stem:
A 32-year-old G2P1 woman at 27+5 weeks gestation attends her local diabetes-in-pregnancy clinic for her routine screening 75 g oral glucose tolerance test. She is asymptomatic. Her booking weight gave a BMI of 29 kg/m2, she gained 4 kg in her last pregnancy with a 3.8 kg baby and no GDM diagnosed retrospectively, and she has no family history of type 2 diabetes. Her previous antenatal visits have been unremarkable. She fasted from midnight as instructed.

Her test results have just come back to the clinic registrar.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse rate 78/min, blood pressure 118/72 mmHg, respiratory rate 14/min, SpO2 99% on room air, temperature 36.5°C
data_table.Examination: Fundal height 28 cm; fetal heart 142/min; no oedema
data_table.Investigations: 75 g OGTT: fasting glucose 5.3 mmol/L; 1 hour 11.4 mmol/L; 2 hour 8.0 mmol/L

lead_in: What is the most appropriate interpretation and immediate management?

options.text: Diagnose gestational diabetes on the 1 hour value and start carbohydrate-counted dietary advice with home glucose monitoring.
options.rationale: ADIPS diagnostic thresholds for GDM on 75 g OGTT are fasting at or above 5.1, 1 hour at or above 10.0, or 2 hour at or above 8.5; one abnormal value makes the diagnosis. (Source: ADIPS 2014 guideline)

options.text: Report the test as normal and repeat screening only if fetal macrosomia develops on subsequent ultrasound.
options.rationale: The 1 hour value of 11.4 exceeds the ADIPS threshold of 10.0 mmol/L, so the test is diagnostic of GDM. (Source: ADIPS 2014 guideline)

options.text: Repeat the entire OGTT at 32 weeks to confirm the diagnosis before instituting any treatment changes.
options.rationale: A single OGTT meeting ADIPS thresholds is diagnostic; routine repeat testing for confirmation is not recommended. (Source: ADIPS 2014 guideline)

options.text: Commence metformin 500 mg twice daily immediately without trialling lifestyle modification first.
options.rationale: First-line initial therapy is dietary modification with glucose monitoring; pharmacotherapy is added if targets are not met. (Source: ADIPS 2014 guideline)

options.text: Order an HbA1c above 6.5 percent threshold to confirm gestational diabetes before any further action.
options.rationale: HbA1c is not the diagnostic test for GDM in Australia; the OGTT is the standard, and HbA1c can be misleading in pregnancy. (Source: ADIPS 2014 guideline)

explanation.summary: Australasian Diabetes in Pregnancy Society diagnostic thresholds on the 75 g OGTT are: fasting at or above 5.1 mmol/L, 1 hour at or above 10.0 mmol/L, or 2 hour at or above 8.5 mmol/L. A single abnormal value confirms gestational diabetes. Initial management is dietary modification, regular physical activity, and self-monitored blood glucose four times a day (fasting and one or two hours post-meal). Metformin or insulin is added if more than 20% of values exceed targets over a 7 to 14 day review.
key_points: ADIPS thresholds: fasting at or above 5.1, 1 hour at or above 10.0, 2 hour at or above 8.5 mmol/L.
One abnormal value confirms GDM.
First-line treatment is diet plus monitoring; pharmacotherapy if glucose targets are missed.
explanation.pearls: Use ADIPS, not the WHO thresholds, in Australian practice; the 1 hour 10.0 threshold is more stringent than the WHO 1 hour 10.0 but identical, and the fasting 5.1 is lower than the older 5.5.

stem:
A 28-year-old G1P0 woman at 28+0 weeks gestation attends her routine antenatal visit at a metropolitan public hospital. She is well with no bleeding, abdominal pain, or recent abdominal trauma. Her booking blood group at 12 weeks was O Rh D-negative with a negative antibody screen; her partner is known to be Rh D-positive. She has had no sensitising events during this pregnancy. Fetal movements are felt regularly and there has been normal fetal growth on her morphology scan.

The antibody screen and group repeat performed at this visit have just returned.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse rate 76/min, blood pressure 112/68 mmHg, respiratory rate 14/min, SpO2 99% on room air, temperature 36.7°C
data_table.Examination: Fundal height 28 cm; fetal heart 148/min; abdomen soft and non-tender
data_table.Investigations: Group O Rh D-negative; antibody screen negative; fetal RhD genotyping not performed

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step?

options.text: Withhold anti-D until 34 weeks because the 28 week dose is not part of routine Australian protocol.
options.rationale: Australian guidelines have recommended dual 28 and 34 week dosing since 2003; withholding is incorrect. (Source: NBA anti-D guidelines)

options.text: Administer Rh D immunoglobulin 625 IU intramuscularly today and again at 34 weeks.
options.rationale: Australian routine antenatal anti-D prophylaxis is 625 IU IM at 28 and 34 weeks for D-negative women with no anti-D antibodies. (Source: NBA anti-D guidelines)

options.text: Wait for postnatal cord blood Rh D typing before giving any antenatal anti-D immunoglobulin.
options.rationale: Cord blood Rh typing guides postpartum dosing, not whether routine antenatal prophylaxis is given. (Source: NBA anti-D guidelines)

options.text: Administer Rh D immunoglobulin 250 IU intramuscularly now and a single repeat at delivery.
options.rationale: 250 IU IM is the standard for first trimester sensitising events; routine antenatal dosing is 625 IU. (Source: NBA anti-D guidelines)

options.text: Send fetal RhD genotyping on maternal plasma and defer immunoglobulin until the fetal status is known.
options.rationale: Fetal cell-free DNA RhD testing is available but not the universal Australian pathway; routine prophylaxis is still recommended. (Source: NBA anti-D guidelines)

explanation.summary: The Australian routine antenatal anti-D prophylaxis schedule for D-negative women with no anti-D antibodies is 625 IU intramuscular Rh D immunoglobulin at both 28 and 34 weeks gestation. The 28 week dose targets feto-maternal haemorrhage in the third trimester before it causes sensitisation, and the 34 week dose covers the period to term. Smaller 250 IU doses are used for first trimester sensitising events such as a small antepartum haemorrhage or chorionic villus sampling.
key_points: Australian routine antenatal anti-D is 625 IU at 28 and 34 weeks.
250 IU is the dose for first trimester sensitising events.
Postpartum dosing depends on cord blood Rh typing and Kleihauer testing for large feto-maternal haemorrhage.
explanation.pearls: If a sensitising event occurs after a routine 28 week dose, give an additional 625 IU within 72 hours rather than relying on the prior dose to cover both indications.

sources.label: RANZCOG statement on Rh D immunoglobulin

stem:
A 30-year-old G2P1 woman at 39+3 weeks gestation has been admitted in established labour, cervix 5 cm dilated with intact membranes. Her vaginal-rectal swab at 36+0 weeks grew group B Streptococcus. She has no documented penicillin allergy and tolerated amoxicillin for a UTI earlier in this pregnancy. Her previous baby was born vaginally at term and did not develop neonatal sepsis. The intrapartum CTG is reactive with normal variability and accelerations.

The midwife is asking for prescription of intrapartum antibiotic prophylaxis.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse rate 82/min, blood pressure 118/70 mmHg, respiratory rate 16/min, SpO2 99% on room air, temperature 36.8°C, fetal heart 140/min reactive
data_table.Examination: Cervix 5 cm dilated, membranes intact, vertex presentation; abdomen soft non-tender
data_table.Investigations: 36 week vaginal-rectal swab: GBS positive; current bloods unremarkable; CTG reactive

lead_in: What is the most appropriate intrapartum antibiotic regimen?

options.text: Oral amoxicillin 500 mg three times daily commenced now and continued for 48 hours postpartum.
options.rationale: Oral antibiotics do not achieve the rapid amniotic fluid levels required for neonatal GBS prophylaxis; IV therapy is essential. (Source: RANZCOG GBS statement)

options.text: IV vancomycin 20 mg/kg over 1 hour given every 8 hours throughout labour until delivery.
options.rationale: Vancomycin is reserved for severe penicillin allergy with confirmed clindamycin resistance, not routine first-line prophylaxis. (Source: RANZCOG GBS statement)

options.text: IV cefazolin 2 g loading dose then 1 g every 8 hours until delivery as first-line therapy.
options.rationale: Cefazolin is the appropriate choice for non-severe penicillin allergy without anaphylaxis history, not first-line over benzylpenicillin. (Source: RANZCOG GBS statement)

options.text: Benzylpenicillin 3 g intravenously as a loading dose then 1.8 g every 4 hours until delivery.
options.rationale: RANZCOG and AMH recommend intrapartum IV benzylpenicillin 3 g load then 1.8 g every 4 hours as first-line for GBS-positive women without penicillin allergy. (Source: RANZCOG GBS statement)

options.text: Defer antibiotics until rupture of membranes occurs because she is currently low risk for transmission.
options.rationale: Antibiotics should be commenced once labour is established to achieve adequate amniotic fluid penetration before delivery. (Source: RANZCOG GBS statement)

explanation.summary: Intrapartum antibiotic prophylaxis for a known GBS-positive woman in established labour is IV benzylpenicillin 3 g loading dose followed by 1.8 g every 4 hours until delivery. The aim is to achieve at least one full dose at least 4 hours before delivery to reduce neonatal early-onset GBS disease. For mild penicillin allergy (rash, no anaphylaxis), cefazolin 2 g IV load then 1 g 8-hourly is the alternative; for severe allergy, clindamycin 600 mg 8-hourly if susceptibility confirmed, else vancomycin.
key_points: First-line: benzylpenicillin 3 g IV load then 1.8 g every 4 hours.
Aim for at least one dose at least 4 hours before delivery.
Cefazolin for mild penicillin allergy; clindamycin or vancomycin for severe.
explanation.pearls: Start antibiotics as soon as labour is established (cervix at least 4 cm and regular contractions, or rupture of membranes), not when membranes rupture, to maximise the chance of a 4-hour cover before birth.

stem:
A 34-year-old G3P3 woman is 25 minutes postpartum following a spontaneous vaginal delivery at 39 weeks with active third stage. Estimated blood loss is now 1100 mL and ongoing from the placental bed; the placenta is complete on inspection. She was treated for gestational hypertension during pregnancy with labetalol 200 mg twice daily and her blood pressure on the labour ward 30 minutes before delivery was 158/108 mmHg. Bimanual compression has been started and a second 16 G IV cannula is in. Oxytocin 10 IU IM has been given as part of active third stage and an oxytocin infusion 40 IU in 1000 mL Hartmann's at 250 mL/hr has been running for 15 minutes.

The consultant is asking what to add next.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse rate 122/min, blood pressure 156/104 mmHg, respiratory rate 22/min, SpO2 97% on room air, temperature 36.7°C
data_table.Examination: Uterus boggy at the umbilicus, blood loss from below ongoing; perineum intact; bladder catheterised and empty
data_table.Investigations: Hb 92 g/L (115-165); platelets 142 x10^9/L; INR 1.1; fibrinogen 2.6 g/L; cross match in progress
data_table.Medications: Labetalol 200 mg bd; oxytocin infusion running

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next pharmacological agent?

options.text: Ergometrine 250 micrograms intramuscularly together with tranexamic acid 1 g intravenously.
options.rationale: Ergometrine causes vasoconstriction and is contraindicated with uncontrolled hypertension, pre-eclampsia, or eclampsia. (Source: RANZCOG PPH guideline)

options.text: Misoprostol 800 micrograms sublingually as a single dose with no additional intravenous therapy.
options.rationale: Misoprostol monotherapy is inadequate at this volume of blood loss when other uterotonic options remain available. (Source: RANZCOG PPH guideline)

options.text: Carbetocin 100 micrograms intravenously as a single bolus dose to replace ongoing oxytocin therapy.
options.rationale: Carbetocin is used at delivery for active management; once oxytocin infusion has failed, the next step is to add a different uterotonic. (Source: RANZCOG PPH guideline)

options.text: Recombinant activated factor VII 90 micrograms/kg intravenously before any further uterotonic doses.
options.rationale: Recombinant factor VIIa is reserved for major haemorrhage refractory to other measures with documented coagulopathy. (Source: RANZCOG PPH guideline)

options.text: Tranexamic acid 1 g intravenously over 10 minutes plus carboprost 250 micrograms intramuscularly.
options.rationale: Ergometrine is contraindicated with active hypertension; tranexamic acid plus carboprost are appropriate next-line agents in PPH. (Source: RANZCOG PPH guideline)

explanation.summary: Postpartum haemorrhage management follows a parallel mechanical, pharmacological, and resuscitation pathway. Pharmacological escalation starts with oxytocin, but the second uterotonic depends on contraindications: ergometrine is contraindicated with hypertension, pre-eclampsia, or eclampsia, because it causes intense vasoconstriction. In this woman, the next pharmacological steps are tranexamic acid 1 g IV (ideally within 3 hours of onset, as per the WOMAN trial), and carboprost (15-methyl prostaglandin F2-alpha) 250 micrograms IM, repeatable every 15 minutes up to 8 doses, avoiding it in asthma.
key_points: Ergometrine is contraindicated with hypertension, pre-eclampsia, or eclampsia.
Tranexamic acid 1 g IV within 3 hours reduces mortality (WOMAN trial).
Carboprost is contraindicated in asthma due to bronchospasm risk.
explanation.pearls: When the woman has both hypertension and asthma, the next-line uterotonic is misoprostol 800 micrograms rectal or sublingual alongside tranexamic acid, because both ergometrine and carboprost are off the menu.

stem:
A 26-year-old G1P0 woman at 34+5 weeks gestation has been admitted with severe headache, visual scotomata, and right upper quadrant pain. Her booking blood pressure was 110/70 mmHg and BMI 24. Two readings 15 minutes apart in triage have been 168/112 mmHg and 162/110 mmHg. Antihypertensive therapy has been commenced with oral labetalol 200 mg and her blood pressure 30 minutes later is 152/96 mmHg. She has 3+ proteinuria on dipstick, normal fetal movements, and a reactive CTG. The on-call obstetrician has decided to deliver in the next 24 hours after a course of betamethasone.

The team is now discussing seizure prophylaxis.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse rate 96/min, blood pressure 152/96 mmHg, respiratory rate 18/min, SpO2 99% on room air, temperature 36.7°C, fetal heart 145/min reactive
data_table.Examination: Brisk reflexes with 2 beats of clonus bilaterally; mild epigastric tenderness; no focal deficit
data_table.Investigations: Platelets 96 x10^9/L; ALT 72 U/L; creatinine 78 micromol/L; urate 0.42 mmol/L; LDH 320 U/L; PCR 320 mg/mmol
data_table.Medications: Labetalol 200 mg orally given; betamethasone 11.4 mg IM started

lead_in: What is the most appropriate magnesium sulfate regimen?

options.text: Magnesium sulfate 4 g IV loading dose over 20 minutes then a maintenance infusion of 1 g/hour.
options.rationale: Australian and Magpie trial protocol for severe pre-eclampsia seizure prophylaxis is 4 g IV loading dose then 1 g per hour maintenance. (Source: SOMANZ pre-eclampsia guideline)

options.text: Magnesium sulfate 6 g IV loading dose over 20 minutes followed by a 2 g per hour maintenance infusion.
options.rationale: Higher dosing regimens were used historically but are not the current Australian standard, which is 4 g and 1 g/hr. (Source: SOMANZ pre-eclampsia guideline)

options.text: Phenytoin 18 mg/kg intravenous loading dose given over 30 minutes for eclampsia seizure prevention.
options.rationale: Magnesium is superior to phenytoin for both prevention and treatment of eclamptic seizures and is the standard of care. (Source: SOMANZ pre-eclampsia guideline)

options.text: Oral nifedipine 30 mg modified release alone, deferring magnesium until a seizure actually occurs.
options.rationale: In severe pre-eclampsia with neurological features and biochemical derangement, prophylactic magnesium is recommended rather than waiting. (Source: SOMANZ pre-eclampsia guideline)

options.text: Diazepam 10 mg intravenously as a single dose with onward titration of labetalol infusion only.
options.rationale: Benzodiazepines are second-line for refractory eclampsia, not standard prophylaxis in severe pre-eclampsia. (Source: SOMANZ pre-eclampsia guideline)

explanation.summary: Severe pre-eclampsia with neurological features (headache, visual disturbance), epigastric pain, hypertension at 160/110 mmHg or above, or biochemical derangement (platelets below 100, ALT raised, urate above 0.4 mmol/L) warrants magnesium sulfate seizure prophylaxis. The Australian SOMANZ regimen, based on the Magpie trial, is a 4 g IV loading dose over 20 minutes followed by 1 g per hour maintenance infusion, continued until 24 hours after delivery or after the last seizure. Monitor patellar reflexes, respiratory rate, and urine output; serum magnesium levels are not routinely required if clinical monitoring is reliable.
key_points: SOMANZ regimen: 4 g IV load over 20 minutes then 1 g/hour for 24 hours postpartum.
Monitor patellar reflexes, respiratory rate, and urine output for toxicity.
Calcium gluconate 10 mL of 10 percent IV is the antidote for magnesium toxicity.
explanation.pearls: Reduce the maintenance to 0.5 g/hour if the creatinine is above 100 micromol/L or urine output falls below 100 mL over 4 hours, because magnesium clearance is renal.

stem:
A 29-year-old G2P0 woman presents to early pregnancy assessment at 7+3 weeks from her last menstrual period with 3 days of mild left iliac fossa pain and minor brown vaginal spotting. She is haemodynamically stable. Her last serum beta-hCG taken at the GP 48 hours ago was 2200 IU/L and today it is 2850 IU/L. Transvaginal ultrasound shows an empty uterine cavity with thin endometrium, a 22 mm left adnexal mass with no fetal pole and no cardiac activity, and a small volume of free fluid in the pouch of Douglas. Her FBC, renal function, and liver function are within normal limits. She has no significant past history, takes no medications, and lives nearby with reliable transport.

She is keen to avoid surgery if possible and has been counselled about the options.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse rate 80/min, blood pressure 118/72 mmHg, respiratory rate 14/min, SpO2 99% on room air, temperature 36.6°C
data_table.Examination: Soft abdomen, mild left iliac fossa tenderness, no peritonism, no cervical motion tenderness
data_table.Investigations: Beta-hCG 48 hour rise 2200 to 2850 IU/L; TVUS left adnexal 22 mm mass, no FH; small free fluid; Hb 132 g/L; LFTs and creatinine normal

lead_in: What is the most appropriate management?

options.text: Expectant management with serial beta-hCG every 48 hours until the value has spontaneously declined.
options.rationale: Expectant management is generally reserved for beta-hCG below 1500 with a clearly declining trend, not the rising value seen here. (Source: RANZCOG ectopic pregnancy guideline)

options.text: Single dose intramuscular methotrexate 50 mg/m2 with follow-up beta-hCG on day 4 and day 7.
options.rationale: She meets RANZCOG methotrexate criteria with beta-hCG under 5000, mass under 3.5 cm, no fetal cardiac activity, stable, and reliable follow-up. (Source: RANZCOG ectopic pregnancy guideline)

options.text: Diagnostic laparoscopy with planned salpingectomy of the affected fallopian tube during the same procedure.
options.rationale: Surgery is appropriate but is not required when methotrexate criteria are met and the patient prefers medical management. (Source: RANZCOG ectopic pregnancy guideline)

options.text: Single dose intramuscular methotrexate 50 mg/m2 plus prophylactic folate 5 mg orally daily for 7 days.
options.rationale: Folate antagonises methotrexate efficacy and should be avoided around treatment. (Source: RANZCOG ectopic pregnancy guideline)

options.text: Emergency theatre for salpingectomy on the basis that any free fluid signals a tubal rupture.
options.rationale: A small volume of free fluid alone in a haemodynamically stable woman is not an indication for emergency surgery. (Source: RANZCOG ectopic pregnancy guideline)

explanation.summary: RANZCOG criteria for methotrexate in tubal ectopic pregnancy are: haemodynamic stability, beta-hCG below 5000 IU/L, no fetal cardiac activity, ectopic mass below 3.5 cm, normal renal and hepatic function, no contraindications (immunosuppression, blood dyscrasia, breastfeeding, hypersensitivity), reliable follow-up, and patient preference. The dose is 50 mg/m2 IM as a single agent. Follow-up beta-hCG is taken on day 4 and day 7; the day 4 to day 7 fall of at least 15% predicts success, otherwise a second dose is considered.
key_points: RANZCOG methotrexate threshold for beta-hCG is below 5000 IU/L, not below 3000.
Day 4 to day 7 beta-hCG must fall by at least 15 percent for success.
Avoid folate, NSAIDs, alcohol, and conception for 3 months after methotrexate.
explanation.pearls: Surgical management is mandated by RANZCOG when beta-hCG is at or above 5000 IU/L, the mass is at or above 3.5 cm, there is fetal cardiac activity, significant pain, or haemodynamic instability.

stem:
A 27-year-old G1P0 woman with a monochorionic-diamniotic twin pregnancy at 22+5 weeks gestation is reviewed at the fetal medicine unit after an outside scan reported amniotic fluid discordance. She has felt well; no antepartum bleeding or contractions. The current detailed scan with paired Doppler studies has just been reported by the maternal-fetal medicine consultant. Both fetuses have normal anatomy. Twin A (the donor) is structurally normal with deepest vertical pocket 1.4 cm; twin B (the recipient) has deepest vertical pocket 9.2 cm with a visible bladder.

Umbilical artery Dopplers and ductus venosus traces are also reported.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse rate 76/min, blood pressure 116/70 mmHg, respiratory rate 14/min, SpO2 99% on room air, temperature 36.7°C
data_table.Examination: Soft abdomen, fundal height 28 cm; cervix on TVUS 36 mm and closed
data_table.Investigations: Twin A EFW 380 g; bladder not visualised; DVP 1.4 cm; UA Doppler with absent end-diastolic flow. Twin B EFW 540 g; visible bladder; DVP 9.2 cm; UA Doppler normal; ductus venosus normal a-wave

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next management step?

options.text: Amnioreduction from the recipient sac alone every 7 days until 28 weeks gestation is reached.
options.rationale: Fetoscopic laser is superior to serial amnioreduction for stage II and above TTTS between 16 and 26 weeks. (Source: NICE multiple pregnancy guideline)

options.text: Expectant management with weekly Dopplers because absent end diastolic flow alone can be transient.
options.rationale: Absent end-diastolic flow in TTTS is Quintero stage III and is not transient; expectant management risks intrauterine death. (Source: RANZCOG multiple pregnancy guideline)

options.text: Refer urgently for fetoscopic laser photocoagulation of the placental vascular anastomoses.
options.rationale: TTTS Quintero stage III (donor absent end-diastolic flow) at 22+5 weeks meets criteria for fetoscopic laser within 16 to 26 weeks. (Source: RANZCOG multiple pregnancy guideline)

options.text: Selective feticide of the donor twin by bipolar cord coagulation to maximise recipient survival.
options.rationale: Selective reduction is reserved for severe fetal anomaly or stage IV TTTS with one twin already moribund. (Source: RANZCOG multiple pregnancy guideline)

options.text: Administer betamethasone 11.4 mg intramuscularly and plan delivery within 48 hours by caesarean.
options.rationale: Delivery at 22+5 weeks is below the threshold of viability and would not address the underlying anastomotic pathology. (Source: RANZCOG multiple pregnancy guideline)

explanation.summary: Twin-twin transfusion syndrome is diagnosed when monochorionic twins show oligohydramnios with deepest vertical pocket below 2 cm in one sac and polyhydramnios with DVP above 8 cm in the other (Quintero stage I). Staging progresses with non-visible donor bladder (II), abnormal Doppler in either twin including donor absent or reversed end-diastolic umbilical artery flow (III), hydrops (IV), and demise (V). For stage II to IV between 16 and 26 weeks, fetoscopic laser photocoagulation of the inter-twin anastomoses is the standard of care, improving survival of at least one twin to around 80 to 90% in expert centres.
key_points: TTTS staging: I oligo plus poly, II absent donor bladder, III abnormal Doppler, IV hydrops, V demise.
Fetoscopic laser is first-line for Quintero stage II to IV between 16 and 26 weeks.
Amnioreduction is now reserved for centres without laser access or for stage I progression.
explanation.pearls: After laser, surveillance for twin anaemia-polycythaemia sequence (TAPS) with weekly middle cerebral artery peak systolic velocity Dopplers is mandatory because residual anastomoses can persist.

stem: A 31-year-old primigravida at 32+2 weeks presents with new severe headache and right upper quadrant pain. Booking blood pressure was 110/70 mmHg. Today her blood pressure is 168/112 mmHg after 30 minutes of rest. She has had three doses of oral nifedipine 20 mg over 90 minutes with blood pressure now 152/98 mmHg. CTG is reassuring. Bloods: platelets 92 x10^9/L (150-400), ALT 96 U/L (5-35), creatinine 96 micromol/L (45-90), urine protein-creatinine ratio 86 mg/mmol. Fetal growth was at the 25th centile two weeks ago.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 96, BP 152/98 mmHg, RR 18, SpO2 99%, temperature 36.8°C, FHR 140
data_table.Examination: Brisk reflexes, no clonus, mild RUQ tenderness, no peripheral oedema documented
data_table.Investigations: Platelets 92, ALT 96 U/L, creatinine 96 micromol/L, urate 0.42 mmol/L, urine PCR 86 mg/mmol; CTG normal variability with accelerations
data_table.Medications: Nifedipine immediate release 20 mg PO x3 over 90 minutes

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step?

options.text: Expectant management until 37 weeks with twice-weekly bloods, CTG and growth scan
options.rationale: Expectant management beyond 34 weeks is not appropriate with severe disease and falling platelets; delivery within 24-48 hours is indicated. (Source: SOMANZ hypertension in pregnancy 2014)

options.text: Discharge home on oral labetalol 200 mg three times daily with weekly review
options.rationale: Severe pre-eclampsia is a hospital diagnosis; discharge with significant end-organ involvement is unsafe. (Source: SOMANZ hypertension in pregnancy 2014)

options.text: Plan delivery within 24-48 hours after IV magnesium and antenatal corticosteroids
options.rationale: Severe pre-eclampsia with hepatic and renal involvement and falling platelets at 32 weeks requires planned delivery within 24-48 hours. Betamethasone 11.4 mg IM x2 (24 hours apart) and IV magnesium sulfate for neuroprotection precede delivery. (Source: SOMANZ hypertension in pregnancy 2014)

options.text: Proceed to immediate emergency caesarean before any steroid loading dose
options.rationale: With reassuring CTG and controlled BP, a 24-48 hour window allows steroid benefit; immediate delivery is reserved for fetal compromise or maternal instability. (Source: SOMANZ hypertension in pregnancy 2014)

options.text: Continue oral nifedipine and add aspirin 100 mg daily for preventive effect
options.rationale: Aspirin prevents pre-eclampsia from the first trimester; it has no role at 32 weeks with established severe disease. (Source: SOMANZ hypertension in pregnancy 2014)

explanation.summary: Severe pre-eclampsia with hepatic transaminitis, renal involvement, and a platelet count under 100 x10^9/L at 32 weeks indicates delivery within 24-48 hours per SOMANZ. The window allows antenatal corticosteroids for fetal lung maturity and IV magnesium for neuroprotection. Immediate caesarean is reserved for non-reassuring CTG or maternal instability. Expectant management is not appropriate once severe features are established.
key_points: Severe pre-eclampsia from 32 weeks: deliver within 24-48 hours after steroids
IV magnesium sulfate is neuroprotective and reduces eclampsia
Aspirin prevents pre-eclampsia from early pregnancy; not a rescue therapy
explanation.pearls: When severe pre-eclampsia is diagnosed remote from term, the question is how to deliver safely, not whether to deliver.

stem: A 34-year-old G2P1 has had a normal vaginal delivery of a 4.1 kg infant after a four-hour second stage. Active management of the third stage was performed with oxytocin 10 IU IM. Twenty minutes after the placenta the uterine fundus is boggy at the umbilicus and 900 mL of blood has been lost. She has been catheterised, the placenta is reported as complete, no genital tract trauma is identified, and there are no clots in the vagina. She had blood pressure 158/104 mmHg in late pregnancy and is on oral labetalol 200 mg three times daily. Current blood pressure is 132/88 mmHg.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 108, BP 132/88 mmHg, RR 20, SpO2 99%, temperature 36.9°C
data_table.Examination: Fundus boggy at umbilicus, ongoing trickle PV, perineum intact, placenta reported complete
data_table.Investigations: Estimated blood loss 900 mL and rising; Hb pending
data_table.Medications: Oxytocin 10 IU IM (third stage), labetalol 200 mg TDS PO, IV access secured with 1 L Hartmann's running

lead_in: Which uterotonic is the most appropriate next step?

options.text: IM ergometrine 250 micrograms with prochlorperazine 12.5 mg for nausea
options.rationale: Ergometrine is contraindicated in any current or past hypertensive disorder of pregnancy due to severe vasoconstriction risk. (Source: RANZCOG PPH 2022)

options.text: Misoprostol 800 micrograms sublingual after one further oxytocin infusion bolus
options.rationale: Misoprostol is third-line in Australia after a parenteral prostaglandin (carboprost), particularly when IV/IM access is available. (Source: RANZCOG PPH 2022)

options.text: IV tranexamic acid 1 g over 10 minutes as the sole pharmacological action
options.rationale: Tranexamic acid is adjunctive and given within 3 hours, but it does not replace a second-line uterotonic when the uterus is atonic. (Source: RANZCOG PPH 2022)

options.text: IM carboprost 250 micrograms while preparing for theatre balloon tamponade
options.rationale: Carboprost (a prostaglandin F2-alpha analogue) is the appropriate second-line uterotonic when ergometrine is contraindicated. It is given IM 250 micrograms, repeatable to 2 mg total, with theatre escalation prepared in parallel. (Source: RANZCOG PPH 2022)

options.text: IV magnesium sulfate 4 g bolus to relax associated arterial spasm and clot
options.rationale: Magnesium is uterine-relaxing and worsens atony; it has no role in active PPH from atony. (Source: RANZCOG PPH 2022)

explanation.summary: Atonic PPH not responding to oxytocin and uterine massage requires a second-line uterotonic. Ergometrine is contraindicated with any current or past hypertensive disorder. The RANZCOG alternative is IM carboprost 250 micrograms, repeatable every 15 minutes to a maximum 2 mg. Misoprostol sublingual 800 micrograms is third-line. Tranexamic acid 1 g IV is an adjunct within three hours of bleeding onset, not a replacement.
key_points: Ergometrine contraindicated in hypertensive disorders of pregnancy
Carboprost 250 mcg IM is second-line uterotonic when ergometrine cannot be used
Tranexamic acid is adjunctive, not a substitute for uterotonic
explanation.pearls: Boggy uterus plus ongoing bleed plus blood pressure history that rules out ergometrine equals carboprost reflex.

stem: A 28-year-old G1P0 at 39+1 weeks attends the birth suite reporting a 'gush' of clear fluid 14 hours ago. She is not in labour. Vaginal speculum confirms pooling of clear amniotic fluid. The cardiotocograph is reactive. Her group B streptococcus swab at 36 weeks was negative. She has had no fevers and reports normal fetal movements. She tells you she would prefer to go home and 'see if labour starts on its own'.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 84, BP 118/72 mmHg, RR 16, SpO2 99%, temperature 36.7°C, FHR 138
data_table.Examination: Speculum confirms amniotic pooling, no offensive discharge, cervix appears 1 cm dilated visually
data_table.Investigations: GBS negative at 36 weeks; CTG reactive

lead_in: What is the most appropriate recommendation?

options.text: Discharge home with a thermometer and review in 48 hours if not in labour
options.rationale: Australian practice offers expectant management up to about 24 hours, but inpatient observation and induction within 24 hours improves neonatal outcomes versus outpatient waiting beyond that. (Source: RANZCOG term PROM 2017)

options.text: Commence oxytocin infusion now in the birth suite with epidural insertion
options.rationale: Immediate oxytocin without informed consent or analgesia discussion bypasses shared decision making; an interval allowing spontaneous labour is offered. (Source: RANZCOG term PROM 2017)

options.text: Insert a Foley balloon for cervical ripening and start prophylactic ampicillin
options.rationale: Mechanical ripening is not first-line in established membrane rupture and routine ampicillin is not given when GBS swab is negative without fever. (Source: RANZCOG term PROM 2017)

options.text: Recommend caesarean section now for prolonged rupture exceeding 12 hours
options.rationale: Term PROM is not by itself an indication for caesarean. (Source: RANZCOG term PROM 2017)

options.text: Offer induction now or within 24 hours of rupture with inpatient monitoring
options.rationale: Term PROM with GBS-negative status is offered induction by 24 hours from rupture. Inpatient monitoring through that window with induction by syntocinon is the RANZCOG-recommended pathway. (Source: RANZCOG term PROM 2017)

explanation.summary: Term prelabour rupture of membranes is managed by offering induction with oxytocin by 24 hours from rupture, with inpatient observation in the interval. GBS-negative women without fever do not need prophylactic antibiotics at this point. Discharge home for outpatient waiting is not the Australian standard, and immediate caesarean is not indicated. Foley ripening is reserved for unfavourable cervix without ruptured membranes.
key_points: Term PROM: offer induction within 24 hours of rupture
GBS-negative term PROM without fever: no prophylactic antibiotics yet
Inpatient monitoring throughout the latency interval
explanation.pearls: Counsel the patient on both options (induction now or wait up to 24 hours) and document her informed choice.

stem: A 26-year-old G2P1 at 19+4 weeks attends fortnightly ultrasound for a known monochorionic-diamniotic twin pregnancy. Today the recipient twin's deepest vertical pocket is 8.6 cm and the donor twin's deepest vertical pocket is 1.4 cm. Both bladders are visible, umbilical artery Dopplers show normal end diastolic flow in both, and venous Doppler waveforms are normal. Both growth percentiles are on track for gestation. Maternal observations are normal and she reports a tight abdomen but no contractions.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 84, BP 118/72 mmHg, RR 16, SpO2 99%, temperature 36.7°C, no contractions on tocograph
data_table.Investigations: Twin A (recipient) DVP 8.6 cm, bladder visible, normal Dopplers; Twin B (donor) DVP 1.4 cm, bladder visible, normal Dopplers; growth concordant

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step?

options.text: Refer urgently to a fetal medicine unit for assessment and laser candidacy
options.rationale: Quintero stage I TTTS (DVP discordance with bladders visible and normal Dopplers) requires urgent referral to a fetal therapy centre. Fetoscopic laser ablation of placental anastomoses is the standard treatment from stage II and is considered case-by-case for stage I. (Source: ISUOG monochorionic twin guideline 2016)

options.text: Continue fortnightly scans and review at the next routine appointment
options.rationale: Quintero stage I TTTS still requires urgent fetal medicine review; routine fortnightly monitoring under local team is not enough. (Source: ISUOG monochorionic twin guideline 2016)

options.text: Perform serial amnioreductions weekly to control polyhydramnios in recipient
options.rationale: Amnioreduction is second-line; laser ablation has better neurological outcomes for stages II to IV. (Source: ISUOG monochorionic twin guideline 2016)

options.text: Plan elective caesarean delivery at 32 weeks after antenatal corticosteroids
options.rationale: Stable monochorionic-diamniotic twins are normally delivered at 36+0 to 36+6 weeks; pre-empting at 32 weeks is not warranted without indication. (Source: ISUOG monochorionic twin guideline 2016)

options.text: Start maternal sildenafil 20 mg three times daily to improve donor perfusion
options.rationale: Sildenafil has no role in TTTS; the STRIDER trial found no benefit and possible fetal harm. (Source: ISUOG monochorionic twin guideline 2016)

explanation.summary: Quintero stage I TTTS is defined by polyhydramnios in the recipient (DVP greater than 8 cm before 20 weeks) and oligohydramnios in the donor (DVP less than 2 cm), with both bladders visible and normal Dopplers. Even stage I requires urgent fetal medicine referral because progression to stages II-IV can be rapid. Fetoscopic laser ablation of placental anastomoses is the standard treatment for stages II-IV and is considered case-by-case for stage I. Amnioreduction is second-line; sildenafil has no role.
key_points: Stage I TTTS: DVP discordance with visible bladders and normal Dopplers
Laser ablation is standard for stages II-IV TTTS
Urgent fetal medicine referral required even at stage I
explanation.pearls: DVP above 8 cm before 20 weeks or above 10 cm from 20 weeks defines polyhydramnios in monochorionic twins; pair with DVP under 2 cm in the co-twin to call TTTS.

sources.label: RANZCOG management of monochorionic twin pregnancy

stem: A 32-year-old G4P0 presents two weeks after her third consecutive first-trimester loss. All three losses occurred between 8 and 11 weeks, two were ultrasound-confirmed missed miscarriages, and one was a complete miscarriage at home. Her menstrual cycles are regular at 28 days. She has no history of thromboembolism, no family history of miscarriage, and no chronic disease. Karyotyping of the most recent products of conception showed 46,XX with no aneuploidy. She is otherwise well and asks what investigations are appropriate now.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 72, BP 118/74 mmHg, RR 14, SpO2 99%, temperature 36.7°C
data_table.Examination: Body mass index 24, no acanthosis, no goitre, no hirsutism
data_table.Investigations: Cycle history regular; recent products of conception karyotype 46,XX

lead_in: What is the most appropriate first-line investigation panel?

options.text: Inherited thrombophilia panel including factor V Leiden and prothrombin gene
options.rationale: Inherited thrombophilia testing is not recommended routinely in recurrent miscarriage without personal or family VTE history. (Source: ESHRE recurrent pregnancy loss 2022)

options.text: Pelvic ultrasound with antiphospholipid screen and thyroid function tests
options.rationale: RANZCOG and ESHRE recommend a structural assessment (pelvic ultrasound or sonohysterogram), lupus anticoagulant plus anticardiolipin plus beta-2-glycoprotein-1 antibodies for antiphospholipid syndrome, and TSH for thyroid disease as first-line in recurrent miscarriage. (Source: ESHRE recurrent pregnancy loss 2022)

options.text: Endometrial biopsy with natural killer cell quantification and HLA typing
options.rationale: Immune cell quantification is not standard of care and is not validated for routine recurrent miscarriage workup. (Source: ESHRE recurrent pregnancy loss 2022)

options.text: Parental karyotyping for both partners and routine sperm DNA fragmentation
options.rationale: Parental karyotyping is not first-line when products of conception have shown normal karyotype; reserved for selected couples after first-line workup. (Source: ESHRE recurrent pregnancy loss 2022)

options.text: Empirical low-dose aspirin and LMWH from positive pregnancy test next cycle
options.rationale: Empirical anticoagulation without confirmed antiphospholipid syndrome does not improve live birth rates and is not recommended. (Source: ESHRE recurrent pregnancy loss 2022)

explanation.summary: Recurrent miscarriage (three or more consecutive first-trimester losses) warrants a structural uterine assessment, antiphospholipid antibody screen, and thyroid function as first-line. Inherited thrombophilia panels, immune assays, and parental karyotyping are reserved for second-line workup in selected cases. Empirical aspirin or LMWH outside antiphospholipid syndrome is not evidence-based and may harm.
key_points: First-line: pelvic ultrasound, APS triple antibody panel, TSH
Inherited thrombophilia testing reserved for personal/family VTE
Empirical anticoagulation outside APS is not recommended
explanation.pearls: APS testing must be repeated 12 weeks apart for confirmation; do not commit to lifelong therapy on a single positive.

stem: A 33-year-old G2P2 was diagnosed with gestational diabetes at 28 weeks during this pregnancy and was managed with diet alone (no insulin or metformin). She has now had an uncomplicated normal vaginal delivery of a healthy 3.6 kg baby at 39+5 weeks. She is six weeks postpartum, breastfeeding, and her finger-prick glucose readings have been 5.6 to 6.4 mmol/L fasting at home. She has no symptoms of hyperglycaemia. She asks what monitoring she needs going forward.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 76, BP 118/74 mmHg, RR 14, SpO2 99%, temperature 36.6°C
data_table.Examination: Body mass index 27.4, no acanthosis nigricans, breastfeeding established
data_table.Investigations: Pregnancy: GDM diagnosed at 28 weeks by 75 g OGTT (fasting 5.4, 1h 11.2, 2h 8.8 mmol/L), diet controlled; postnatal: home fasting glucose 5.6 to 6.4 mmol/L

lead_in: What follow-up plan is most appropriate?

options.text: Repeat 75 g OGTT only at the start of any subsequent pregnancy as routine
options.rationale: Early-pregnancy testing in the next pregnancy is offered, but lifetime monitoring outside pregnancy is also required. (Source: ADIPS postnatal management of women with GDM 2022)
source_refs: ADIPS postnatal management of women with GDM 2022

options.text: Annual fasting plasma glucose only and reassess if she conceives again
options.rationale: Single fasting glucose has lower sensitivity than OGTT or HbA1c and the lifetime risk extends beyond reproductive years. (Source: ADIPS postnatal management of women with GDM 2022)
source_refs: ADIPS postnatal management of women with GDM 2022

options.text: 75 g OGTT at 6-12 weeks postpartum and HbA1c every 1-3 years thereafter
options.rationale: ADIPS recommends a 75 g OGTT at 6-12 weeks postpartum then HbA1c or 75 g OGTT every 1-3 years for life given the elevated lifetime type 2 diabetes risk. (Source: ADIPS postnatal management of women with GDM 2022)
source_refs: ADIPS postnatal management of women with GDM 2022

options.text: Commence metformin 500 mg daily empirically to prevent type 2 diabetes
options.rationale: Empirical metformin without confirmed prediabetes or T2DM is not recommended; lifestyle remains first-line. (Source: ADIPS postnatal management of women with GDM 2022)
source_refs: ADIPS postnatal management of women with GDM 2022

options.text: Refer to endocrinology now for insulin initiation given fasting near 6 mmol/L
options.rationale: Home fasting capillary glucose of 5.6-6.4 mmol/L during established breastfeeding does not by itself indicate insulin; formal venous testing comes first. (Source: ADIPS postnatal management of women with GDM 2022)
source_refs: ADIPS postnatal management of women with GDM 2022

explanation.summary: ADIPS recommends a 75 g oral glucose tolerance test 6-12 weeks postpartum to detect persistent hyperglycaemia, followed by HbA1c (or repeat OGTT) every 1-3 years for life because the lifetime risk of type 2 diabetes is roughly 50-70%. Early-pregnancy testing should also be offered in subsequent pregnancies. Lifestyle remains first-line; empirical metformin is not routine. Home capillary glucose is not diagnostic for diabetes in this context.
key_points: 75 g OGTT at 6-12 weeks postpartum
HbA1c or OGTT every 1-3 years lifelong
Early-pregnancy retesting in next pregnancy
explanation.pearls: GDM is a stress test; about half will develop type 2 diabetes within 10 years - schedule the OGTT before discharge from the postnatal clinic.

sources.label: ADIPS postnatal management of women with GDM 2022

stem: A 16-year-old presents with oligomenorrhoea (cycles every 70-90 days for the last 2 years), mild facial hirsutism (Ferriman-Gallwey 10), and acne unresponsive to topical therapy. She is not sexually active. Body mass index 28.5. Bloods: total testosterone 2.8 nmol/L (0.5-2.4), SHBG 28 nmol/L (30-90), TSH 1.6 mU/L, prolactin 240 mU/L, 17-OH progesterone 4 nmol/L, fasting glucose 5.3 mmol/L. Pelvic ultrasound is reported as showing more than 20 small follicles per ovary. She wants help with cycle regulation and acne. Her mother is concerned about long-term endometrial protection.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 76, BP 118/72 mmHg, RR 14, SpO2 99%, temperature 36.7°C
data_table.Examination: BMI 28.5, Ferriman-Gallwey 10, comedonal and inflammatory acne over face and back
data_table.Investigations: Testosterone 2.8 nmol/L, SHBG 28 nmol/L, TSH 1.6 mU/L, prolactin 240 mU/L, 17-OH progesterone 4 nmol/L, fasting glucose 5.3 mmol/L, more than 20 follicles per ovary on ultrasound

lead_in: What is the most appropriate first-line management?

options.text: Spironolactone 100 mg daily without concurrent contraception cover
options.rationale: Spironolactone is teratogenic and is only used with effective contraception; not appropriate as monotherapy initial step. (Source: International PCOS guideline 2023)

options.text: Metformin 500 mg twice daily as monotherapy for menstrual regulation
options.rationale: Metformin can be added when metabolic features predominate but is not first-line for cycle regulation and hyperandrogenism. (Source: International PCOS guideline 2023)

options.text: Cyclic medroxyprogesterone acetate 10 mg for 10 days every 3 months
options.rationale: Cyclic progestogen provides endometrial protection only and does not address hyperandrogenism. (Source: International PCOS guideline 2023)

options.text: Combined oral contraceptive containing 30 mcg ethinylestradiol with levonorgestrel
options.rationale: International PCOS guideline 2023 recommends combined hormonal contraception first-line for cycle regulation and hyperandrogenism in adolescents; lower-dose preparations are preferred. (Source: International PCOS guideline 2023)

options.text: Letrozole 2.5 mg daily on cycle days 3-7 to induce ovulation each month
options.rationale: Ovulation induction is not the goal in an adolescent not seeking pregnancy. (Source: International PCOS guideline 2023)

explanation.summary: Adolescents with PCOS who seek cycle regulation and management of hyperandrogenism are offered combined hormonal contraception first-line per the 2023 international PCOS guideline, which is endorsed by RANZCOG. Lower-dose formulations are preferred. Lifestyle modification is paired with pharmacotherapy. Metformin is added when metabolic features predominate or after lifestyle alone has failed for impaired glucose tolerance. Spironolactone requires concurrent contraception.
key_points: Combined hormonal contraception first-line for cycle and hyperandrogenism in PCOS
Lifestyle pairs with pharmacotherapy
Spironolactone requires effective contraception due to teratogenicity
explanation.pearls: In adolescents, PCOS diagnosis requires both oligo-anovulation and hyperandrogenism; polycystic ovarian morphology is not used for diagnosis in this age group.

stem: A 29-year-old G3P3 is seen at her six-week postnatal review. Her delivery was an uncomplicated normal vaginal birth. She is fully breastfeeding and her baby has not been formula-supplemented. Her menstrual periods have not returned. She is in a stable relationship and asks about a copper intrauterine device because she does not want hormonal contraception. She has no history of pelvic infection or heavy menstrual bleeding.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 72, BP 116/72 mmHg, RR 14, SpO2 99%, temperature 36.7°C
data_table.Examination: Uterus involuted, lochia minimal, no offensive discharge, perineum healed

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step?

options.text: Refer to gynaecology theatre for insertion under general anaesthesia next month
options.rationale: Outpatient insertion is appropriate and avoids unnecessary general anaesthesia. (Source: Family Planning Australia contraception guide 2023)

options.text: Defer copper IUD insertion until 12 weeks postpartum to reduce expulsion
options.rationale: Insertion from four weeks postpartum is acceptable; deferring routinely leaves a gap with no contraception. (Source: Family Planning Australia contraception guide 2023)

options.text: Recommend condoms only and review again in six months for the IUD
options.rationale: Condom-only contraception has high typical-use failure rates and the patient has requested LARC. (Source: Family Planning Australia contraception guide 2023)

options.text: Start the progestogen-only pill today and insert copper IUD at six months
options.rationale: She has specifically requested non-hormonal contraception; offering POP overrides her stated preference. (Source: Family Planning Australia contraception guide 2023)

options.text: Insert the copper intrauterine device today after current pregnancy is excluded
options.rationale: Postnatal copper IUD insertion from four weeks postpartum is supported by Faculty of Sexual and Reproductive Health and Family Planning Australia after excluding pregnancy. Fully breastfeeding with amenorrhoea further lowers risk. (Source: Family Planning Australia contraception guide 2023)

explanation.summary: Copper IUD can be inserted immediately postpartum within 48 hours of delivery or any time from four weeks postpartum once the uterus has involuted, after excluding current pregnancy. Lactational amenorrhoea provides additional safety but is not relied upon alone for LARC users. Outpatient insertion at six weeks postnatal review is standard. Honour the patient's request for non-hormonal contraception rather than substituting a hormonal alternative.
key_points: Copper IUD: immediate postpartum (within 48 hours) or from 4 weeks
Exclude pregnancy before insertion
Patient autonomy: honour non-hormonal preference
explanation.pearls: Combining the six-week postnatal review with LARC insertion is the highest-yield contact for unmet contraceptive need.

stem:
A 30-year-old G3P1 at 32 weeks' gestation presents after a 200 mL painless fresh vaginal bleed at home. The bleed has now stopped. Her anomaly scan documented a complete placenta praevia. Her blood group is A positive. The fetus is moving normally and CTG shows a reassuring trace with baseline 140 bpm, variability 10 bpm, accelerations present, no decelerations. Speculum was deferred. Bedside ultrasound confirms cephalic presentation and placenta covering the os. Haemoglobin is 112 g/L (115-165) and platelets 198 x10^9/L (150-400).

The maternal fetal medicine team is on-site.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 88, BP 124/78 mmHg, RR 16, SpO2 99%, temperature 36.7°C, fetal HR 140
data_table.Examination: Soft abdomen, no uterine tenderness, no contractions
data_table.Investigations: Haemoglobin 112 g/L, platelets 198 x10^9/L, fibrinogen 4.2 g/L, blood group A positive; ultrasound complete praevia, cephalic, normal EFW

lead_in: What is the most appropriate management plan?

options.text: Admit, betamethasone IM, cross-match 2 units, and plan caesarean at 36-37 weeks
options.rationale: RANZCOG advises inpatient observation for sentinel praevia bleeds, corticosteroids 24-34+6 weeks, and elective caesarean at 36-37 weeks for complete praevia. (Source: RANZCOG Placenta Praevia 2022)

options.text: Discharge home with safety netting after 4 hours of observation
options.rationale: A sentinel bleed in placenta praevia mandates admission; the next bleed is often the dangerous one. (Source: RANZCOG Placenta Praevia 2022)

options.text: Immediate category 1 caesarean section regardless of fetal status
options.rationale: Category 1 is reserved for ongoing haemorrhage, maternal compromise, or non-reassuring CTG; bleeding has settled and CTG is reassuring. (Source: RANZCOG Placenta Praevia 2022)

options.text: Induction of labour with vaginal prostaglandin and aim for vaginal birth
options.rationale: Complete placenta praevia is an absolute contraindication to vaginal birth; the placenta covers the os. (Source: RANZCOG Placenta Praevia 2022)

options.text: Outpatient management with twice-weekly midwifery review and aspirin 100 mg
options.rationale: Outpatient management is only appropriate after no bleeding for at least 48 hours, immediate hospital access, and stable haemoglobin; aspirin is not indicated. (Source: RANZCOG Placenta Praevia 2022)

explanation.summary: A painless antepartum haemorrhage with confirmed placenta praevia at 32 weeks requires inpatient observation after the sentinel bleed because the next bleed is often heavier and unpredictable. Antenatal corticosteroids are given between 24 and 34+6 weeks for fetal lung maturation if delivery within 7 days is anticipated. Cross-match is held given the bleeding risk. Complete praevia mandates elective caesarean at 36+0 to 37+0 weeks; vaginal birth is contraindicated. Outpatient management is only considered after at least 48 hours of stability and immediate hospital access.
key_points: Sentinel praevia bleed: admit for observation
Steroids 24-34+6 weeks if delivery within 7 days possible
Complete praevia: elective caesarean 36-37 weeks
explanation.pearls: If the placenta is anterior and there was a previous caesarean, screen for placenta accreta spectrum with grey-scale plus colour Doppler ultrasound before delivery planning.

stem:
A 34-year-old G2P2 has just delivered a healthy 3.8 kg infant by emergency caesarean at 39 weeks for failure to progress. Her BMI booking weight was 41 kg/m^2. She has no personal or family history of VTE. The operation was uncomplicated with an estimated blood loss of 600 mL. She has no current bleeding and her blood pressure has returned to baseline. She has not received any anticoagulation. Her platelet count is 220 x10^9/L (150-400) and her creatinine is 64 micromol/L (45-90).

The postnatal ward team is preparing her discharge medications.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 82, BP 122/76 mmHg, RR 14, SpO2 99%, temperature 36.7°C
data_table.Examination: Wound clean and dry, uterus contracted, lochia minimal
data_table.Investigations: Haemoglobin 108 g/L, platelets 220 x10^9/L, creatinine 64 micromol/L

lead_in: What is the most appropriate VTE prophylaxis plan?

options.text: Enoxaparin 40 mg subcutaneous daily for 6 weeks postpartum
options.rationale: BMI >=40 plus caesarean section is two risk factors; RANZCOG recommends LMWH thromboprophylaxis for at least 6 weeks postpartum for high-risk women. (Source: RANZCOG Maternal VTE Prevention 2020)

options.text: Aspirin 100 mg orally daily for one week as sole prophylaxis
options.rationale: Aspirin is not adequate VTE prophylaxis postpartum for a high-risk woman; LMWH is the AU standard. (Source: RANZCOG Maternal VTE Prevention 2020)

options.text: Enoxaparin 40 mg subcutaneous daily for 10 days only
options.rationale: 10 days is the standard postpartum duration after uncomplicated caesarean with only one risk factor; this patient has two risk factors and warrants 6 weeks. (Source: RANZCOG Maternal VTE Prevention 2020)

options.text: Mechanical prophylaxis with calf compression and mobilisation
options.rationale: Mechanical alone is insufficient for a woman with BMI 41 plus caesarean; LMWH is required. (Source: RANZCOG Maternal VTE Prevention 2020)

options.text: Apixaban 2.5 mg orally twice daily for 6 weeks postpartum
options.rationale: DOACs are not approved during breastfeeding by AMH; LMWH is preferred postpartum. (Source: AMH: Apixaban)

explanation.summary: Postpartum VTE risk peaks in the first six weeks. RANZCOG and ANZSPM categorise risk: caesarean delivery, BMI >=30, age >=35, parity >=3, smoking, immobility, and family or personal VTE history each add risk. Two or more risk factors warrant LMWH for the full 6 weeks postpartum; a single intermediate risk factor warrants 10 days. DOACs are avoided in breastfeeding women per AMH because of limited safety data.
key_points: Two risk factors postpartum: 6 weeks LMWH
One intermediate risk factor: 10 days LMWH
DOACs avoided in breastfeeding
explanation.pearls: Weight-adjust enoxaparin to 0.5 mg/kg twice daily for BMI >=40 or weight >=100 kg, since fixed 40 mg daily is subtherapeutic in higher-weight women.

stem:
A 28-year-old G2P1 at 38 weeks is admitted in spontaneous labour. After artificial rupture of membranes a midwife feels a pulsating loop of cord through the cervix. The cervix is 4 cm dilated and the fetal head is at -3 station. CTG shows variable decelerations to 70 bpm with slow recovery. The bedside theatre team has been activated and the obstetric consultant is en route. The mother is in the antenatal ward bed.

The team has been briefed and she gives full consent.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 96, BP 128/74 mmHg, RR 18, SpO2 99%, temperature 36.8°C, fetal HR 70 (decelerations)
data_table.Examination: Cervix 4 cm dilated, fetal head -3 station, pulsating cord in vagina
data_table.Investigations: CTG variable decelerations to 70 bpm

lead_in: What is the most appropriate immediate action while waiting for caesarean?

options.text: Knee-chest or steep Trendelenburg, elevating the presenting part
options.rationale: Manual elevation of the presenting part plus gravity position relieves cord compression until delivery; both knee-chest and Trendelenburg are AU first-line. (Source: RANZCOG Cord Prolapse 2020)

options.text: Cover the cord with warm saline-soaked gauze and otherwise leave undisturbed
options.rationale: Warming gauze does not relieve compression; the priority is to elevate the presenting part off the cord. (Source: RANZCOG Cord Prolapse 2020)

options.text: Push the cord back into the uterus and start oxytocin to expedite delivery
options.rationale: Replacing the cord is contraindicated; oxytocin would worsen compression. (Source: RANZCOG Cord Prolapse 2020)

options.text: Insert catheter and infuse 500-750 mL into bladder for transfer
options.rationale: Bladder filling is an alternative when manual elevation is not feasible (e.g. transfer to a distant facility); manual elevation is faster when theatre is on site. (Source: RANZCOG Cord Prolapse 2020)

options.text: Start magnesium sulfate 4 g IV bolus to suppress contractions
options.rationale: Tocolysis (terbutaline 250 mcg SC) is an option to relieve contractions during transfer but is second to elevation; magnesium is not the AU tocolytic choice in cord prolapse. (Source: RANZCOG Cord Prolapse 2020)

explanation.summary: Cord prolapse with fetal compromise is a category 1 obstetric emergency. Immediate priority is to relieve compression of the cord against the presenting part: the examiner keeps two fingers in the vagina elevating the presenting part while the patient is placed in knee-chest or steep Trendelenburg. Tocolysis (terbutaline) and bladder filling are reserved for prolonged transfers. Delivery is by category 1 caesarean unless full dilatation allows immediate instrumental.
key_points: Manual elevation plus gravity position is first-line
Category 1 caesarean unless full dilatation
Bladder fill for prolonged transfers only
explanation.pearls: Decision-to-delivery interval should be under 30 minutes for category 1 caesarean; document time of prolapse and time of delivery for clinical governance.

stem:
A 33-year-old G3P2 at 34 weeks presents with sudden severe constant abdominal pain that began two hours ago. She reports no vaginal bleeding. She is normotensive with mild tachycardia. The uterus is tense and tender between contractions. CTG shows a sinusoidal pattern with reduced variability and late decelerations. Maternal haemoglobin is 92 g/L (115-165), platelets 88 x10^9/L (150-400), fibrinogen 1.4 g/L (2.0-4.5), INR 1.4 (0.9-1.2). Ultrasound shows a retroplacental clot with no praevia.

The team has been briefed and consent obtained.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 118, BP 116/72 mmHg, RR 24, SpO2 98%, temperature 36.8°C, fetal HR sinusoidal
data_table.Examination: Tense tender uterus, no external bleeding
data_table.Investigations: Haemoglobin 92 g/L, platelets 88 x10^9/L, fibrinogen 1.4 g/L, INR 1.4; ultrasound retroplacental clot

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step?

options.text: Category 1 caesarean section with massive transfusion protocol activation
options.rationale: Concealed abruption with non-reassuring CTG and developing DIC is a category 1 emergency; delivery and blood product support cannot be delayed. (Source: RANZCOG Placental Abruption 2020)

options.text: Tocolysis with nifedipine and steroids, plan delivery at 36 weeks
options.rationale: Tocolysis is contraindicated in significant abruption; fetal compromise and DIC mandate immediate delivery. (Source: RANZCOG Placental Abruption 2020)

options.text: Induction of labour with oxytocin aiming for vaginal birth
options.rationale: Vaginal birth is possible only if fetus is dead or rapidly deliverable; a sinusoidal CTG with active DIC requires caesarean. (Source: RANZCOG Placental Abruption 2020)

options.text: Conservative management with continuous CTG and serial coagulation
options.rationale: Conservative management is reserved for stable, small abruption with reassuring CTG and no coagulopathy. (Source: RANZCOG Placental Abruption 2020)

options.text: Cryoprecipitate alone targeting fibrinogen >2 g/L, then reassess delivery
options.rationale: Cryoprecipitate is part of resuscitation but does not replace delivery; the source of DIC must be removed. (Source: RANZCOG Placental Abruption 2020)

explanation.summary: Concealed placental abruption can hide a major haemorrhage; tense uterus, anaemia, thrombocytopenia, hypofibrinogenaemia and a sinusoidal CTG together indicate DIC with fetal compromise. Immediate category 1 caesarean is required, with massive transfusion protocol activation. Fibrinogen below 2 g/L in obstetric haemorrhage predicts severe haemorrhage; replacement with cryoprecipitate or fibrinogen concentrate is included in the protocol.
key_points: Concealed abruption with DIC + non-reassuring CTG: category 1 caesarean
Activate massive transfusion protocol
Fibrinogen <2 g/L is the obstetric red flag
explanation.pearls: Couvelaire uterus (myometrial bleeding) seen at caesarean is not an indication for hysterectomy unless uterine atony does not respond to uterotonics.

stem:
A 32-year-old G1P0 at 40 weeks has been pushing for 30 minutes. The head delivers but retracts firmly against the perineum and external rotation fails. McRoberts hyperflexion has been performed and suprapubic pressure applied for 30 seconds without delivery. Estimated fetal weight at 38 weeks was 4.0 kg. The mother is fully dilated. The shoulders remain impacted. CTG had been reassuring until head-on-perineum sign.

The team is in position around the bed.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 102, BP 134/84 mmHg, RR 20, SpO2 99%, temperature 36.9°C, fetal HR not currently auscultatable
data_table.Examination: Fetal head retracted against perineum, external rotation failed
data_table.Investigations: Cervix fully dilated; fetus presumed cephalic

lead_in: What is the next most appropriate manoeuvre?

options.text: Rubin II internal rotation by pushing the anterior shoulder forward
options.rationale: After McRoberts and suprapubic pressure fail, the next HELPERR step in AU practice is an internal manoeuvre, commencing with Rubin II to reduce shoulder diameter. (Source: RANZCOG Shoulder Dystocia 2020)

options.text: Symphysiotomy under local anaesthetic to widen the pelvic outlet
options.rationale: Symphysiotomy is a last-resort manoeuvre with high maternal morbidity, after all internal manoeuvres and Zavanelli have failed. (Source: RANZCOG Shoulder Dystocia 2020)

options.text: Apply axial traction with stronger maternal pushing efforts
options.rationale: Stronger axial traction risks brachial plexus injury and does not resolve impaction; internal manoeuvres are required. (Source: RANZCOG Shoulder Dystocia 2020)

options.text: Zavanelli manoeuvre with cephalic replacement and immediate caesarean
options.rationale: Zavanelli is reserved for failure of internal manoeuvres; it is the AU last-resort before symphysiotomy. (Source: RANZCOG Shoulder Dystocia 2020)

options.text: Fundal pressure to drive the anterior shoulder under the symphysis
options.rationale: Fundal pressure worsens impaction and is contraindicated in shoulder dystocia. (Source: RANZCOG Shoulder Dystocia 2020)

explanation.summary: Shoulder dystocia is a time-critical emergency. The HELPERR sequence is: call for Help, evaluate for Episiotomy, McRoberts hyperflexion of maternal legs, suprapubic Pressure, then internal manoeuvres (Enter the vagina) including Rubin II and Wood's screw, deliver the posterior arm (Reach), and Roll the patient onto all fours. If all manoeuvres fail, Zavanelli or symphysiotomy are last resorts. Fundal pressure is contraindicated throughout.
key_points: After McRoberts and suprapubic, go internal
Rubin II reduces bisacromial diameter
Fundal pressure is contraindicated
explanation.pearls: Each manoeuvre is given approximately 30 seconds; the head-to-body delivery interval is associated with hypoxic injury when it exceeds 5 minutes.

stem:
A 36-year-old G2P1 at 38 weeks presents with progressive shortness of breath for ten days, two-pillow orthopnoea, and bilateral pitting oedema to the knees. She has no history of cardiac disease. There is no chest pain. Echocardiogram shows global LV hypokinesis with LVEF 28%, no valvular lesion, and a moderate pericardial effusion. NT-proBNP is 5400 ng/L (normal <300). CTG is reassuring. She is currently in spontaneous early labour with the cervix 3 cm dilated, fetus cephalic, no membrane rupture.

Multidisciplinary delivery planning is in progress.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 118, BP 106/64 mmHg, RR 28, SpO2 94%, temperature 36.7°C, fetal HR 140
data_table.Examination: Raised JVP 5 cm, bibasal crackles, bilateral pitting oedema, S3 gallop
data_table.Investigations: LVEF 28%, NT-proBNP 5400 ng/L; CTG reassuring; cervix 3 cm dilated

lead_in: What is the most appropriate delivery plan?

options.text: Assisted vaginal birth under epidural with shortened second stage
options.rationale: In peripartum cardiomyopathy without obstetric indication for caesarean, vaginal birth with epidural and assisted second stage reduces cardiac stress compared with caesarean; multidisciplinary input is essential. (Source: ESC Cardiovascular Disease in Pregnancy 2018)

options.text: Immediate category 1 caesarean section under general anaesthetic now
options.rationale: Category 1 caesarean is for fetal or maternal compromise; haemodynamics are stable and CTG reassuring. (Source: ESC Cardiovascular Disease in Pregnancy 2018)

options.text: Nifedipine tocolysis and elective caesarean section at 40 weeks
options.rationale: Nifedipine reduces preload and may worsen output; prolonging pregnancy in PPCM does not benefit either patient. (Source: ESC Cardiovascular Disease in Pregnancy 2018)

options.text: Bromocriptine 2.5 mg twice daily to delay delivery for optimisation
options.rationale: Bromocriptine is investigational adjunct postpartum; it does not replace delivery in established labour. (Source: ESC Cardiovascular Disease in Pregnancy 2018)

options.text: Insert intra-aortic balloon pump pre-emptively before delivery
options.rationale: Mechanical circulatory support is reserved for cardiogenic shock or severe pulmonary oedema unresponsive to medical therapy. (Source: ESC Cardiovascular Disease in Pregnancy 2018)

explanation.summary: Peripartum cardiomyopathy with LVEF <30% at term is high-risk for decompensation. AU multidisciplinary delivery planning favours vaginal birth with regional anaesthesia in stable patients because caesarean fluid shifts and supine compression worsen failure. Invasive arterial monitoring is used. A shortened second stage with instrumental delivery limits Valsalva. Caesarean is reserved for usual obstetric indications or maternal collapse. Anticoagulation, beta-blockade, and bromocriptine are postpartum considerations.
key_points: PPCM stable: vaginal birth with epidural preferred
Caesarean reserved for obstetric indications
Shortened second stage with instrumental
explanation.pearls: Bromocriptine 2.5 mg twice daily added to standard heart failure therapy postpartum has been associated with improved LV recovery in PPCM in IPAC and BRO-HF trials.

stem:
A 30-year-old G1P0 at 33 weeks presents with right upper quadrant pain and nausea for 18 hours. She has had no previous antenatal hypertension. Examination shows tender liver edge. Urine dipstick 3+ protein. Bloods: haemoglobin 92 g/L (115-165), platelets 40 x10^9/L (150-400), AST 380 U/L (0-40), ALT 410 U/L (0-40), LDH 920 U/L (140-280), creatinine 102 micromol/L (45-90), uric acid 0.48 mmol/L (0.15-0.35), fibrinogen 2.8 g/L. INR 1.0. Blood film shows fragmentation. CTG is reassuring.

The team has been briefed and consent obtained for delivery.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 96, BP 168/108 mmHg, RR 18, SpO2 99%, temperature 36.7°C, fetal HR 142
data_table.Examination: RUQ tenderness, hyperreflexia, no clonus
data_table.Investigations: Haemoglobin 92 g/L, platelets 40 x10^9/L, AST 380 U/L, ALT 410 U/L, LDH 920 U/L, creatinine 102 micromol/L, urate 0.48 mmol/L, fibrinogen 2.8 g/L, INR 1.0; film fragmentation

lead_in: What is the most appropriate plan for delivery and anaesthesia?

options.text: Caesarean under GA after labetalol, magnesium, and platelets >50
options.rationale: Platelets <50 x10^9/L contraindicates neuraxial anaesthesia; HELLP at 33 weeks with BP control and seizure prophylaxis warrants delivery under general. (Source: RANZCOG Hypertension in Pregnancy 2023)

options.text: Epidural and assisted vaginal birth after platelet transfusion
options.rationale: Even after transfusion, neuraxial is high-risk in HELLP because of falling platelets and bleeding tendency; vaginal birth has prolonged exposure. (Source: RANZCOG Hypertension in Pregnancy 2023)

options.text: Spinal anaesthesia without platelet transfusion at current platelet count
options.rationale: Spinal at platelet <50 x10^9/L carries unacceptable spinal haematoma risk. (Source: RANZCOG Hypertension in Pregnancy 2023)

options.text: Conservative management with steroids; reassess delivery at 48 h
options.rationale: HELLP at >=34 weeks or with severe maternal complications requires delivery; conservative management beyond steroid window is not standard for severe HELLP. (Source: RANZCOG Hypertension in Pregnancy 2023)

options.text: Induction of labour with oxytocin and IV pethidine for analgesia
options.rationale: Pethidine is contraindicated in HELLP because of seizure threshold and accumulation of norpethidine; induction with severe HELLP risks deterioration during prolonged labour. (Source: AMH: Pethidine)

explanation.summary: HELLP at 33 weeks with platelets 40, AST and ALT >400, and LDH >600 represents Mississippi Class 1 severe disease. Delivery is the only definitive treatment. Severe hypertension is controlled to <160/110 with IV labetalol or hydralazine; magnesium sulfate 4 g IV loading then 1 g/hour prevents eclamptic seizures. Neuraxial anaesthesia requires platelets >=70-80 x10^9/L for epidural and >=50 x10^9/L for spinal per individual unit thresholds, with falling counts a relative contraindication. General anaesthetic is preferred when platelets are <50 and falling.
key_points: Severe HELLP needs delivery, no temporising beyond steroid window
Platelets <50 contraindicate neuraxial when falling
Magnesium sulfate plus IV antihypertensive precede delivery
explanation.pearls: Dexamethasone for HELLP improves laboratory values but not maternal or neonatal outcomes; the Cochrane review found no benefit beyond fetal lung maturity dosing.

stem:
A 32-year-old G2P2 has just had a spontaneous vaginal delivery of a 3.9 kg baby at 39 weeks gestation. The placenta delivered intact. Within 10 minutes she has lost an estimated 900 mL of bright red blood, and the uterus is boggy on palpation. She had pre-eclampsia in this pregnancy and is on labetalol; her booking BMI was 28 kg/m^2.

IV oxytocin 10 units intramuscularly was given with active third-stage management. An IV infusion of oxytocin 40 units in 1 L of Hartmann's is now running. Bimanual uterine massage has been started.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 115, BP 162/106 mmHg, RR 22, SpO2 98%, temperature 36.8 °C
data_table.Examination: Boggy uterus 20 cm above symphysis, ongoing PV trickle of bright red blood, no obvious vaginal or cervical laceration
data_table.Investigations: Hb 96 g/L (115-165), platelets 165 × 10^9/L (150-400), coags within normal limits
data_table.Medications: Labetalol 200 mg PO TDS during pregnancy, oxytocin infusion running

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next uterotonic to add?

options.text: Ergometrine 250 mcg intramuscular bolus, repeated once after 30 minutes if needed
options.rationale: Ergometrine causes vasoconstriction and is contraindicated in hypertension and pre-eclampsia; using it in this woman with BP 162/106 mmHg risks accelerated hypertension and stroke. (Source: RANZCOG Management of Postpartum Haemorrhage 2021)

options.text: Carboprost (15-methyl PGF2α) 250 mcg intramuscular, repeated every 15 minutes
options.rationale: Carboprost is the appropriate next-line uterotonic when ergometrine is contraindicated (hypertension, pre-eclampsia); RANZCOG advises avoiding ergometrine when BP exceeds 140/90 mmHg. (Source: RANZCOG Management of Postpartum Haemorrhage 2021)

options.text: Misoprostol 800 mcg sublingual single dose, no further uterotonic for 30 minutes
options.rationale: Misoprostol is an adjunct option but in established atonic PPH with hypertension the recommended escalation is parenteral carboprost; misoprostol takes longer to act and is less effective for refractory atony. (Source: RANZCOG Management of Postpartum Haemorrhage 2021)

options.text: Tranexamic acid 1 g intravenous as the only further pharmacological adjunct given
options.rationale: Tranexamic acid is an adjunct to uterotonics not a replacement; the WOMAN trial shows benefit when given within 3 hours, but atonic PPH still requires a second uterotonic to address the bleeding mechanism. (Source: RANZCOG Management of Postpartum Haemorrhage 2021)

options.text: Increase the oxytocin infusion rate to 80 units in 1 L Hartmann's over 4 hours
options.rationale: Increasing the oxytocin concentration beyond standard regimens does not improve atony response and increases hyponatraemia risk because of its antidiuretic effect; the AU step is to add a second uterotonic. (Source: RANZCOG Management of Postpartum Haemorrhage 2021)

explanation.summary: Postpartum haemorrhage is the leading cause of maternal mortality globally and a major morbidity contributor in Australia. The AU approach pairs mechanical (massage, bimanual compression, balloon tamponade) and pharmacological (uterotonics, tranexamic acid) measures with rapid resuscitation and surgical escalation. The uterotonic ladder is oxytocin first, then ergometrine, then carboprost, with misoprostol as an alternative if injectable options are unavailable. Ergometrine is contraindicated in hypertension and pre-eclampsia; carboprost is contraindicated in asthma. Tranexamic acid 1 g IV should be given within 3 hours of bleeding onset.
key_points: First-line: oxytocin bolus and infusion plus mechanical measures.
Ergometrine contraindicated in hypertension or pre-eclampsia.
Carboprost contraindicated in asthma.
Tranexamic acid 1 g IV within 3 hours of bleeding onset (WOMAN trial).
explanation.pearls: RANZCOG PPH ladder: oxytocin → ergometrine (avoid if BP >140/90) → carboprost (avoid in asthma) → misoprostol; TXA 1 g IV adjunct.

stem:
A 28-year-old G1P0 at 33+5 weeks is reviewed in the day-assessment unit after self-monitoring elevated home blood pressures. She reports a mild headache but no visual disturbance or epigastric pain. She is on no regular medications.

Urine dipstick shows protein 3+. Bloods show platelets 220 × 10^9/L, ALT 28 U/L (5-30), creatinine 58 micromol/L (45-90), urate 0.41 mmol/L. CTG shows a normal trace at 140 bpm with variability and accelerations. There has been no antenatal antihypertensive treatment to date.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 88, BP 168/112 mmHg confirmed on repeat, RR 16, SpO2 99%, temperature 36.7 °C, fetal HR 140 bpm
data_table.Examination: Reflexes brisk but no clonus, no epigastric tenderness, no peripheral oedema beyond ankles, fundoscopy unremarkable
data_table.Investigations: Urine PCR 320 mg/mmol, platelets 220 × 10^9/L, ALT 28 U/L, creatinine 58 micromol/L, urate 0.41 mmol/L

lead_in: What is the most appropriate immediate antihypertensive choice?

options.text: Sublingual nifedipine immediate-release 10 mg, repeated as needed up to 30 mg
options.rationale: Sublingual short-acting nifedipine causes unpredictable rapid drops in BP and is contraindicated in pregnancy; oral immediate-release is acceptable but not sublingual. (Source: SOMANZ Guideline for the Management of Hypertensive Disorders of Pregnancy 2023)
source_refs: SOMANZ Guideline for the Management of Hypertensive Disorders of Pregnancy 2023

options.text: Oral methyldopa 250 mg three times daily as the slow-titrated initial agent
options.rationale: Methyldopa is a slow-onset oral agent used for outpatient chronic management; it is not appropriate for severe acute hypertension where BP must be reduced within an hour. (Source: SOMANZ Guideline for the Management of Hypertensive Disorders of Pregnancy 2023)
source_refs: SOMANZ Guideline for the Management of Hypertensive Disorders of Pregnancy 2023

options.text: Intravenous labetalol 20 mg bolus, doubled every 10 minutes to a maximum of 220 mg
options.rationale: SOMANZ recommends rapid-acting parenteral labetalol (or IV hydralazine or oral immediate-release nifedipine) as first-line for severe hypertension in pregnancy with BP ≥160/110 mmHg, with the aim to drop BP into the 140-150 systolic range within an hour. (Source: SOMANZ Guideline for the Management of Hypertensive Disorders of Pregnancy 2023)
source_refs: SOMANZ Guideline for the Management of Hypertensive Disorders of Pregnancy 2023

options.text: Intravenous magnesium sulfate 4 g as the only initial pharmacological treatment
options.rationale: Magnesium sulfate is for seizure prophylaxis and treatment in eclampsia, not direct BP control; it must be paired with a true antihypertensive when BP ≥160/110 mmHg. (Source: SOMANZ Guideline for the Management of Hypertensive Disorders of Pregnancy 2023)
source_refs: SOMANZ Guideline for the Management of Hypertensive Disorders of Pregnancy 2023

options.text: Intravenous furosemide 40 mg bolus alone to reduce intravascular volume and BP
