options.rationale: Loop diuretics are not first-line in pre-eclampsia because intravascular volume is often already reduced; they are reserved for pulmonary oedema, not severe hypertension control. (Source: SOMANZ Guideline for the Management of Hypertensive Disorders of Pregnancy 2023)
source_refs: SOMANZ Guideline for the Management of Hypertensive Disorders of Pregnancy 2023

explanation.summary: Severe hypertension in pregnancy (BP ≥160/110 mmHg) is a hypertensive emergency. SOMANZ first-line options are intravenous labetalol, intravenous hydralazine, or oral immediate-release nifedipine; magnesium sulfate is given concurrently for seizure prophylaxis in pre-eclampsia. The target is BP 140-150/90-100 mmHg within an hour. After acute control, transition to a maintenance oral agent (labetalol, nifedipine controlled-release, or methyldopa). ACE inhibitors and ARBs are teratogenic and contraindicated. Delivery timing is decided by gestation, severity, fetal status, and end-organ involvement.
key_points: Severe HT threshold in pregnancy = ≥160/110 mmHg.
First-line acute agents: IV labetalol, IV hydralazine, oral immediate-release nifedipine.
Magnesium sulfate is for seizure prophylaxis, not BP control.
Sublingual nifedipine and ACE-I/ARBs are contraindicated.
explanation.pearls: SOMANZ: aim BP 140-150/90-100 mmHg within 1 hour using IV labetalol, IV hydralazine, or oral immediate-release nifedipine.

sources.label: SOMANZ Guideline for the Management of Hypertensive Disorders of Pregnancy 2023

stem:
A 29-year-old G1P0 attends her 26-week antenatal appointment after her routine 75 g oral glucose tolerance test. She has been well, is gaining weight along expected centiles, and has no symptoms. Her booking BMI was 26 kg/m^2. She has no family history of diabetes and is not on any regular medications.

Her fasting plasma glucose was 4.8 mmol/L. The 1-hour value was 10.4 mmol/L. The 2-hour value was 7.8 mmol/L. Her HbA1c at booking was 5.0%. Her urinalysis today is negative for glucose and protein.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 80, BP 118/72 mmHg, RR 14, SpO2 100%, temperature 36.6 °C, fetal HR 145 bpm
data_table.Examination: Fundal height appropriate for dates, normal symphysis-fundal growth chart, no oedema
data_table.Investigations: OGTT fasting 4.8 mmol/L, 1-hour 10.4 mmol/L, 2-hour 7.8 mmol/L, booking HbA1c 5.0%, urinalysis negative

lead_in: What is the most appropriate interpretation of these results?

options.text: Normal glucose tolerance because the fasting and 2-hour values are below threshold
options.rationale: ADIPS criteria treat any single threshold breach as diagnostic; a normal fasting and 2-hour result does not override an elevated 1-hour result. (Source: ADIPS Consensus Guidelines for GDM 2014)

options.text: Gestational diabetes diagnosed on the 1-hour OGTT value alone, no repeat needed
options.rationale: ADIPS Australian criteria diagnose GDM when ANY single OGTT value meets the threshold: fasting ≥5.1, 1-hour ≥10.0, or 2-hour ≥8.5 mmol/L; this patient's 1-hour 10.4 mmol/L is diagnostic. (Source: ADIPS Consensus Guidelines for GDM 2014)

options.text: Repeat the OGTT in 4 weeks because only one value is elevated on this test
options.rationale: ADIPS does not require repeat OGTT after a single elevated value; repeating delays management and increases fetal exposure to hyperglycaemia. (Source: ADIPS Consensus Guidelines for GDM 2014)

options.text: Pre-existing type 2 diabetes because the HbA1c at booking was above 5.5%
options.rationale: Her booking HbA1c of 5.0% is well below the type 2 diabetes diagnostic threshold of 6.5% and is also below the early-pregnancy GDM threshold of 5.9%. (Source: ADIPS Consensus Guidelines for GDM 2014)

options.text: Impaired glucose tolerance only, not gestational diabetes, on these OGTT values
options.rationale: Australian pregnancy guidance does not use an 'impaired glucose tolerance' category separate from GDM during pregnancy; any single OGTT breach is GDM. (Source: ADIPS Consensus Guidelines for GDM 2014)

explanation.summary: Australian GDM diagnosis is based on the 75 g OGTT performed at 24-28 weeks, with ADIPS thresholds of fasting ≥5.1, 1-hour ≥10.0, and 2-hour ≥8.5 mmol/L. Any single elevated value is diagnostic. Earlier OGTT (booking) is recommended for women with risk factors (prior GDM, BMI ≥30, prior macrosomic baby, ethnicity from a high-prevalence group, age ≥40, family history). Once diagnosed, first-line management is dietary advice and self-monitoring; insulin or metformin is added when glycaemic targets are not met.
key_points: ADIPS OGTT thresholds: fasting ≥5.1, 1-h ≥10.0, 2-h ≥8.5 mmol/L.
Any single elevated value is diagnostic; no repeat required.
Early OGTT for high-risk women at booking.
First-line management is diet and SMBG; insulin or metformin if targets unmet.
explanation.pearls: ADIPS: GDM diagnosed by a single OGTT value at or above fasting 5.1, 1-h 10.0, or 2-h 8.5 mmol/L.

stem:
A 31-year-old G2P0 presents to the early pregnancy unit with 2 weeks of intermittent right iliac fossa discomfort. Her last menstrual period was 7 weeks ago. She has no syncope, no shoulder-tip pain, and no significant bleeding. She lives 20 minutes from the hospital and can attend twice-weekly follow-up.

Transvaginal ultrasound shows a 3.1 cm right tubal mass without fetal cardiac activity and no free fluid. Beta-hCG is 4200 IU/L. Her LFTs and UEC are within normal limits. She has had no prior abdominal surgery and no contraindications to methotrexate.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 76, BP 118/72 mmHg, RR 14, SpO2 100%, temperature 36.6 °C
data_table.Examination: Soft abdomen, mild right adnexal tenderness, no peritonism, no cervical motion tenderness
data_table.Investigations: TV ultrasound 3.1 cm right tubal mass, no fetal cardiac activity, no free fluid, beta-hCG 4200 IU/L, UEC and LFTs within normal limits

lead_in: What is the most appropriate management option?

options.text: Emergency laparotomy with salpingectomy regardless of haemodynamic stability
options.rationale: Laparotomy is reserved for haemodynamic instability or where laparoscopy is not feasible; this stable patient with mild symptoms does not need open surgery. (Source: RANZCOG Tubal Ectopic Pregnancy Statement 2024)

options.text: Laparoscopic salpingectomy of the right tube as definitive surgical management
options.rationale: Salpingectomy is preferred when surgery is needed but this patient meets RANZCOG criteria for medical management; surgery here over-treats and removes a tube whose future fertility role matters. (Source: RANZCOG Tubal Ectopic Pregnancy Statement 2024)

options.text: Laparoscopic salpingostomy with conservation of the right tube and bhCG follow-up
options.rationale: Salpingostomy is the surgical option chosen when the contralateral tube is absent or damaged; with a normal opposite tube and methotrexate criteria met, surgery is not indicated. (Source: RANZCOG Tubal Ectopic Pregnancy Statement 2024)

options.text: Expectant management with serial beta-hCG and no methotrexate or surgery
options.rationale: Expectant management is acceptable only with bhCG <1000-1500 IU/L and falling, low symptom burden, and small mass; at bhCG 4200 IU/L the risk of progression and tubal rupture is too high. (Source: RANZCOG Tubal Ectopic Pregnancy Statement 2024)

options.text: Single-dose intramuscular methotrexate 50 mg/m^2 with serial beta-hCG monitoring
options.rationale: RANZCOG GPS criteria for methotrexate include beta-hCG <5000 IU/L, mass <3.5 cm, no fetal cardiac activity, no significant pain, reliable follow-up, and no contraindications; this patient meets all six. (Source: RANZCOG Tubal Ectopic Pregnancy Statement 2024)

explanation.summary: Tubal ectopic pregnancy management in Australia follows RANZCOG GPS criteria. Methotrexate is preferred when beta-hCG <5000 IU/L, mass <3.5 cm, no fetal cardiac activity, no significant pain, reliable follow-up access, and no contraindications (active hepatic or renal disease, immunodeficiency, peptic ulcer, breastfeeding, or known sensitivity). Surgery is indicated for higher bhCG, large mass, fetal cardiac activity, significant pain, haemodynamic instability, or failed medical therapy. Salpingectomy is preferred over salpingostomy when the contralateral tube is healthy.
key_points: Methotrexate threshold (RANZCOG): bhCG <5000 IU/L plus the full criteria set.
Surgical management when bhCG ≥5000, mass ≥3.5 cm, FCA present, significant pain, or instability.
Salpingectomy preferred over salpingostomy when the opposite tube is healthy.
Day 4 and day 7 bhCG: ≥15% fall expected with successful methotrexate.
explanation.pearls: RANZCOG threshold for ectopic surgery vs methotrexate is bhCG 5000 IU/L (not 3000), with the full criteria set met.

stem:
A 32-year-old G2P2 presents on day 4 after a forceps-assisted vaginal delivery with a 12-hour history of fever and lower abdominal pain. She had prolonged rupture of membranes (28 hours) before delivery. Her lochia is heavy and foul-smelling.

On arrival to the postnatal ward she is alert and orientated. There is no calf swelling, no respiratory symptoms, and no flank pain. The uterus is tender on bimanual examination at the level of the umbilicus. Initial bloods show a raised CRP and a left shift on FBC.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 118, BP 102/64 mmHg, RR 22, SpO2 98%, temperature 38.6 °C
data_table.Examination: Tender boggy uterus at umbilicus, foul-smelling lochia, no calf swelling, chest clear, mild suprapubic tenderness without peritonism
data_table.Investigations: WCC 18.4 × 10^9/L (4-11), CRP 145 mg/L (<5), lactate 1.8 mmol/L, urine MCS sent, blood cultures sent

lead_in: What is the most appropriate empirical antibiotic regimen?

options.text: Computed tomography abdomen and pelvis prior to starting any antibiotic therapy
options.rationale: Imaging is reserved for suspected abscess, retained products, or atypical course; empiric antibiotics should not be delayed for CT in a febrile tachycardic postpartum woman. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic)

options.text: Oral cefalexin 500 mg four times daily as outpatient treatment for 7 days
options.rationale: Oral monotherapy with a first-generation cephalosporin does not cover anaerobes or enterococci and is inadequate for febrile inpatient endometritis with tachycardia. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic)

options.text: Intravenous piperacillin-tazobactam 4.5 g eight-hourly as broad-spectrum monotherapy
options.rationale: Piperacillin-tazobactam is broader-spectrum than needed for first-line endometritis; the AU step-up regimen is amox-gent-metronidazole, with piperacillin-tazobactam reserved for non-response or sepsis. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic)

options.text: Intravenous vancomycin 25 mg/kg load then 15 mg/kg twelve-hourly as monotherapy
options.rationale: Vancomycin covers MRSA and gram-positive organisms but misses gram-negatives and anaerobes; it is not first-line empirical therapy for endometritis. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic)

options.text: Intravenous amoxicillin, gentamicin, and metronidazole until afebrile for 24 hours
options.rationale: Therapeutic Guidelines empirical regimen for puerperal endometritis is IV ampicillin or amoxicillin plus gentamicin plus metronidazole to cover polymicrobial genital tract organisms including anaerobes. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic)

explanation.summary: Puerperal endometritis is a polymicrobial ascending genital tract infection that presents with fever, uterine tenderness, and offensive lochia in the first 10 days postpartum. Risk factors include caesarean section, prolonged rupture of membranes, instrumental delivery, and chorioamnionitis. The AU empirical regimen is IV amoxicillin or ampicillin plus gentamicin plus metronidazole, switched to oral once afebrile for 24-48 hours. Imaging is reserved for failed response, retained products, or suspected abscess. Septic pelvic thrombophlebitis is a differential when fever persists despite antibiotics.
key_points: AU empirical: IV amoxicillin or ampicillin plus gentamicin plus metronidazole.
Cover polymicrobial including anaerobes (genital tract flora).
Switch to oral once afebrile 24-48 hours; total 7-14 days.
Failed response should prompt imaging for retained products or abscess.
explanation.pearls: Postpartum endometritis: IV amoxicillin plus gentamicin plus metronidazole; persisting fever after 48 h suggests retained products or septic pelvic thrombophlebitis.

stem:
A 34-year-old G2P1 is seen in the antenatal clinic at 32 weeks gestation to discuss mode of delivery. Her first pregnancy was 3 years ago at 35 weeks for severe early pre-eclampsia. The operation note from that admission records 'extension of lower segment incision required, vertical extension up the uterine body, repaired in two layers'.

This pregnancy has been uncomplicated. The fetus is cephalic, AFI 14 cm, EFW 50th centile. Placenta is fundal. She has been counselled about VBAC versus elective caesarean and asks for your advice.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 78, BP 118/72 mmHg, RR 14, SpO2 100%, temperature 36.6 °C, fetal HR 142 bpm
data_table.Examination: Fundal height 32 cm, cephalic presentation, no scar tenderness
data_table.Investigations: Ultrasound at 32 weeks: fundal anterior placenta, AFI 14 cm, EFW 50th centile, fetal Dopplers normal

lead_in: Which feature is the strongest absolute contraindication to attempting VBAC?

options.text: Estimated fetal weight on the 50th centile at 32 weeks gestation review today
options.rationale: A normally grown fetus is not a contraindication to VBAC; macrosomia (>4 kg estimated) is a relative concern but not absolute. (Source: RANZCOG Birth After Previous Caesarean Section Statement 2023)
source_refs: RANZCOG Birth After Previous Caesarean Section Statement 2023

options.text: Maternal age 34 with a body mass index of 28 kg/m^2 at booking visit
options.rationale: Maternal age and overweight BMI modestly reduce VBAC success rates but neither is an absolute contraindication to attempted vaginal birth after caesarean. (Source: RANZCOG Birth After Previous Caesarean Section Statement 2023)
source_refs: RANZCOG Birth After Previous Caesarean Section Statement 2023

options.text: A single previous lower-segment caesarean section in the immediately prior pregnancy
options.rationale: A single previous LSCS is the standard indication for VBAC counselling and is not a contraindication; success rates are 60-80% with no upper-segment scar. (Source: RANZCOG Birth After Previous Caesarean Section Statement 2023)
source_refs: RANZCOG Birth After Previous Caesarean Section Statement 2023

options.text: Previous classical (vertical) uterine incision documented in the operation note
options.rationale: RANZCOG lists previous classical or T-shaped uterine incision as an absolute contraindication because the upper-segment myometrium has a uterine-rupture risk of 4-9% in labour. (Source: RANZCOG Birth After Previous Caesarean Section Statement 2023)
source_refs: RANZCOG Birth After Previous Caesarean Section Statement 2023

options.text: Past medical history of severe early-onset pre-eclampsia in the first pregnancy
options.rationale: Previous pre-eclampsia is an indication for aspirin and surveillance in this pregnancy but is not by itself a contraindication to attempting VBAC in a low-risk uncomplicated current pregnancy. (Source: RANZCOG Birth After Previous Caesarean Section Statement 2023)
source_refs: RANZCOG Birth After Previous Caesarean Section Statement 2023

explanation.summary: Vaginal birth after caesarean is recommended in suitable candidates because of lower morbidity than repeat caesarean, but it requires a low-segment scar in the prior surgery. Absolute contraindications include previous classical or T-shaped (upper-segment) incision, previous uterine rupture, more than two prior caesareans, placenta praevia or vasa praevia, and any other contraindication to vaginal birth. Relative factors that lower success include higher BMI, advanced maternal age, induction with prostaglandins, and short interpregnancy interval. Counselling must include uterine rupture risk of approximately 0.5% with one prior LSCS.
key_points: Absolute contraindications: classical/T incision, prior rupture, >2 caesareans, praevia/vasa praevia.
Single previous LSCS: VBAC offered with informed counselling; success 60-80%.
Uterine rupture risk with one prior LSCS ~0.5%.
Prostaglandin induction increases rupture risk; mechanical methods preferred.
explanation.pearls: RANZCOG: previous classical or T-shaped uterine incision is an absolute VBAC contraindication; rupture risk 4-9% versus ~0.5% with low-segment scar.

sources.label: RANZCOG Birth After Previous Caesarean Section Statement 2023
NHMRC Mode of birth after caesarean

stem:
A 32-year-old G3P2 at 40+2 weeks is brought into the birth suite by ambulance with spontaneous rupture of membranes 30 minutes ago. Her previous two pregnancies were uncomplicated vaginal deliveries. She declined external cephalic version at 37 weeks because she was not comfortable with the procedure. Her last ultrasound at 38 weeks showed a footling breech.

On arrival vaginal examination reveals 4 cm dilated cervix with a foot palpable below the cord and no cord prolapse identified. CTG is reassuring at baseline 140 bpm. The on-call obstetrician and paediatric team are present.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 92, BP 122/76 mmHg, RR 18, SpO2 99%, temperature 36.6 °C, fetal HR 140 bpm
data_table.Examination: Cervix 4 cm dilated, footling breech with right foot palpable through cervix, no cord prolapse, contractions every 4 minutes
data_table.Investigations: Bedside ultrasound confirms footling breech, EFW 3.6 kg, AFI 6 cm post-SROM, no nuchal cord visualised

lead_in: What is the most appropriate management?

options.text: Induction of labour with augmentation by oxytocin and continuous fetal monitoring
options.rationale: Augmenting a footling breech increases cord prolapse and uterine hyperstimulation risk and does not solve the underlying contraindication to vaginal breech birth. (Source: RANZCOG Breech Presentation at Term Statement 2022)
source_refs: RANZCOG Breech Presentation at Term Statement 2022

options.text: Vaginal breech delivery with epidural analgesia and experienced obstetric assistance
options.rationale: Vaginal breech delivery has acceptable outcomes for selected frank or complete breech with strict criteria; footling breech is specifically excluded because of cord prolapse and head entrapment risk. (Source: RANZCOG Breech Presentation at Term Statement 2022)
source_refs: RANZCOG Breech Presentation at Term Statement 2022

options.text: Emergency caesarean section as soon as the operating theatre is available
options.rationale: RANZCOG and the Term Breech Trial findings make planned caesarean the safer route for footling breech in particular because of much higher cord prolapse and head entrapment risk than frank or complete breech. (Source: RANZCOG Breech Presentation at Term Statement 2022)
source_refs: RANZCOG Breech Presentation at Term Statement 2022

options.text: External cephalic version now under bedside ultrasound guidance after SROM
options.rationale: ECV is contraindicated after spontaneous rupture of membranes due to reduced amniotic fluid and increased risk of cord prolapse and abruption during the manipulation. (Source: RANZCOG Breech Presentation at Term Statement 2022)
source_refs: RANZCOG Breech Presentation at Term Statement 2022

options.text: Internal podalic version with breech extraction by the on-call obstetric registrar
options.rationale: Internal podalic version is reserved for the second twin with non-cephalic presentation in a planned vaginal birth; it has no role in a singleton footling breech in active labour. (Source: RANZCOG Breech Presentation at Term Statement 2022)
source_refs: RANZCOG Breech Presentation at Term Statement 2022

explanation.summary: Footling breech presentation in singleton pregnancies at term carries higher risk than frank or complete breech because of cord prolapse with each contraction and trapped after-coming head when only one or two limbs lead. Even centres that still offer planned vaginal breech birth for selected frank or complete breeches exclude footling breech. After SROM with the cord at risk, the operative pathway is rapid caesarean section. ECV is contraindicated once membranes are ruptured. Internal podalic version belongs to second-twin delivery, not singleton breech at term.
key_points: Footling breech is an absolute exclusion from planned vaginal breech birth.
Cord prolapse risk is high enough that delivery should be expedited.
ECV is contraindicated after SROM.
Internal podalic version is a second-twin manoeuvre, not singleton.
explanation.pearls: Footling breech with SROM = emergency caesarean; cord prolapse and head entrapment risk excludes vaginal breech in this subtype.

sources.label: RANZCOG Breech Presentation at Term Statement 2022

subtopic_detail: Refractory primary PPH escalation - mechanical tamponade vs surgical
stem:
A 32-year-old G3P3 woman has delivered a live male infant by spontaneous vaginal birth. She had a precipitate second stage. Within 15 minutes of delivery she has had brisk ongoing bleeding from the genital tract. She has already received: oxytocin 10 IU IM, ergometrine 250 micrograms IM, oxytocin infusion 40 IU in 1000 mL Hartmann's at 250 mL/hour, tranexamic acid 1 g IV, and bimanual uterine compression for 10 minutes.

Vaginal and perineal lacerations have been sutured. The placenta is intact on examination. Estimated blood loss is now 1500 mL. She has no known medical conditions, no anticoagulants, no pre-eclampsia, and her blood pressure is currently stable on a unit of packed red cells running.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 124, BP 96/62 mmHg, RR 22, SpO2 98% on 4 L/min, temperature 36.6 °C
data_table.Examination: Uterus boggy and soft despite uterotonics, ongoing brisk red bleeding per vagina, no expanding haematoma, perineum repaired and dry
data_table.Investigations: Hb 86 g/L (115-160), platelets 154 x10^9/L (150-400), fibrinogen 2.4 g/L (2.0-4.5), APTT and INR within normal limits, fibrinogen falling on serial samples
data_table.Medications: Oxytocin infusion, tranexamic acid given, one unit packed red cells running

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step?

options.text: Insert a Bakri intrauterine balloon and inflate to tamponade while preparing theatre
options.rationale: RANZCOG escalation for atonic PPH refractory to medical uterotonics (oxytocin, ergometrine, prostaglandin) and TXA is mechanical tamponade with a Bakri balloon while theatre is prepared. Balloon tamponade controls bleeding in about 85% of cases and buys time for surgical options if needed. B-Lynch and hysterectomy are surgical options reserved for tamponade failure. (Source: RANZCOG: Postpartum Haemorrhage)

options.text: Transfer to interventional radiology for uterine artery embolisation now
options.rationale: Uterine artery embolisation is an option only in haemodynamically stable patients where IR is immediately available and other measures have failed. With ongoing brisk bleeding and falling fibrinogen, tamponade and proceeding to theatre is faster than IR mobilisation. MTP activation may also be appropriate but is not the next surgical step. (Source: RANZCOG: Postpartum Haemorrhage)

options.text: Repeat ergometrine 250 micrograms intramuscularly with monitoring of blood pressure
options.rationale: Maximum total ergometrine dose is 500 micrograms in 24 hours; she has already had 250 micrograms so one further dose is technically allowed but unlikely to resolve a refractory atonic PPH and delays the next-line mechanical step. (Source: RANZCOG: Postpartum Haemorrhage)

options.text: Proceed straight to B-Lynch compression suture under anaesthesia in theatre
options.rationale: B-Lynch is the next surgical step if mechanical tamponade fails or in patients already having a laparotomy; jumping to laparotomy when balloon tamponade has not been tried bypasses a less invasive intervention that resolves the majority of cases. (Source: RANZCOG: Postpartum Haemorrhage)

options.text: Give intramuscular carboprost 250 micrograms and repeat once in 15 minutes
options.rationale: Carboprost is the next-line uterotonic when oxytocin and ergometrine fail, but with brisk ongoing bleeding past 1500 mL and continuing atony despite oxytocin and ergometrine and TXA, escalation to mechanical tamponade is the appropriate parallel step rather than further pharmacological delays. Carboprost remains an adjunct. (Source: RANZCOG: Postpartum Haemorrhage)

explanation.summary: RANZCOG PPH algorithm: medical uterotonics (oxytocin, ergometrine, carboprost or misoprostol) plus TXA first; then mechanical (bimanual compression, Bakri balloon); then surgical (B-Lynch, uterine artery ligation, internal iliac artery ligation, hysterectomy). IR embolisation is an option in stable patients with immediate access.
key_points: Bakri balloon controls atonic PPH in about 85% of cases as the bridge between medical and surgical management
Maximum 24-hour ergometrine dose is 500 micrograms (two doses)
Carboprost contraindicated in asthma; misoprostol 800 micrograms PR is the asthma alternative
explanation.pearls: Activate MTP early when blood loss exceeds 1500 mL with ongoing bleeding or fibrinogen falling below 2 g/L. RANZCOG includes a structured 4Ts mnemonic (tone, trauma, tissue, thrombin) - check that perineal and cervical tears have been completely repaired and that no retained placental tissue is missed.

subtopic_detail: Tubal ectopic with prior contralateral salpingectomy - surgical choice
stem:
A 31-year-old G3P1 woman, last menstrual period 7 weeks 2 days ago, presents with right iliac fossa pain and a small amount of dark vaginal spotting. She had a left tubal ectopic pregnancy 2 years ago treated by laparoscopic salpingectomy. She has been trying to conceive for the past 12 months and this is her first positive pregnancy test since the salpingectomy. She had a postpartum tubal contralateral preservation note in her previous operative report.

Her obstetric team has reviewed her. The on-call gynaecology consultant has had a detailed antenatal discussion of the choices with her partner and her present.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 86, BP 118/74 mmHg, RR 16, SpO2 99% in room air, temperature 36.7 °C
data_table.Examination: Soft abdomen with mild right iliac fossa tenderness, no peritonism, no rebound, cervical os closed
data_table.Investigations: Beta-hCG 4200 IU/L, transvaginal ultrasound shows a 28 mm right tubal mass with no fetal cardiac activity, no free fluid in the pouch of Douglas, empty uterus, the left adnexa shows surgical absence of the tube as expected, anti-D negative

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step?

options.text: Laparoscopic right salpingostomy with conservation of the tube
options.rationale: Salpingostomy in the standard case preserves fertility but in a woman with a prior contralateral salpingectomy this tube is her only remaining tube and recurrent ipsilateral ectopic in that same tube is the dominant risk. The benefit-risk balance flips - AU practice favours salpingectomy and IVF over a high-risk single retained tube. (Source: RANZCOG: Tubal Ectopic Pregnancy)

options.text: Laparoscopic right salpingectomy with planning for future IVF
options.rationale: Standard teaching is that salpingostomy preserves fertility in women with one tube; however when the contralateral tube is already absent (prior salpingectomy), the affected tube is the only remaining tube and the risk of recurrent ipsilateral ectopic in that same tube after salpingostomy is dominant. AU practice favours salpingectomy in this T14-lever scenario because future fertility is best served by IVF rather than carrying ipsilateral recurrence risk in a single tube. (Source: RANZCOG: Tubal Ectopic Pregnancy)

options.text: Methotrexate 50 mg/m^2 intramuscularly with weekly serial beta-hCG
options.rationale: RANZCOG methotrexate criteria require beta-hCG under 5000 IU/L AND mass under 3.5 cm AND no fetal cardiac activity AND no significant pain AND reliable follow-up AND no contraindications. She meets the laboratory threshold but has ongoing pain, which is a relative contraindication, and the surgical option is decisive. (Source: RANZCOG: Tubal Ectopic Pregnancy)

options.text: Expectant management with serial beta-hCG every 48 hours
options.rationale: Expectant management requires a falling beta-hCG (usually below 1500 to 2000 IU/L) and a small asymptomatic ectopic. This patient has a 4200 IU/L beta-hCG with a 28 mm mass and active pain, none of which qualify her for expectant management. (Source: RANZCOG: Tubal Ectopic Pregnancy)

options.text: Laparotomy and total abdominal hysterectomy with right salpingectomy
options.rationale: Hysterectomy is a destructive option reserved for life-threatening haemorrhage from a ruptured cornual ectopic that cannot be controlled by lesser measures; the patient is haemodynamically stable with no free fluid and laparoscopy is appropriate. (Source: RANZCOG: Tubal Ectopic Pregnancy)

explanation.summary: Standard teaching that salpingostomy preserves fertility in women with one functional tube flips in patients with a prior contralateral salpingectomy: the affected tube is the only remaining tube and ipsilateral recurrence risk dominates. AU practice favours salpingectomy and IVF over a high-risk retained tube. This is the historical-bilaterality flip (T14 lever).
key_points: Salpingostomy is preferred for tubal ectopic in patients with a normal contralateral tube
When the contralateral tube is absent, salpingectomy is preferred because ipsilateral recurrence risk dominates
Methotrexate threshold for surgical management is beta-hCG ≥5000 IU/L (RANZCOG)
explanation.pearls: Anti-D 250 IU prophylaxis required for Rh-negative women with ectopic pregnancy. Methotrexate criteria are stringent: bhCG <5000, mass <3.5 cm, no fetal heart, no significant pain, no haemorrhage, reliable follow-up. The decision tree benefits from a documented antenatal discussion before theatre.

subtopic_detail: HELLP syndrome with thrombocytopenia - delivery and anaesthesia decision
stem:
A 28-year-old G2P0 woman at 34 weeks 2 days presents with a 2-day history of right upper quadrant pain. She has known pre-eclampsia treated with oral labetalol 200 mg three times daily since 32 weeks. Magnesium sulfate was loaded 1 hour ago and a maintenance infusion at 1 g/hour is running. Fetal heart rate is normal with reactive CTG.

Decision-to-deliver has been made and platelet count has dropped on serial samples over the last 6 hours. The on-call anaesthetic registrar has been called and the consultant obstetrician is in the unit.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 102, BP 165/110 mmHg, RR 18, SpO2 98% in room air, temperature 36.8 °C, fetal HR 145 reactive
data_table.Examination: Right upper quadrant tender to palpation, hyperreflexic with 3 beats of clonus, no scotomata reported
data_table.Investigations: Hb 102 g/L (115-160), platelets 64 x10^9/L (150-400, was 110 four hours ago), LDH 820 U/L (<280), AST 240 U/L (<35), ALT 198 U/L (<35), bilirubin 38 micromol/L (<20), INR 1.0, fibrinogen 3.4 g/L (2.0-4.5), uric acid 0.46 mmol/L (<0.36), urinalysis protein 3+
data_table.Medications: Labetalol 200 mg PO TDS, magnesium sulfate infusion 1 g/hour

lead_in: What is the most appropriate anaesthetic and delivery plan?

options.text: Continue expectant management at 34 weeks with daily inpatient monitoring
options.rationale: Once HELLP is established with downtrending platelets, RUQ pain, and rising LFTs, delivery is the only definitive treatment. Expectant management between 34 and 37 weeks risks placental abruption, eclampsia, hepatic capsular rupture, and DIC. (Source: SOMANZ: Hypertension in Pregnancy)

options.text: Administer high-dose intravenous dexamethasone to delay delivery for 48 hours
options.rationale: Antenatal corticosteroids for fetal lung maturity below 34 weeks may be given but they do not reverse maternal HELLP. At 34 weeks 2 days the fetus is past the steroid-benefit window and the mother's worsening HELLP requires immediate delivery, not delay. (Source: SOMANZ: Hypertension in Pregnancy)

options.text: Augment labour for vaginal delivery under epidural analgesia today
options.rationale: Epidural placement at platelet 64 with downtrending kinetics raises epidural haematoma risk; vaginal delivery may also take long enough that progression to lower counts intra-partum becomes more likely. (Source: SOMANZ: Hypertension in Pregnancy)

options.text: Proceed to category 2 caesarean section under general anaesthesia urgently
options.rationale: Platelet count of 64 x10^9/L with a downtrending trajectory (110 to 64 in 4 hours) is the kinetic warning that platelets may be below the regional anaesthesia threshold by the time the needle is placed. ANZCA / RANZCOG guidance uses a 70 to 80 x10^9/L static cut-off for neuraxial in obstetrics, with a strong caveat against placing a block in a downtrending count. General anaesthesia avoids the epidural haematoma risk in this trajectory. (Source: SOMANZ: Hypertension in Pregnancy)

options.text: Caesarean under spinal anaesthesia after platelet transfusion to above 100
options.rationale: Platelet transfusion to lift the count above 100 takes time, may be ineffective in HELLP (consumption is ongoing), and exposes her to transfusion reactions in a setting where regional may still not be safe due to platelet dysfunction beyond the number. AU current consensus is that GA is the safer pathway with a downtrending count. (Source: SOMANZ: Hypertension in Pregnancy)

explanation.summary: HELLP at 34 weeks with downtrending platelets and active maternal end-organ involvement mandates delivery. AU consensus uses a platelet count of 70 to 80 x10^9/L as the static threshold for neuraxial anaesthesia in obstetrics; a downtrending kinetic count is a stronger contraindication than a stable one above that threshold. General anaesthesia is the safer pathway in that scenario.
key_points: HELLP with downtrending platelets to under 80 x10^9/L is a contraindication to neuraxial - GA is preferred
Delivery is the only definitive treatment for HELLP
Magnesium sulfate prophylaxis against eclampsia is continued during and 24 hours after delivery
explanation.pearls: Hepatic capsular rupture is a rare but catastrophic HELLP complication suggested by hypotension and rising abdominal pain post-delivery; CT and emergency hepatic packing may be needed. Magnesium sulfate is continued 24 hours postpartum because eclampsia can occur in that window.

subtopic_detail: Twin-twin transfusion syndrome Quintero staging - laser timing
stem:
A 27-year-old G1P0 woman with a monochorionic-diamniotic twin pregnancy at 19 weeks 4 days is referred from her local fetal medicine unit. The amniotic fluid volume has changed rapidly over the last 2 weeks. She has been previously well.

The maternal fetal medicine consultant has reviewed the ultrasound and the staging discussion has just concluded. Both fetuses appear structurally normal.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 78, BP 116/72 mmHg, RR 16, SpO2 99% in room air, temperature 36.7 °C, fetal heart rates both reactive
data_table.Examination: Soft non-tender uterus consistent with 24 weeks size, no contractions, cervical length 32 mm
data_table.Investigations: Monochorionic-diamniotic twins. Twin 1 (donor): deepest vertical pocket 1.4 cm, empty bladder, umbilical artery Doppler with persistent absent end-diastolic flow. Twin 2 (recipient): deepest vertical pocket 10.4 cm, visible distended bladder, normal umbilical artery Doppler, normal ductus venosus a-wave, no hydrops

lead_in: What is the most appropriate management?

options.text: Maternal sildenafil 20 mg three times daily to improve uteroplacental flow
options.rationale: Sildenafil for fetal growth restriction has been withdrawn from trials after concerns about neonatal pulmonary hypertension (Dutch STRIDER trial). It has no role in TTTS. (Source: RANZCOG: Twin and Multiple Pregnancy)

options.text: Selective fetal reduction of the donor twin by radiofrequency ablation
options.rationale: Selective fetal reduction is reserved for severe TTTS with a structurally abnormal twin or unfavourable laser anatomy, or for severe selective intrauterine growth restriction. With both fetuses structurally normal and stable, laser is the standard. (Source: RANZCOG: Twin and Multiple Pregnancy)

options.text: Fetoscopic laser photocoagulation of placental anastomoses
options.rationale: Twin-twin transfusion syndrome staged at Quintero 3 (donor with absent or reversed umbilical end-diastolic flow OR recipient with absent or reversed ductus venosus a-wave) and presenting between 16 and 26 weeks is best managed by fetoscopic laser ablation of placental anastomoses (eg Solomon technique). Laser is the only treatment that addresses the pathophysiology and is supported by AU fetal medicine centres for TTTS at Quintero stage 2 or above. (Source: RANZCOG: Twin and Multiple Pregnancy)

options.text: Serial amnioreduction every 1 to 2 weeks until viability is reached
options.rationale: Amnioreduction reduces maternal symptoms and preterm labour from polyhydramnios but does not address the underlying vascular anastomoses; the Eurofetus randomised trial showed laser has substantially better dual-survival and neurological outcomes than amnioreduction for Quintero ≥2. Amnioreduction is reserved for centres without laser access or after laser. (Source: RANZCOG: Twin and Multiple Pregnancy)

options.text: Conservative observation with weekly Doppler velocimetry studies
options.rationale: Quintero stage 3 has an untreated mortality above 70 to 90% without intervention; conservative observation is not appropriate. (Source: RANZCOG: Twin and Multiple Pregnancy)

explanation.summary: Twin-twin transfusion syndrome is staged by Quintero criteria: stage 1 oligohydramnios in donor + polyhydramnios in recipient; stage 2 absent donor bladder; stage 3 abnormal Dopplers (donor UA AEDF or recipient DV a-wave reversal); stage 4 hydrops; stage 5 demise. Quintero stage 2 or above between 16 and 26 weeks should be referred for fetoscopic laser.
key_points: Fetoscopic laser is first-line for TTTS Quintero 2 or above between 16 and 26 weeks
Amnioreduction is symptomatic and reserved for centres without laser or as adjunct
Sildenafil has no role and was associated with neonatal pulmonary hypertension in STRIDER
explanation.pearls: After laser, twins are monitored weekly with biometry and Dopplers for the recurrence of TTTS or twin anaemia-polycythaemia sequence (TAPS), now reduced by the Solomon laser technique (equator-to-equator dichorionisation).

subtopic_detail: HELLP syndrome and timing of delivery
stem:
A 28-year-old G2P1 woman at 32+3 weeks gestation is admitted to the high-risk obstetrics ward with right upper quadrant pain and headache. Her previous pregnancy was uncomplicated. She has no chronic hypertension. Her booking BP was 110/70 mmHg. She had no prior obstetric admissions this pregnancy. She received antenatal corticosteroids (betamethasone) for fetal lung maturity 14 hours ago after her platelet count began to fall.

Over the last 6 hours her platelets have dropped further despite stable BP control with oral labetalol. She remains alert and oriented. Cardiotocograph shows a reassuring trace.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 92, BP 146/94 mmHg (on labetalol), RR 18, SpO2 99% in room air, temperature 36.8 °C, fetal heart rate 145 bpm with reactive trace
data_table.Examination: Right upper quadrant tenderness without peritonism, 3+ proteinuria on dipstick, no clonus, normal reflexes, no facial oedema
data_table.Investigations: Platelets 62 x10^9/L (down from 95 6 hours ago, baseline 220), AST 320 U/L (<35), ALT 280 U/L (<35), LDH 820 U/L (<250), haemoglobin 96 g/L with schistocytes on film, creatinine 92 micromol/L (45-90), urate 0.42 mmol/L (<0.36), urine PCR 580 mg/mmol
data_table.Medications: Labetalol 200 mg PO TDS, magnesium sulfate IV (loading 4 g + 1 g/hour maintenance), betamethasone 11.4 mg IM doses x 2 (last dose 14 hours ago)

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step?

options.text: Continue expectant management with daily bloods until 34 weeks then plan delivery
options.rationale: Falling platelets with HELLP criteria met is not stable disease - it is HELLP syndrome with progression. Expectant management beyond 48 hours after steroid completion is not justified in HELLP because of risks of placental abruption, hepatic haematoma rupture, DIC and maternal death. RANZCOG and the SOMANZ pre-eclampsia guideline recommend delivery once HELLP is established and the steroid window is complete or near complete. (Source: RANZCOG Statements)

options.text: Increase the labetalol dose and continue magnesium sulfate, review at 12 hours
options.rationale: Antihypertensive intensification and seizure prophylaxis do not address the underlying disease. HELLP at 32 weeks with progressive thrombocytopenia and after a completed steroid course requires planned delivery. (Source: RANZCOG Statements)

options.text: Transfuse a single adult dose of platelets and continue expectant management
options.rationale: Platelet transfusion is only indicated for active bleeding or before regional anaesthesia/operative delivery with platelets below 50 x10^9/L. Prophylactic transfusion to continue expectancy does not change the natural history of HELLP. (Source: RANZCOG Statements)

options.text: Commence intravenous heparin for presumed HELLP thrombotic microangiopathy
options.rationale: Heparin is not used for HELLP. The condition is a placental disorder of pre-eclamptic origin, not a primary thrombotic microangiopathy like TTP/aHUS; the treatment is delivery, not anticoagulation. (Source: RANZCOG Statements)

options.text: Plan delivery within 6 to 12 hours by the most appropriate route after steroids
options.rationale: HELLP at 32+ weeks with completed antenatal corticosteroid course (last dose at least 12 to 24 hours ago) and progressive disease (platelets dropping from 95 to 62) is an indication for delivery. Corticosteroids do NOT reverse HELLP - they improve neonatal lung outcome and a brief window (up to 48 hours after steroid completion) may be permitted if stable, but progressive thrombocytopenia disqualifies further delay. Mode of delivery is dictated by Bishop score, fetal status and platelet count for regional anaesthesia. Magnesium continues until 24 hours postpartum. (Source: RANZCOG Statements)

explanation.summary: HELLP syndrome (haemolysis, elevated liver enzymes, low platelets) at any gestation above 34 weeks mandates delivery. Between 24 and 34 weeks, antenatal corticosteroids are given and delivery planned once the steroid window is maximised (typically 24 to 48 hours), with earlier delivery if disease progresses or maternal status deteriorates. Continue magnesium for 24 hours postpartum. Platelet transfusion only for active bleeding or imminent operative/regional anaesthesia.
key_points: HELLP at 34 weeks or more: immediate delivery
HELLP at 24-34 weeks: steroids then delivery within 24-48 hours, sooner if progressive
Magnesium continues 24 hours postpartum
explanation.pearls: A subcapsular hepatic haematoma is a life-threatening HELLP complication; sudden worsening of right-upper-quadrant pain with hypotension requires urgent CT or focused ultrasound and may need interventional radiology embolisation or surgery.

stem:
A 31-year-old G2P1 woman at 19+5 weeks gestation with a monochorionic-diamniotic twin pregnancy is referred to a tertiary fetal medicine centre after her routine fortnightly ultrasound. Her previous pregnancy was a term singleton delivery. She has no chronic medical conditions. First-trimester combined screening showed both fetuses with normal nuchal translucency and chorionicity confirmed as monochorionic-diamniotic at 12 weeks.

She has noticed increased abdominal girth over the past week. The fetal medicine consultant has reviewed her in clinic.

data_table.Vital signs: Within normal limits
data_table.Examination: Uterus equivalent to 26 weeks size, soft, no contractions
data_table.Investigations: Ultrasound deepest vertical pocket of donor twin 1.2 cm (oligohydramnios less than 2 cm), deepest vertical pocket of recipient twin 9.4 cm (polyhydramnios greater than 8 cm); donor bladder visible; both fetuses with normal Doppler waveforms in umbilical arteries, middle cerebral arteries and ductus venosus; no hydrops in either twin; estimated fetal weight discordance 18%

lead_in: What is the most appropriate management?

options.text: Refer for fetoscopic laser photocoagulation of placental anastomoses
options.rationale: This is Quintero stage 2 twin-to-twin transfusion syndrome (oligohydramnios in donor with non-visible bladder threshold not yet crossed - actually donor bladder remains visible, so this is stage 1 to 2 transition; with oligo+poly criteria met it qualifies as stage 1 minimum and progresses readily). Fetoscopic laser photocoagulation of placental anastomoses (Solomon technique) is the standard of care for stage 2 and above before 26 weeks gestation and is now recommended in selected stage 1 cases with progression. Eurofetus and other trials show improved perinatal survival compared with amnioreduction. (Source: RANZCOG Statements)

options.text: Serial amnioreduction every 1 to 2 weeks until fetal lung maturity
options.rationale: Amnioreduction temporises symptoms in the recipient but does not address the underlying vascular communications and is inferior to laser photocoagulation in published trials (Eurofetus). It is reserved for laser-unsuitable anatomy or post-26-week disease. (Source: RANZCOG Statements)

options.text: Selective fetocide of the donor twin by bipolar cord coagulation
options.rationale: Selective reduction is reserved for severe discordant anomaly, imminent demise of one twin, or salvage when laser has failed. It is not first-line for TTTS at this stage when both fetuses are viable. (Source: RANZCOG Statements)

options.text: Continue fortnightly ultrasound surveillance with no intervention
options.rationale: Surveillance without intervention in established TTTS (poly-oligo sequence with DVPs at the criteria) carries a survival rate as low as 10 to 20% without treatment. Intervention is needed once Quintero stage 1 is established with progression risk. (Source: RANZCOG Statements)

options.text: Plan elective delivery by classical caesarean section at 28 weeks
options.rationale: Delivery at 19 weeks is not viable. Once a viable gestation is reached, delivery may be considered for non-laser-amenable progression but is not the management at 19 weeks. (Source: RANZCOG Statements)

explanation.summary: TTTS arises from unbalanced placental vascular anastomoses in monochorionic-diamniotic twins. Quintero staging: I poly-oligo only, II donor bladder not visible, III abnormal Dopplers (umbilical AEDV/REDV, ductus venosus reversed a-wave), IV hydrops, V demise. Fetoscopic laser is first-line for stage 2 to 4 before 26 weeks (Solomon technique includes equator dichorionisation). Amnioreduction is salvage or for laser-unsuitable cases. Survival without treatment in stage 2 to 3 is 10 to 20%; with laser, dual survival 60 to 70%.
key_points: Quintero staging: I poly-oligo, II donor bladder absent, III Doppler abnormal, IV hydrops, V demise
Fetoscopic laser first-line for stage 2+ before 26 weeks (Solomon technique)
Amnioreduction is salvage, not first-line
explanation.pearls: Always confirm chorionicity in the first trimester (lambda vs T sign); a monochorionic pregnancy needs fortnightly ultrasound from 16 weeks for early TTTS or TAPS detection.

stem:
A 33-year-old G2P0 woman at 32 weeks gestation is referred to a tertiary fetal medicine unit after her morphology scan and follow-up imaging. She conceived via IVF with a fresh embryo transfer. Her first pregnancy ended in a missed miscarriage at 9 weeks. The 20-week morphology scan reported a low-lying placenta with a succenturiate lobe; a follow-up transvaginal scan at 30 weeks confirmed a velamentous cord insertion with a fetal vessel running across the internal cervical os.

She is asymptomatic with no bleeding and good fetal movements. The maternal-fetal medicine consultant has reviewed her in clinic.

data_table.Vital signs: Within normal limits
data_table.Examination: Soft non-tender abdomen, no uterine activity, fundal height 30 cm, cervix long and closed on transabdominal assessment
data_table.Investigations: Transvaginal ultrasound with colour Doppler confirms a fetal vessel crossing the internal cervical os within 2 cm; placenta no longer praevia (lower edge 4 cm from internal os); estimated fetal weight 50th centile; reactive CTG; FBC, group and hold normal

lead_in: What is the most appropriate plan?

options.text: Continue routine antenatal care with delivery at 39 weeks unless labour intervenes
options.rationale: Routine term delivery exposes the fetus to a high risk of vessel rupture once cervical change begins. Vasa praevia carries a 60% fetal mortality if undiagnosed and ruptures, falling to less than 3% with planned prelabour caesarean. (Source: RANZCOG Statements)

options.text: Inpatient admission 30-32 weeks with steroids and elective caesarean 34 to 36 weeks
options.rationale: RANZCOG recommends inpatient admission from around 30 to 32 weeks, antenatal corticosteroids before 34+6 weeks for fetal lung maturity, and elective caesarean section at 34 to 36 weeks gestation. Inpatient admission allows immediate caesarean if labour or membrane rupture occurs. The trade-off is small prematurity-related morbidity versus catastrophic fetal exsanguination from ruptured fetal vessels. (Source: RANZCOG Statements)

options.text: Plan elective caesarean at 39 weeks with cross-matched blood and neonatal team
options.rationale: Vasa praevia is at substantial risk of vessel rupture before 39 weeks (especially with cervical shortening or early labour). Delivery is brought forward to 34 to 36 weeks to balance prematurity against rupture risk. (Source: RANZCOG Statements)

options.text: Perform an emergency caesarean today because vasa praevia is now confirmed on ultrasound
options.rationale: There is no emergency indication. Antenatal corticosteroids and planned delivery at 34 to 36 weeks offers better neonatal outcomes than immediate delivery at 32 weeks. (Source: RANZCOG Statements)

options.text: Outpatient weekly cervical length monitoring with planned vaginal delivery anyway
options.rationale: Vasa praevia is an absolute indication for caesarean section irrespective of cervical length, because rupture of the fetal vessel during labour kills the fetus rapidly. (Source: RANZCOG Statements)

explanation.summary: Vasa praevia is unprotected fetal vessels traversing membranes within 2 cm of the internal cervical os, typically from velamentous cord insertion or a succenturiate placental lobe. Diagnosis is by transvaginal ultrasound with colour Doppler. Management: inpatient admission from 30 to 32 weeks, antenatal corticosteroids before 34+6 weeks, planned caesarean at 34 to 36 weeks. Undiagnosed vasa praevia has 60% fetal mortality with vessel rupture; with planned delivery it falls to under 3%.
key_points: Inpatient admission 30-32 weeks for monitoring
Antenatal corticosteroids before 34+6 weeks
Elective caesarean 34-36 weeks (not 39)
explanation.pearls: IVF and second-trimester low-lying placenta are risk factors for vasa praevia - always evaluate cord insertion with colour Doppler in these patients at the morphology scan.

stem:
A 24-year-old G1P0 woman at 35 weeks gestation presents to the birth suite by ambulance with headache and visual flashing. Her booking blood pressure was 110/68 mmHg. She has had two BP readings at home of 165/108 and 168/110 mmHg this morning. She has had no proteinuria at previous antenatal visits. She has no chronic hypertension or other comorbidities. Her partner is with her.

On arrival she is anxious but oriented. The obstetric registrar is at the bedside and intravenous access has been established.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 96, BP 168/112 mmHg, RR 18, SpO2 99% in room air, temperature 36.7 °C, fetal heart rate 140 bpm reactive
data_table.Examination: 3+ proteinuria on dipstick, brisk reflexes with 2 beats of clonus, no facial oedema, no abdominal tenderness, CTG reassuring
data_table.Investigations: FBC haemoglobin 124 g/L, platelets 188 x10^9/L (150-400), AST 32 U/L (<35), ALT 28 U/L (<35), creatinine 78 micromol/L (45-90), urate 0.38 mmol/L (<0.36), urine PCR 220 mg/mmol

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step for acute blood pressure control?

options.text: Oral nifedipine immediate-release 20 mg given by the sublingual route as crisis dose
options.rationale: Sublingual nifedipine is contraindicated in pregnancy because of rapid uncontrolled BP drop and risk of placental hypoperfusion. Oral immediate-release nifedipine 10 mg by swallowed dose is acceptable but sublingual is not. (Source: RANZCOG Statements)

options.text: Intravenous magnesium sulfate 4 g bolus then 1 g per hour as the primary BP agent
options.rationale: Magnesium is for seizure prophylaxis, not blood pressure control. It should be started concurrently in severe pre-eclampsia with neurological symptoms but does not replace an antihypertensive. (Source: RANZCOG Statements)

options.text: Intravenous labetalol 20 mg bolus with repeat doses to a maximum 220 mg cumulative
options.rationale: Severe hypertension in pregnancy (BP at or above 160/110 mmHg sustained) is a hypertensive emergency requiring acute BP lowering within 15 to 60 minutes. IV labetalol 20 mg bolus, repeated at 10-minute intervals with escalating doses (40 mg, then 80 mg) to a maximum cumulative 220 mg, is first-line in the SOMANZ/RANZCOG pre-eclampsia guideline. Concurrent IV magnesium sulfate for seizure prophylaxis and planning for delivery are also required. Target BP is 140-150/80-100 mmHg to avoid overshooting. (Source: RANZCOG Statements)

options.text: Intravenous nitroprusside infusion titrated to a target BP under 140/90 mmHg
options.rationale: Nitroprusside causes cyanide toxicity in the fetus and is contraindicated in pregnancy. (Source: RANZCOG Statements)

options.text: Oral methyldopa 250 mg three times daily as a maintenance antihypertensive agent
options.rationale: Methyldopa is used for ongoing antihypertensive maintenance in pregnancy but its onset is too slow for acute severe hypertension; it does not control BP in the next 15 to 60 minutes. (Source: RANZCOG Statements)

explanation.summary: Severe hypertension in pregnancy (BP at or above 160/110 mmHg) requires acute BP lowering within 15 to 60 minutes. First-line options in Australian practice: IV labetalol (escalating 20-40-80 mg, max 220 mg cumulative) or oral immediate-release nifedipine 10 mg (swallowed, not sublingual), or IV hydralazine. Target 140-150/80-100 mmHg. Concurrent magnesium sulfate for seizure prophylaxis (4 g IV bolus then 1 g/hour). Plan for delivery after maternal stabilisation.
key_points: First-line acute BP control: IV labetalol, oral nifedipine, IV hydralazine
Sublingual nifedipine and IV nitroprusside contraindicated
Target BP 140-150/80-100, not aggressive normalisation
explanation.pearls: Magnesium does not lower BP but prevents eclamptic seizure; both BP control and seizure prophylaxis run in parallel in severe pre-eclampsia.

stem:
A 34-year-old G3P3 woman has just had a vaginal delivery of her third child following a syntocinon-augmented labour for slow progress. The placenta delivered intact but soon afterwards she developed brisk fresh PV bleeding. Her uterus felt boggy. She is in the birth suite with the obstetric registrar and anaesthetic registrar at the bedside; the obstetric consultant has been called.

Over the last 25 minutes she has received IV syntocinon infusion, ergometrine 250 mcg IM, intramuscular carboprost 250 mcg, tranexamic acid 1 g IV, bimanual compression and a Bakri balloon inflated to 500 mL. She has bled approximately 2200 mL total and continues to bleed around the balloon at about 200 mL every 5 minutes. She has had 4 units of packed cells, 2 units FFP and 1 platelet pool transfused. Her perineal repair is intact. Theatre is being prepared.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 132, BP 92/56 mmHg, RR 26, SpO2 97% on 6 L/min via mask, temperature 36.2 °C
data_table.Examination: Pale, cool peripheries, capillary refill 4 seconds, uterus firm with Bakri balloon in situ, continued PV bleeding around the balloon, no perineal source
data_table.Investigations: Haemoglobin 78 g/L (post-transfusion, baseline 118), platelets 78 x10^9/L (150-400), fibrinogen 1.6 g/L (>2 intrapartum target), INR 1.6, calcium 0.94 mmol/L ionised (1.16-1.32), lactate 4.2; fibrinogen concentrate 2 g being prepared
data_table.Medications: Syntocinon 40 IU/L infusion, ergometrine 250 mcg IM, carboprost 250 mcg IM, tranexamic acid 1 g IV, packed cells x4, FFP x2, platelets x1

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step?

options.text: Repeat carboprost 250 micrograms intramuscularly as the fourth uterotonic dose
options.rationale: Carboprost has a maximum total dose of 2 mg over 24 hours and is given at 15 to 90 minute intervals. Additional doses are unlikely to help once first-line uterotonics have failed and the uterus is firm but bleeding continues - the lesion is likely lower-segment atony or a vascular bleed that pharmacology will not control. (Source: RANZCOG Statements)

options.text: Transfuse an additional 4 units of packed cells before any surgical intervention
options.rationale: Ongoing blood loss requires concurrent transfusion AND definitive haemorrhage control. Delaying surgery for further transfusion alone will not stop the bleeding. Massive transfusion protocol continues alongside surgical management. (Source: RANZCOG Statements)

options.text: Insert a second Bakri balloon transvaginally on top of the existing balloon now
options.rationale: Stacking balloons does not increase tamponade effect and risks misplacement. Once balloon tamponade has failed, escalation to surgical or interventional radiological techniques is required. (Source: RANZCOG Statements)

options.text: Transfer to theatre for examination and surgical haemostasis with IR backup if stable
options.rationale: Refractory PPH after stepwise medical, mechanical and tranexamic acid management requires surgical management. RANZCOG recommends transfer to theatre for examination under anaesthesia to confirm no retained tissue or genital tract trauma, then progression through B-Lynch or modified compression suture, bilateral uterine artery or internal iliac ligation, and ultimately peripartum hysterectomy if bleeding continues. In a haemodynamically borderline patient who can be transported safely, uterine artery embolisation by interventional radiology is also a valid intermediate step; in collapse, proceed directly to hysterectomy. The massive transfusion protocol continues alongside. (Source: RANZCOG Statements)

options.text: Commence intravenous recombinant factor VIIa 90 mcg/kg as an off-label haemostatic
options.rationale: Recombinant factor VIIa is a last-resort adjunct after correction of fibrinogen above 2 g/L, platelets above 50, pH above 7.2 and temperature above 35 °C. It does not replace definitive surgical haemostasis and carries thromboembolic risk. (Source: RANZCOG Statements)

explanation.summary: Refractory PPH after stepwise medical (uterotonics, tranexamic acid) and mechanical (balloon tamponade) management requires surgical or interventional radiological control. Step ladder: B-Lynch or modified compression sutures, bilateral uterine artery ligation, bilateral internal iliac ligation, peripartum hysterectomy. Uterine artery embolisation is a valid alternative in stable patients. Massive transfusion protocol runs in parallel with replacement of fibrinogen (target above 2 g/L), platelets (above 50), and warmed products.
key_points: Refractory PPH after balloon: theatre for surgical haemostasis OR IR for embolisation if stable
Massive transfusion protocol runs in parallel - replace fibrinogen, platelets, warm products
Recombinant factor VIIa is a last-resort adjunct, not first-line
explanation.pearls: If a multiparous woman bleeds around an apparently well-positioned Bakri balloon, suspect lower-segment or cervical source not covered by intrauterine tamponade - examination under anaesthesia is essential before further escalation.

stem:
A 32-year-old G2P1 woman with diet-controlled gestational diabetes is in the second stage of labour at 39+5 weeks. Her previous pregnancy resulted in a 4.4 kg infant delivered vaginally without complications. Estimated fetal weight on a growth scan two weeks ago was 4.3 kg. Her labour has progressed normally and the head has just delivered with the chin pointing toward the maternal left thigh; the head retracts against the perineum.

Routine downward traction has failed to deliver the anterior shoulder. The midwife has called for help and the obstetric registrar is at the bedside.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 96, BP 122/74 mmHg, RR 18, SpO2 99% in room air, temperature 36.8 °C, fetal heart rate decelerating to 90 bpm
data_table.Examination: Head delivered, turtle sign positive, no anterior shoulder descent with maternal effort and routine traction, mother positioned in semi-recumbent
data_table.Investigations: Not applicable - this is an intrapartum emergency

lead_in: What is the most appropriate immediate next step?

options.text: Apply suprapubic pressure and pull harder with fundal pressure to dislodge the shoulder
options.rationale: Fundal pressure is contraindicated in shoulder dystocia because it impacts the anterior shoulder further behind the symphysis pubis and may cause uterine rupture. Suprapubic pressure (Rubin I) is appropriate; fundal pressure is not. (Source: RANZCOG Statements)

options.text: Cut a generous mediolateral episiotomy and continue routine downward traction now
options.rationale: Episiotomy alone does not address the bony obstruction. It may be performed selectively to allow internal manoeuvres, but is not the first step before McRoberts and suprapubic pressure. (Source: RANZCOG Statements)

options.text: Proceed immediately to deliberate clavicular fracture (cleidotomy) as initial step
options.rationale: Deliberate cleidotomy is a last resort after all other manoeuvres including internal rotation, delivery of posterior arm and all-fours position have failed. It is not first-line. (Source: RANZCOG Statements)

options.text: Apply Zavanelli manoeuvre by replacing the head and proceed to emergency caesarean
options.rationale: Zavanelli is a last-resort manoeuvre after all standard interventions have failed. It is not the first response. (Source: RANZCOG Statements)

options.text: Perform McRoberts manoeuvre (hyperflex maternal thighs) with suprapubic pressure
options.rationale: RANZCOG/RCOG follow the HELPERR mnemonic - Help, Evaluate for episiotomy, Legs (McRoberts), Pressure (suprapubic), Enter (internal manoeuvres: Rubin II, Woods, reverse Woods), Remove the posterior arm, Roll the woman onto all fours. McRoberts hyperflexion plus suprapubic pressure resolves up to 90% of shoulder dystocia by widening the pelvic outlet and pushing the anterior shoulder into the oblique. Fundal pressure is contraindicated; routine downward traction must be substituted by axial traction only. (Source: RANZCOG Statements)

explanation.summary: Shoulder dystocia is diagnosed when the anterior shoulder fails to deliver with routine downward traction after delivery of the head. HELPERR: Help, Evaluate for episiotomy, Legs (McRoberts), Pressure (suprapubic), Enter (internal manoeuvres), Remove posterior arm, Roll to all fours. McRoberts plus suprapubic pressure resolves up to 90%. Avoid fundal pressure (uterine rupture, worsens impaction). Document time-line and which manoeuvres used.
key_points: HELPERR mnemonic structures stepwise response
McRoberts plus suprapubic pressure first - 90% success
Fundal pressure CONTRAINDICATED; axial (not lateral) traction only
explanation.pearls: After every shoulder dystocia document the head-to-body interval, the manoeuvres used, the position of the fetal head at presentation and any newborn injury (brachial plexus, clavicle); this is a high-medico-legal-risk event and contemporaneous notes are critical.

stem:
A 26-year-old G1P0 woman at 35+6 weeks gestation with a twin pregnancy is admitted to the high-risk obstetric ward with a week of malaise, anorexia and nausea, and 3 days of right upper quadrant discomfort. She has been increasingly drowsy over the last 24 hours. She has no past medical history and her pregnancy was uncomplicated until now. Her BP at the last antenatal visit was 118/74 mmHg.

On admission she is jaundiced and sleepy but rousable. Her partner reports she has been confused about names of family members this morning. The obstetric registrar and gastroenterology registrar are at the bedside.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 108, BP 134/84 mmHg, RR 22, SpO2 98% in room air, temperature 37.1 °C, fetal heart rates both reactive
data_table.Examination: Sclera icteric, jaundice on skin, mild RUQ tenderness, no peripheral oedema, mild asterixis, BSL 2.4 mmol/L, no peritonism
data_table.Investigations: AST 580 U/L (<35), ALT 480 U/L (<35), bilirubin 142 micromol/L (3-20) predominantly conjugated, ALP 280 U/L, GGT 220 U/L, INR 2.4, fibrinogen 1.2 g/L (>2 intrapartum target), platelets 102 x10^9/L (150-400), creatinine 138 micromol/L (45-90), urate 0.46 mmol/L (<0.36), urine PCR 80 mg/mmol, BSL 2.4 mmol/L (low), ammonia 110 micromol/L (<50), white cell count 16 x10^9/L, viral hepatitis screen negative, abdominal ultrasound shows hyperechoic liver with no focal lesion

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step?

options.text: Stabilise hypoglycaemia and coagulopathy and arrange urgent delivery
options.rationale: This presentation - jaundice, encephalopathy, hypoglycaemia, hyperammonaemia, coagulopathy with low fibrinogen, normal-to-mild AST/ALT elevation relative to disease severity, twin pregnancy at 35+6 weeks and mild proteinuria - meets Swansea criteria for acute fatty liver of pregnancy. AFLP is a microvesicular fatty infiltration linked to defective fetal long-chain 3-hydroxyacyl-CoA dehydrogenase (LCHAD). Delivery is the only definitive treatment and must be expedited regardless of fetal lung maturity; maternal mortality without delivery is high. Stabilise hypoglycaemia (10% dextrose), reverse coagulopathy (FFP, cryoprecipitate to fibrinogen above 1.5 to 2.0 g/L, vitamin K), correct electrolytes and proceed to delivery (vaginal if rapid progress or caesarean if not) within hours. (Source: RANZCOG Statements)

options.text: Commence empirical N-acetylcysteine and admit to intensive care without delivery
options.rationale: N-acetylcysteine is the treatment for paracetamol-induced hepatotoxicity. There is no history of paracetamol ingestion and the clinical picture is gestational. Without delivery, AFLP progresses to multi-organ failure regardless of medical support. (Source: RANZCOG Statements)

options.text: Transfer for emergency liver transplantation assessment and continue the pregnancy
options.rationale: Liver transplantation may be needed in a small minority of post-delivery patients with progressive liver failure but is not first-line and is irrelevant unless delivery has already happened. Continuing the pregnancy is unsafe. (Source: RANZCOG Statements)

options.text: Diagnose HELLP syndrome and proceed to delivery after a course of betamethasone
options.rationale: HELLP and AFLP overlap clinically but AFLP is distinguished by hypoglycaemia, encephalopathy, hyperammonaemia, INR elevation out of proportion to platelet drop, and elevated bilirubin out of proportion to AST/ALT. A 24 to 48-hour delay for steroids is dangerous in established AFLP. (Source: RANZCOG Statements)

options.text: Treat as fulminant viral hepatitis and isolate while awaiting hepatitis E PCR
options.rationale: Viral hepatitis serology is negative on initial testing. The Swansea features are characteristic of AFLP. Waiting for hepatitis E PCR would delay delivery. (Source: RANZCOG Statements)

explanation.summary: Acute fatty liver of pregnancy is a rare but life-threatening third-trimester disorder of microvesicular fatty hepatic infiltration linked to fetal LCHAD deficiency. Swansea criteria require 6+ features (vomiting, abdominal pain, polydipsia/polyuria, encephalopathy, raised bilirubin, hypoglycaemia, raised urate, leucocytosis, ascites or bright liver on ultrasound, raised transaminases, raised ammonia, renal impairment, coagulopathy, microvesicular steatosis on biopsy). The only treatment is prompt delivery; mode is determined by maternal status and cervical favourability.
key_points: Swansea criteria distinguish AFLP from HELLP (hypoglycaemia, ammonia, encephalopathy key)
Delivery is the only definitive treatment; do not delay for steroids
Fetal LCHAD deficiency requires postpartum testing and newborn screen
explanation.pearls: Babies of mothers with AFLP should be tested for LCHAD deficiency because the disease can recur in subsequent pregnancies and the affected infant develops hypoketotic hypoglycaemia in the first months of life if undiagnosed.

stem:
A 32-year-old woman in her first pregnancy attends her 28-week antenatal review. Her BMI at booking was 31 kg/m^2 and her mother has type 2 diabetes. The dating ultrasound and 20-week morphology scan were normal. She is otherwise well and on routine pregnancy vitamins.

She has returned today for the results of her 75 g oral glucose tolerance test performed at 27 weeks after an 8-hour fast. Her fasting plasma glucose is 5.4 mmol/L, 1-hour post-load 9.8 mmol/L, and 2-hour post-load 8.0 mmol/L. She has no symptoms of polyuria, polydipsia or weight loss.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 78, BP 118/74 mmHg, RR 16, SpO2 99% on room air, temperature 36.6 °C
data_table.Examination: Symphysis-fundal height 27 cm at 28 weeks, fetal heart rate 142, no oedema
data_table.Investigations: 75 g OGTT: fasting 5.4 mmol/L (<5.1), 1-hour 9.8 mmol/L (<10), 2-hour 8.0 mmol/L (<8.5)
data_table.Medications: Iodine 150 mcg, folic acid 500 mcg, vitamin D

lead_in: What is the most appropriate diagnosis and next step?

options.text: Normal test; reassure and continue routine antenatal care with no further glucose monitoring
options.rationale: Her fasting plasma glucose of 5.4 mmol/L exceeds the ADIPS threshold of 5.1 mmol/L for gestational diabetes; any single value above its threshold makes the diagnosis. (Source: ADIPS Consensus)

options.text: Gestational diabetes; commence dietitian-led medical nutrition therapy with self-monitoring of blood glucose
options.rationale: ADIPS diagnoses GDM when any one value meets or exceeds fasting 5.1 mmol/L, 1-hour 10.0 mmol/L, or 2-hour 8.5 mmol/L; her fasting at 5.4 confirms GDM. AU first-line management is dietitian-led medical nutrition therapy plus capillary BSL monitoring (fasting and 1- or 2-hour post-prandials), with metformin or insulin added if targets are not met after 1-2 weeks. (Source: ADIPS Consensus)

options.text: Gestational diabetes; commence insulin glargine 10 units nocte immediately as the proposed approach
options.rationale: Pharmacotherapy is added when lifestyle measures do not achieve glycaemic targets (fasting under 5.0, 1-hour under 7.4, or 2-hour under 6.7 mmol/L) after a 1-2 week trial, not at diagnosis. (Source: ADIPS Consensus)

options.text: Type 2 diabetes overt in pregnancy; commence insulin and refer to endocrinology urgently
options.rationale: Overt diabetes in pregnancy is diagnosed by fasting plasma glucose at or above 7.0 mmol/L, random glucose at or above 11.1 mmol/L, or HbA1c at or above 6.5%. Her fasting of 5.4 mmol/L meets GDM criteria only. (Source: ADIPS Consensus)

options.text: Borderline result; repeat the OGTT in 2 weeks before any diagnostic label as the proposed approach
options.rationale: ADIPS does not recommend repeating an OGTT when a single value crosses a threshold; the diagnosis stands and management starts. (Source: ADIPS Consensus)

explanation.summary: ADIPS uses fasting 5.1 / 1-hour 10.0 / 2-hour 8.5 mmol/L thresholds; any single value at or above its threshold diagnoses GDM. First-line is dietitian-led medical nutrition therapy plus capillary BSL monitoring, with pharmacotherapy added after 1-2 weeks if targets are not met. Targets are fasting under 5.0, 1-hour under 7.4, or 2-hour under 6.7 mmol/L. Overt diabetes in pregnancy uses different thresholds.
key_points: ADIPS OGTT thresholds: 5.1 / 10.0 / 8.5 mmol/L
Any single value at threshold diagnoses GDM
First-line: medical nutrition therapy + capillary BSL monitoring
Targets: fasting <5.0, 1-hour <7.4, 2-hour <6.7 mmol/L
explanation.pearls: ADIPS thresholds are lower and more sensitive than older 2-step approaches; AU practice catches more milder GDM and manages most cases without pharmacotherapy.

stem:
A 24-year-old woman attends your GP clinic to discuss contraception. She has been on a combined oral contraceptive pill (ethinylestradiol 30 mcg / levonorgestrel 150 mcg) for the past 2 years with good cycle control. Over the last 6 months she has developed two episodes of unilateral visual scintillations lasting 20 minutes followed by a unilateral throbbing headache; her GP previously documented migraine without aura.

She smokes 3 cigarettes daily, BMI is 24 kg/m^2, blood pressure today is 122/78 mmHg, and her family history is unremarkable. She is sexually active in a monogamous relationship and wants long-term reliable contraception with low maintenance.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 72, BP 122/78 mmHg, RR 14, SpO2 99% on room air, temperature 36.5 °C
data_table.Examination: Cardiovascular and neurological examination normal, no carotid bruit, no visual field defect
data_table.Investigations: Cervical screening up to date and normal; routine bloods within normal limits 6 months ago
data_table.Medications: Combined oral contraceptive ethinylestradiol 30 mcg / levonorgestrel 150 mcg daily

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step in contraception?

options.text: Insert a 52 mg levonorgestrel intrauterine system after counselling on insertion and bleeding patterns
options.rationale: Migraine with aura makes combined hormonal contraception UKMEC 4 and progestogen-only options become preferred. A 52 mg levonorgestrel IUS is UKMEC 1 in migraine with aura, provides 5-8 years of highly effective contraception, and aligns with her preference for long-term reliable low-maintenance contraception. (Source: UKMEC)

options.text: Switch to a 20 mcg ethinylestradiol combined pill and review symptoms in 3 months
options.rationale: Migraine with aura at any age is a UKMEC category 4 (absolute contraindication) for combined hormonal contraception regardless of oestrogen dose because of the ischaemic stroke risk; switching to a lower-dose combined pill does not mitigate this. (Source: UKMEC)

options.text: Continue current pill and add aspirin 100 mg daily for stroke prophylaxis as the proposed approach
options.rationale: Aspirin does not reduce the oestrogen-related stroke risk in migraine with aura to acceptable levels and adds bleeding risk; contraindicated hormonal use should be ceased, not pharmacologically counterbalanced. (Source: UKMEC)

options.text: Switch to the vaginal ring (etonogestrel/ethinylestradiol) and review in 3 months
options.rationale: The vaginal ring is a combined oestrogen-progestogen method and carries the same UKMEC 4 contraindication in migraine with aura. (Source: UKMEC)

options.text: Recommend condoms alone with cessation of all hormonal contraception as the proposed approach
options.rationale: Condoms are user-dependent with typical-use failure around 13% per year and do not meet her stated preference for long-term reliable low-maintenance contraception; progestogen-only LARC is preferable. (Source: FSRH)

explanation.summary: Migraine with aura at any age is UKMEC 4 for combined hormonal contraception because of ischaemic stroke risk. Progestogen-only methods (levonorgestrel IUS, etonogestrel implant, depot, progestogen-only pill) are all safe in this scenario. A 52 mg LNG-IUS is UKMEC 1 with 5-8 years of high-efficacy contraception that aligns with this patient's stated preference. Lower-dose combined pills, the ring, and adjunctive aspirin do not solve the contraindication.
key_points: Migraine with aura = UKMEC 4 for combined hormonal contraception
Progestogen-only methods are UKMEC 1-2
LNG-IUS = 5-8 years, highly effective, low maintenance
Stroke risk drives the contraindication, not headache itself
explanation.pearls: Migraine with aura roughly doubles stroke risk; adding combined hormonal contraception multiplies the risk further. The aura - not the headache - is the discriminator triggering UKMEC 4.

stem:
A 28-year-old woman in her second pregnancy presents to the birth suite at 39 weeks and 2 days with regular painful contractions every 4 minutes and ruptured membranes 30 minutes ago. Her booking visit was uncomplicated and her 36-week vaginal-rectal swab grew Streptococcus agalactiae. Her first child was born at term with no neonatal infection.

On examination her cervix is 5 cm dilated and the cephalic presenting part is engaged. Fetal heart rate is 138 with normal variability. She has no penicillin allergy.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 88, BP 122/76 mmHg, RR 16, SpO2 99% on room air, temperature 36.9 °C, fetal heart rate 138
data_table.Examination: Cervix 5 cm dilated, fully effaced, vertex at -1 station, clear liquor draining
data_table.Investigations: Antenatal 36-week vaginal-rectal GBS swab positive; FBC and group-and-hold within normal limits

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step in management?

options.text: Give a single dose of oral amoxicillin 1 g now and arrange home discharge until contractions intensify
options.rationale: Oral antibiotics do not achieve fetal-protective intrapartum levels reliably; intravenous benzylpenicillin is the standard. Home discharge with ruptured membranes in active labour is unsafe. (Source: RANZCOG GBS)

options.text: Withhold antibiotics and observe for clinical chorioamnionitis before treating as the proposed approach
options.rationale: Intrapartum antibiotic prophylaxis is offered based on the antenatal screen, not on clinical infection criteria; waiting for chorioamnionitis means accepting preventable early-onset neonatal GBS disease. (Source: RANZCOG GBS)

options.text: Give intravenous clindamycin 900 mg 8-hourly until birth with the proposed clinical action
options.rationale: Clindamycin is an alternative agent for women with severe penicillin allergy and confirmed clindamycin susceptibility; in a non-allergic woman benzylpenicillin is first-line and provides better in-utero penetration. (Source: RANZCOG GBS)

options.text: Commence intravenous benzylpenicillin 3 g loading dose now, then 1.8 g every 4 hours until birth
options.rationale: RANZCOG and Therapeutic Guidelines recommend intrapartum benzylpenicillin 3 g IV loading then 1.8 g every 4 hours until delivery for any woman with a positive antenatal GBS screen presenting in labour or with rupture of membranes. The first dose is the most important; effective prophylaxis ideally requires at least 4 hours before delivery but should not be delayed. (Source: RANZCOG GBS)

options.text: Defer antibiotic prophylaxis as her previous child was unaffected and prior unaffected pregnancy reduces neonatal risk
