options.rationale: Prior unaffected pregnancy does not reduce GBS colonisation risk in the current pregnancy and does not waive the indication for prophylaxis with a current positive screen. (Source: RANZCOG GBS)

explanation.summary: AU intrapartum GBS prophylaxis uses benzylpenicillin 3 g IV loading then 1.8 g every 4 hours until delivery for women with positive antenatal screen, prior infant with GBS disease, GBS bacteriuria in this pregnancy, or unknown status with risk factors. Clindamycin is reserved for confirmed severe penicillin allergy with susceptibility. Oral antibiotics are insufficient. The first dose is the most important; do not delay.
key_points: RANZCOG: IV benzylpenicillin 3 g load then 1.8 g 4-hourly until birth
Indications: positive screen, prior GBS infant, GBS bacteriuria, unknown + risk
Clindamycin only if severe penicillin allergy + susceptibility
First dose timing matters most; ideal ≥4 hours before delivery
explanation.pearls: Cefazolin replaces benzylpenicillin only for non-anaphylactic penicillin allergy; severe (anaphylaxis) allergy with confirmed clindamycin susceptibility uses clindamycin instead.

stem:
A 29-year-old woman attends your fertility clinic with 18 months of primary infertility. Her cycles are irregular, occurring every 45 to 90 days with light flow. She has hirsutism on the chin and lower abdomen, acne, and her BMI is 27 kg/m^2. Pelvic ultrasound shows enlarged ovaries with multiple peripheral follicles bilaterally. Her partner's semen analysis is normal.

Day-3 hormonal profile shows raised LH:FSH ratio, mildly raised testosterone, and normal prolactin and TSH. Hysterosalpingogram demonstrates patent fallopian tubes. She has been counselled on weight optimisation and lifestyle changes for 6 months without conception.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 76, BP 124/78 mmHg, RR 16, SpO2 99% on room air, temperature 36.6 °C
data_table.Examination: BMI 27 kg/m^2, Ferriman-Gallwey 12, mild acne, no acanthosis nigricans
data_table.Investigations: FSH 5 IU/L (3-10), LH 14 IU/L (2-12), testosterone 2.6 nmol/L (<2.0), prolactin 380 mIU/L (60-560), TSH 1.8 mIU/L (0.4-4.0), AMH 64 pmol/L (12-49); HSG patent bilateral tubes; partner sperm density 32 million/mL with normal motility and morphology

lead_in: What would you first recommend as ovulation induction therapy?

options.text: Recombinant FSH gonadotrophin injections from cycle day 3 with transvaginal ultrasound monitoring
options.rationale: Gonadotrophins are second-line ovulation induction after oral agents fail and require close cycle monitoring because of multiple-pregnancy and ovarian hyperstimulation risks; they are not first-line in PCOS. (Source: RANZCOG PCOS)

options.text: Clomifene citrate 50 mg orally daily on cycle days 2-6 for up to six ovulatory cycles
options.rationale: Clomifene was historically first-line but letrozole has been shown superior in live-birth rates with similar safety in PCOS infertility and is now preferred. Clomifene remains a reasonable option where letrozole is not accessible. (Source: International PCOS Guideline)

options.text: Metformin extended-release 1500 mg daily as ovulation induction monotherapy
options.rationale: Metformin improves ovulation rates modestly and is used as an adjunct (particularly with BMI over 30) or where letrozole is contraindicated, but is not first-line as monotherapy for ovulation induction in this BMI band. (Source: International PCOS Guideline)

options.text: Letrozole 2.5 mg orally daily on cycle days 2-6 for up to six ovulatory cycles
options.rationale: The international PCOS guideline and RANZCOG endorse letrozole as first-line ovulation induction in PCOS-related anovulatory infertility, with higher live-birth rates than clomifene (PPCOS-II trial) and a lower multiple-pregnancy rate. The starting dose is 2.5 mg cycle days 2-6, titrated up to 7.5 mg if anovulatory, continued for up to six ovulatory cycles. (Source: International PCOS Guideline)

options.text: Laparoscopic ovarian drilling as the initial ovulation induction approach as the proposed approach
options.rationale: Laparoscopic ovarian drilling is reserved for clomifene or letrozole resistance or where ovarian surgery is otherwise indicated; it is not a first-line approach because of surgical risk and uncertain durability. (Source: RANZCOG PCOS)

explanation.summary: Letrozole is the first-line ovulation induction agent for PCOS-related infertility per the 2023 International PCOS Guideline and RANZCOG. It outperforms clomifene in live-birth rate (PPCOS-II) with lower multiple-pregnancy risk. Metformin is an adjunct in higher-BMI women or alternative when letrozole is contraindicated. Gonadotrophins and ovarian drilling are second-line.
key_points: First-line: letrozole 2.5 mg cycle days 2-6, up to 6 cycles
Titrate to 7.5 mg if anovulatory
Clomifene second choice; metformin adjunct in BMI >30
Gonadotrophins and drilling for resistance
explanation.pearls: Letrozole has a shorter half-life than clomifene and avoids anti-oestrogenic endometrial effects, explaining the higher live-birth rate at equivalent ovulation rates.

stem:
A 30-year-old woman in her first pregnancy attends for her 11-week-plus-4-day dating ultrasound. The scan confirms a live twin pregnancy with two fetuses each measuring crown-rump length consistent with her last menstrual period. The intervening membrane meets the placental surface in a T-shape (no lambda sign), with a single placental mass and a thin intervening membrane. Both fetuses appear morphologically appropriate for gestation with present nasal bones and normal nuchal translucency measurements.

She is otherwise healthy with a BMI of 23 kg/m^2 and no significant medical or family history. She asks how her pregnancy will be monitored.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 76, BP 116/72 mmHg, RR 14, SpO2 99% on room air, temperature 36.5 °C
data_table.Examination: Soft non-tender abdomen, no visible scars
data_table.Investigations: Dating ultrasound 11+4 weeks: live twin pregnancy, T-sign at membrane-placenta interface, single placental mass, normal NT measurements bilaterally

lead_in: What is the most appropriate surveillance plan?

options.text: Four-weekly ultrasound from 20 weeks with growth assessment and delivery at 37-38 weeks as the proposed approach
options.rationale: Four-weekly surveillance starting at 20 weeks is the schedule for dichorionic-diamniotic twins; MCDA twins require fortnightly scans from 16 weeks because of the higher TTTS, sFGR, and TAPS risks. (Source: RANZCOG Twin Pregnancy)

options.text: Fortnightly ultrasound from 16 weeks with growth and amniotic fluid assessment, fetal Doppler studies and timed delivery at 36-37 weeks
options.rationale: T-sign at the membrane-placenta interface indicates a monochorionic-diamniotic (MCDA) twin pregnancy. RANZCOG and the AU monochorionic twin pathway recommend fortnightly ultrasound from 16 weeks to screen for twin-to-twin transfusion syndrome (DVP discordance, bladder visualisation), selective fetal growth restriction (EFW discordance, UA Doppler), and TAPS (MCA-PSV); planned delivery is 36-37 weeks because of late stillbirth risk. (Source: RANZCOG Twin Pregnancy)

options.text: Routine antenatal care as for a singleton pregnancy with delivery at 40 weeks with the proposed clinical action
options.rationale: Twin pregnancies of any chorionicity require enhanced surveillance and earlier planned delivery because of increased perinatal mortality and morbidity compared to singletons. (Source: RANZCOG Twin Pregnancy)

options.text: Weekly cardiotocograph from 28 weeks with delivery at 34 weeks as the proposed approach with the proposed clinical action
options.rationale: Routine CTG is not the surveillance modality for MCDA twins; ultrasound for fetal Doppler, growth and amniotic fluid is the primary surveillance. Delivery at 34 weeks is too early without specific complications. (Source: RANZCOG Twin Pregnancy)

options.text: Refer for early elective caesarean section at 32 weeks because of the chorionicity as the proposed approach
options.rationale: Uncomplicated MCDA twins do not require delivery at 32 weeks; this would impose iatrogenic prematurity. Planned delivery is at 36-37 weeks, mode determined by presentation and other obstetric factors. (Source: RANZCOG Twin Pregnancy)

explanation.summary: First-trimester ultrasound determines chorionicity reliably. T-sign = MCDA; lambda sign = DCDA. MCDA twins require fortnightly ultrasound from 16 weeks for TTTS, sFGR, and TAPS screening and planned delivery at 36-37 weeks. DCDA twins have four-weekly scans from 20 weeks and delivery at 37-38 weeks. Monochorionic-monoamniotic twins are managed with inpatient surveillance from 28-32 weeks and delivered at 32-34 weeks by caesarean.
key_points: T-sign at 11-14 weeks = monochorionic-diamniotic
MCDA: fortnightly US from 16 weeks; delivery 36-37 weeks
DCDA: four-weekly US from 20 weeks; delivery 37-38 weeks
MCMA: inpatient surveillance 28-32 weeks; caesarean 32-34 weeks
explanation.pearls: Lambda sign reflects placental tissue insinuating between two separate placentae (DCDA); T-sign reflects a single placental mass with a thin two-layer dividing membrane (MCDA).

stem:
A 32-year-old woman with a 4-year history of endometriosis is referred to your clinic with worsening cyclical pelvic pain, dyschezia, and rectal bleeding with menstruation over the past 6 months. She has tried a combined oral contraceptive in continuous regimen and the levonorgestrel IUS without adequate symptom control. Her CA125 is 65 U/mL.

Pelvic ultrasound shows a 4 cm right ovarian endometrioma and a 2 cm bowel wall hypoechoic mass at the rectosigmoid junction with loss of the normal hyperechoic submucosal layer. MRI confirms a 25 mm full-thickness rectal nodule infiltrating the muscularis and approaching the mucosa, with a separate uterosacral ligament nodule.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 80, BP 118/72 mmHg, RR 14, SpO2 99% on room air, temperature 36.5 °C
data_table.Examination: Tenderness in the pouch of Douglas, fixed retroverted uterus, no palpable rectal mass
data_table.Investigations: Pelvic ultrasound: 4 cm right ovarian endometrioma; 2 cm rectosigmoid bowel wall lesion. MRI: 25 mm deep infiltrating endometriotic nodule of anterior rectum + uterosacral nodule. CA125 65 U/mL (<35)
data_table.Medications: Continuous COC trial failed; levonorgestrel IUS trial failed

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step in management?

options.text: Commence GnRH agonist therapy with add-back tibolone as definitive management as the proposed approach
options.rationale: GnRH agonists can reduce pain in endometriosis but do not address deep infiltrating bowel disease anatomically; failure of two adequate hormonal trials and structural disease point to surgical planning. GnRH agonists may be used as a bridge to surgery, not as definitive management of DIE with bowel involvement. (Source: RANZCOG Endometriosis)

options.text: Refer to a tertiary endometriosis multidisciplinary clinic with colorectal and minimally invasive gynaecology input
options.rationale: Deep infiltrating endometriosis with bowel involvement requires multidisciplinary surgical planning; shaving versus disc excision versus segmental resection is decided by lesion size, depth, and proximity to mucosa with input from colorectal surgery, complex gynaecology, and radiology. RANZCOG and the AU endometriosis action plan direct DIE with bowel involvement to a specialised endometriosis MDT centre. (Source: RANZCOG Endometriosis)

options.text: Proceed with laparoscopic ablation of visible peritoneal endometriosis at the local hospital
options.rationale: Ablation alone is inadequate for deep infiltrating endometriosis; excision is required and bowel involvement warrants specialist colorectal-gynaecology MDT input rather than ablation at a non-specialist centre. (Source: RANZCOG Endometriosis)

options.text: Initiate aromatase inhibitor letrozole plus norethisterone as third-line hormonal therapy
options.rationale: Aromatase inhibitors have a role in refractory endometriosis but do not substitute for surgical evaluation of structural bowel disease, and require co-prescription with progestogen to prevent ovarian cyst formation in pre-menopausal women. They are not the next step here. (Source: RANZCOG Endometriosis)

options.text: Schedule total abdominal hysterectomy and bilateral salpingo-oophorectomy as first-line definitive surgery
options.rationale: At 32 years with fertility implications, hysterectomy is not first-line; conservative excisional surgery preserving fertility with MDT planning is preferred. Hysterectomy may be considered for women who have completed family with persistent symptoms after conservative surgery. (Source: RANZCOG Endometriosis)

explanation.summary: Deep infiltrating endometriosis with bowel involvement requires multidisciplinary care because surgical decisions (shave, disc, or segmental resection) depend on lesion size, depth, and proximity to mucosa, with colorectal and complex gynaecology input. Failed hormonal therapy with structural bowel disease is not adequately managed by additional medical therapy alone. Hysterectomy is rarely first-line in a 32-year-old.
key_points: DIE with bowel involvement = tertiary MDT clinic
Surgical options: shave / disc excision / segmental resection
Failed hormonal therapy + structural disease drives surgical referral
Hysterectomy is rarely first-line for fertility-aware patients
explanation.pearls: Cyclical rectal bleeding plus dyschezia in a woman with known endometriosis = highly suspicious for bowel DIE; MRI defines depth and shave-versus-resection planning.

stem:
A 34-year-old woman in her fourth pregnancy at 32 weeks gestation is referred to the maternal-fetal medicine unit. She has had three previous caesarean sections, all uncomplicated. Her current pregnancy was complicated by an anterior placenta praevia identified at the morphology scan. Detailed expert ultrasound at 28 weeks identified multiple placental lacunae, loss of the uteroplacental clear zone, retroplacental hypervascularity, and bridging vessels into the bladder. MRI confirms anterior placental tissue invading the bladder wall.

She is otherwise well, BMI 26 kg/m^2, has had a course of antenatal corticosteroids at 31 weeks, and her haemoglobin today is 124 g/L. She has been counselled on placenta percreta in the previous antenatal multidisciplinary meeting. She is asking when delivery should be planned, given she has small children at home.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 88, BP 122/78 mmHg, RR 16, SpO2 99% on room air, temperature 36.6 °C, fetal heart rate 142
data_table.Examination: Soft non-tender abdomen, three lower-segment caesarean scars, fetal cephalic presentation
data_table.Investigations: MRI: anterior placental tissue traversing myometrium with bladder wall invasion. Ultrasound: lacunae, loss of clear zone, hypervascularity, bridging vessels. Haemoglobin 124 g/L (115-160), platelets 232 x10^9/L (150-400), fibrinogen 4.2 g/L, group A positive, antibodies negative
data_table.Medications: Iron supplement, antenatal corticosteroids course completed at 31 weeks

lead_in: What would you first recommend regarding timing and mode of delivery?

options.text: Planned caesarean hysterectomy at 34-35 weeks gestation in a tertiary placenta accreta spectrum centre with interventional radiology standby, cross-matched blood, and pre-arranged urology input
options.rationale: RANZCOG and AU placenta accreta spectrum (PAS) pathway recommend planned delivery at 34-35 weeks for placenta percreta to balance preterm risk against the high risk of antepartum bleeding precipitating emergency surgery. Steroids have already been given at 31 weeks. Delivery must be in a specialised PAS centre with multidisciplinary team (anaesthesia, IR, urology, obstetrics, neonatology), cross-matched blood and cell salvage. Caesarean hysterectomy with placenta left in situ at delivery is the recommended primary approach for percreta. (Source: RANZCOG PAS)

options.text: Planned vaginal delivery at 39 weeks with active management of the third stage as the proposed approach with the proposed clinical action as the proposed clinical action
options.rationale: Placenta praevia alone contraindicates vaginal delivery; placenta percreta makes vaginal delivery actively dangerous because of catastrophic haemorrhage on placental separation. (Source: RANZCOG PAS)

options.text: Planned caesarean section at 39 weeks with manual removal of the placenta at delivery in the local maternity unit with the proposed clinical action
options.rationale: Manual placental removal in percreta causes massive haemorrhage; the recommended approach leaves the placenta in situ at hysterectomy. Local maternity units lack the multidisciplinary resources for PAS and term delivery without antepartum bleeding is unlikely. (Source: RANZCOG PAS)

options.text: Emergency caesarean section today regardless of fetal lung maturity to avoid antenatal haemorrhage as the proposed approach with the proposed clinical action
options.rationale: There is no current bleeding or other emergency indication; planned delivery at 34-35 weeks balances fetal maturity against bleeding risk. Emergency delivery at 32 weeks adds significant neonatal morbidity without immediate maternal benefit. (Source: RANZCOG PAS)

options.text: Conservative management with methotrexate and leaving the placenta in situ after caesarean delivery, with serial bhCG follow-up as the proposed approach
options.rationale: Conservative management leaving placenta in situ with delayed delivery and serial bhCG is an option in selected cases with future fertility desire and ability to monitor closely, but is high-risk in percreta with bladder invasion and is not first-line; methotrexate has no proven benefit. (Source: RANZCOG PAS)

explanation.summary: Placenta percreta with bladder invasion requires planned caesarean hysterectomy at 34-35 weeks in a specialised PAS centre with multidisciplinary preparation. The placenta is left in situ at the time of hysterectomy to avoid catastrophic haemorrhage. Antenatal corticosteroids precede delivery. Conservative methotrexate and term delivery approaches are not appropriate for bladder-invasive percreta. The disconfirming finding here is bladder wall invasion which kills conservative options and forces hysterectomy planning.
key_points: Percreta with bladder invasion = caesarean hysterectomy at 34-35 weeks
Placenta left in situ at hysterectomy
MDT centre: anaesthesia, IR, urology, obstetrics, neonatology
Antenatal corticosteroids; cross-match and cell salvage ready
explanation.pearls: Bladder invasion on MRI is the disconfirming finding that converts a 'maybe conservative' percreta into a mandatory caesarean hysterectomy at 34-35 weeks in a specialist centre.

subtopic_detail: HPV not 16-18 with LSIL reflex cytology
stem:
A 28-year-old woman attends your general practice clinic for results of her routine 5-yearly Cervical Screening Test. She has no abnormal bleeding, no postcoital bleeding, and no pelvic pain. She had a previous screening test 5 years ago that was negative. She is sexually active with a single male partner of 3 years, uses combined oral contraception, and has had no abnormal cervical results in the past. She is not pregnant.

Her current Cervical Screening Test reports oncogenic HPV detected (non-16, non-18 type) with reflex liquid-based cytology showing low-grade squamous intraepithelial lesion (possible LSIL). Speculum at sample-taking was unremarkable; the cervix appeared smooth and there were no contact-bleeding findings noted. She is up to date with her HPV vaccination history (3-dose schedule in adolescence). She asks 'do I need a biopsy now?'.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 72, BP 116/74 mmHg, RR 14, SpO2 99% on room air, temperature 36.6 °C
data_table.Examination: Speculum: cervix smooth, no friable lesion, no contact bleeding, no abnormal discharge
data_table.Investigations: Cervical Screening Test: HPV non-16/18 detected; reflex liquid-based cytology low-grade squamous intraepithelial lesion (possible LSIL)

lead_in: What is the most appropriate management?

options.text: Repeat the Cervical Screening Test in 12 months irrespective of cytology grade or HPV genotype reported
options.rationale: Twelve-month repeat applies after HPV non-16/18 with negative or low-grade reflex cytology in a routine intermediate-risk pathway; the description fits but the discriminator is the symptom set and prior negative test. This option phrasing is incomplete because it omits the 12-month and 24-month consecutive logic; the official program ties the management to the cytology grade. (Source: NCSP Guidelines)

options.text: Refer to a gynaecologist for diagnostic excisional biopsy (large loop excision of the transformation zone) within 6 weeks
options.rationale: Excisional procedures are reserved for biopsy-confirmed high-grade squamous intraepithelial lesion (HSIL) or higher; LSIL on screening cytology with non-16/18 HPV does not warrant immediate excision. (Source: NCSP Guidelines)

options.text: Refer urgently to colposcopy clinic for diagnostic assessment and directed cervical biopsies within 8 weeks
options.rationale: Direct colposcopy is the AU intermediate-risk referral pathway only after a second HPV non-16/18 with persistent low-grade abnormality at 12 months, or any reflex HSIL result. A first-occasion HPV non-16/18 with possible LSIL is managed by 12-month repeat. (Source: NCSP Guidelines)

options.text: Treat her empirically with vaginal imiquimod and repeat the Cervical Screening Test in 3 months
options.rationale: Topical imiquimod is not part of the AU screening program management; empirical treatment without histological diagnosis is not recommended. (Source: NCSP Guidelines)

options.text: Repeat the Cervical Screening Test in 12 months and refer to colposcopy if HPV remains detected at that point
options.rationale: An HPV non-16/18 result with reflex possible LSIL or LSIL is intermediate risk under the AU NCSP and is managed by repeat Cervical Screening Test at 12 months. If HPV (any oncogenic type) is still detected at the 12-month repeat, colposcopy referral is required regardless of cytology. If the 12-month repeat is HPV-negative, she returns to 5-yearly screening. (Source: NCSP Guidelines)

explanation.summary: The Australian National Cervical Screening Program uses primary HPV testing every 5 years from age 25 to 74. HPV 16/18 detection triggers direct colposcopy referral; HPV non-16/18 results are stratified by reflex cytology. Negative or low-grade reflex cytology with HPV non-16/18 leads to a 12-month repeat test (intermediate risk pathway). HSIL or higher on reflex cytology, or persistent HPV at 12-month repeat, triggers colposcopy. Self-collection from age 25 is available for under-screened women.
key_points: HPV 16/18: direct colposcopy regardless of cytology
HPV non-16/18 with negative or low-grade cytology: 12-month repeat
Persistent HPV (any type) at 12-month repeat: colposcopy
Self-collection available from age 25 for under-screened women
explanation.pearls: AU intermediate-risk pathway: HPV non-16/18 with negative or low-grade reflex cytology returns at 12 months; if still HPV-positive at that visit, colposcopy is the next step regardless of cytology grade.

stem:
A 32-year-old woman attends your general practice clinic 4 months postpartum complaining of palpitations, tremor, weight loss of 4 kg despite a good appetite, and feeling 'hot all the time'. Her mother says 'she has been tearful and snappy, she's not herself'. She is breastfeeding and has not had a postnatal contraceptive review. Her last menstrual period before pregnancy was regular. She denies eye pain, double vision, or visual changes.

On examination she has a fine tremor of outstretched hands, a smooth non-tender symmetrical small goitre without bruit, and no proptosis or lid lag. There is no pretibial myxoedema. Edinburgh Postnatal Depression Scale score is 9. Initial bloods show TSH 0.04 mIU/L (0.5-4.0), free T4 28 pmol/L (10-22), and free T3 9 pmol/L (3.5-6.5). She wonders 'is it just my hormones from feeding?'.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 108 regular, BP 124/76 mmHg, RR 18, SpO2 99% on room air, temperature 36.9 °C
data_table.Examination: Fine tremor, smooth small symmetrical goitre, no bruit, no proptosis or lid lag, no pretibial myxoedema, lactating
data_table.Investigations: TSH 0.04 mIU/L (0.5-4.0), free T4 28 pmol/L (10-22), free T3 9 pmol/L (3.5-6.5), EPDS 9; TSH-receptor antibody pending, thyroid uptake scan not yet performed

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next investigation to clarify the cause?

options.text: Twenty-four-hour urinary iodine excretion testing before considering any further investigation steps
options.rationale: Iodine excretion testing assesses iodine status at a population level and does not differentiate thyroiditis from Graves disease in an individual. (Source: ATA Postpartum Thyroiditis Guideline)

options.text: Repeat thyroid function tests in 4 weeks without any further immediate biochemical or imaging testing
options.rationale: Both postpartum thyroiditis and Graves can persist or progress; differentiation needs to happen now because antithyroid drug therapy is appropriate only for Graves and not for transient thyroiditis. (Source: ATA Postpartum Thyroiditis Guideline)

options.text: Refer for radioactive iodine uptake scanning this week to differentiate Graves from thyroiditis
options.rationale: Radioactive iodine is contraindicated in breastfeeding women; a technetium scan with milk withholding could be used but is not the first-line discriminator. (Source: ATA Postpartum Thyroiditis Guideline; AMH)

options.text: Order TSH-receptor antibody and TPO antibody titres in addition to a small thyroid ultrasound now
options.rationale: TSH-receptor antibody (TRAb) is the key discriminator: positive supports Graves disease; negative with TPO antibody positivity supports postpartum thyroiditis. Ultrasound shows diffuse hypervascularity in Graves and patchy hypoechogenicity in thyroiditis. TRAb-positive results steer the patient toward antithyroid drug therapy with breastfeeding-compatible carbimazole at low dose; TRAb-negative directs symptomatic management. (Source: ATA Postpartum Thyroiditis Guideline; RANZCOG)

options.text: Commence empirical carbimazole 15 mg orally daily for biochemical hyperthyroidism while awaiting any further work
options.rationale: Empirical antithyroid drug therapy is wrong if the cause is postpartum thyroiditis (a destructive process not responsive to antithyroid medication) and exposes a breastfeeding mother unnecessarily; discriminate first. (Source: AMH)

explanation.summary: Postpartum thyroiditis affects up to 5% of women within 12 months of delivery and is a destructive autoimmune process producing transient hyperthyroidism followed by hypothyroidism and recovery in most cases. Graves disease in the postpartum period is autoimmune-stimulatory and persists. TRAb positivity, diffuse hypervascular goitre on ultrasound, and ophthalmopathy point to Graves. TPO antibody positivity with normal vascularity and a transient course points to thyroiditis. Carbimazole is the AU breastfeeding-compatible antithyroid drug at low dose; propylthiouracil reserved for first trimester or carbimazole intolerance.
key_points: TRAb is the key discriminator: positive = Graves, negative = thyroiditis
Radioactive iodine uptake contraindicated in breastfeeding women
Carbimazole low-dose is the AU breastfeeding-compatible antithyroid agent
Postpartum thyroiditis usually self-resolves; surveillance for permanent hypothyroidism
explanation.pearls: Breastfeeding-compatible carbimazole up to 20 mg per day is supported by AMH where serum testing in the infant has been used and infant thyroid function followed at intervals; propylthiouracil is preferred only for first trimester.

subtopic_detail: Hyperemesis gravidarum admission and refeeding risk
stem:
A 24-year-old gravida 1 para 0 woman presents to your emergency department at 9 weeks gestation with severe vomiting for 10 days. She tells you 'I can't keep water down for more than a few minutes'. She has lost 5 kg from her pre-pregnancy weight of 64 kg. She has had ginger, B6, oral metoclopramide, and ondansetron prescribed by her general practitioner without lasting effect. She has no abdominal pain, no fever, and no urinary symptoms.

On examination she has dry mucous membranes and a soft abdomen. Urinalysis shows ketones 3+ with no nitrites or leukocytes. Bloods show sodium 132 mmol/L (135-145), potassium 2.9 mmol/L (3.5-5.0), chloride 90 mmol/L, bicarbonate 30 mmol/L, urea 8 mmol/L, creatinine 84 micromol/L. Beta-hCG is appropriate for gestation; thyroid function is mildly suppressed (TSH 0.3 mIU/L). She has not eaten reliably for nearly two weeks.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 112, BP 100/60 mmHg standing 92/56 mmHg, RR 18, SpO2 98% on room air, temperature 36.7 °C
data_table.Examination: Dry mucous membranes, sunken eyes, capillary refill 3 seconds, abdomen soft non-tender, fundus not palpable
data_table.Investigations: Urinalysis ketones 3+; sodium 132 mmol/L (135-145), potassium 2.9 mmol/L (3.5-5.0), bicarbonate 30 mmol/L, urea 8 mmol/L, creatinine 84 micromol/L; beta-hCG appropriate for gestation; TSH 0.3 mIU/L; transabdominal ultrasound single live intrauterine pregnancy matched for dates
data_table.Medications: Ondansetron 8 mg orally (last dose 6 hours ago), metoclopramide PRN, ginger, pyridoxine 25 mg three times daily

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step in management?

options.text: Admit for intravenous thiamine, intravenous fluid with potassium replacement, then escalate antiemetics
options.rationale: Severe hyperemesis with ketonuria, hypokalaemia, and orthostatic hypotension warrants admission. Intravenous thiamine 100 mg is given BEFORE any dextrose-containing fluid (Wernicke prevention), followed by isotonic crystalloid with potassium replacement and then escalation to combination antiemetic therapy (e.g. ondansetron with cyclizine, or short-course oral prednisolone in refractory cases). (Source: RANZCOG; AMH)

options.text: Commence intravenous 5% dextrose 1 L over 1 hour with intramuscular cyclizine for symptom control
options.rationale: Dextrose-containing fluid before thiamine in a malnourished hyperemesis patient risks precipitating Wernicke encephalopathy; thiamine is always given first. (Source: RANZCOG)

options.text: Discharge with oral doxylamine-pyridoxine combination tablet and outpatient antenatal follow-up next week
options.rationale: Doxylamine-pyridoxine is appropriate first-line outpatient therapy for mild nausea, but this patient has dehydration, electrolyte derangement, and treatment failure on standard antiemetics; she needs admission. (Source: RANZCOG)

options.text: Arrange immediate termination of pregnancy referral given the severity of the maternal vomiting and weight loss
options.rationale: Termination is reserved for life-threatening maternal compromise that does not respond to maximal therapy; standard escalation including IV fluids and steroids has not yet been tried. (Source: RANZCOG)

options.text: Commence high-dose oral prednisolone 60 mg daily before any intravenous fluid or thiamine is given to her
options.rationale: Oral steroids are a salvage therapy for refractory hyperemesis after standard antiemetics and intravenous rehydration fail; they are not first-line and the patient cannot reliably absorb oral medication when actively vomiting. (Source: RANZCOG)

explanation.summary: Hyperemesis gravidarum is severe nausea and vomiting in pregnancy producing weight loss, dehydration, electrolyte abnormality, and ketonuria. Admission criteria include failure of outpatient management, dehydration, electrolyte derangement, or significant weight loss. Thiamine 100 mg must precede any dextrose-containing fluid because malnourished women are at risk of Wernicke encephalopathy. Stepwise antiemetics include ondansetron, metoclopramide, cyclizine, and short-course corticosteroids for refractory cases.
key_points: Thiamine before dextrose - Wernicke prevention is non-negotiable
Admit for IV fluids if ketonuria, electrolyte derangement, or treatment-failed outpatient
Stepwise antiemetics: doxylamine-pyridoxine, metoclopramide, ondansetron, cyclizine, steroids
Mildly suppressed TSH from beta-hCG cross-reactivity is benign in early pregnancy
explanation.pearls: Intravenous thiamine 100 mg in 100 mL saline given over 30 minutes precedes any dextrose-containing fluid in malnourished hyperemesis admissions to prevent acute Wernicke encephalopathy.

stem:
A 29-year-old primigravida attends your antenatal clinic at 14 weeks gestation for routine review. She is well, with no urinary symptoms, no flank pain, and no contraction-like discomfort. Her booking-visit midstream urine culture has just returned: Escherichia coli at greater than 10^8 CFU/L, sensitive to nitrofurantoin, trimethoprim, cefalexin, and amoxicillin-clavulanate. She has no penicillin allergy and no other medical history. Booking renal function and blood pressure are normal.

On examination she is afebrile. Abdomen is soft with a fundus consistent with dates. Urinalysis at the clinic visit is now negative for nitrites or leukocyte esterase. She asks 'do I really need antibiotics if I feel fine?'.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 78, BP 110/68 mmHg, RR 14, SpO2 99% on room air, temperature 36.6 °C
data_table.Examination: Abdomen soft, fundus consistent with dates, no renal angle tenderness, no costovertebral tenderness
data_table.Investigations: Booking midstream urine culture E. coli >10^8 CFU/L, sensitivities as above; today urinalysis nitrites and leukocyte esterase negative; routine antenatal bloods within normal limits
data_table.Medications: Pregnancy multivitamin including iodine and folate

lead_in: What is the most appropriate management?

options.text: Reassure that asymptomatic bacteriuria does not need antibiotic treatment in a healthy pregnancy and rescreen routinely
options.rationale: Untreated asymptomatic bacteriuria in pregnancy substantially increases the risk of acute pyelonephritis and preterm birth; the AU standard is to treat after a confirmed positive culture. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic; RANZCOG)

options.text: Commence oral nitrofurantoin 100 mg twice daily for 5 days and repeat midstream urine culture 7 days post-treatment
options.rationale: Asymptomatic bacteriuria in pregnancy is treated to reduce pyelonephritis and preterm birth. Nitrofurantoin is AU first-line in the first and second trimester (avoid at term and in glucose-6-phosphate dehydrogenase deficiency given neonatal haemolysis risk); a follow-up culture confirms eradication. Cefalexin or amoxicillin-clavulanate are reasonable alternatives if nitrofurantoin is contraindicated. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic; RANZCOG)

options.text: Repeat the urine culture in 2 weeks before deciding whether antibiotic treatment is justified for this woman
options.rationale: Two consecutive positive cultures from voided samples are reassuring of true bacteriuria, but a single positive midstream culture at greater than 10^8 CFU/L in pregnancy still warrants treatment in AU practice. (Source: RANZCOG)

options.text: Prescribe a single oral dose of fosfomycin 3 g once and arrange routine clinic follow-up at 6 weeks
options.rationale: Single-dose fosfomycin is acceptable for non-pregnant women with uncomplicated cystitis; in pregnancy, AU practice favours a longer course with documented test-of-cure. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic)

options.text: Refer to obstetric medicine for inpatient intravenous antibiotic treatment regardless of symptom status today
options.rationale: IV antibiotics are indicated for pyelonephritis or systemic illness, not asymptomatic bacteriuria; outpatient oral therapy is appropriate. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic)

explanation.summary: Asymptomatic bacteriuria in pregnancy is screened universally at booking. Treatment reduces the risk of pyelonephritis (which complicates approximately 30% of untreated cases) and preterm birth. AU first-line is nitrofurantoin or cefalexin for 5-7 days, with a test-of-cure culture afterwards. Trimethoprim is avoided in the first trimester; nitrofurantoin is avoided at term and where neonatal G6PD deficiency is suspected due to haemolysis risk. Group B streptococcus bacteriuria of any colony count is treated and triggers intrapartum prophylaxis.
key_points: Universal booking screen for ASB; treat all positive cultures
Nitrofurantoin or cefalexin first-line in pregnancy; avoid trimethoprim in T1
Group B streptococcus in any concentration triggers intrapartum prophylaxis
Follow up with test-of-cure culture to confirm eradication
explanation.pearls: Nitrofurantoin 100 mg orally twice daily for 5 days is the AU first-line for asymptomatic bacteriuria in the first and second trimester; avoid at term and where the neonate is at risk of G6PD-deficiency related haemolysis.

stem:
A 24-year-old woman presents to your general practice clinic with worsening cyclical pelvic pain for 3 years, dyspareunia for 6 months, and heavy menstrual bleeding requiring tampon and pad together with overnight changes. She tells you 'the pain takes over for the first 2 days every month and I have to call in sick'. She is currently not in a relationship and does not want pregnancy in the next 2 years, but would like to preserve fertility for the future.

On bimanual examination there is uterosacral nodularity and mild tenderness; the uterus is mobile. There is no adnexal mass. Pelvic transvaginal ultrasound shows a 2 cm endometrioma on the left ovary and no other significant findings. She has no medical comorbidity, is a non-smoker, has a body mass index of 24, and her blood pressure is normal. She has tried ibuprofen and mefenamic acid which have not been adequate.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 72, BP 116/72 mmHg, RR 14, SpO2 99% on room air, temperature 36.6 °C
data_table.Examination: Bimanual: uterosacral nodularity and mild tenderness, mobile uterus, no adnexal mass
data_table.Investigations: Transvaginal ultrasound: 2 cm left ovarian endometrioma, normal uterus and right ovary; FBC haemoglobin 119 g/L (115-165), ferritin 18 micrograms/L (30-300)
data_table.Medications: Ibuprofen 400 mg as needed; mefenamic acid 500 mg three times daily; oral iron

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step?

options.text: Refer for diagnostic laparoscopy and definitive excision of all peritoneal endometriotic deposits
options.rationale: Laparoscopy is reserved for failed medical therapy, severe disease unresponsive to first-line, or large endometriomas requiring surgical management. AU practice escalates medical options first when fertility is desired and the endometrioma is small. (Source: RANZCOG; NICE NG73)

options.text: Trial GnRH agonist therapy with add-back hormone replacement for 6 months as the first hormonal option
options.rationale: GnRH analogues are second-line after first-line hormonal therapy fails because of bone density and vasomotor cost; add-back is used to mitigate these but it is not first-line. (Source: RANZCOG; AMH)

options.text: Commence continuous combined oral contraception or a 52 mg levonorgestrel intrauterine system with NSAIDs for breakthrough pain
options.rationale: AU first-line medical management of endometriosis-related pain is continuous combined oral contraception or progestogen-based therapy (oral progestogen, depot, or 52 mg levonorgestrel intrauterine system). The 52 mg LNG-IUS additionally treats heavy menstrual bleeding and preserves fertility. NSAIDs are added for breakthrough pain. Six-month trial is expected before escalation. (Source: RANZCOG; NICE NG73)

options.text: Refer for ovarian endometrioma cystectomy now given the 2 cm finding on transvaginal ultrasound today
options.rationale: Endometriomas under 4 cm with no diagnostic uncertainty are typically managed medically when fertility is desired; surgery is reserved for larger lesions, severe symptoms, or suspicion of malignancy. (Source: RANZCOG)

options.text: Commence danazol 200 mg orally daily for 6 months with monthly clinical and biochemical monitoring
options.rationale: Danazol is rarely used in AU practice due to androgenic adverse effects; safer hormonal options are first-line. (Source: AMH)

explanation.summary: Endometriosis-related pain is initially managed with NSAIDs and AU first-line hormonal options (continuous combined oral contraception or progestogen-only therapy including the 52 mg levonorgestrel intrauterine system). The LNG-IUS is particularly useful when heavy menstrual bleeding coexists and fertility preservation is desired. Failed first-line therapy escalates to GnRH analogues (with add-back) or laparoscopic excision. Small endometriomas (under 4 cm) without diagnostic uncertainty are followed medically; larger lesions or suspicion of malignancy prompt surgical referral.
key_points: First-line medical: continuous combined OCP, oral progestogen, or 52 mg LNG-IUS
GnRH analogues with add-back are second-line
Endometriomas under 4 cm: medical first; larger or suspicious: surgical
NSAIDs as adjunct, not stand-alone
explanation.pearls: The 52 mg levonorgestrel intrauterine system reduces dysmenorrhoea, heavy menstrual bleeding, and endometriotic disease activity simultaneously, and preserves fertility - ideal first-line for women not currently planning pregnancy.

stem:
A 28-year-old woman gravida 2 para 1 presents to your tertiary delivery suite at 31 weeks plus 2 days with a confirmed gush of clear fluid 2 hours ago. She is not contracting. Her last delivery was a normal vaginal birth at term. She is well in herself. Her booking screen for group B streptococcus was negative; she has no other infection risk factors. The fetus is in cephalic presentation with reassuring antenatal records.

On sterile speculum examination, clear pooling is seen in the posterior fornix and a positive amniotic fluid test confirms ruptured membranes. The cervix appears uneffaced and closed. Maternal temperature, uterine tenderness, and fetal heart rate tracing are normal. Bedside transabdominal ultrasound shows a single fetus in cephalic position with significantly reduced amniotic fluid index but persistent fetal movements and no fetal anomalies. She has not received antenatal steroids in this pregnancy.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 86, BP 116/74 mmHg, RR 16, SpO2 99% on room air, temperature 36.7 °C; fetal heart rate baseline 140 bpm with reactive trace
data_table.Examination: Sterile speculum: clear pooling, no offensive odour, cervix closed; abdomen soft, non-tender, no contractions palpable
data_table.Investigations: FBC and CRP within normal limits; amniotic fluid test positive; transabdominal ultrasound single cephalic fetus, AFI reduced

lead_in: What is the most appropriate management bundle?

options.text: Immediate caesarean section regardless of cervical status given the gestation and rupture of membranes today
options.rationale: Caesarean is reserved for established labour with malpresentation, fetal compromise, chorioamnionitis with deteriorating fetus, or other obstetric indication; expectant management is the AU default at this gestation. (Source: RANZCOG PPROM)

options.text: Antenatal corticosteroids, erythromycin 10 days, magnesium sulfate if delivery within 24 hours, and expectant management with daily review
options.rationale: PPROM at 24+0 to 33+6 is managed expectantly with the AU bundle: antenatal corticosteroids (single course, 24 to 34+6 weeks), erythromycin 250 mg orally four times daily for 10 days, magnesium sulfate neuroprotection if delivery is anticipated within 24 hours, and daily clinical and CTG surveillance for chorioamnionitis or fetal compromise. Delivery is planned at 36 to 37 weeks unless infection, abruption, or non-reassuring fetal status intervenes. (Source: RANZCOG PPROM; ACOG)

options.text: Single dose corticosteroids and immediate induction of labour with synthetic oxytocin via continuous infusion
options.rationale: Induction at 31 weeks PPROM accelerates extreme preterm birth without infection drivers; expectant management improves neonatal outcomes. (Source: RANZCOG PPROM)

options.text: Administer tocolysis with nifedipine for 48 hours and discharge home with twice-weekly outpatient surveillance
options.rationale: Tocolysis in PPROM is controversial and limited to enabling steroid completion or in-utero transfer; home discharge is unsafe given infection risk. (Source: RANZCOG PPROM)

options.text: Commence amoxicillin and clavulanic acid orally for 10 days as antibiotic prophylaxis from time of confirmed rupture
options.rationale: Amoxicillin-clavulanate is avoided in PPROM (associated with necrotising enterocolitis in ORACLE-I); erythromycin is the AU first-line agent. (Source: RANZCOG PPROM)

explanation.summary: Preterm prelabour rupture of membranes (PPROM) from 24 to 33+6 weeks is managed expectantly to maximise gestation while monitoring for chorioamnionitis. The AU bundle pairs antenatal corticosteroids, erythromycin (NOT amoxicillin-clavulanate; ORACLE-I showed increased neonatal necrotising enterocolitis), magnesium sulfate neuroprotection within 24 hours of anticipated birth, and inpatient surveillance. Planned delivery is at 36 to 37 weeks. Earlier delivery is indicated for chorioamnionitis, non-reassuring fetal status, or abruption.
key_points: Erythromycin for 10 days; never amoxicillin-clavulanate (NEC risk per ORACLE-I)
Antenatal corticosteroids 24 to 34+6 weeks
Magnesium sulfate neuroprotection if delivery within 24 hours
Plan delivery at 36 to 37 weeks unless infection or compromise
explanation.pearls: Erythromycin 250 mg orally four times daily for 10 days is the AU PPROM prophylactic regimen; amoxicillin-clavulanate is contraindicated by ORACLE-I neonatal necrotising enterocolitis signal.

stem:
A 32-year-old woman attends your reproductive medicine clinic after three first-trimester miscarriages over 18 months, all confirmed by ultrasound as missed miscarriages between 7 and 9 weeks gestation. She had a calf deep vein thrombosis 4 years ago after a long-haul flight, treated with 3 months of warfarin. She is currently not pregnant, has regular menstrual cycles, normal pelvic ultrasound and uterine cavity assessment, and a normal partner semen analysis.

Initial screening 6 weeks ago detected a weakly positive lupus anticoagulant by dilute Russell viper venom time on a single occasion. Anti-cardiolipin IgG and anti-beta2-glycoprotein-I antibodies were both negative. Antinuclear antibody screen was negative. Inherited thrombophilia panel was negative. Karyotype on both partners and products of conception are normal. She asks 'should I just start aspirin and heparin if I get pregnant again?'.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 70, BP 118/74 mmHg, RR 14, SpO2 99% on room air, temperature 36.6 °C
data_table.Examination: Soft non-tender abdomen, no oedema, no rash, no synovitis
data_table.Investigations: Lupus anticoagulant weakly positive (dilute Russell viper venom time) on single sample 6 weeks ago; anti-cardiolipin IgG negative; anti-beta2-glycoprotein-I negative; ANA negative; inherited thrombophilia screen negative; parental karyotype normal; products of conception karyotype normal; pelvic ultrasound normal

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step in management?

options.text: Commence low-dose aspirin and low-molecular-weight heparin now and continue when she next becomes pregnant
options.rationale: Aspirin and heparin combination treats confirmed antiphospholipid syndrome with obstetric criteria; a single weakly positive lupus anticoagulant is not yet diagnostic and the treatment carries bleeding risk without proven benefit until criteria are met. (Source: ISTH; RANZCOG)

options.text: Refer for in vitro fertilisation with preimplantation genetic testing for aneuploidy on every embryo created
options.rationale: Recurrent miscarriage without parental karyotypic abnormality or persistent embryonic aneuploidy does not benefit from PGT-A; this leaps over the diagnostic step. (Source: RANZCOG)

options.text: Commence empirical prednisolone 10 mg daily from a positive pregnancy test for empirical immune modulation
options.rationale: Empirical prednisolone for unexplained recurrent miscarriage is not supported by evidence and increases gestational diabetes and preterm birth risk; specific diagnosis comes first. (Source: RANZCOG)

options.text: Refer for hysteroscopy and adhesion assessment under general anaesthetic prior to any further conception attempt
options.rationale: Uterine cavity has already been assessed as normal on imaging; further hysteroscopy without indication is not warranted. (Source: RANZCOG)

options.text: Repeat the lupus anticoagulant assay 12 weeks after the initial positive sample before any treatment decision
options.rationale: Antiphospholipid syndrome (Sapporo / Sydney criteria) requires PERSISTENT positivity of lupus anticoagulant or anticardiolipin or anti-beta2GP-I, confirmed at least 12 weeks apart, plus an obstetric or vascular criterion. A single positive result can reflect transient post-infective antibodies. Aspirin and heparin commit a woman to anticoagulation across pregnancy and should not be started on a single transient result. (Source: ISTH; RANZCOG)

explanation.summary: Antiphospholipid syndrome is diagnosed by persistent (over 12 weeks apart) positivity of lupus anticoagulant, anti-cardiolipin, or anti-beta2-glycoprotein-I antibodies, plus obstetric criteria (three or more first-trimester losses, one or more second-trimester loss, or early severe pre-eclampsia or placental insufficiency) or vascular criteria (arterial or venous thromboembolism). A single positive result can be transiently provoked by infection. Treatment of obstetric APS with low-dose aspirin and prophylactic low-molecular-weight heparin requires confirmed diagnosis; a transient positive does not justify the bleeding and procedural cost.
key_points: APS diagnosis: persistent positivity 12 weeks apart PLUS clinical criterion
Treat obstetric APS with aspirin + LMWH; never empirically
Single positive lupus anticoagulant: repeat in 12 weeks before labelling
Inherited thrombophilia testing not indicated for unexplained recurrent miscarriage
explanation.pearls: The Sapporo (Sydney) criteria require two persistent positive results at least 12 weeks apart - single positive lupus anticoagulant is not enough to label antiphospholipid syndrome or to start anticoagulation.

stem:
A 28-year-old primigravida at 34+4 weeks gestation is admitted to your delivery suite with a 1-day history of frontal headache and right upper quadrant pain. Her midwife says 'her blood pressure has been creeping up and the protein-creatinine ratio came back high'. She has had three booking visits with normal blood pressure and a normal 20-week morphology scan. She has no history of seizures and no chronic hypertension.

On examination she is alert, GCS 15, with normal cranial nerves. Reflexes are brisk symmetrically with 2 beats of clonus at both ankles. Abdomen is gravid with mild right upper quadrant tenderness and a single live fetus on cardiotocography with a reassuring trace. Her vital signs include BP 168/112 mmHg confirmed on repeat manual reading 15 minutes apart. Bloods show platelets 122 x10^9/L (150-450), ALT 96 U/L (under 35), creatinine 88 micromol/L (45-90), urate 0.42 mmol/L (0.16-0.36), and urine protein-to-creatinine ratio 78 mg/mmol (under 30).

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 92, BP 168/112 mmHg confirmed on repeat manual reading, RR 18, SpO2 98% on room air, temperature 36.7 °C, fetal HR 142 bpm reassuring
data_table.Examination: Alert, GCS 15, brisk reflexes with 2 beats clonus bilaterally, RUQ tenderness, gravid abdomen, single fetus on CTG
data_table.Investigations: Platelets 122 x10^9/L (150-450), ALT 96 U/L (under 35), creatinine 88 micromol/L (45-90), urate 0.42 mmol/L (0.16-0.36), urine PCR 78 mg/mmol (under 30)
data_table.Medications: Nil regular antenatally; intravenous labetalol bolus 20 mg given prior to your review

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next pharmacological step?

options.text: Commence intravenous magnesium sulfate loading 4 g over 20 minutes then 1 g per hour as eclampsia prophylaxis
options.rationale: Severe pre-eclampsia (severe-range BP plus end-organ involvement) requires magnesium sulfate seizure prophylaxis: 4 g IV loading over 20 minutes followed by 1 g/hour infusion. Magnesium is continued for 24 hours after delivery or after the last seizure. Calcium gluconate is the antidote for toxicity. (Source: RANZCOG; SOMANZ Hypertension in Pregnancy)

options.text: Add oral nifedipine immediate release for ongoing blood pressure control without seizure prophylaxis cover
options.rationale: Antihypertensive therapy controls severe BP but does not reduce seizure risk; magnesium prophylaxis is indicated in severe disease. (Source: SOMANZ Hypertension in Pregnancy)

options.text: Commence intravenous phenytoin loading dose for seizure prophylaxis instead of magnesium sulfate
options.rationale: Phenytoin is inferior to magnesium for eclampsia seizure prevention; magnesium is the AU and international first-line. (Source: SOMANZ Hypertension in Pregnancy)

options.text: Hold further therapy pending repeat blood pressure in 30 minutes and bedside ultrasound for fetal wellbeing
options.rationale: BP is already confirmed severe-range on repeat measurement; further delay risks eclampsia and acute hypertensive complications. (Source: SOMANZ Hypertension in Pregnancy)

options.text: Administer intramuscular betamethasone alone for fetal lung maturation and arrange transfer to tertiary unit
options.rationale: Antenatal corticosteroids are given for delivery anticipated within 7 days at 34 weeks or earlier, but magnesium prophylaxis is concurrent and not deferred for steroids. (Source: RANZCOG)

explanation.summary: Pre-eclampsia is new-onset hypertension at or after 20 weeks gestation with end-organ dysfunction (renal, hepatic, neurological, haematological, fetal growth restriction, placental). Severe features include BP at or above 160/110 mmHg, severe headache, visual disturbance, epigastric pain, pulmonary oedema, hepatocellular dysfunction, thrombocytopaenia, renal injury, or eclamptic seizure. Magnesium sulfate 4 g IV load then 1 g/hour reduces seizure risk by half and is the AU first-line. Antihypertensive control targets BP under 160/110 mmHg without overshoot to preserve placental perfusion.
key_points: Severe features include BP >=160/110 mmHg confirmed on repeat
Magnesium sulfate 4 g IV load then 1 g/hour for prophylaxis
Continue magnesium for 24 hours after delivery or last seizure
Calcium gluconate is the antidote for magnesium toxicity
explanation.pearls: Magnesium toxicity progression: loss of patellar reflex around 4 mmol/L, respiratory depression at 6 mmol/L, cardiac arrest above 12 mmol/L; calcium gluconate 1 g IV is the antidote.

stem:
A 32-year-old G3P3 has just had a normal vaginal birth at 39+5 weeks gestation. The placenta delivered intact 12 minutes ago and the midwife says 'the uterus feels boggy and there's a steady fresh red trickle of blood'. Estimated blood loss is now 800 mL and continuing. Active management of the third stage was used with intramuscular oxytocin 10 IU.

On examination her airway is patent, she is talking but slightly anxious, and her conjunctivae are pink. The fundus is palpable above the umbilicus and not contracted. The vulva and lower vagina are inspected and there are no genital tract lacerations needing suture; the placenta is intact when re-examined. Bedside coagulation testing has been sent and is pending. Bimanual uterine massage has been initiated and the bladder has been emptied with a urinary catheter that has just been inserted. Intravenous access is established with a 16 G cannula running 0.9% sodium chloride.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 108 regular, BP 102/64 mmHg, RR 18, SpO2 99% on room air, temperature 36.7 °C
data_table.Examination: Boggy poorly contracted uterus above the umbilicus, no perineal laceration, placenta inspected and intact, fresh red ongoing trickle, catheter inserted, 16 G IV access
data_table.Investigations: FBC, coags, fibrinogen, group and hold sent; bedside lactate 2.1 mmol/L (under 2.0)
data_table.Medications: Active third stage included intramuscular oxytocin 10 IU

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next pharmacological step?

options.text: Administer intravenous oxytocin 5 IU slowly then commence an oxytocin infusion 40 IU in 1000 mL over 4 hours
options.rationale: Uterine atony is the most common cause of primary postpartum haemorrhage. First-line pharmacological treatment after concurrent uterine massage and bladder emptying is intravenous oxytocin 5 IU slowly followed by an oxytocin infusion; ergometrine, carboprost, and intramyometrial carboprost are the next steps if atony persists. Tranexamic acid is given in parallel within 3 hours of onset. (Source: RANZCOG PPH Statement; AMH)

options.text: Inject intramuscular ergometrine 250 mcg without prior assessment of blood pressure or pre-eclampsia history
options.rationale: Ergometrine is a second-line uterotonic and is contraindicated in hypertension or pre-eclampsia; oxytocin is preferred first. (Source: AMH)

options.text: Administer rectal misoprostol 800 mcg as the only uterotonic without intravenous oxytocin or massage
options.rationale: Misoprostol is a useful adjunct, particularly in low-resource settings, but is not the AU first-line when intravenous oxytocin is available. (Source: RANZCOG PPH Statement)

options.text: Proceed directly to balloon tamponade with a Bakri balloon as the first step in pharmacological management
options.rationale: Balloon tamponade is a non-pharmacological adjunct used after first-line uterotonics fail to control bleeding; uterotonic escalation precedes it. (Source: RANZCOG PPH Statement)

options.text: Withhold further uterotonics and observe for spontaneous uterine contraction over the next 15 minutes
options.rationale: Ongoing bleeding with uterine atony requires escalation; observation worsens haemodynamic compromise. (Source: RANZCOG PPH Statement)

explanation.summary: Primary postpartum haemorrhage is blood loss greater than 500 mL after vaginal birth or greater than 1000 mL after caesarean within 24 hours; the 4 Ts framework identifies tone, trauma, tissue, and thrombin causes. Atony is the commonest cause. Management is concurrent (call for help, two large-bore IVs, FBC/coags/fibrinogen/group and hold/crossmatch, massage, empty bladder, uterotonic escalation, tranexamic acid within 3 hours). The uterotonic ladder is oxytocin then ergometrine (if no hypertension) then carboprost (if no asthma) then intrauterine balloon tamponade then surgical interventions. Tranexamic acid is given regardless of the immediate cause within the 3-hour window.
key_points: 4 Ts: tone, trauma, tissue, thrombin
Uterotonic ladder: oxytocin -> ergometrine (no hypertension) -> carboprost (no asthma)
Tranexamic acid 1 g IV within 3 hours of onset
Balloon tamponade after uterotonic failure
explanation.pearls: Carboprost (PGF2alpha) 250 mcg intramuscular every 15 minutes up to 8 doses is reserved for atony refractory to oxytocin and ergometrine; it is contraindicated in asthma.

stem:
A 22-year-old woman attends your general practice clinic for advice about missed combined oral contraceptive pills. She says 'I forgot two active pills in a row, the ones in the second week of the packet, and we had sex 24 hours after the second missed pill without protection'. She has been on the same monophasic 30 microgram ethinylestradiol pill for 18 months with no breakthrough bleeding. Her last menstrual period started on day 1 of her current packet 9 days ago.

She has no recent illness, no diarrhoea or vomiting, and is not taking any enzyme-inducing medication. She has not had unprotected sex earlier in the cycle. She wishes to continue the pill but is anxious about pregnancy risk. She has no past history of venous thromboembolism, migraine with aura, or breast cancer. Her BMI is 24 kg/m squared. She asks whether she needs emergency contraception now, when to start her next packet, and how to handle the rest of this packet.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 74, BP 118/76 mmHg, RR 14, SpO2 99% on room air, temperature 36.8 °C
data_table.Examination: Well, no abdominal tenderness, no breast lump on screening
data_table.Investigations: Urinary pregnancy test today negative
data_table.Medications: Monophasic combined oral contraceptive 30 mcg ethinylestradiol; no enzyme inducers

lead_in: What is the single best management plan?

options.text: Take the most recent missed pill, continue the rest of the packet, and omit the inactive pills at packet end
options.rationale: For 2 missed combined pills in week 2, the user takes the most recent missed pill, continues the rest of the packet, and goes straight from the active pills into the next packet without taking the inactive (placebo) pills. Emergency contraception is NOT required when 7 consecutive active pills have been taken in the week before the missed pills. (Source: RANZCOG; Family Planning Australia)

options.text: Take the most recent missed pill, finish the current packet, and use condoms for the next 7 days as backup
options.rationale: This plan misses the key step of skipping the inactive pills between packets to prevent ovulation; condoms alone do not address the loss of pituitary suppression. (Source: Family Planning Australia)

options.text: Stop the current pill packet immediately, give emergency contraception now, and restart pills next cycle
options.rationale: Stopping the pill removes ongoing contraceptive cover and worsens pregnancy risk; the missed-pill rules continue the packet rather than discarding it. (Source: Family Planning Australia)

options.text: Provide ulipristal acetate emergency contraception, continue current pills, and use condoms for 5 days
options.rationale: Ulipristal is reserved for cases where 7 consecutive active pills have not been taken before the missed pills, or other criteria are met; it is not required for missed pills in week 2 with preceding pill-taking. (Source: AMH; Family Planning Australia)

options.text: Take both missed pills together with the next scheduled pill and continue the inactive pills as planned
options.rationale: Doubling up the missed pill is acceptable, but continuing the inactive pills between packets re-introduces a hormone-free interval and risks ovulation; skip the inactive pills. (Source: Family Planning Australia)

explanation.summary: Combined oral contraceptive missed-pill rules depend on how many pills are missed and where in the cycle. Missing 1 pill at any time: take it as soon as possible and continue. Missing 2 or more in week 1: take the most recent missed pill, continue, use condoms for 7 days, and consider emergency contraception if there was unprotected sex during the hormone-free interval or week 1. Missing 2 or more in week 2: take the most recent missed pill and continue (no emergency contraception needed if 7 consecutive active pills were taken before). Missing 2 or more in week 3: skip the inactive pills and go straight to the next packet. Vomiting within 2 hours or severe diarrhoea is equivalent to missing a pill.
key_points: Missed 2 in week 2 with prior 7 consecutive active pills: no emergency contraception needed
Missed 2 in week 3: skip inactive pills to next packet
Vomiting within 2 hours or severe diarrhoea equates to missed pill
Enzyme inducers reduce efficacy - alternative method recommended
explanation.pearls: Levonorgestrel emergency contraception 1.5 mg is most effective within 72 hours; ulipristal acetate 30 mg extends the window to 120 hours and is more effective at the late end.

subtopic_detail: Gestational diabetes diagnosis and insulin initiation
stem:
A 31-year-old G2P1 at 28+2 weeks gestation attends your antenatal clinic for review of her oral glucose tolerance test results. She is asymptomatic. Her previous pregnancy was uncomplicated with a baby weighing 3.4 kg born at term. Her BMI is 30 kg/m squared and she has no personal history of impaired glucose tolerance.

Her 75 g OGTT results are: fasting venous plasma glucose 5.4 mmol/L (under 5.1), 1-hour 11.4 mmol/L (under 10.0), 2-hour 8.9 mmol/L (under 8.5). Antenatal blood pressure has been normal. The 28-week scan shows estimated fetal weight on the 60th centile, normal amniotic fluid index, and normal umbilical artery Dopplers. She has commenced ADIPS-style structured education with the diabetes educator and lifestyle measures for 2 weeks. A home glucose diary shows fasting glucose values consistently 5.6 to 5.9 mmol/L and 2-hour postprandial values 8.2 to 9.4 mmol/L, despite good adherence to dietary advice.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 84, BP 118/72 mmHg, RR 16, SpO2 99% on room air, temperature 36.7 °C, fetal HR 148 bpm
data_table.Examination: Symphysis-fundal height 28 cm, no oedema, no contractions
data_table.Investigations: 75 g OGTT fasting 5.4 mmol/L (under 5.1), 1-hour 11.4 mmol/L (under 10.0), 2-hour 8.9 mmol/L (under 8.5); home glucose diary fasting 5.6-5.9 and postprandial 8.2-9.4 mmol/L

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step?

options.text: Continue lifestyle measures alone for a further 2 weeks before any consideration of pharmacological treatment
options.rationale: After a 1-2 week lifestyle trial with persistent fasting glucose above target and postprandial values above target, pharmacological therapy is indicated; further delay accumulates fetal exposure to hyperglycaemia. (Source: ADIPS Gestational Diabetes Guideline)

options.text: Commence subcutaneous insulin therapy with isophane (NPH) at night and short-acting insulin with main meals
options.rationale: Insulin is the first-line pharmacological agent for gestational diabetes failing lifestyle measures in Australia. A basal-bolus regimen with isophane at night for fasting hyperglycaemia and rapid-acting insulin with meals for postprandial hyperglycaemia is the AU standard. Metformin can be added or used as an alternative based on patient preference and access. (Source: ADIPS Gestational Diabetes Guideline; AMH)

options.text: Commence empirical glibenclamide as oral hypoglycaemic monotherapy without a discussion of insulin alternative
options.rationale: Glibenclamide crosses the placenta and is not recommended as first-line gestational diabetes therapy in Australia; insulin and metformin are preferred. (Source: ADIPS Gestational Diabetes Guideline)

options.text: Repeat the oral glucose tolerance test in 4 weeks to confirm gestational diabetes before any treatment escalation
options.rationale: GDM is a single-test diagnosis when ADIPS thresholds are met; repeating the OGTT delays fetal protection. (Source: ADIPS Gestational Diabetes Guideline)

options.text: Plan induction of labour at 37+0 weeks irrespective of current glycaemic control or fetal growth trajectory
options.rationale: Timing of birth in GDM is individualised on glycaemic control, fetal growth, and other obstetric risk; routine 37-week induction is not the AU default for diet-controlled GDM and most insulin-treated cases proceed to 38-39 weeks. (Source: ADIPS Gestational Diabetes Guideline)

explanation.summary: Gestational diabetes is diagnosed by 75 g OGTT at 24-28 weeks with the ADIPS-WHO thresholds: fasting at or above 5.1 mmol/L, 1-hour at or above 10.0 mmol/L, or 2-hour at or above 8.5 mmol/L. Lifestyle measures (medical nutrition therapy, exercise, glucose monitoring) are first-line for 1-2 weeks. Insulin is the AU first-line pharmacological therapy with basal-bolus regimens for persistent fasting and postprandial hyperglycaemia. Metformin is an acceptable alternative or adjunct. Timing of birth is individualised on glycaemia, fetal growth, and other obstetric factors.
key_points: ADIPS criteria: fasting 5.1, 1-hour 10.0, 2-hour 8.5 mmol/L
Lifestyle trial 1-2 weeks before pharmacological escalation
Insulin first-line; metformin alternative or adjunct
Avoid glibenclamide in Australia
explanation.pearls: Postnatal 75 g OGTT at 6-12 weeks postpartum is recommended for all gestational diabetes pregnancies to detect persistent dysglycaemia; up to half develop type 2 diabetes within 10 years.

stem:
A 34-year-old G3P2 at 30+5 weeks gestation is brought by ambulance with a 2-hour history of painless bright red fresh vaginal bleeding. She says 'I noticed a gush of blood when I went to the toilet, no warning, no pain'. Estimated blood loss at home was about 200 mL and continues as a steady trickle. She has had two previous lower-segment caesarean births.

On examination she is anxious but talking, with no abdominal pain or tenderness. The uterus is soft and non-irritable. Speculum examination has NOT been performed yet. Fetal heart rate is reassuring with no decelerations on cardiotocography. Her 20-week morphology scan reported a posterior placenta with the lower edge 8 mm from the internal os. A repeat scan at 28 weeks confirmed placental edge covering the internal os (Grade 4 placenta praevia) with hyperechoic placental lacunae and loss of clear zone, raising suspicion of placenta accreta spectrum.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 108 regular, BP 108/64 mmHg, RR 20, SpO2 99% on room air, temperature 36.8 °C, fetal HR 142 bpm reassuring on CTG
data_table.Examination: Soft non-tender non-irritable uterus, fresh ongoing trickle visible at vulva, no speculum or digital examination performed
data_table.Investigations: FBC, coags, fibrinogen, group and screen sent; bedside Hb 108 g/L; 28-week scan: placenta covering os (Grade 4 praevia) with lacunae and loss of clear zone

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step?

options.text: Perform a digital vaginal examination to assess the cervix and the cause of the antepartum haemorrhage
options.rationale: Digital vaginal examination is contraindicated in suspected or known placenta praevia until placenta praevia has been excluded by imaging; it precipitates catastrophic haemorrhage. (Source: RANZCOG Placenta Praevia and Accreta)

options.text: Admit, secure two large-bore IV cannulae, administer antenatal corticosteroids, and arrange tertiary transfer
options.rationale: Confirmed placenta praevia at 30+5 with active bleeding requires admission, resuscitation, two large-bore IVs, FBC/coags/group and screen, and Rh anti-D if Rh negative. Antenatal corticosteroids (betamethasone 11.4 mg IM two doses 24 hours apart) are given for fetal lung maturation. Magnesium sulfate is considered for neuroprotection if delivery within 24 hours is anticipated under 30 weeks. Transfer to a unit with paediatric ICU and accreta-spectrum surgical expertise is required given the suspected accreta. (Source: RANZCOG Placenta Praevia and Accreta)

options.text: Proceed immediately to emergency caesarean delivery under general anaesthetic regardless of maternal stability
options.rationale: Emergency caesarean is reserved for maternal compromise, non-reassuring fetal status, or torrential haemorrhage; this woman is currently stable and the fetus is reassuring, allowing time for steroids and tertiary transfer. (Source: RANZCOG Placenta Praevia and Accreta)

options.text: Discharge home after bleeding settles with strict bed rest, daily kick chart, and review in 1 week clinic
options.rationale: A first significant antepartum haemorrhage from placenta praevia, particularly with suspected accreta and two prior caesareans, requires inpatient observation and surgical planning rather than outpatient management. (Source: RANZCOG Placenta Praevia and Accreta)

options.text: Commence intramuscular ergometrine 250 mcg for uterine tone in suspected placental abruption with bleeding
options.rationale: Ergometrine is contraindicated in pregnancy outside the third stage; this presentation is also not abruption (which is painful, with a tender uterus and concealed component possible). (Source: AMH)

explanation.summary: Placenta praevia is placental implantation in the lower uterine segment overlying the internal os. It presents as painless bright red vaginal bleeding, typically in the third trimester. Definitive diagnosis is by transvaginal ultrasound. Two or more prior caesarean births raise placenta accreta spectrum risk substantially; antenatal ultrasound features include lacunae, loss of the retroplacental clear zone, abnormal bladder-uterine interface, and bridging vessels. Management is admission, resuscitation, antenatal corticosteroids 24+0 to 34+6 weeks, magnesium for neuroprotection if under 30+0 weeks within 24 hours of birth, and elective caesarean delivery at 36-37 weeks in a tertiary unit (earlier if recurrent bleeding).
key_points: Painless bright red bleeding - never digital examination until praevia excluded
Two or more prior caesareans raise accreta risk; image with TVUS and MRI
Antenatal corticosteroids 24+0 to 34+6
Elective caesarean 36-37 weeks in tertiary unit
explanation.pearls: Antenatal betamethasone 11.4 mg intramuscular two doses 24 hours apart reduces neonatal respiratory distress, intraventricular haemorrhage, necrotising enterocolitis, and mortality between 24+0 and 34+6 weeks.

stem:
A 30-year-old G2P1 at 37+0 weeks gestation with a dichorionic diamniotic (DCDA) twin pregnancy attends your antenatal clinic for delivery planning. Her pregnancy has been uncomplicated. Both fetuses are cephalic on this morning's growth scan, with concordant estimated fetal weights (twin 1 estimated 2.8 kg, twin 2 estimated 2.7 kg, both above the 10th centile). Amniotic fluid volumes are normal in both sacs and umbilical artery Dopplers are normal.

She has no prior caesarean and her previous singleton birth was a spontaneous vaginal delivery at term. Maternal blood pressure has been normal throughout. There is no diabetes, no cholestasis, and no growth restriction. The booking ultrasound at 11+3 weeks documented dichorionic diamniotic placentation with a lambda sign. She is keen for vaginal birth if safe and asks about timing.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 78, BP 116/72 mmHg, RR 16, SpO2 99% on room air, temperature 36.7 °C, twin 1 HR 138 bpm, twin 2 HR 144 bpm
data_table.Examination: Symphysis-fundal height 40 cm, both twins cephalic on scan, no contractions
data_table.Investigations: Growth scan today: twin 1 EFW 2.8 kg (>10th), twin 2 EFW 2.7 kg (>10th), normal AFI and umbilical Dopplers both

lead_in: What is the most appropriate plan for timing of birth?

options.text: Plan elective caesarean delivery at 36+0 weeks gestation regardless of presentation of the twins
options.rationale: DCDA twins with twin 1 cephalic do not routinely require caesarean and 36+0 weeks is earlier than the AU recommended timing of birth for uncomplicated DCDA. (Source: RANZCOG Multiple Pregnancy)

options.text: Recommend planned birth at 37+0 to 38+0 weeks gestation by mode appropriate to fetal presentation at the time
options.rationale: Uncomplicated DCDA twins are recommended for planned birth at 37+0 to 38+0 weeks gestation in Australia; continuing pregnancy beyond this raises stillbirth risk relative to comparable singletons. Mode of birth is guided by twin 1 presentation: cephalic twin 1 allows planned vaginal birth (with continuous fetal monitoring of both twins and an obstetrician immediately available for twin 2). (Source: RANZCOG Multiple Pregnancy; Royal Women's Hospital Vic Multiple Pregnancy Guideline)
source_refs: Royal Women's Hospital Vic Multiple Pregnancy Guideline

options.text: Defer until 40+0 weeks gestation provided cardiotocography, growth, and Dopplers remain normal weekly
options.rationale: DCDA twins beyond 38 weeks have higher stillbirth risk than comparable singletons; routine continuation to 40 weeks is not the AU position. (Source: RANZCOG Multiple Pregnancy)

options.text: Plan elective caesarean delivery at 38+0 weeks gestation because both twins are cephalic and concordant
options.rationale: Cephalic-cephalic concordant uncomplicated DCDA twins are candidates for planned vaginal birth; caesarean is not the default. (Source: RANZCOG Multiple Pregnancy)

options.text: Plan vaginal birth at 39+0 to 40+0 weeks regardless of presentations because the pregnancy has been uneventful
options.rationale: Even uneventful DCDA twin pregnancies are advised birth at 37+0 to 38+0 weeks; the increased stillbirth risk in twin pregnancies past this point is documented in AU and international cohorts. (Source: RANZCOG Multiple Pregnancy)

explanation.summary: Twin pregnancy timing of birth depends on chorionicity. Uncomplicated dichorionic diamniotic (DCDA): plan birth 37+0 to 38+0 weeks. Uncomplicated monochorionic diamniotic (MCDA): plan birth 36+0 to 37+0 weeks. Monochorionic monoamniotic (MCMA): plan caesarean 32+0 to 34+0 weeks. Mode of birth is guided by twin 1 presentation: cephalic twin 1 is candidate for vaginal birth with continuous monitoring of both fetuses and immediate obstetric availability for twin 2. Twin 2 management options include cephalic-cephalic delivery, breech extraction, or internal podalic version with breech extraction (operator-skill dependent).
key_points: DCDA: birth 37+0 to 38+0 weeks
MCDA: birth 36+0 to 37+0 weeks
MCMA: planned caesarean 32+0 to 34+0 weeks
Cephalic twin 1: planned vaginal birth candidate
explanation.pearls: For cephalic-cephalic DCDA twins, the inter-delivery interval target for twin 2 is under 30 minutes; longer intervals correlate with acidosis and may prompt operative delivery of twin 2.

sources.label: Royal Women's Hospital Vic Multiple Pregnancy Guideline

subtopic_detail: Adnexal mass risk of malignancy assessment
stem:
A 58-year-old postmenopausal woman attends your general gynaecology clinic with 6 weeks of vague bloating and early satiety. She says 'my pants feel tight at the waistband, my appetite is off, and food sits in me for ages'. There is no abnormal vaginal bleeding, no haematuria, and no abdominal pain. Her mother and maternal aunt had breast cancer; she does not know whether either had ovarian cancer. She had a normal age-appropriate Cervical Screening Test 1 year ago.

On examination her abdomen is mildly distended without ascites detectable clinically. Bimanual examination palpates a non-tender right adnexal mass approximately 10 cm in diameter. Pelvic ultrasound performed by the radiology department reports a 9 by 8 by 7 cm right ovarian mass with multilocular solid components, papillary projections more than 7 mm, no acoustic shadowing, and Doppler colour score 4 (very strong vascularity); ascites volume mild. Serum CA-125 is 480 kU/L (under 35) and HE4 is markedly raised. ROMA score is in the high-risk range.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 78, BP 132/82 mmHg, RR 16, SpO2 98% on room air, temperature 36.8 °C
data_table.Examination: Mildly distended abdomen, mild shifting dullness equivocal, non-tender right adnexal mass approximately 10 cm bimanually
data_table.Investigations: TVUS: 9x8x7 cm right ovarian multilocular solid mass with papillary projections >7 mm, Doppler colour score 4, mild ascites; CA-125 480 kU/L (under 35); HE4 raised; ROMA high-risk; FBC and UEC within normal limits

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step?

options.text: Refer urgently to a gynaecological oncologist for staging laparotomy and intraoperative tumour assessment
