options.rationale: A complex adnexal mass with papillary projections, multilocular solid components, Doppler colour score 4, ascites, and raised CA-125 with high-risk ROMA in a postmenopausal woman is high risk for ovarian malignancy. Cancer Council Australia recommends referral to gynaecological oncology for staging laparotomy; outcomes are improved when surgery is performed by a gynaecological oncologist. Image-guided biopsy is generally avoided to prevent peritoneal seeding. (Source: Cancer Council Australia Ovarian Cancer Guideline; RANZCOG)
source_refs: Cancer Council Australia Ovarian Cancer Guideline

options.text: Arrange image-guided percutaneous biopsy of the ovarian mass before any operative management discussion
options.rationale: Percutaneous biopsy of an ovarian mass risks peritoneal seeding and upstaging; surgical staging is the standard initial approach. (Source: Cancer Council Australia Ovarian Cancer Guideline)
source_refs: Cancer Council Australia Ovarian Cancer Guideline

options.text: Trial 3 months of cyclical combined oral contraceptive therapy to assess for functional cyst regression
options.rationale: Functional cysts are uncommon in postmenopausal women and are resolved with observation rather than cyclical hormones; this mass is high risk for malignancy. (Source: RANZCOG)

options.text: Repeat pelvic ultrasound and CA-125 measurement in 6 weeks before referring for any specialist opinion
options.rationale: Repeating imaging in a high-risk mass delays diagnosis and definitive surgery; the high-risk findings already warrant gynaecological oncology referral now. (Source: Cancer Council Australia Ovarian Cancer Guideline)
source_refs: Cancer Council Australia Ovarian Cancer Guideline

options.text: Commence empirical letrozole therapy for presumed oestrogen-driven ovarian neoplasm before surgical evaluation
options.rationale: Letrozole is used in selected hormone-receptor positive ovarian and endometrial cancers, generally adjuvant or for recurrent disease, not as empirical pre-surgical therapy on imaging alone. (Source: eviQ)

explanation.summary: Ovarian malignancy is suspected when an adnexal mass has complex sonographic features (multilocular solid, papillary projections, irregular borders, Doppler colour score 3-4, ascites) and tumour marker elevation (CA-125 in postmenopausal women, HE4, ROMA, IOTA simple rules). Risk assessment integrates clinical, imaging, and biochemical features. High-risk masses are referred to a gynaecological oncologist for staging laparotomy. Genetic testing (BRCA1/2, BRIP1, RAD51C/D, MMR genes) is offered routinely on diagnosis of non-mucinous epithelial ovarian cancer in Australia, with cascade family testing if positive.
key_points: Complex features: papillary projections, Doppler colour 3-4, ascites
Refer to gynaecological oncology for staging laparotomy
Avoid percutaneous biopsy in suspected ovarian malignancy
Routine BRCA1/2 testing on non-mucinous epithelial ovarian cancer diagnosis
explanation.pearls: Even non-familial high-grade serous ovarian cancer at any age warrants BRCA1/2 testing in Australia at diagnosis; up to 15% carry a germline pathogenic variant relevant for PARP inhibitor eligibility.

sources.label: Cancer Council Australia Ovarian Cancer Guideline

stem:
You are the obstetric registrar at a regional referral hospital. You are called to a labour room at 3 am for a 26-year-old G2P1 at 36+4 weeks gestation. She has spontaneous rupture of membranes 5 minutes ago. The midwife says 'when her waters broke I could see a loop of cord at the introitus, and the heart rate has dropped'. The baby was breech on the morning scan and she had been awaiting external cephalic version this week.

On examination the cord is visible and pulsatile at the introitus. The presenting part is high and not engaged. Cardiotocography shows a sustained fetal bradycardia at 70 bpm without recovery for the past 3 minutes. The cervix is 5 cm dilated. The mother has no epidural in situ and has had no recent oral intake. Theatre is on the same floor and immediately accessible; anaesthetic and paediatric teams have been activated. She is haemodynamically stable. There is no PPH and no bleeding. The cord pH from a small sample is not available.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 96, BP 124/76 mmHg, RR 18, SpO2 99% on room air, temperature 36.8 °C, fetal HR sustained 70 bpm on CTG
data_table.Examination: Pulsatile cord visible at introitus, presenting part high, breech presentation, cervix 5 cm dilated, no PPH
data_table.Investigations: Fetal heart trace shows sustained bradycardia; no cord pH available; cross-match pending

lead_in: What is the most appropriate immediate single best action?

options.text: Manually elevate the presenting part to relieve cord compression and proceed to emergency caesarean delivery now
options.rationale: Cord prolapse with fetal bradycardia is a category 1 (immediate-threat) obstetric emergency. The immediate manoeuvre is manual elevation of the presenting part off the cord (using a fist or by filling the bladder with 500-700 mL warmed saline through a catheter that is then clamped) while urgently transferring to theatre for category 1 caesarean. The knee-chest or Trendelenburg position can complement bladder filling. Tocolysis (terbutaline 250 mcg subcutaneous) may be considered if delay is anticipated. (Source: RANZCOG Cord Prolapse; Royal Women's Vic)

options.text: Attempt manual cord reduction back through the cervix into the uterus and proceed with vaginal breech delivery
options.rationale: Manual cord reduction is not recommended; it traumatises the cord and rarely succeeds. The cervix is not fully dilated and vaginal breech is not feasible. (Source: RANZCOG Cord Prolapse)

options.text: Wrap the prolapsed cord in warmed saline gauze, attempt vaginal examination repeatedly, and observe in delivery suite
options.rationale: Warming and protecting the cord is reasonable adjunct care, but observation rather than immediate caesarean during sustained bradycardia is unsafe. (Source: RANZCOG Cord Prolapse)

options.text: Commence intravenous terbutaline as tocolysis and arrange routine category 2 caesarean within 75 minutes
options.rationale: Fetal bradycardia with cord prolapse is category 1 (decision-to-delivery interval target 30 minutes), not category 2; tocolysis is a delay-only adjunct, not a substitute for category 1 timing. (Source: RANZCOG Cord Prolapse)

options.text: Wait 5 minutes for spontaneous heart rate recovery before deciding between vaginal breech and operative delivery
options.rationale: Each minute of sustained fetal bradycardia at the level seen risks irreversible hypoxic injury; delay is not appropriate. (Source: RANZCOG Cord Prolapse)

explanation.summary: Umbilical cord prolapse is the descent of the cord through the cervix beyond the presenting part with ruptured membranes, leading to cord compression and fetal hypoxia. Risk factors include malpresentation (breech, transverse), polyhydramnios, prematurity, multiple pregnancy, low-lying placenta, and procedures that destabilise the presenting part (amniotomy with high head, external cephalic version, manual rotation). Diagnosis is by visual inspection of cord at the introitus or palpation on vaginal examination after rupture of membranes with abnormal fetal heart rate. Management is category 1 caesarean while relieving compression by manual elevation, bladder filling, knee-chest position, and tocolysis if delay is unavoidable.
key_points: Manual elevation, bladder filling, knee-chest position to relieve compression
Category 1 caesarean target decision-to-delivery 30 minutes
Tocolysis (terbutaline) for unavoidable delay only
Avoid handling the prolapsed cord more than necessary
explanation.pearls: Bladder filling with 500-700 mL of warmed saline through a catheter (then clamped) elevates the presenting part for transfer, comparable to manual elevation and freeing hands for theatre preparation.

stem:
A 27-year-old G2P1 at 39+2 weeks gestation is in your delivery suite in active second stage of labour with vertex presentation. The midwife performs a vaginal examination after a sudden gush of fluid and calls you saying 'there's a pulsating loop of cord palpable past the vertex and the fetal heart rate has dropped'. The cervix is fully dilated and the head is at station plus 1.

On examination she is alert and lying on her back. She has had an uncomplicated antenatal course apart from gestational hypertension controlled on labetalol. Her last vaginal examination 30 minutes ago showed full dilatation and station plus 1. The CTG had been reactive prior to the current event. The on-call obstetric consultant and anaesthetist are 3 minutes away. The theatre is empty and ready for a category 1 caesarean if needed. The bladder is empty. Her epidural is functioning well with adequate sensory block to the umbilicus.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 108, BP 134/82 mmHg, RR 18, SpO2 99% on room air, temperature 36.7 °C, fetal HR 70 bpm sustained
data_table.Examination: Cervix fully dilated, head at station plus 1, pulsating cord palpable past the vertex, intact membranes ruptured
data_table.Investigations: CTG previously reactive, now sustained bradycardia fetal HR 70 bpm
data_table.Medications: Epidural with adequate block to umbilicus

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step?

options.text: Place the mother in steep Trendelenburg position and arrange transfer to theatre for category 1 caesarean section
options.rationale: Category 1 caesarean is the default route for cord prolapse with fetal compromise when birth is not imminent, but when the cervix is fully dilated with low station, instrumental vaginal birth may be faster and is the preferred route here. (Source: RANZCOG Cord Prolapse Statement)

options.text: Manually elevate the presenting part with a gloved hand and fill the bladder with 500-700 mL of saline
options.rationale: Manual elevation and bladder filling are correct temporising measures when caesarean is the planned route, but when the cervix is fully dilated with the head at +1, instrumental vaginal birth is faster than transfer to theatre. (Source: RANZCOG Cord Prolapse Statement)

options.text: Proceed to immediate instrumental vaginal birth with vacuum or forceps assistance in the delivery room now
options.rationale: Cord prolapse with a fully dilated cervix and low station (+1 or lower) in an effective epidural with cooperative mother allows operative vaginal birth to be quicker than caesarean. Delivery time is the prime determinant of fetal outcome; the fastest safe route is the right route. Instrumental delivery is the AU recommended approach in this configuration. (Source: RANZCOG Cord Prolapse Statement; RANZCOG Instrumental Vaginal Birth Statement)

options.text: Push the cord back above the presenting part and continue active second stage with directed pushing efforts
options.rationale: Attempting to replace the cord is associated with vasospasm and worsening fetal compromise; the cord is kept warm and unhandled while the route of delivery is decided. (Source: RANZCOG Cord Prolapse Statement)

options.text: Administer intravenous terbutaline 250 microgram tocolysis and arrange urgent magnetic resonance imaging
options.rationale: Tocolysis is used to facilitate transfer to theatre when caesarean is the planned route; imaging has no place in acute cord prolapse management. (Source: RANZCOG Cord Prolapse Statement)

explanation.summary: Umbilical cord prolapse is an obstetric emergency. Management hinges on the fastest safe route to deliver the baby and minimise cord compression. When the cervix is not fully dilated, category 1 caesarean is the route, with concurrent manual elevation of the presenting part, knee-chest or steep Trendelenburg position, bladder filling 500-700 mL, and tocolysis (terbutaline 250 microgram subcutaneous) to facilitate transfer. When the cervix is fully dilated with low station and an effective epidural, operative vaginal birth is faster and preferred. The cord is kept warm and unhandled to avoid vasospasm.
key_points: Fastest safe route to delivery is the principle
Not fully dilated: category 1 caesarean with temporising measures
Fully dilated and low station: instrumental vaginal birth
Cord kept warm and unhandled to avoid vasospasm
explanation.pearls: Bladder filling 500-700 mL via a Foley catheter elevates the presenting part and reduces cord compression more reliably than manual elevation alone when transfer to theatre is anticipated.

stem:
A 31-year-old G1P0 is referred to your fetal medicine clinic at 29+3 weeks gestation for severe early-onset fetal growth restriction. She has had one prior morphology scan at 20 weeks (normal) and a growth scan at 28 weeks showed estimated fetal weight at the 2nd centile. She has had no antepartum haemorrhage and no abdominal pain. Her booking visit blood pressure was 110/70 mmHg.

The current scan today shows estimated fetal weight 850 g (under 3rd centile), abdominal circumference under 3rd centile, head circumference at the 25th centile, amniotic fluid index 4 cm (deepest pool 2 cm), umbilical artery Doppler with absent end-diastolic flow, middle cerebral artery pulsatility index 0.78 (under 5th centile for gestation), and ductus venosus a-wave absent. She has had a normal full antenatal screen for infection and a normal karyotype. CTG shows reduced short-term variability over a 60-minute computerised assessment. Her blood pressure is 142/92 mmHg today and a spot urine protein-to-creatinine ratio is 36 mg/mmol.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 92, BP 142/92 mmHg, RR 18, SpO2 99% on room air, temperature 36.7 °C, fetal HR 142 bpm
data_table.Examination: Symphysio-fundal height 24 cm, soft abdomen, no tenderness
data_table.Investigations: EFW 850 g under 3rd centile; AC under 3rd centile; AFI 4 cm; UA Doppler absent end-diastolic flow; MCA PI 0.78; ductus venosus a-wave absent; computerised CTG reduced STV; urine PCR 36 mg/mmol
data_table.Medications: Two doses intramuscular betamethasone 11.4 mg given 24 and 12 hours ago; intravenous magnesium sulfate infusion started 4 hours ago for neuroprotection

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step?

options.text: Continue inpatient observation with twice-daily computerised CTG and Doppler in 1 week for ongoing monitoring
options.rationale: Absent or reversed ductus venosus a-wave with reduced short-term variability on computerised CTG signals imminent decompensation; weekly review is unsafe. (Source: RANZCOG IUGR Statement)

options.text: Wait until 30 weeks completed gestation before commencing any plan for delivery for additional fetal maturity
options.rationale: Ductus venosus a-wave loss combined with reduced computerised CTG STV at 29+3 weeks crosses the threshold for delivery; waiting risks intrauterine demise. (Source: TRUFFLE study)

options.text: Proceed to category 2 caesarean section once magnesium sulfate neuroprotection is complete with neonatal team in attendance
options.rationale: The TRUFFLE trial and RANZCOG IUGR guidance use ductus venosus a-wave (absent or reversed) plus reduced short-term variability on computerised CTG as the trigger for delivery in severe early-onset IUGR. Betamethasone is complete and magnesium sulfate for fetal neuroprotection has been started; once the second dose interval is met, category 2 caesarean delivery with neonatal team in attendance is the route. (Source: RANZCOG IUGR Statement; TRUFFLE study)

options.text: Induce labour with oral mifepristone followed by a vaginal prostaglandin pessary and aim for vaginal birth
options.rationale: Severe IUGR with absent end-diastolic flow and ductus venosus a-wave loss does not tolerate labour; the route of delivery is caesarean. (Source: RANZCOG IUGR Statement)

options.text: Treat the maternal blood pressure with labetalol and reassess fetal status after 48 hours of antihypertensive control
options.rationale: Maternal blood pressure control is warranted but does not change the fetal trigger; delivery is the response to the fetal indication. (Source: SOMANZ Hypertension in Pregnancy)

explanation.summary: Early-onset severe fetal growth restriction is the highest-risk subset for stillbirth and severe perinatal morbidity. The TRUFFLE trial established ductus venosus a-wave waveform changes plus reduced short-term variability on computerised CTG as superior to umbilical artery Doppler alone for delivery timing. RANZCOG triggers delivery when both criteria are met after corticosteroid completion and magnesium sulfate for fetal neuroprotection (under 30 weeks). Caesarean section is the route because severe IUGR fetuses tolerate labour poorly. Magnesium for neuroprotection is given for delivery at or before 30 weeks (some units extend to 32 weeks).
key_points: TRUFFLE trigger: ductus venosus a-wave absent/reversed plus reduced CTG STV
Magnesium sulfate for fetal neuroprotection at or before 30 weeks
Betamethasone before delivery at gestations less than 34+6 weeks
Caesarean is the preferred route in severe IUGR with abnormal Dopplers
explanation.pearls: Umbilical artery absent end-diastolic flow alone allows surveillance with delivery by 33+6; ductus venosus a-wave absent or reversed shifts delivery forward regardless of gestation between 26 and 32 weeks.

stem:
You are the obstetric registrar in delivery suite. A 34-year-old G3P3 has just delivered a 4.1 kg baby vaginally. Active management of the third stage was given. The midwife was applying cord traction when there was a sudden gush of blood and the mother became pale and clammy. The midwife says 'the fundus has disappeared and I can feel something like a bag at the introitus'.

On examination she is conscious but pale and diaphoretic. There is a large dark red mass visible at the introitus. The uterine fundus is no longer palpable abdominally. Estimated blood loss is now 1500 mL and increasing. She is in significant pain. Intravenous access has been established with a 16 G cannula and 0.9% sodium chloride is running. The anaesthetic registrar is in the room. The placenta is not yet delivered and appears still attached to the inverted uterine fundus. Bedside coagulation is pending. Bedside lactate is 3.6 mmol/L (under 2.0).

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 128 thready, BP 78/42 mmHg, RR 22, SpO2 99% on 6 L/min mask oxygen, temperature 36.4 °C
data_table.Examination: Conscious pale diaphoretic, large dark red mass at the introitus, no fundus palpable abdominally, placenta still attached to inverted fundus
data_table.Investigations: FBC and coags sent, bedside lactate 3.6 mmol/L (under 2.0)
data_table.Medications: Active third stage included intramuscular oxytocin 10 IU; 0.9% sodium chloride running through 16 G cannula

lead_in: What is the most appropriate immediate management priority?

options.text: Cease all uterotonics, leave the placenta attached, and immediately attempt manual replacement of the inverted fundus
options.rationale: Acute uterine inversion is reduced immediately by manual replacement (Johnson manoeuvre) WITHOUT removing the placenta first; placental removal before reduction worsens haemorrhage. Uterotonics are STOPPED to allow uterine relaxation; tocolysis (terbutaline subcutaneous, magnesium sulfate, or general anaesthesia with halothane) is added if simple manual replacement fails. Once reduced, uterotonics are restarted, the placenta is removed, and PPH management continues. (Source: RANZCOG PPH Statement; RANZCOG Acute Uterine Inversion Guideline)

options.text: Remove the placenta manually first to reduce blood loss, then attempt replacement of the inverted fundus
options.rationale: Removing the placenta from the inverted fundus before reduction sharply increases haemorrhage; the placenta is left in situ until after reduction. (Source: RANZCOG Acute Uterine Inversion Guideline)

options.text: Commence intravenous ergometrine 250 microgram before any attempt at manual reduction of the uterine fundus
options.rationale: Uterotonics increase uterine tone and oppose reduction; they are STOPPED for inversion. The sequence is reduce first, then uterotonics. (Source: RANZCOG Acute Uterine Inversion Guideline)

options.text: Immediately transfer to theatre for emergency abdominal hysterectomy under general anaesthesia as the first step
options.rationale: Hysterectomy is reserved for irreducible inversion or major haemorrhage uncontrolled by reduction and uterotonics; first-line is manual replacement. (Source: RANZCOG Acute Uterine Inversion Guideline)

options.text: Apply firm bimanual compression with two hands and administer intramuscular carboprost 250 microgram immediately
options.rationale: Bimanual compression and carboprost treat ongoing atony AFTER the inversion is reduced; before reduction they impede the manoeuvre. (Source: RANZCOG Acute Uterine Inversion Guideline)

explanation.summary: Acute uterine inversion is a rare but life-threatening obstetric emergency, classically presenting with maternal collapse, haemorrhage out of proportion to the visible loss, disappearing fundus on abdominal palpation, and a mass visible or palpable at the introitus. Treatment priority is immediate manual replacement (Johnson manoeuvre) with placenta still attached; uterotonics are STOPPED to allow uterine relaxation. If simple manual replacement fails, tocolysis is added (terbutaline 250 microgram subcutaneous, magnesium sulfate, or general anaesthesia with halothane) and a second attempt is made. Once reduced, uterotonics are restarted, placenta is delivered, and PPH management continues. Resuscitation runs in parallel.
key_points: Stop uterotonics; reduce first, then deliver placenta
Johnson manoeuvre: cup the fundus and push it back through the cervix
Tocolysis (terbutaline/magnesium/halothane) for failed first attempt
Hysterectomy for irreducible inversion or uncontrolled haemorrhage
explanation.pearls: The disappearance of the uterine fundus on abdominal palpation in a recently delivered woman with collapse is pathognomonic of inversion; vagal-mediated bradycardia can accompany the haemodynamic collapse.

stem:
A 33-year-old G2P1 at 37+0 weeks gestation is on your delivery suite for a planned induction. She had a velamentous cord insertion identified at her 20-week morphology scan with vasa praevia confirmed on transvaginal scan at 32 weeks. Antenatal corticosteroids were given at 32 and 34 weeks, and she has been admitted as an inpatient since 34 weeks for monitoring.

A few minutes after artificial rupture of membranes by the registrar (at 4 cm cervical dilation), the midwife reports a small painless gush of bright red blood. CTG immediately shows a sinusoidal trace with reduced variability and a baseline of 130 bpm. The previously reactive trace before ARM had a baseline of 140 bpm with moderate variability. Maternal observations remain stable. Theatre is staffed and the anaesthetic team is already in the room. Her booking blood group is O positive with no antibodies. She has had no prior caesarean and her epidural is functioning.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 92, BP 124/78 mmHg, RR 18, SpO2 99% on room air, temperature 36.8 °C, fetal HR 130 bpm sinusoidal
data_table.Examination: Cervix 4 cm dilated, membranes ruptured, small bright red painless gush ongoing, fetal head at station 0
data_table.Investigations: CTG sinusoidal trace; Kleihauer test sent; FBC, group and hold available
data_table.Medications: Two doses antenatal betamethasone 11.4 mg at 32 and 34 weeks; functioning epidural

lead_in: What is the most appropriate immediate next step?

options.text: Continue induction of labour and aim for vaginal birth with continuous CTG monitoring and operative delivery if needed
options.rationale: Vasa praevia bleeding is fetal blood loss and the fetal exsanguination window is minutes; vaginal birth is not safe once vasa praevia has bled. (Source: RANZCOG Vasa Praevia Statement)

options.text: Administer maternal intravenous tranexamic acid 1 g and arrange fetal blood transfusion in the neonatal unit
options.rationale: Maternal tranexamic acid does not address fetal bleeding from a ruptured fetal vessel; the only effective treatment is immediate delivery. (Source: RANZCOG Vasa Praevia Statement)

options.text: Perform manual digital tamponade against the bleeding vessel and observe CTG for spontaneous recovery over 15 minutes
options.rationale: Digital tamponade is not a recognised treatment and delays delivery; fetal exsanguination occurs within minutes once the vessel ruptures. (Source: RANZCOG Vasa Praevia Statement)

options.text: Activate the category 1 caesarean section pathway with delivery within 30 minutes and neonatal team in attendance
options.rationale: Vasa praevia with bleeding and a sinusoidal fetal heart trace is a category 1 caesarean indication; the bleeding is fetal and exsanguination occurs within minutes (fetal blood volume is approximately 80-100 mL/kg). Delivery within 30 minutes is the goal, neonatal resuscitation including O-negative crossmatched blood is prepared, and the baby is delivered by caesarean. (Source: RANZCOG Vasa Praevia Statement)

options.text: Send urgent Kleihauer test and Apt test for fetal blood differentiation before deciding mode of delivery
options.rationale: Kleihauer and Apt tests confirm fetal origin retrospectively; the diagnosis is clinical (known vasa praevia + bleeding after ARM + sinusoidal trace) and delivery cannot wait for laboratory confirmation. (Source: RANZCOG Vasa Praevia Statement)

explanation.summary: Vasa praevia is a fetal vessel running through the membranes within 2 cm of the internal cervical os, unsupported by placenta or cord. Risk factors include velamentous cord insertion, bilobed or succenturiate placenta, and twin pregnancy. Antenatal diagnosis by transvaginal Doppler is the standard. Confirmed cases are admitted between 30-34 weeks with antenatal corticosteroids and delivered by elective caesarean between 34-36 weeks before labour. Acute bleeding from ruptured vasa praevia is fetal in origin and produces rapid exsanguination; the fetal heart rate becomes sinusoidal and then bradycardic. Category 1 caesarean section is the only effective treatment. Neonatal resuscitation includes O-negative crossmatched blood for the baby.
key_points: Vasa praevia: fetal vessel within 2 cm of internal os, unsupported
Antenatal admission 30-34 weeks; delivery by elective caesarean 34-36 weeks
Acute rupture: category 1 caesarean within 30 minutes
Neonatal O-negative blood preparation for fetal exsanguination
explanation.pearls: Fetal blood volume is approximately 80-100 mL/kg; a fetus can exsanguinate within minutes of vasa praevia rupture, making this one of the few true obstetric emergencies with a minute-by-minute window.

stem:
A 29-year-old G1P1 woman is brought to your emergency department day 4 after a normal vaginal birth at term. Her partner says 'she's been getting more confused all day, her tummy is rock hard and she's gone really cold and shaky'. She had a brief sore throat the day before delivery. There is no history of antenatal infection and her group B streptococcus screen was negative.

On examination she is drowsy (GCS 13), with cool peripheries and mottled lower limbs. She has marked uterine tenderness, foul-smelling pinkish lochia, and a rigid abdomen. There is no breast erythema. Bedside lactate is 5.8 mmol/L (under 2.0); white cell count is 28 x10^9/L (4-11) with 92% neutrophils; CRP is 320 mg/L (under 5); creatinine has risen from 60 to 132 micromol/L. Bedside ultrasound shows retained products of conception 32 mm. She is exclusively breastfeeding a healthy term baby. The pelvic examination reveals an open cervical os with passage of foul-smelling discharge.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 138, BP 78/40 mmHg, RR 28, SpO2 95% on room air, temperature 39.4 °C
data_table.Examination: Drowsy GCS 13, cool peripheries with mottled lower limbs, rigid abdomen with uterine tenderness, foul-smelling lochia, open cervical os
data_table.Investigations: Lactate 5.8 mmol/L (under 2.0), WCC 28 x10^9/L (4-11) 92% neutrophils, CRP 320 mg/L (under 5), creatinine 132 micromol/L (45-90), retained products of conception 32 mm on bedside ultrasound

lead_in: What is the most appropriate antibiotic regimen?

options.text: Intravenous oral metronidazole monotherapy with intravenous fluids and observation for 6 hours
options.rationale: Monotherapy fails to cover gram-positive cocci including group A streptococcus, which is a leading cause of fulminant puerperal sepsis. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic)

options.text: Intravenous benzylpenicillin alone with intravenous fluids and immediate transfer to the postnatal ward
options.rationale: Penicillin alone does not cover anaerobes from retained products and lacks toxin suppression for group A streptococcus; broad-spectrum cover plus clindamycin is required. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic)

options.text: Intravenous ceftriaxone 2 g, metronidazole 500 mg, plus clindamycin 600 mg every 8 hours and urgent surgical evacuation
options.rationale: Postpartum septic shock with retained products in Australia is treated with broad gram-positive, gram-negative, and anaerobic cover plus clindamycin for its toxin-suppression effect on group A streptococcus and staphylococcal exotoxins. Therapeutic Guidelines lists ceftriaxone plus metronidazole plus clindamycin for severe puerperal sepsis with septic shock features. Source control by surgical evacuation of retained products is essential and is the most time-critical intervention. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic; RANZCOG Puerperal Sepsis Statement)

options.text: Intravenous oral cefalexin and oral metronidazole pending culture results with outpatient follow-up in 48 hours
options.rationale: Oral therapy is inadequate for septic shock with end-organ dysfunction; intravenous broad-spectrum cover is required. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic)

options.text: Intravenous vancomycin alone for presumed methicillin-resistant Staphylococcus aureus puerperal mastitis
options.rationale: This presentation is not lactational mastitis; vancomycin monotherapy lacks anaerobic and gram-negative cover required for endometritis and septic shock. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic)

explanation.summary: Puerperal sepsis is sepsis arising from a genital tract source within 6 weeks of birth, miscarriage, or termination of pregnancy. Group A streptococcus (GAS) is a leading cause of fulminant disease; sore throat exposure in the days before or after delivery is a classic risk factor. Antibiotic choice covers gram-positive cocci, gram-negatives, anaerobes, and adds clindamycin for toxin suppression. Therapeutic Guidelines specifies ceftriaxone plus metronidazole plus clindamycin for severe puerperal sepsis. Source control (surgical evacuation of retained products, drainage of pelvic collections, hysterectomy in irreversible necrotising endometritis) is the most time-critical intervention. Resuscitation runs in parallel with the hour-1 sepsis bundle.
key_points: Empirical IV ceftriaxone + metronidazole + clindamycin in severe puerperal sepsis
Clindamycin added for GAS and staphylococcal toxin suppression
Source control: surgical evacuation of retained products
Hour-1 sepsis bundle in parallel
explanation.pearls: In the breastfeeding patient, ceftriaxone, metronidazole, and clindamycin are all considered acceptable; brief lactation interruption is unnecessary in routine practice and exclusive expressed breastmilk feeding continues.

stem:
You are the antenatal clinic registrar at a regional hospital seeing a 33-year-old G2P1 woman at 36 weeks for a planning discussion about her mode of birth. Her previous birth was an emergency lower segment caesarean section at term two years ago for arrest of dilation at 6 cm despite syntocinon augmentation; the baby was 3.6 kg and the operation note describes a transverse lower segment incision with no extension. She has had no other pregnancies.

This pregnancy has been uncomplicated. The fetus is cephalic, estimated fetal weight on a growth scan two days ago is 3.4 kg with normal umbilical artery dopplers, and the placenta is fundal. Her body mass index at booking was 28 kg/m2. She has had no interpregnancy interval issues and is keen to attempt a vaginal birth. The regional hospital has a 24/7 obstetrician on call, an in-house anaesthetist, blood bank availability, and a 30 minute decision-to-delivery audit.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 78/min, BP 118/72 mmHg, RR 16/min, SpO2 99% room air, temperature 36.7 °C, fetal heart 142/min
data_table.Examination: Symphysis fundal height 36 cm, longitudinal lie, cephalic, free 4/5; uterus soft and non tender
data_table.History: G2P1; previous LSCS at term for arrest of dilation; transverse lower segment incision; current EFW 3.4 kg; BMI 28

lead_in: What is the most appropriate counselling recommendation?

options.text: Advise that vaginal birth is contraindicated because of her body mass index of 28 kg/m2
options.rationale: A BMI of 28 is not a contraindication to VBAC; obesity reduces success rates but does not preclude trial of labour. (Source: RANZCOG Birth After Previous Caesarean Section)
source_refs: RANZCOG Birth After Previous Caesarean Section

options.text: Recommend elective repeat caesarean section at 39 weeks given prior arrest of dilation
options.rationale: Prior labour arrest is not an absolute contraindication to VBAC; success rates fall modestly but remain above 50% and an elective ERCS removes maternal choice based on a non-absolute factor. (Source: RANZCOG Birth After Previous Caesarean Section)
source_refs: RANZCOG Birth After Previous Caesarean Section

options.text: Induce labour at 39 weeks with prostaglandin gel to optimise her chance of vaginal birth
options.rationale: Prostaglandin induction of VBAC is associated with a 2 to 3 fold rise in uterine rupture compared with spontaneous labour and is generally avoided; mechanical induction (Foley) is preferred if induction is needed. (Source: RANZCOG Birth After Previous Caesarean Section)
source_refs: RANZCOG Birth After Previous Caesarean Section

options.text: Offer trial of labour after caesarean with continuous CTG and IV access from established labour
options.rationale: She is a good VBAC candidate (single prior low transverse LSCS, no other uterine surgery, cephalic presentation, average EFW, supportive hospital infrastructure); RANZCOG supports VBAC with continuous CTG once in established labour and intravenous access, with reported success rates 60-80% and uterine rupture risk approximately 0.5%. (Source: RANZCOG Birth After Previous Caesarean Section)
source_refs: RANZCOG Birth After Previous Caesarean Section

options.text: Arrange external cephalic version at 37 weeks before any further mode of birth discussion
options.rationale: The fetus is already cephalic; ECV is not indicated and does not change the VBAC discussion. (Source: RANZCOG External Cephalic Version)

explanation.summary: Trial of labour after caesarean is supported by RANZCOG for women with a single prior low transverse LSCS, no other uterine scar, cephalic presentation, no contraindication to vaginal birth and access to facilities able to perform emergency caesarean within 30 minutes. Reported success rates are 60-80% and uterine rupture risk is approximately 0.5%. Continuous CTG is mandatory in established labour because fetal heart rate change is the earliest sign of rupture. Prostaglandin induction is generally avoided due to elevated rupture risk; mechanical methods are preferred. Two prior caesareans, classical scar, T or J incision, or low transverse extension are absolute contraindications.
key_points: VBAC candidate: 1 prior low transverse LSCS, cephalic, supportive infrastructure
Uterine rupture risk approximately 0.5% in spontaneous VBAC labour
Continuous CTG mandatory from established labour onward
Avoid prostaglandin induction; mechanical (Foley) preferred
explanation.pearls: RANZCOG recommends decision-to-delivery within 30 minutes for category 1 emergency caesarean; this is the critical infrastructure prerequisite that allows VBAC at a regional hospital.

sources.label: RANZCOG Birth After Previous Caesarean Section

stem:
You are the obstetric registrar called to the assessment unit at 11pm for a 28-year-old G1P0 woman at 32+4 weeks brought in by her partner with a frontal headache for 6 hours and three episodes of vomiting. She has been seeing a midwife at a low-risk shared care clinic. Booking BP was 110/70 mmHg.

On arrival she is reactive but withdrawn. Repeat manual BP measurements over 15 minutes are 168/112, 172/108 and 165/110 mmHg. Reflexes are brisk with 3 beats of ankle clonus. There is no visual scotoma. Urine dipstick shows protein 3+. CTG shows a baseline of 145/min with normal variability and accelerations, no decelerations. The bed manager confirms a tertiary neonatal unit cot is available 90 minutes away by retrieval.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 98/min, BP 168/112 mmHg, RR 18/min, SpO2 99% room air, temperature 36.7 °C, fetal heart 145/min
data_table.Examination: Reactive, withdrawn; brisk reflexes with 3 beats clonus; no scotoma; no epigastric tenderness; SFH 33 cm
data_table.Investigations: Urine dipstick protein 3+; platelets 142 x10^9/L (150-400); ALT 78 U/L (<40); creatinine 88 micromol/L; uric acid raised; PlGF assay pending
data_table.CTG: Baseline 145/min, normal variability, accelerations present, no decelerations

lead_in: What is the most appropriate immediate management?

options.text: Administer intravenous furosemide 40 mg as a single bolus for pulmonary oedema prophylaxis
options.rationale: Routine furosemide is not part of acute severe pre-eclampsia management and may worsen placental perfusion; it is reserved for confirmed pulmonary oedema. (Source: SOMANZ Hypertension in Pregnancy)

options.text: Commence betamethasone 11.4 mg IM and plan delivery in the morning by elective caesarean
options.rationale: Antenatal corticosteroid is correct at this gestation, but delaying acute BP control and magnesium until morning risks eclampsia or stroke; both are time critical. (Source: SOMANZ Hypertension in Pregnancy)

options.text: Oral nifedipine 20 mg immediate-release and IV magnesium sulfate 4 g loading dose, then arrange retrieval
options.rationale: Severe hypertension (BP ≥160/110) plus pre-eclampsia symptoms requires immediate acute antihypertensive (oral nifedipine 10 to 20 mg or IV labetalol 20 mg) plus magnesium sulfate 4 g loading then 1 g/hour for eclampsia prophylaxis; tertiary in utero transfer is appropriate at 32+4 weeks if mother stabilises. (Source: SOMANZ Hypertension in Pregnancy; RANZCOG Hypertension in Pregnancy)

options.text: Discharge home on oral labetalol 100 mg three times daily with day-stay review tomorrow
options.rationale: Severe hypertension with symptoms and proteinuria is an admission with magnesium prophylaxis; home management at this severity is unsafe. (Source: SOMANZ Hypertension in Pregnancy)

options.text: Start an intravenous glyceryl trinitrate infusion targeting mean arterial pressure under 80 mmHg
options.rationale: GTN is reserved for pre-eclampsia with pulmonary oedema; first-line acute antihypertensives are oral nifedipine or IV labetalol or IV hydralazine. (Source: SOMANZ Hypertension in Pregnancy)

explanation.summary: Pre-eclampsia with severe features (BP ≥160/110, symptoms of impending eclampsia such as headache, scotoma, epigastric pain, hyperreflexia, or end-organ involvement) requires admission, immediate acute antihypertensive, magnesium sulfate for eclampsia prophylaxis, and a delivery plan. The SOMANZ first-line acute agents are oral nifedipine 10 to 20 mg, IV labetalol 20 mg (escalating), or IV hydralazine 5 mg. Magnesium sulfate 4 g IV loading then 1 g/hour infusion halves the risk of eclampsia. At pre-term gestations between 24 and 34 weeks, antenatal corticosteroids and consideration of in utero transfer to a tertiary centre are part of the package. Delivery timing depends on maternal and fetal stability; at 32 to 34 weeks, expectant management is appropriate if both are stable.
key_points: Severe BP threshold = 160/110 mmHg
Acute antihypertensive: nifedipine PO or labetalol IV or hydralazine IV
Magnesium sulfate 4 g IV load then 1 g/hour for eclampsia prophylaxis
Tertiary transfer at 32+ weeks if mother and fetus stable
explanation.pearls: Magnesium sulfate halves eclampsia risk in severe pre-eclampsia (NNT approximately 100); monitor patellar reflex, respiratory rate and urine output and check magnesium level if signs of toxicity emerge.

stem:
You are the obstetric medicine registrar reviewing a 35-year-old G2P1 woman at 32+0 weeks gestation in the joint obstetric-endocrine clinic. She was diagnosed with gestational diabetes at 26 weeks on a 75g OGTT (fasting 5.3, 1 hour 11.2, 2 hour 9.4 mmol/L). She has been on dietary modification plus metformin 1 g twice daily for the last four weeks. She is otherwise well; her BMI at booking was 31 kg/m2 and her previous pregnancy was complicated by a 4.1 kg neonate at term without operative delivery.

Her blood glucose monitoring diary over the last 14 days shows fasting capillary glucoses ranging 5.6 to 6.1 mmol/L (target <5.1), one hour postprandial values ranging 7.5 to 8.4 mmol/L (target <7.4), and she reports good dietary adherence with a low GI breakfast. Her HbA1c last week was 5.8%. A growth ultrasound today shows estimated fetal weight on the 92nd centile with a normal abdominal circumference to head circumference ratio.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 82/min, BP 122/76 mmHg, RR 16/min, SpO2 99% room air, temperature 36.7 °C, fetal heart 140/min
data_table.BGL diary: Fasting 5.6 to 6.1 mmol/L (target <5.1); 1 hour postprandial 7.5 to 8.4 mmol/L (target <7.4)
data_table.Investigations: HbA1c 5.8%; EFW 92nd centile; AC:HC ratio normal; amniotic fluid index 18 cm

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step?

options.text: Add bedtime intermediate-acting insulin isophane 8 units and continue metformin
options.rationale: Persistent fasting hyperglycaemia above target on maximal metformin requires addition of basal insulin (typically isophane at bedtime); this targets overnight gluconeogenesis specifically and is the ADIPS-endorsed escalation. (Source: ADIPS Consensus Guidelines GDM; RANZCOG Diabetes in Pregnancy)

options.text: Increase metformin to 1.5 g twice daily and reassess in two weeks
options.rationale: Maximum daily metformin dose in pregnancy is 2 g/day (per ADIPS); she is already at maximum, and ongoing hyperglycaemia mandates insulin addition. (Source: ADIPS Consensus Guidelines GDM)

options.text: Switch from metformin to glibenclamide 5 mg twice daily as an alternative oral agent
options.rationale: Glibenclamide crosses the placenta, carries higher neonatal hypoglycaemia and macrosomia rates than insulin, and is not first-line in Australia. (Source: ADIPS Consensus Guidelines GDM)

options.text: Plan elective induction of labour at 37 weeks for fetal macrosomia prophylaxis
options.rationale: Induction discussion belongs at 38 to 39 weeks for diet/metformin GDM; current management is to first achieve glycaemic targets with insulin escalation. (Source: RANZCOG Diabetes in Pregnancy)

options.text: Continue current management as her HbA1c of 5.8% indicates adequate overall control
options.rationale: HbA1c in late pregnancy is unreliable due to red cell turnover and underestimates postprandial peaks; capillary targets, not HbA1c, govern treatment escalation. (Source: ADIPS Consensus Guidelines GDM)

explanation.summary: GDM in Australia is treated to capillary targets of fasting <5.1 mmol/L and either 1 hour postprandial <7.4 mmol/L or 2 hour postprandial <6.7 mmol/L. First line is medical nutrition therapy plus exercise; second line is metformin (max 2 g/day in pregnancy); third line is insulin. Insulin is added rather than substituted for metformin: basal isophane targets fasting glucose, rapid analogues target postprandial peaks. HbA1c is unreliable in late pregnancy. Fetal growth above 90th centile with disproportionate abdominal circumference signals fetal hyperinsulinism and is an additional indication for tighter control.
key_points: Capillary targets: fasting <5.1, 1 hour <7.4, 2 hour <6.7 mmol/L
Maximum metformin in pregnancy 2 g/day
Add basal insulin (isophane) rather than swap, for fasting hyperglycaemia
HbA1c unreliable in pregnancy; use capillary diary
explanation.pearls: Persistent fasting hyperglycaemia on maximum metformin in GDM is best addressed by adding bedtime isophane targeting overnight gluconeogenesis; switching to glibenclamide is not Australian first-line practice.

stem:
You are the postnatal ward registrar reviewing a 36-year-old G3P3 woman who delivered 8 hours ago by emergency lower segment caesarean at 38+5 weeks for failure to progress after a 14-hour labour. The procedure was uncomplicated; estimated blood loss was 750 mL. Her booking BMI was 34 kg/m2. Her mother had an unprovoked DVT at age 55 and her sister had a pulmonary embolism on the combined oral contraceptive pill in her twenties. She is otherwise well, mobilising with assistance, and the urinary catheter has been removed.

A thrombophilia screen taken at booking by her general practitioner before this admission showed her to be heterozygous for the factor V Leiden mutation. She is not breastfeeding by choice. Today's full blood count is normal, renal function is preserved (creatinine 68 micromol/L, eGFR >90), and there is no active bleeding from her wound or her vagina. The midwife asks you to prescribe thromboprophylaxis.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 84/min, BP 118/72 mmHg, RR 16/min, SpO2 99% room air, temperature 36.7 °C
data_table.Examination: Comfortable, mobilising with assistance; dry wound; lochia normal; calves soft and non tender
data_table.Investigations: Full blood count within normal limits; creatinine 68 micromol/L; eGFR >90 mL/min; factor V Leiden heterozygous

lead_in: What is the most appropriate thromboprophylaxis prescription?

options.text: Enoxaparin 40 mg subcutaneously daily for 7 days only, then mechanical prophylaxis
options.rationale: Seven days covers the immediate caesarean risk, but factor V Leiden plus family history extends the high-risk window; current Australian guidelines extend pharmacological prophylaxis to 6 weeks. (Source: RANZCOG Venous Thromboembolism in Pregnancy and Postpartum)
source_refs: RANZCOG Venous Thromboembolism in Pregnancy and Postpartum

options.text: Subcutaneous enoxaparin 40 mg daily for 6 weeks plus graduated compression stockings
options.rationale: She has multiple postpartum VTE risk factors (caesarean, BMI >30, age >35, low-risk thrombophilia, family history) totalling >=4 RANZCOG/RCOG risk points, which warrants prophylactic LMWH for 6 weeks postpartum plus mechanical prophylaxis. (Source: RANZCOG Venous Thromboembolism in Pregnancy and Postpartum; RCOG Green-top 37a)
source_refs: RANZCOG Venous Thromboembolism in Pregnancy and Postpartum

options.text: Graduated compression stockings alone for 6 weeks without pharmacological prophylaxis
options.rationale: Mechanical prophylaxis alone is inadequate when the risk score reaches the LMWH threshold; this approach underdoses her postpartum risk. (Source: RANZCOG Venous Thromboembolism in Pregnancy and Postpartum)
source_refs: RANZCOG Venous Thromboembolism in Pregnancy and Postpartum

options.text: Aspirin 100 mg orally daily for 6 weeks for venous thromboembolism prevention
options.rationale: Aspirin has limited evidence in obstetric VTE prevention and is not the recommended agent for postpartum prophylaxis; LMWH is the standard. (Source: RANZCOG Venous Thromboembolism in Pregnancy and Postpartum)
source_refs: RANZCOG Venous Thromboembolism in Pregnancy and Postpartum

options.text: Therapeutic enoxaparin 1 mg/kg twice daily for 3 months given factor V Leiden
options.rationale: Treatment doses are reserved for proven VTE or very high risk profiles (previous VTE, antiphospholipid syndrome, homozygous mutations); heterozygous factor V Leiden without prior VTE warrants prophylactic not therapeutic dosing. (Source: RANZCOG Venous Thromboembolism in Pregnancy and Postpartum)
source_refs: RANZCOG Venous Thromboembolism in Pregnancy and Postpartum

explanation.summary: Postpartum VTE risk is stratified using the RANZCOG and RCOG risk scoring systems. Major factors (previous VTE, antiphospholipid syndrome, homozygous thrombophilia) attract treatment-dose LMWH and 6 weeks duration. Multiple intermediate factors (caesarean, BMI >30, age >35, parity >3, smoking, low-risk thrombophilia, prolonged labour, postpartum haemorrhage >1L, family history) attract prophylactic LMWH for variable durations of 10 days to 6 weeks depending on score. Enoxaparin 40 mg subcutaneously daily is the standard prophylactic dose; weight-adjusted dosing (60 mg if 90-130 kg) applies in obesity. Graduated compression stockings are adjunctive, not alternative, in this risk band.
key_points: RANZCOG VTE risk scoring drives dose and duration
Enoxaparin 40 mg daily for 6 weeks if multiple intermediate factors
Mechanical prophylaxis adjunctive, not alternative
Weight-banded dosing in BMI >40 or weight >90 kg
explanation.pearls: Heterozygous factor V Leiden alone does NOT trigger postpartum LMWH, but combined with caesarean, BMI >30, and family history it crosses the threshold for 6 weeks of prophylactic enoxaparin.

sources.label: RANZCOG Venous Thromboembolism in Pregnancy and Postpartum

stem:
You are the antenatal day-assessment registrar reviewing a 29-year-old G2P1 woman at 36+6 weeks gestation who has been referred from her shared-care GP for a breech presentation noted clinically and confirmed on a presentation scan today. She had a normal vaginal birth at term with her first pregnancy two years ago.

This pregnancy has been uncomplicated. Symphysis fundal height is 36 cm, the presenting part is high, and CTG today is normal. The growth scan two weeks ago showed an estimated fetal weight on the 55th centile, amniotic fluid index 14 cm, and the placenta was reported as fundo-anterior with no praevia. Today's presentation scan confirms a frank breech with extended legs and re-states the placenta as fundo-anterior. There is no rupture of membranes, no antepartum haemorrhage and no history of previous uterine surgery. She is keen to attempt a vaginal birth and asks about turning the baby.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 82/min, BP 118/72 mmHg, RR 16/min, SpO2 99% room air, temperature 36.7 °C, fetal heart 142/min
data_table.Examination: SFH 36 cm; presenting part high; uterus soft and non tender; no PV bleeding; no rupture of membranes
data_table.Investigations: Presentation scan: frank breech with extended legs; AFI 14 cm; placenta fundo-anterior; no praevia

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step?

options.text: Defer all action and rescan at 38 weeks to allow possible spontaneous version to occur
options.rationale: Spontaneous version after 36 weeks is uncommon (approximately 5%); ECV should be offered at 37 weeks rather than waiting passively. (Source: RANZCOG External Cephalic Version)

options.text: Recommend elective caesarean section at 39 weeks without first offering external cephalic version
options.rationale: Skipping the offer of ECV deprives her of a chance at vaginal birth; routine ECV before elective caesarean is standard RANZCOG practice. (Source: RANZCOG External Cephalic Version)

options.text: Plan a trial of vaginal breech birth at term with continuous CTG monitoring as first option
options.rationale: Planned vaginal breech is permissible after counselling about increased perinatal mortality and morbidity but is offered after ECV failure or refusal, not as first option. (Source: RANZCOG External Cephalic Version)

options.text: Refer for moxibustion at acupuncture point BL67 daily for 14 days before any further decision
options.rationale: Moxibustion has weak supporting evidence; it can be offered as an adjunct but does not substitute for the ECV discussion. (Source: RANZCOG External Cephalic Version)

options.text: Schedule external cephalic version at 37 weeks with terbutaline tocolysis and post-procedure CTG
options.rationale: She is an excellent ECV candidate with no contraindications (uncomplicated singleton, frank breech, normal AFI, fundo-anterior placenta, no scar, no praevia); RANZCOG recommends offering ECV from 37 weeks with tocolysis improving success rates to approximately 60%. (Source: RANZCOG External Cephalic Version)

explanation.summary: External cephalic version is offered from 37 weeks for uncomplicated breech presentations. Success rates are approximately 50% nulliparous and 60% multiparous, improved with tocolysis (salbutamol or terbutaline). Absolute contraindications are placenta praevia, antepartum haemorrhage, ruptured membranes, multiple pregnancy (except second twin), fetal compromise, major fetal anomaly and a previous classical caesarean. Relative contraindications include oligohydramnios, prior caesarean (success and safety similar to no scar in observational data, but discussion required) and small for gestational age. Anti-D is given to Rh negative women. Pre and post procedure CTG is mandatory and immediate caesarean must be available.
key_points: Offer ECV from 37 weeks for uncomplicated breech
Tocolysis improves success (terbutaline or salbutamol)
Anti-D for Rh negative women
Absolute contraindications: praevia, APH, ROM, fetal compromise
explanation.pearls: ECV success is around 60% with multiparity, normal liquor and a posterior or fundo-anterior (not anterior) placenta; tocolysis with terbutaline 250 mcg subcutaneous lifts success by approximately 10 percentage points.

stem:
You are the obstetric registrar in the high-risk antenatal clinic reviewing a 31-year-old G3P1 woman at 14+0 weeks gestation. Her first pregnancy ended in a painless second-trimester loss at 22 weeks following spontaneous rupture of membranes preceded by silent cervical dilation; her second pregnancy ended in a similar loss at 20 weeks. Neither loss had infective features and both placentas showed no chorioamnionitis on histology. She has no other gynaecological history and her first-trimester anatomy and screening have been low risk.

A transvaginal ultrasound today shows a closed external os with a cervical length of 28 mm and no funnelling. Her current pregnancy is singleton, the fetus is structurally normal at the 12-week morphology scan, and the placenta is fundal. She has no vaginal bleeding, no abdominal pain, and no signs of preterm labour. There is no history of cervical surgery or LLETZ. She asks what can be done to reduce the chance of losing this pregnancy.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 78/min, BP 110/68 mmHg, RR 16/min, SpO2 99% room air, temperature 36.7 °C, fetal heart 158/min
data_table.Examination: Closed external os on speculum; no PV bleeding; uterus appropriate for gestation
data_table.Investigations: Transvaginal ultrasound: cervical length 28 mm, no funnelling; singleton; structural anatomy normal

lead_in: What is the most appropriate intervention?

options.text: History indicated cerclage now plus daily vaginal progesterone 200 mg from 16 weeks
options.rationale: Two or more consecutive painless second-trimester losses meet RANZCOG criteria for history-indicated (prophylactic) cerclage placed at 12 to 14 weeks; vaginal progesterone is an evidence-supported adjunct for preterm birth prevention. (Source: RANZCOG Cervical Insufficiency; SMFM Cerclage Guideline)

options.text: Serial transvaginal cervical length scans every 2 weeks and intervene only if shortening
options.rationale: Surveillance is appropriate when the history is equivocal or there has been one prior loss; with two consecutive painless second-trimester losses, history-indicated cerclage is preferred over waiting for sonographic shortening. (Source: SMFM Cerclage Guideline)

options.text: Bed rest at home from 16 weeks until 36 weeks with avoidance of intercourse
options.rationale: Bed rest has no proven benefit in preventing preterm birth and increases maternal VTE and deconditioning risks; it is not a substitute for cerclage where indicated. (Source: RANZCOG Cervical Insufficiency)

options.text: Place an abdominal cerclage by laparoscopy at 12 weeks given two previous failures
options.rationale: Abdominal cerclage is reserved for failed transvaginal cerclage or absent vaginal cervix; first attempt should be a McDonald or Shirodkar transvaginal procedure. (Source: RANZCOG Cervical Insufficiency)

options.text: Administer betamethasone 11.4 mg IM weekly from 24 weeks prophylactically
options.rationale: Antenatal corticosteroids are not given prophylactically by schedule; they are administered when preterm birth is anticipated within 7 days and a single rescue dose at most. (Source: RANZCOG Antenatal Corticosteroids)

explanation.summary: Cervical insufficiency presents as painless, progressive second-trimester cervical dilation often with bulging membranes and is diagnosed by history when there are two or more consecutive second-trimester losses without other cause. Management options are history-indicated cerclage (12 to 14 weeks, recommended for >=2 prior losses), ultrasound-indicated cerclage (offered if cervical length falls below 25 mm before 24 weeks with one prior preterm birth), and physical-examination-indicated (rescue) cerclage for asymptomatic cervical dilation. Vaginal progesterone 200 mg daily from 16 weeks reduces preterm birth in women with a short cervix or prior preterm birth and complements cerclage. McDonald cerclage is the most common technique; Shirodkar and abdominal cerclage are reserved for selected cases.
key_points: >=2 consecutive painless second trimester losses = history-indicated cerclage at 12-14 weeks
Vaginal progesterone 200 mg daily from 16 weeks is adjunctive
Ultrasound-indicated cerclage if cervix <25 mm before 24 weeks with prior preterm
Bed rest has no proven benefit and harms maternal health
explanation.pearls: History-indicated cerclage at 12 to 14 weeks plus daily vaginal progesterone 200 mg from 16 weeks is the RANZCOG recommended package for women with two or more consecutive painless second-trimester losses.

stem:
You are the on-call obstetric registrar reviewing a 26-year-old G1P0 woman in active labour at 39+4 weeks gestation. Her membranes ruptured 22 hours ago and she has had spontaneous progress to 5 cm dilation with regular contractions. She had a prolonged second stage planned and is on an epidural. Her group B streptococcus swab at 36 weeks was negative.

Over the last hour her temperature has risen from 36.9 °C to 38.4 °C, recorded by the midwife on two readings 20 minutes apart. Her maternal heart rate is 118/min. Fetal CTG shows a baseline of 168/min with reduced variability and no decelerations. The amniotic fluid drained at vaginal examination is cloudy and offensive. She is otherwise stable, with a normal blood pressure and respiratory rate, and is comfortable on epidural with no abdominal tenderness between contractions. She is not allergic to penicillin or to any other medication.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 118/min, BP 122/72 mmHg, RR 18/min, SpO2 99% room air, temperature 38.4 °C, fetal heart 168/min baseline
data_table.Examination: 5 cm dilation; cloudy offensive amniotic fluid; no abdominal tenderness; epidural in situ
data_table.Investigations: Maternal CTG baseline 168/min reduced variability no decelerations; WCC pending; GBS swab negative at 36 weeks

lead_in: What is the most appropriate antibiotic regimen?

options.text: Withhold antibiotics until blood cultures return and target therapy then
options.rationale: Empirical broad spectrum cover must start immediately when chorioamnionitis is diagnosed; waiting for cultures risks neonatal sepsis. (Source: RANZCOG Intrapartum Fever)

options.text: Intravenous benzylpenicillin 1.2 g 4-hourly alone for GBS coverage
options.rationale: GBS monotherapy is appropriate intrapartum prophylaxis with positive screen, NOT chorioamnionitis treatment; once infection is established, broader gram-negative cover is needed. (Source: RANZCOG Intrapartum Fever)

options.text: Intravenous ceftriaxone 1 g daily plus metronidazole 500 mg 12-hourly
options.rationale: Ceftriaxone-metronidazole is an alternative for severe penicillin allergy, but is not the standard first-line regimen in Australia which uses ampicillin plus gentamicin. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines Antibiotic)

options.text: Oral cefalexin 500 mg 6-hourly plus expectant management of labour
options.rationale: Oral antibiotics are inadequate for established intrapartum infection; IV therapy is required and continued until 24 hours post-delivery (or per institutional protocol). (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines Antibiotic)

options.text: Intravenous ampicillin 2 g 6-hourly plus gentamicin 5 mg/kg daily
options.rationale: Intrapartum chorioamnionitis empiric therapy in Australia is IV ampicillin 2 g 6-hourly plus gentamicin 5 mg/kg daily; this covers ascending genital tract organisms including GBS, E. coli and Enterococcus. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines Antibiotic; RANZCOG Intrapartum Fever)

explanation.summary: Clinical chorioamnionitis is diagnosed by maternal fever >=38 °C plus one of fetal tachycardia, maternal tachycardia, uterine tenderness or purulent amniotic fluid. Empirical IV antibiotics target ascending genital flora including GBS, E. coli and Enterococcus; the Australian first-line is ampicillin plus gentamicin. Add clindamycin or metronidazole if caesarean delivery occurs to cover anaerobes. Delivery is the definitive treatment; antibiotics typically continue for 24 hours postpartum, longer if features of sepsis persist. The neonatal team should attend delivery given increased early-onset sepsis risk.
key_points: Fever >=38 °C plus one of fetal/maternal tachycardia, uterine tenderness, purulent liquor
Empirical IV ampicillin 2 g 6h plus gentamicin 5 mg/kg daily
Add clindamycin or metronidazole if caesarean (anaerobe cover)
Delivery is definitive; neonatal team to attend
explanation.pearls: Australian first-line for clinical chorioamnionitis is ampicillin 2 g IV 6-hourly plus gentamicin 5 mg/kg IV daily; ceftriaxone-metronidazole is the alternative for severe penicillin allergy, not first-line.

stem:
You are the senior obstetric registrar at a tertiary delivery suite called urgently to a 34-year-old G4P3 woman who collapsed two minutes after the spontaneous vaginal birth of a 4.2 kg male infant at 41+2 weeks. The third stage had been managed actively with intramuscular oxytocin 10 IU. The placenta is in situ.

While you arrive she becomes unresponsive, has a witnessed seizure, and stops breathing. Pulse is impalpable centrally. Cardiopulmonary resuscitation is commenced immediately. The midwife reports she became suddenly breathless, said she felt cold, and complained of impending doom moments before losing consciousness. There was a small amount of pink frothy sputum at her mouth. She has no past history of asthma or epilepsy, did not receive epidural, and a peripheral cannula sited 30 minutes ago for hydration has been kept patent. The first bloods drawn during resuscitation show a fibrinogen of 0.8 g/L (1.5-4.0), platelets 78 x10^9/L, INR 2.4 and pH 6.98.

data_table.Vital signs: No central pulse; previously: pulse 142/min, BP 70/40 mmHg, SpO2 unrecordable, RR 0 (apnoeic)
data_table.Examination: Unresponsive after seizure; pink frothy sputum at mouth; uterus tone unclear with placenta in situ; no obvious haemorrhage source
data_table.Investigations: Fibrinogen 0.8 g/L (1.5-4.0); platelets 78 x10^9/L; INR 2.4; pH 6.98; lactate 9.2 mmol/L

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step?

options.text: Defer resuscitation and arrange urgent CT pulmonary angiogram to confirm pulmonary embolism
options.rationale: A peri-arrest collapse cannot wait for imaging; treatment is empiric supportive ALS with MTP, and CTPA is not part of acute AFE management. (Source: ANZCOR ALS)

options.text: Give intravenous adrenaline 100 mcg boluses for presumed anaphylaxis to active third stage oxytocin
options.rationale: Oxytocin anaphylaxis is extremely rare and does NOT explain the DIC; treating AFE as anaphylaxis delays appropriate resuscitation and coagulopathy correction. (Source: RANZCOG Amniotic Fluid Embolism)

options.text: Administer intravenous magnesium sulfate 4 g for presumed eclampsia and continue observation
options.rationale: Without preceding pre-eclampsia or hypertension, eclampsia is unlikely; the DIC and pink frothy sputum point to AFE, and magnesium does not address the haemodynamic collapse. (Source: SOMANZ Hypertension in Pregnancy)

options.text: Continue CPR, secure airway, activate massive transfusion protocol, escalate to obstetric and ICU consultants
options.rationale: The collapse plus seizure plus DIC profile is amniotic fluid embolism until proven otherwise; management is supportive ALS plus aggressive correction of coagulopathy with MTP, with team-based escalation. (Source: ANZCOR ALS; RANZCOG Amniotic Fluid Embolism; SOMANZ AFE)

options.text: Start tranexamic acid 1 g intravenously and observe response before further escalation
options.rationale: TXA is given as part of PPH management but is not a substitute for full massive transfusion and ALS in cardiovascular collapse with established DIC. (Source: RANZCOG Postpartum Haemorrhage)

explanation.summary: Amniotic fluid embolism is a catastrophic obstetric event characterised by sudden cardiorespiratory collapse, hypoxia, neurological compromise (seizure or altered consciousness) and disseminated intravascular coagulation, usually around delivery or in the immediate postpartum period. The clinical picture - obstetric peripartum timing plus collapse plus DIC - is itself the diagnosis; no laboratory test is pathognomonic. Management is bundles-based: ANZCOR ALS for cardiac arrest, early airway control, supportive ventilation, aggressive correction of coagulopathy with massive transfusion protocol (red cells, FFP, cryoprecipitate, platelets), fibrinogen replacement, and consideration of veno-arterial ECMO at tertiary centres. Mortality remains 20-60%. Documentation and structured debriefing are mandatory.
key_points: Diagnosis is clinical: peripartum collapse + DIC + hypoxia +/- seizure
ANZCOR ALS plus airway plus MTP plus team escalation
Fibrinogen <2 g/L is a strong AFE marker, replace with cryoprecipitate
Consider VA-ECMO at tertiary centres
explanation.pearls: AFE often presents in two phases: an initial pulmonary hypertensive/cardiogenic shock phase from amniotic debris in the pulmonary vasculature, followed within an hour by florid DIC; fibrinogen below 2 g/L is the strongest single discriminator from haemorrhagic shock with secondary coagulopathy.

stem:
A 32-year-old woman attends your general practice clinic with a 12-month history of progressively heavier periods. She reports cycles every 28 days lasting 8 days, soaks through a super tampon and a pad together every 1 to 2 hours on day 2 and 3, and has passed coin-sized clots. She is increasingly tired but works full time. She and her partner plan to conceive in around 12 months and want to avoid hormonal contraception. There is no dyspareunia, no intermenstrual or post coital bleeding, and no family history of bleeding disorder.

On examination she is comfortable; abdomen is soft and non tender and no pelvic mass is palpable. Speculum and bimanual examination are normal. Cervical screening (HPV-based) is current and negative. Pelvic ultrasound is reported as a normal sized anteverted uterus with regular endometrial echotexture, no submucosal fibroid, no adenomyosis features and normal ovaries. Full blood count shows haemoglobin 104 g/L (115-160), MCV 72 fL (80-95), ferritin 8 mcg/L (30-150). Coagulation profile and von Willebrand panel are within normal limits.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 76/min, BP 112/68 mmHg, RR 16/min, SpO2 99% room air, temperature 36.7 °C
data_table.Examination: Abdomen soft, non tender, no pelvic mass; speculum and bimanual normal; cervical screening current negative
data_table.Investigations: Pelvic US: normal uterus, no fibroid, no adenomyosis, normal ovaries; Hb 104 g/L, MCV 72 fL, ferritin 8 mcg/L; coagulation and von Willebrand panel within normal limits

lead_in: What is the most appropriate first-line pharmacological treatment?

options.text: Combined oral contraceptive pill containing ethinylestradiol 30 mcg and levonorgestrel 150 mcg
options.rationale: COCP reduces bleeding but is hormonal and contraceptive, which the patient has declined; choosing it ignores her stated preference. (Source: RANZCOG Heavy Menstrual Bleeding)

options.text: Endometrial ablation under outpatient hysteroscopy after diagnostic curettage at the same sitting
options.rationale: Endometrial ablation is a permanent solution that precludes future pregnancy and is contraindicated in a woman planning to conceive. (Source: RANZCOG Heavy Menstrual Bleeding)

options.text: GnRH agonist depot injection monthly for 6 months with low dose oestrogen add-back
options.rationale: GnRH agonists are reserved for short-term use before surgery and are not first-line for uncomplicated ovulatory heavy menstrual bleeding. (Source: RANZCOG Heavy Menstrual Bleeding)

options.text: Tranexamic acid 1 g orally three times daily for the first 4 days of each menstrual cycle
options.rationale: Tranexamic acid reduces menstrual blood loss by approximately 40 to 60% and is non hormonal; it is the recommended first-line for ovulatory heavy menstrual bleeding in a woman who has declined hormonal therapy and wishes to conceive. (Source: RANZCOG Heavy Menstrual Bleeding; AMH)

options.text: Levonorgestrel-releasing intrauterine system inserted at the next available appointment
options.rationale: The Mirena IUS is highly effective for heavy menstrual bleeding but is a hormonal contraceptive that the patient has declined; first-line for women seeking conception within 12 months is non-hormonal tranexamic acid. (Source: RANZCOG Heavy Menstrual Bleeding)

explanation.summary: Heavy menstrual bleeding affects up to 25% of women and is defined as excessive bleeding interfering with quality of life. Initial workup includes FBC, ferritin, TSH, coagulation profile and von Willebrand panel if any bleeding history, plus pelvic ultrasound to exclude structural causes. RANZCOG and NICE first-line pharmacotherapy for ovulatory HMB without structural cause is tranexamic acid 1 g three times daily during menses for women not requiring contraception. The Mirena IUS is preferred for women happy with hormonal contraception. NSAIDs are an alternative for women with associated dysmenorrhoea. Iron supplementation runs concurrently and the patient here needs both oral iron and treatment of the bleeding.
key_points: Workup: FBC, ferritin, TSH, von Willebrand, pelvic ultrasound
First-line non hormonal: tranexamic acid 1 g three times daily during menses
First-line hormonal: Mirena LNG-IUS
Treat iron deficiency in parallel
explanation.pearls: Tranexamic acid is contraindicated only in active thromboembolism or history of arterial thrombosis; routine VTE risk does not preclude use per AMH and RANZCOG guidance.

stem:
A 28-year-old G1P1 woman is referred to your gynaecology clinic with 9 months of secondary amenorrhoea. Her cycle had previously been regular every 28 days. She had a normal vaginal delivery 14 months ago, complicated by retained products of conception that required ultrasound-guided suction curettage at 6 weeks postpartum after antibiotic treatment for endometritis. She has had cyclical pelvic pain in the lower abdomen each month for the last 6 months without any associated bleeding. She is not breastfeeding.

On examination she is healthy and well. Body mass index 24 kg/m2. Abdomen is soft. Speculum examination reveals a clean cervix; bimanual examination is unremarkable. Beta-hCG is negative. Serum TSH, prolactin, FSH, LH, oestradiol and androgen panel are within the normal range. A progesterone withdrawal challenge with medroxyprogesterone 10 mg daily for 10 days produced no bleeding. Transvaginal ultrasound shows a thin discontinuous endometrium with focal anechoic areas suggesting adhesions; a saline infusion sonohysterogram shows fibrous bands crossing the uterine cavity.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 72/min, BP 116/72 mmHg, RR 14/min, SpO2 99% room air, temperature 36.7 °C
data_table.Examination: Healthy, BMI 24; abdomen soft; speculum and bimanual unremarkable
data_table.Investigations: Beta-hCG negative; TSH, prolactin, FSH, LH, oestradiol and androgens within normal limits; progesterone withdrawal: no bleed; TV US: thin discontinuous endometrium; saline sonohysterogram: intrauterine adhesions

lead_in: What is the most appropriate management?

options.text: Diagnostic laparoscopy with chromopertubation to exclude tubal disease before any treatment
options.rationale: The diagnosis is intracavity not tubal; laparoscopy is not the next step and adds operative risk. (Source: RANZCOG Asherman Syndrome)

options.text: Repeat dilation and curettage to clear suspected retained tissue with antibiotic cover
options.rationale: Blind dilation and curettage created the adhesions and risks creating more; hysteroscopic adhesiolysis under direct vision is the correct procedure. (Source: RANZCOG Asherman Syndrome)

options.text: Empirical GnRH agonist therapy for 3 months and reassess endometrial pattern by ultrasound
options.rationale: GnRH agonists suppress ovulation and are used pre fibroid surgery; they do not lyse adhesions and worsen the endometrial thinning. (Source: RANZCOG Asherman Syndrome)

options.text: Combined oral contraceptive pill for 6 months and reassess menstrual return after cessation
options.rationale: COCP does not treat established adhesions; even high dose oestrogen alone cannot lyse fibrous bands and ongoing amenorrhoea will continue. (Source: RANZCOG Asherman Syndrome)

options.text: Hysteroscopic adhesiolysis under direct vision with post operative oestrogen for 8 weeks
options.rationale: Hysteroscopic adhesiolysis is the standard treatment for Asherman syndrome; postoperative oestrogen stimulates endometrial regeneration and reduces adhesion reformation. (Source: RANZCOG Asherman Syndrome)

explanation.summary: Asherman syndrome describes intrauterine adhesions that follow uterine instrumentation, especially curettage in the postpartum or post miscarriage state when endometrial vulnerability is highest. Patients present with hypomenorrhoea or amenorrhoea, cyclical pain from haematometra, and secondary infertility. The diagnostic gold standard is hysteroscopy but saline infusion sonohysterography is a reasonable non invasive screen. Treatment is hysteroscopic adhesiolysis with cold scissors or fine bipolar to preserve endometrium, followed by postoperative oestrogen and intracavity barriers (intrauterine balloon, hyaluronic acid gel) to reduce reformation. Severe disease may require staged procedures.
key_points: Cause: uterine instrumentation in vulnerable endometrium, e.g. postpartum
Presentation: amenorrhoea, cyclical pain, infertility
Diagnosis: hysteroscopy (gold standard); SIS as a screen
Treatment: hysteroscopic adhesiolysis plus post op oestrogen plus barrier
explanation.pearls: Postoperative oestrogen replacement (oestradiol valerate 2 mg twice daily for 6 to 8 weeks) is recommended after hysteroscopic adhesiolysis in Asherman syndrome to stimulate endometrial regrowth and reduce adhesion reformation per RANZCOG.

stem:
A 29-year-old nulliparous woman presents to your general practice for the third time in 9 months distressed by severe irritability, low mood, anxiety, breast tenderness and bloating that begin around 7 days before menses and resolve fully within 2 days of menses starting. She has used the eCOPE prospective symptom diary for 3 consecutive cycles which shows at least 5 symptoms in the luteal phase with full resolution in the follicular phase and no symptoms outside the luteal phase.

On examination she is well, with a normal mood when reviewed in the follicular phase today. PHQ-9 outside the luteal phase is 2 of 27 and GAD-7 is 1 of 21; both rise sharply in the luteal phase. She has tried regular exercise and dietary change for 4 months without benefit. There is no history of bipolar affective disorder, no current alcohol or recreational drug use, no concomitant medications and no contraception is in use because she and her partner are happy with condoms.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 70/min, BP 116/72 mmHg, RR 14/min, SpO2 99% room air, temperature 36.7 °C
data_table.Examination: Well, mood reactive; eCOPE diary: at least 5 luteal symptoms, full follicular resolution across 3 cycles
data_table.Investigations: PHQ-9 follicular 2/27 (rises sharply in luteal phase); GAD-7 follicular 1/21; TSH within normal limits

lead_in: What is the most appropriate first-line pharmacological treatment?

options.text: Sertraline 50 mg orally daily commenced 14 days before expected menses each cycle
options.rationale: Luteal phase dosing of SSRI is supported by NICE and RANZCOG for premenstrual dysphoric disorder and works within hours rather than weeks; symptom improvement begins from the first treated cycle. (Source: RANZCOG Premenstrual Disorders; AMH; RANZCP)

options.text: Lithium carbonate 600 mg taken nightly with monthly serum lithium concentration monitoring
options.rationale: Lithium has no role in PMDD without bipolar disorder; it is a mood stabiliser for bipolar affective disorder and risks toxicity without indication. (Source: RANZCP Practice Guidelines)

options.text: Intravenous magnesium sulfate 2 g infusion during severe luteal flares in the day clinic
options.rationale: IV magnesium for PMDD flares is not standard care; oral magnesium has weak evidence but IV use lacks support and exposes the patient to procedural risk. (Source: RANZCOG Premenstrual Disorders)

options.text: Lamotrigine titrated over 6 weeks to 100 mg daily with rash monitoring during build up
options.rationale: Lamotrigine is used in bipolar depression maintenance; it is not first-line for PMDD and has rash risk that does not justify use here. (Source: AMH)

options.text: Combined oral contraceptive pill containing drospirenone taken cyclically with a 4 day break
options.rationale: Drospirenone COCP is an option for PMDD but typically used continuously or with a 4-day break, with mixed evidence; for women not requiring contraception, luteal phase SSRI is preferred first line. (Source: RANZCOG Premenstrual Disorders)

explanation.summary: Premenstrual dysphoric disorder is the severe end of the premenstrual disorder spectrum, affecting around 3 to 8% of menstruating women. DSM-5 requires at least 5 symptoms confined to the luteal phase across 2 prospective cycles with full follicular phase remission and functional impairment. First-line pharmacotherapy is SSRI: either continuous, luteal-phase only (14 days before expected menses), or symptom onset. Luteal phase dosing is convenient and effective from the first cycle, unlike SSRIs in major depression. Combined oral contraceptive pills with drospirenone are an alternative for women also seeking contraception. Cognitive behaviour therapy and lifestyle measures (exercise, sleep, reduced caffeine) are adjuncts.
key_points: DSM-5 PMDD: at least 5 symptoms, luteal only, functional impairment, prospective diary
First-line: SSRI continuous or luteal phase only
Alternative: drospirenone COCP if contraception also wanted
Onset of SSRI benefit in PMDD is within hours, not weeks
