explanation.pearls: Luteal phase dosing of sertraline 50 mg from cycle day 14 until day 1 of menses produces response from the first treated cycle in PMDD; this rapid action distinguishes PMDD treatment from SSRI use in major depressive disorder where weeks of dosing are needed.

stem:
A 30-year-old G2P2 woman presents to your general practice at 6 weeks postpartum for her routine review. She has had two uncomplicated vaginal deliveries; the youngest is exclusively breastfed and feeding 3 to 4 hourly day and night. Her previous postnatal contraception was a progesterone only pill that she found unreliable and she has a 12 year history of menorrhagia previously controlled on combined oral contraceptive pill. She and her partner have completed their family but are not yet committed to permanent sterilisation. She has had no bleeding for the last 7 days and there has been no resumption of menses.

On examination she is well. Body mass index is 25 kg/m2. Blood pressure is 118/72 mmHg. Speculum examination shows a clean cervix and bimanual examination reveals a normally involuted uterus, no adnexal tenderness and no mass. A urine pregnancy test in the consulting room is negative. There is no current pelvic infection and she has had no STI risk in the last 6 months.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 70/min, BP 118/72 mmHg, RR 14/min, SpO2 99% room air, temperature 36.7 °C
data_table.Examination: Well, BMI 25; speculum clean cervix; bimanual: involuted uterus, no adnexal tenderness
data_table.Investigations: Urine pregnancy test negative; no current STI symptoms; no high-risk sexual contact in last 6 months

lead_in: What is the most appropriate contraceptive recommendation today?

options.text: Commence the combined oral contraceptive pill starting today and continuing without breaks
options.rationale: COCP is contraindicated in breastfeeding women under 6 weeks postpartum and cautioned until 6 months; it can reduce milk supply and is not the best option here. (Source: RANZCOG Contraception)

options.text: Insert a levonorgestrel releasing intrauterine system in the same consultation today
options.rationale: At 6 weeks postpartum after lochia has settled, LNG-IUS can be safely inserted; it provides effective contraception, treats her menorrhagia history, and is compatible with breastfeeding. (Source: RANZCOG Contraception; Family Planning Australia)

options.text: Insert a copper intrauterine device at 12 weeks postpartum after a repeat speculum examination
options.rationale: Copper IUD is an option but delays initiation by 6 weeks unnecessarily; it also worsens menstrual bleeding which is undesirable given her menorrhagia history. (Source: RANZCOG Contraception)

options.text: Defer all contraception until resumption of menses then start the progesterone only pill
options.rationale: Lactational amenorrhoea is not sufficiently reliable beyond 6 months or after introduction of solids; gaps in contraception in an actively partnered woman risks unplanned pregnancy. (Source: RANZCOG Contraception)

options.text: Administer depot medroxyprogesterone 150 mg intramuscular injection today and repeat every 12 weeks
options.rationale: Depot is an option but is associated with weight gain and bone density loss with long use; the patient prefers a long acting reversible method that also treats her menorrhagia. (Source: RANZCOG Contraception)

explanation.summary: Long-acting reversible contraception is recommended as a first-line postpartum option for women not seeking immediate further pregnancy. LNG-IUS can be inserted at the time of caesarean section, within 48 hours of vaginal birth (immediate), or after 4 weeks postpartum (delayed); insertion between 48 hours and 4 weeks carries higher expulsion risk and is avoided. By 4 to 6 weeks lochia has typically settled and the uterus has involuted; the LNG-IUS is safe and effective in breastfeeding women and reduces menstrual blood loss substantially. The copper IUD is an alternative but increases bleeding, which is undesirable in women with prior menorrhagia. Combined hormonal methods are contraindicated under 6 weeks postpartum due to VTE risk and may impair lactation; progesterone only methods are compatible with breastfeeding throughout.
key_points: Postpartum LNG-IUS: at delivery, within 48 hours, or after 4 weeks
Avoid insertion 48 hours to 4 weeks (high expulsion)
LNG-IUS safe in breastfeeding and treats menorrhagia
COCP contraindicated under 6 weeks; progesterone only methods OK
explanation.pearls: Immediate postpartum LNG-IUS insertion within 48 hours of vaginal birth is now supported in Australian practice but carries an expulsion rate of approximately 15 to 20% at 6 months; delayed insertion at 4 to 6 weeks balances expulsion risk and ease of access per Family Planning Australia.

stem:
You are the obstetric registrar called to the high dependency obstetric area for a 36-year-old G2P1 woman at 35+2 weeks being managed for severe pre-eclampsia. Two hours ago she had a 4 g intravenous magnesium sulfate loading dose followed by a 1 g/hour maintenance infusion. Her blood pressure is now controlled on a labetalol infusion. She has had no seizure and the cardiotocograph remains reassuring.

The bedside midwife calls you because over the last 30 minutes the patient has become progressively drowsy, slurring her speech. Patellar reflexes are now absent bilaterally. Respiratory rate has fallen to 9 breaths per minute and she is not coughing on suctioning. Hourly urine output has dropped from 60 mL/hour to 15 mL/hour over the last 2 hours. The renal team reports her serum creatinine has risen from 78 to 156 micromol/L since admission. The point of care magnesium concentration just back from the laboratory is 4.5 mmol/L (therapeutic 2 to 3.5 mmol/L).

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 78/min, BP 138/86 mmHg, RR 9/min, SpO2 94% room air, temperature 36.7 °C, fetal heart 140/min
data_table.Examination: Drowsy with slurred speech; patellar reflexes absent; not coughing on suctioning; urine output 15 mL/hour
data_table.Investigations: Magnesium 4.5 mmol/L (therapeutic 2-3.5); creatinine 156 micromol/L (was 78); CTG: baseline 140/min, normal variability, no decelerations

lead_in: What is the most appropriate immediate management?

options.text: Intravenous naloxone 400 mcg titrated for respiratory depression and reassess every 5 minutes
options.rationale: Naloxone reverses opioid not magnesium toxicity; she has had no opioid and her respiratory depression is from supratherapeutic magnesium. (Source: AMH)

options.text: Intubate immediately and ventilate at FiO2 100% until magnesium clearance restores breathing
options.rationale: Intubation and ventilation are supportive but calcium gluconate is the direct antidote and should be given first; intubation is only required if calcium plus airway support fails to restore respiratory drive. (Source: SOMANZ Hypertension in Pregnancy)

options.text: Cease the magnesium infusion and administer intravenous calcium gluconate 10% 10 mL over 3 minutes
options.rationale: Magnesium toxicity in pre-eclampsia is reversed with intravenous calcium gluconate 1 g (10 mL of 10% solution) given over 3 minutes plus immediate cessation of the magnesium infusion; this antagonises magnesium at the neuromuscular junction. (Source: SOMANZ Hypertension in Pregnancy; RANZCOG Hypertensive Disorders)

options.text: Switch antihypertensive control to oral nifedipine 20 mg and continue the magnesium infusion
options.rationale: Switching antihypertensives does not reverse magnesium toxicity, and continued magnesium with falling renal clearance will worsen the neuromuscular and respiratory depression. (Source: SOMANZ Hypertension in Pregnancy)

options.text: Intravenous furosemide 40 mg to accelerate magnesium clearance and a fluid bolus of 250 mL saline
options.rationale: Furosemide accelerates magnesium clearance but the priority is immediate antagonism with calcium; a fluid bolus in the context of pre-eclampsia and oliguria risks pulmonary oedema. (Source: SOMANZ Hypertension in Pregnancy)

explanation.summary: Magnesium sulfate halves eclampsia risk and is standard for severe pre-eclampsia. Toxicity is dose dependent and renal clearance dependent. Therapeutic concentration is 2 to 3.5 mmol/L; loss of patellar reflexes appears around 3.5 to 5 mmol/L, respiratory depression around 5 to 6.5 mmol/L, and cardiac arrest above 6.5 mmol/L. Oliguria and rising creatinine cut magnesium clearance, so urine output and renal function must be monitored. Treatment of toxicity is immediate cessation of the magnesium infusion and intravenous calcium gluconate 10% 10 mL over 3 minutes; supportive ventilation is added if respiratory depression persists. Magnesium concentration should be checked 6-hourly in renal impairment and the infusion rate halved when creatinine clearance falls.
key_points: Therapeutic Mg 2 to 3.5 mmol/L; toxicity from 3.5 upwards
Loss of reflexes first, then respiratory depression, then arrest
Antidote: calcium gluconate 10% 10 mL over 3 minutes
Renal impairment cuts clearance; reduce or stop infusion
explanation.pearls: In severe pre-eclampsia, hourly patellar reflexes, respiratory rate and urine output are the bedside markers of magnesium safety; a fall in urine output below 30 mL/hour over 4 hours mandates magnesium concentration check and infusion rate review per SOMANZ guidance.

stem:
A 33-year-old G1P0 woman presents to the early pregnancy assessment service at 7 weeks gestation after a fresh embryo transfer through her local IVF clinic. She has had right iliac fossa pain over the last 24 hours, described as constant and rated 4 of 10. There has been a small amount of pink spotting today. There is no shoulder tip pain, no syncope and no significant per vaginal bleeding.

On examination she is haemodynamically stable. Abdomen is soft with mild right iliac fossa tenderness, no rebound and no guarding. Speculum examination shows a closed cervix with a small amount of fresh blood. Bimanual examination reveals fullness in the right adnexa. Transvaginal ultrasound shows an intrauterine gestational sac at 7 weeks with a fetal pole, crown rump length 10 mm and fetal cardiac activity present; a separate 3 cm complex right adnexal mass adjacent to the right ovary and a small amount of free fluid in the pouch of Douglas. Serum beta-hCG is 14,200 IU/L; haemoglobin 124 g/L; her blood group is A positive.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 86/min, BP 116/72 mmHg, RR 16/min, SpO2 99% room air, temperature 36.7 °C
data_table.Examination: Abdomen soft, mild right iliac fossa tenderness, no peritonism; speculum closed cervix small fresh blood; bimanual right adnexal fullness
data_table.Investigations: TV US: viable 7-week intrauterine pregnancy with fetal cardiac activity; 3 cm complex right adnexal mass; small POD fluid; beta-hCG 14,200 IU/L; Hb 124 g/L; group A positive

lead_in: What is the most appropriate management?

options.text: Suction curettage of the uterine cavity followed by methotrexate for the adnexal pregnancy
options.rationale: Suction curettage destroys a viable intrauterine pregnancy that this patient wishes to continue; it is not the standard management for heterotopic pregnancy. (Source: RANZCOG Ectopic Pregnancy)

options.text: Single dose intramuscular methotrexate 50 mg/m2 with weekly beta-hCG monitoring thereafter
options.rationale: Methotrexate is teratogenic and contraindicated when a concurrent viable intrauterine pregnancy is present; it cannot be used in heterotopic pregnancy. (Source: RANZCOG Ectopic Pregnancy)

options.text: Expectant management with serial beta-hCG and ultrasound surveillance over the next 7 days
options.rationale: An adnexal mass over 3.5 cm or with significant pain warrants surgical management; expectant management cannot be safely offered with active symptoms and a viable intrauterine pregnancy to protect. (Source: RANZCOG Ectopic Pregnancy)

options.text: Laparoscopic salpingectomy of the affected tube while preserving the intrauterine pregnancy
options.rationale: In heterotopic pregnancy with a symptomatic adnexal mass, surgical removal (typically laparoscopic salpingectomy of the affected tube) is recommended; the intrauterine pregnancy is preserved by careful technique avoiding uterine manipulation. (Source: RANZCOG Ectopic Pregnancy)

options.text: Administer anti-D immunoglobulin 625 IU and discharge with early pregnancy unit review in 48 hours
options.rationale: She is rhesus positive so anti-D is not indicated; discharge with symptomatic heterotopic pregnancy risks tubal rupture and miscarriage of the intrauterine pregnancy. (Source: RANZCOG Anti-D Immunoglobulin)

explanation.summary: Heterotopic pregnancy (concurrent intrauterine and ectopic pregnancy) is rare in spontaneous conception (1 in 30,000) but occurs in approximately 1 in 100 IVF pregnancies. Diagnosis is missed when an early intrauterine pregnancy is found and the adnexae are not carefully scanned. Beta-hCG is unreliable for diagnosis because the intrauterine pregnancy produces normally rising hCG. Methotrexate is contraindicated because of teratogenicity to the intrauterine pregnancy. Management is surgical: laparoscopic salpingectomy of the affected tube while minimising uterine manipulation. Reported intrauterine pregnancy survival after surgical management of heterotopic pregnancy is approximately 60 to 70%.
key_points: Heterotopic risk approximately 1 in 100 in IVF pregnancies
Always scan adnexae even if intrauterine pregnancy is seen after IVF
Methotrexate contraindicated due to teratogenicity to intrauterine pregnancy
Surgical: laparoscopic salpingectomy with minimal uterine manipulation
explanation.pearls: Among IVF pregnancies, approximately 1 in 100 are heterotopic versus 1 in 30,000 of spontaneously conceived pregnancies; in any IVF pregnancy with adnexal pain the contralateral tube must be carefully assessed despite the comfort of a confirmed intrauterine sac.

stem:
A 35-year-old woman is referred to your colposcopy clinic with a positive cervical screening result. Eighteen months ago she had a large loop excision of the transformation zone for histologically confirmed HSIL (CIN 3) with clear excision margins of 4 mm. She had a routine test of cure cervical screening at 12 months which was reported as HPV oncogenic types not detected and she was advised to return to the routine 5 yearly screening cycle. She presented for an opportunistic test 6 months early following a recent change of general practitioner.

The current result reports HPV oncogenic type 16 detected, with reflex liquid based cytology showing HSIL. She is asymptomatic, with no intermenstrual or postcoital bleeding and no abnormal discharge. She is in a stable monogamous relationship and uses condoms intermittently. Her general health is good and her last menstrual period was 2 weeks ago. On examination the cervix appears macroscopically healthy with no visible lesion; bimanual is unremarkable. Pelvic ultrasound has been arranged but is not yet completed.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 72/min, BP 116/72 mmHg, RR 14/min, SpO2 99% room air, temperature 36.7 °C
data_table.Examination: Cervix macroscopically healthy with no visible lesion; bimanual unremarkable
data_table.Investigations: HPV oncogenic type 16 detected; reflex cytology HSIL; prior LLETZ for CIN 3 with 4 mm clear margins; 12-month test of cure HPV not detected

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step?

options.text: Proceed to total abdominal hysterectomy without prior colposcopy or histology confirmation
options.rationale: Hysterectomy is not justified before histological confirmation and the patient deserves the option of fertility-sparing excisional treatment. (Source: NCSP Guidelines)

options.text: Repeat HPV based cervical screening in 12 months without colposcopy or biopsy intervention
options.rationale: HSIL cytology with HPV type 16 cannot be observed; the recurrence risk after prior CIN 3 is too high to defer histological assessment. (Source: NCSP Guidelines)

options.text: Order pelvic magnetic resonance imaging to stage suspected invasive cervical malignancy first
options.rationale: There is no clinical evidence of invasive disease; staging MRI is appropriate only after histological confirmation of invasion, not before colposcopy. (Source: NCSP Guidelines)

options.text: Repeat cone biopsy by cold knife conisation in the operating theatre under regional anaesthesia
options.rationale: Cold knife conisation is reserved for cases where colposcopy cannot adequately visualise the lesion or where adenocarcinoma in situ is suspected; LLETZ remains preferred for repeat squamous excision. (Source: NCSP Guidelines)

options.text: Colposcopy with directed biopsy and consideration of repeat excisional treatment if confirmed
options.rationale: HPV type 16 with HSIL cytology after prior CIN 3 treatment requires colposcopy with biopsy; further excisional treatment is offered if recurrence is confirmed because residual or recurrent CIN occurs in approximately 5 to 10% even with clear margins. (Source: NCSP Guidelines; RANZCOG Cervical Screening)

explanation.summary: Following excisional treatment for high grade squamous intraepithelial lesion, the Australian National Cervical Screening Program recommends a test of cure (co-test HPV plus liquid based cytology) at 12 months. A negative test of cure returns the woman to routine 5 yearly screening. A positive HPV result or any cytological abnormality at test of cure requires colposcopy. Recurrent or persistent CIN affects approximately 5 to 10% of women after LLETZ even with clear margins because HPV is a field disease and reinfection or persistence at the new transformation zone can occur. HPV type 16 carries the highest risk of invasive progression. Management of recurrence is repeat colposcopy with biopsy and repeat excisional treatment if confirmed; hysterectomy is reserved for older women who have completed family or where excision is technically not feasible.
key_points: Australian test of cure: HPV + cytology at 12 months post LLETZ
Any HPV positive or cytology abnormal: colposcopy
5 to 10% recurrence even with clear margins
HPV type 16: highest invasive progression risk
explanation.pearls: HPV type 16 carries approximately twice the absolute progression risk of other oncogenic HPV types per Australian NCSP modelling; positivity at test of cure mandates colposcopy regardless of cytology result.

stem:
A 22-year-old G1P0 woman had suction evacuation 4 weeks ago for a complete hydatidiform molar pregnancy diagnosed at 9 weeks gestation by uterine size larger than dates, theca lutein cysts, and 'snowstorm' ultrasound. Histology confirmed a complete mole with no evidence of invasive trophoblast on initial review. She is being followed in the Australian gestational trophoblastic registry through your tertiary unit.

Her pre-evacuation beta-hCG was 250,000 IU/L. Weekly serial concentrations have been 18,000 on day 7, 12,000 on day 14, 13,000 on day 21 and 14,000 today on day 28. She is otherwise well, with no abdominal pain, no abnormal bleeding and no respiratory or neurological symptoms. Her chest radiograph is clear without nodules. Pelvic ultrasound today shows a normally involuted uterus, no residual molar tissue and normal adnexae. Liver and renal function are within normal limits. She and her partner use barrier contraception.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 76/min, BP 118/72 mmHg, RR 14/min, SpO2 99% room air, temperature 36.7 °C
data_table.Examination: Well; uterus involuted; no abnormal bleeding; chest clear; no neurological deficits
data_table.Investigations: Beta-hCG day 7: 18,000; day 14: 12,000; day 21: 13,000; day 28: 14,000 IU/L; CXR clear; pelvic US no residual molar tissue; LFTs and renal within normal limits

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step?

options.text: Single agent methotrexate chemotherapy 50 mg intramuscular on day 1, 3, 5, 7 every 2 weeks
options.rationale: The patient meets FIGO criteria for post-molar GTN (beta-hCG plateau over 3 weeks of 4 values within plus or minus 10%); with a FIGO low-risk score, single agent methotrexate is the standard initial chemotherapy. (Source: RANZCOG GTN; FIGO 2018)

options.text: Combination chemotherapy with EMA-CO protocol (etoposide, methotrexate, dactinomycin, vincristine)
options.rationale: EMA-CO is reserved for high-risk GTN (WHO/FIGO prognostic score 7 or higher) or methotrexate-resistant disease; her low-risk score puts her in the single agent group first. (Source: RANZCOG GTN; FIGO 2018)

options.text: Repeat suction curettage of the uterine cavity for presumed retained molar tissue under anaesthesia
options.rationale: There is no ultrasound evidence of residual molar tissue and repeat evacuation does not improve outcome for GTN; chemotherapy is the recommended treatment for the rising or plateau beta-hCG. (Source: RANZCOG GTN; FIGO 2018)

options.text: Continue weekly beta-hCG monitoring without any intervention until 6 months post evacuation
options.rationale: Plateau over 3 weeks meets FIGO criteria for GTN diagnosis; further surveillance without treatment risks progression to choriocarcinoma. (Source: RANZCOG GTN; FIGO 2018)

options.text: Total abdominal hysterectomy with preservation of both ovaries as the definitive treatment
options.rationale: Hysterectomy may be offered for low-risk GTN in women who have completed family but is not first-line in a nulliparous 22-year-old; chemotherapy preserves fertility with equivalent cure rates. (Source: RANZCOG GTN)

explanation.summary: Following evacuation of a complete hydatidiform mole, beta-hCG surveillance detects gestational trophoblastic neoplasia (GTN) which develops in approximately 15 to 20% of complete moles and 1 to 5% of partial moles. FIGO criteria for GTN are (1) plateau of 4 beta-hCG values over 3 weeks within plus or minus 10%, (2) rise of 10% or more over 3 consecutive weekly values, (3) persistent detectable beta-hCG at 6 months post evacuation, or (4) histological choriocarcinoma. Once GTN is diagnosed, staging (FIGO 2018) plus the WHO prognostic score determines low risk (score under 7) versus high risk treatment. Single agent methotrexate (with folinic acid rescue) is first-line for low risk disease; high risk disease requires EMA-CO. Cure rates approach 100% in low risk and 80 to 90% in high risk GTN; subsequent fertility is preserved.
key_points: FIGO post-molar GTN criteria: plateau, rise, persistent at 6 months, or histology
Score under 7 = low risk: single agent methotrexate
Score 7 or higher = high risk: EMA-CO combination
Cure rates approach 100% low risk, 80 to 90% high risk, fertility preserved
explanation.pearls: After successful chemotherapy for low-risk gestational trophoblastic neoplasia in Australia, contraception is recommended for at least 12 months and pregnancy avoided to ensure beta-hCG surveillance is interpretable and to allow detection of late recurrence.

subtopic_detail: Atonic PPH second-line uterotonic with TXA
stem:
You are the obstetric registrar at a tertiary maternity unit reviewing a G3P3 woman who had a spontaneous vaginal delivery 30 minutes ago. The placenta delivered intact. The midwife now reports a steady fresh trickle and an estimated blood loss of 1500 mL over the last 10 minutes. She has had 10 units IM oxytocin at delivery and bimanual uterine compression has been commenced. There is no perineal laceration above first degree.

On assessment she is alert and oriented but cool peripherally. Her fundus is at the umbilicus and boggy on palpation. She has no history of hypertension and no asthma. She has 2 large bore cannulae and a group and hold has been sent with crossmatch in progress. The anaesthetics registrar is on the way.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 116/min, BP 100/65 mmHg, RR 22/min, SpO2 99% room air, temperature 36.6 °C
data_table.Examination: Alert; cool peripheries; fundus at umbilicus, boggy; ongoing fresh PV bleeding; perineum first degree tear, sutured
data_table.Investigations: Estimated blood loss 1500 mL; Hb on antenatal bloods 118 g/L (115-160); coags and lactate sent

lead_in: What is the single most appropriate next uterotonic and adjunct?

options.text: IM ergometrine 250 mcg plus IV tranexamic acid 1 g over 10 minutes
options.rationale: She has no hypertension or pre-eclampsia, so ergometrine is the appropriate second-line uterotonic; TXA reduces death from bleeding when given within 3 hours of PPH onset (WOMAN trial). (Source: RANZCOG Statement: Management of postpartum haemorrhage)
source_refs: RANZCOG Statement: Management of postpartum haemorrhage

options.text: IM carboprost 250 mcg repeated every 15 minutes to a maximum of 8 doses
options.rationale: Carboprost (PGF2-alpha) is reserved when oxytocin and ergometrine have failed; jumping past ergometrine ignores the established uterotonic ladder and incurs bronchospasm risk. (Source: RANZCOG Statement: Management of postpartum haemorrhage)
source_refs: RANZCOG Statement: Management of postpartum haemorrhage

options.text: Misoprostol 800 mcg per rectum as the sole second-line agent
options.rationale: Misoprostol has slow onset and is an adjunct rather than first-line second agent; AU practice prefers ergometrine for rapid uterotonic effect. (Source: RANZCOG Statement: Management of postpartum haemorrhage)
source_refs: RANZCOG Statement: Management of postpartum haemorrhage

options.text: Insert Bakri balloon tamponade now without further pharmacological therapy
options.rationale: Balloon tamponade is appropriate when pharmacological therapy fails or as a bridge to theatre; it should not replace a trial of second-line uterotonic in a haemodynamically stable woman. (Source: RANZCOG Statement: Management of postpartum haemorrhage)
source_refs: RANZCOG Statement: Management of postpartum haemorrhage

options.text: Continue uterine massage and further IV oxytocin infusion as sole therapy
options.rationale: Persisting with oxytocin alone after 1500 mL loss without additional uterotonic class change delays effective control; switching mechanism is the standard escalation. (Source: RANZCOG Statement: Management of postpartum haemorrhage)
source_refs: RANZCOG Statement: Management of postpartum haemorrhage

explanation.summary: Atonic postpartum haemorrhage with 1500 mL loss in a woman without hypertension or pre-eclampsia is escalated with ergometrine as the second-line uterotonic and intravenous tranexamic acid within 3 hours. The WOMAN trial established TXA mortality benefit in PPH. Carboprost and misoprostol are third-line agents for ongoing atony.
key_points: Uterotonic ladder: oxytocin → ergometrine (if no HT/PE) → carboprost (if no asthma) → misoprostol.
TXA 1 g IV within 3 hours of onset of PPH reduces mortality.
Ergometrine is contraindicated in hypertension, pre-eclampsia, and ischaemic heart disease.
Carboprost is contraindicated in asthma.
explanation.pearls: The single most missed step in PPH is intravenous TXA in the first 3 hours; it sits alongside the uterotonic ladder, not after it.

sources.label: RANZCOG Statement: Management of postpartum haemorrhage

subtopic_detail: Severe pre-eclampsia BP control and magnesium
stem:
You are the obstetric registrar on call. A G1 primigravida at 32+4 weeks is referred from a regional hospital with severe pre-eclampsia. She reports an occipital headache and blurred vision for the past hour. She has no past medical history and was on no medications. The retrieval team is en route to transfer her to a tertiary centre with neonatal intensive care 90 minutes away.

On arrival in your obstetric unit she is alert and orientated but uncomfortable. Reflexes are brisk with no clonus. Fetal heart rate trace is reactive at 145/min with no decelerations. The midwife has just established a peripheral cannula and your consultant is on the way. Steroids for fetal lung maturity have been given by the referring hospital.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 96/min, BP 168/115 mmHg, RR 18/min, SpO2 98% room air, temperature 36.8 °C, fetal HR 145/min
data_table.Examination: Alert, uncomfortable; reflexes brisk no clonus; epigastric tenderness; lower limb oedema 2+
data_table.Investigations: Platelets 95 x10^9/L (150-400), ALT 88 U/L (5-35), creatinine 92 micromol/L (45-90), urine PCR 800 mg/mmol, urate 0.42 mmol/L

lead_in: What is the single most appropriate immediate management bundle?

options.text: IV nifedipine 10 mg bolus plus IV magnesium sulfate 4 g loading dose
options.rationale: Nifedipine is given orally, not intravenously, and the AU first-line IV antihypertensive in severe pre-eclampsia is labetalol or hydralazine; oral nifedipine is acceptable but not in IV form. (Source: SOMANZ Hypertension in Pregnancy Guideline)

options.text: IV labetalol 20 mg plus IV magnesium 4 g loading then 1 g/hour, target BP <160/110
options.rationale: AU first-line acute antihypertensives in severe pre-eclampsia are IV labetalol or hydralazine, with magnesium sulfate 4 g loading then 1 g/hour for seizure prophylaxis; BP target is under 160/110 mmHg. (Source: SOMANZ Hypertension in Pregnancy Guideline)

options.text: IV hydralazine 10 mg every 20 minutes plus dexamethasone 12 mg for fetal maturity
options.rationale: Steroids have already been given by the referring team and dose-repeating them is not indicated here; magnesium is the missing critical adjunct. (Source: SOMANZ Hypertension in Pregnancy Guideline)

options.text: Continuous IV nicardipine infusion and immediate category 1 caesarean section
options.rationale: Immediate delivery without first achieving BP control and magnesium loading exposes the woman to intrapartum stroke and seizure; stabilisation precedes delivery decision. (Source: SOMANZ Hypertension in Pregnancy Guideline)

options.text: Low-dose aspirin 150 mg orally plus magnesium 6 g IV loading dose only
options.rationale: Aspirin is for prevention of pre-eclampsia in at-risk women before 20 weeks; it has no role in acute management of established severe pre-eclampsia. (Source: SOMANZ Hypertension in Pregnancy Guideline)

explanation.summary: Severe pre-eclampsia with headache, visual disturbance, and BP at or above 160/110 mmHg requires acute antihypertensive therapy plus magnesium seizure prophylaxis. AU first-line IV agents are labetalol and hydralazine; nifedipine is oral. Magnesium sulfate is given as a 4 g loading dose over 20 minutes then a 1 g/hour maintenance infusion, with monitoring of reflexes and respiratory rate for toxicity.
key_points: AU first-line acute IV antihypertensive: labetalol or hydralazine; nifedipine is oral.
BP target in severe pre-eclampsia under 160/110 mmHg.
Magnesium sulfate 4 g loading over 20 minutes then 1 g/hour for seizure prophylaxis.
Calcium gluconate is the reversal antidote for magnesium toxicity.
explanation.pearls: Stabilise first, deliver second: severe pre-eclampsia needs BP control and magnesium before transfer or delivery, not in parallel.

subtopic_detail: Shoulder dystocia escalation after McRoberts and suprapubic pressure
stem:
You are the senior O and G registrar attending an emergency call from the labour ward. A G2P1 woman at 38+0 weeks has just delivered the fetal head spontaneously after a 2 hour second stage with epidural anaesthesia. The head is turtling against the perineum and the shoulders have not delivered with the next contraction. The estimated fetal weight on the 36 week growth scan was 4100 g.

The team has applied McRoberts manoeuvre with hyperflexion of the maternal hips and suprapubic pressure (Rubin I) for the past 30 seconds without delivery. The midwife is timing each manoeuvre and the obstetric consultant has been paged and is 4 minutes away. The mother is calm with epidural anaesthesia.

data_table.Vital signs: Maternal pulse 95/min, BP 122/72 mmHg, RR 16/min, SpO2 99% room air, fetal HR last recorded 140/min before head delivery
data_table.Examination: Fetal head delivered, turtling sign present; shoulders not delivered; perineum intact apart from small first-degree graze; bladder catheterised
data_table.Investigations: Estimated fetal weight 4100 g at 36 weeks; no GDM; previous baby 3650 g; current head-to-body delivery interval 60 seconds

lead_in: What is the single most appropriate next manoeuvre?

options.text: Continue McRoberts and suprapubic pressure for another 60 seconds before escalating
options.rationale: Sustained reliance on first-line manoeuvres beyond 30 seconds without delivery delays effective release; each manoeuvre is allowed approximately 30 seconds before escalation. (Source: RANZCOG Statement: Shoulder dystocia)

options.text: Zavanelli (cephalic replacement) and prepare theatre for category 1 caesarean
options.rationale: Zavanelli is a last-resort manoeuvre when all other manoeuvres including internal rotations and posterior arm delivery have failed; it is associated with severe fetal injury when used too early. (Source: RANZCOG Statement: Shoulder dystocia)

options.text: Internal rotation manoeuvre (Rubin II or Wood's screw) or delivery of the posterior arm
options.rationale: After 30 seconds of failed McRoberts and suprapubic pressure, the HELPERR escalation moves to internal manoeuvres (Rubin II, Wood's screw) or delivery of the posterior arm, both of which significantly improve resolution rates. (Source: RANZCOG Statement: Shoulder dystocia)

options.text: Symphysiotomy under local anaesthesia at the bedside before any further manoeuvre
options.rationale: Symphysiotomy is reserved for resource-limited settings where caesarean is unavailable and carries high maternal morbidity; it is not part of the Australian shoulder dystocia algorithm. (Source: RANZCOG Statement: Shoulder dystocia)

options.text: Deliberate clavicle fracture by direct suprasternal pressure as next manoeuvre
options.rationale: Deliberate clavicle fracture is a last-resort manoeuvre after internal manoeuvres have failed; performing it before internal rotation skips effective lower-risk steps. (Source: RANZCOG Statement: Shoulder dystocia)

explanation.summary: After approximately 30 seconds of unsuccessful McRoberts plus suprapubic pressure in shoulder dystocia, the HELPERR mnemonic escalates to internal manoeuvres (Rubin II or Wood's screw) or delivery of the posterior arm. Zavanelli, symphysiotomy, and deliberate clavicle fracture are last-resort manoeuvres reserved for failure of all other techniques.
key_points: HELPERR mnemonic: call for Help, Evaluate for episiotomy, Legs (McRoberts), Pressure (suprapubic), Enter (internal rotations), Remove posterior arm, Roll (all fours).
Allow approximately 30 seconds per manoeuvre before escalating.
Internal manoeuvres and posterior arm delivery resolve most cases that fail first-line manoeuvres.
Document time of head delivery, each manoeuvre and its duration, and time of body delivery.
explanation.pearls: The commonest error in shoulder dystocia is staying too long with McRoberts; the next step at 30 seconds is internal rotation or posterior arm, not more pulling.

sources.label: RCOG Green-top Guideline No 42 Shoulder dystocia

subtopic_detail: Cord prolapse in regional setting with delayed transfer
stem:
You are the sole obstetric medical officer at a small regional hospital without on-site theatre or operative obstetric capability. A G2P1 woman at 37+5 weeks with a breech presentation presents with spontaneous rupture of membranes 20 minutes ago and has just been transferred from triage. On vaginal examination you palpate a pulsating umbilical cord below the presenting part. Cervix is 4 cm dilated.

The nearest tertiary maternity unit with theatre is 90 minutes away by ambulance. The retrieval team is being mobilised. The midwife is supporting the woman in left lateral position. Fetal heart rate by intermittent auscultation is 130/min with no decelerations heard so far. The mother is calm and oriented, in mild discomfort. You have IV access established.

data_table.Vital signs: Maternal pulse 92/min, BP 118/72 mmHg, RR 18/min, SpO2 99% room air, temperature 36.7 °C, fetal HR 130/min by Pinard
data_table.Examination: Cervix 4 cm dilated, breech presentation, pulsating cord palpable below presenting part
data_table.Investigations: Fetal HR 130/min reassuring; bedside ultrasound confirms ongoing cardiac activity

lead_in: What is the single most appropriate immediate management before retrieval?

options.text: Vertical transfer with continuous digital elevation of the presenting part throughout
options.rationale: Sustained digital elevation for 90 minutes en route is impractical and unreliable; AU guidance favours retrograde bladder filling for delayed transfer to maintain elevation hands-free. (Source: RANZCOG Statement: Cord prolapse)

options.text: Manually replace the cord into the uterus and observe with continuous CTG monitoring
options.rationale: Cord replacement (funic reduction) is not recommended outside controlled trials due to risk of vasospasm and further prolapse; standard practice is elevation of the presenting part, not replacement of the cord. (Source: RANZCOG Statement: Cord prolapse)

options.text: Allow labour to proceed expectantly at 4 cm cervical dilatation given breech presentation
options.rationale: Cord prolapse with reassuring fetal heart rate still requires expedited delivery (usually caesarean if not imminently deliverable); awaiting full dilatation risks fetal demise. (Source: RANZCOG Statement: Cord prolapse)

options.text: Knee-chest, retrograde bladder fill 500-700 mL warm saline via Foley, urgent caesarean
options.rationale: When transfer is delayed, AU and UK practice is bladder filling with 500-700 mL of warmed saline via Foley to elevate the presenting part hands-free, combined with knee-chest or steep Trendelenburg positioning; urgent caesarean is the definitive treatment. (Source: RANZCOG Statement: Cord prolapse)

options.text: Augment with IV oxytocin infusion to expedite vaginal delivery despite cord prolapse
options.rationale: Augmentation of labour worsens cord compression with each contraction; oxytocin is contraindicated in cord prolapse and delivery must be by caesarean unless vaginal birth is imminent. (Source: RANZCOG Statement: Cord prolapse)

explanation.summary: Cord prolapse with delayed transfer is managed by retrograde bladder filling with warmed saline to elevate the presenting part hands-free, combined with knee-chest or steep Trendelenburg positioning during transport. This is the AU and UK approach when sustained digital elevation throughout a long ambulance journey is impractical. Definitive treatment is urgent caesarean section unless vaginal birth is imminent and the fetal heart rate remains reassuring.
key_points: Retrograde fill the bladder with 500-700 mL warm saline via Foley for hands-free elevation.
Position in knee-chest or steep Trendelenburg during transfer.
Avoid manual cord replacement (funic reduction) and tocolysis is debated.
Definitive treatment is urgent caesarean unless vaginal birth is imminent.
explanation.pearls: For cord prolapse with a 90 minute transfer, fill the bladder and tip the woman head-down; sustained digital elevation in transit is not reliable.

sources.label: RCOG Green-top Guideline No 50 Cord prolapse

subtopic_detail: Maternal cardiac arrest perimortem caesarean timing
stem:
You are the obstetric registrar in a tertiary ED resus when a 32-year-old G1 at 28+2 weeks gestation collapses suddenly at 11:02 with witnessed cardiac arrest. CPR is commenced immediately with continuous chest compressions, manual left uterine displacement, bag-mask ventilation, and intravenous adrenaline 1 mg every 3 to 4 minutes. By 11:05 she has had three cycles of ACLS without return of spontaneous circulation.

A brief bedside ultrasound earlier in the day showed a normal fetal heart rate of 145/min at 28+2 weeks. The fundus is palpable above the umbilicus. The ED consultant is performing the airway and the anaesthetist has arrived. A surgical pack is in the resus bay. The team confirms ongoing high-quality CPR and pulselessness.

data_table.Vital signs: Maternal pulseless, no organised rhythm; ETCO2 18 mmHg during chest compressions; fetal HR not yet rechecked since arrest
data_table.Examination: Pulseless on continuous CPR; fundus 2 cm above umbilicus; no obvious bleeding; left uterine displacement maintained
data_table.Investigations: Earlier same-day ultrasound fetal HR 145/min; rhythm strip shows pulseless electrical activity

lead_in: What is the single most appropriate next action?

options.text: Continue CPR for another 10 minutes before considering caesarean section
options.rationale: Delay beyond 4-5 minutes of arrest with a viable gravid uterus reduces both maternal resuscitation success and fetal neurological outcome; the 4 minute rule mandates earlier action. (Source: ANZCOR Guideline 11.10 Resuscitation in pregnancy)

options.text: Perform bedside ultrasound to confirm fetal viability before deciding on caesarean
options.rationale: Perimortem caesarean is performed primarily for maternal benefit (improving venous return); fetal viability is not a prerequisite at any gestation when uterus is above the umbilicus. (Source: ANZCOR Guideline 11.10 Resuscitation in pregnancy)

options.text: Transfer urgently to theatre for caesarean section under general anaesthesia
options.rationale: Transfer interrupts CPR and adds delay; perimortem caesarean is performed at the site of arrest with minimal preparation, not in theatre. (Source: ANZCOR Guideline 11.10 Resuscitation in pregnancy)

options.text: Cease resuscitation given likely amniotic fluid embolism or massive pulmonary embolism
options.rationale: Ceasing resuscitation at 3 minutes of arrest without exhausting reversible causes is premature and forfeits the benefit of caesarean-assisted maternal CPR. (Source: ANZCOR Guideline 11.10 Resuscitation in pregnancy)

options.text: Perimortem caesarean in resus bay at 11:06 (within 4 minutes of arrest), continue CPR
options.rationale: ANZCOR and AU resuscitation in pregnancy guidance mandates perimortem caesarean within 4-5 minutes of maternal arrest when uterus is above the umbilicus, performed at the site of arrest to improve maternal venous return and oxygen delivery; fetal outcome is secondary. (Source: ANZCOR Guideline 11.10 Resuscitation in pregnancy)

explanation.summary: Perimortem caesarean section is performed within 4 to 5 minutes of maternal cardiac arrest when the uterus is palpable above the umbilicus, primarily to improve maternal venous return and oxygenation by relieving aortocaval compression. The procedure is done at the site of arrest, not in theatre, with CPR continuing throughout. Fetal viability is not a prerequisite to proceed.
key_points: 4-5 minute rule: incise at 4 minutes if no ROSC and uterus above umbilicus.
Performed at the site of arrest; do not transfer to theatre.
Primary indication is maternal benefit; fetus is a secondary beneficiary.
Continue CPR throughout and maintain left uterine displacement until uterus is emptied.
explanation.pearls: If the fundus is above the umbilicus and you do not have ROSC by 4 minutes, the scalpel goes in next; ultrasound for fetal heart is not a prerequisite.

subtopic_detail: Placental abruption with fetal compromise at 34 weeks
stem:
A 32-year-old G3P2 woman at 34+5 weeks gestation presents to the obstetric assessment unit with sudden onset severe constant abdominal pain and dark vaginal bleeding starting 60 minutes ago. Her two previous deliveries were emergency caesarean sections. She has chronic hypertension managed on labetalol 200 mg twice daily; antenatal care has otherwise been uncomplicated and the fetus has been growing on the 50th centile.

On examination the uterus is tense, painful, and woody-hard to palpation. The cardiotocograph shows a sustained fetal bradycardia at 90 bpm with reduced variability. Vaginal examination reveals approximately 300 mL of dark blood, cervix posterior, 1 cm dilated, no cord felt. The patient is alert and oriented but anxious.

data_table.Vital signs: Maternal pulse 110/min, BP 145/95 mmHg, RR 22/min, SpO2 99% room air, temperature 36.7 °C; fetal HR 90/min sustained
data_table.Examination: Tense painful woody uterus; CTG sustained fetal bradycardia 90 bpm reduced variability; vaginal exam 300 mL dark blood, cervix 1 cm posterior, no cord palpable
data_table.Investigations: Group and save sent; FBC haemoglobin 105 g/L (115-165), platelets 195 x10⁹/L (150-400); coagulation studies pending; bedside ultrasound shows retroplacental clot

lead_in: What is the most appropriate immediate management?

options.text: Activate massive transfusion protocol, two large bore IV cannulae, IV crystalloid resuscitation, and category 1 caesarean section within 30 minutes by the on call obstetric team
options.rationale: Sustained fetal bradycardia with abruption and maternal compromise mandates category 1 caesarean (decision-to-delivery <30 min); MTP activation pre-empts coagulopathy from abruption-induced DIC. (Source: RANZCOG Antepartum haemorrhage)

options.text: Perform immediate amniotomy to expedite assisted vaginal delivery with low cavity forceps once cervix is fully dilated under regional anaesthesia, with continuous CTG monitoring during birth
options.rationale: Cervix is 1 cm dilated and not amenable to expedited vaginal birth; abruption with bradycardia and 2 prior CS requires category 1 caesarean. (Source: RANZCOG Antepartum haemorrhage)

options.text: Commence tocolysis with nifedipine 20 mg orally and antenatal betamethasone 11.4 mg intramuscular before delivery to optimise fetal lung maturity before scheduling caesarean within 24 hours
options.rationale: Tocolysis is contraindicated in active significant abruption with fetal compromise; the fetus requires immediate delivery, not lung maturation that will not benefit in 12-24 hours. (Source: RANZCOG Antepartum haemorrhage)

options.text: Conservative management with strict bedrest, continuous CTG monitoring on the antenatal ward, and reassessment for delivery decision after 24 hours of observation and serial bloods
options.rationale: Conservative management is reserved for stable abruption without fetal compromise or coagulopathy; sustained bradycardia mandates immediate delivery. (Source: RANZCOG Antepartum haemorrhage)

options.text: Attempt external cephalic version to confirm cephalic presentation followed by induction of labour with oxytocin and amniotomy under continuous CTG monitoring during the next 6 hours
options.rationale: ECV in active abruption with bradycardia would worsen abruption; induction takes time the fetus does not have; immediate caesarean is required. (Source: RANZCOG Antepartum haemorrhage)

explanation.summary: Placental abruption with fetal compromise (CTG bradycardia or repetitive late decelerations) and maternal haemodynamic concern is a category 1 obstetric emergency requiring delivery within 30 minutes. Risk factors include hypertension (chronic or pre-eclampsia), trauma, smoking, cocaine use, and prior abruption. Major haemorrhage is associated with DIC due to placental tissue factor release - MTP activation should be considered early. Maternal blood loss is often underestimated as concealed retroplacental haemorrhage. Disseminated intravascular coagulation, acute kidney injury, and postpartum haemorrhage are major sequelae.
key_points: Cat 1 caesarean: decision-to-delivery <30 minutes.
MTP activation early to pre-empt DIC.
Concealed haemorrhage often underestimated.
Tocolysis contraindicated in active abruption with compromise.
DIC, AKI, and PPH are major sequelae.
explanation.pearls: Tense painful woody uterus plus sustained fetal bradycardia is a 30 minute clock - activate MTP at the same time as you call category 1, because abruption DIC starts before you cut.

stem:
A 29-year-old woman is seen in the fertility clinic with 18 months of primary infertility. She has oligomenorrhoea since menarche (4-6 cycles per year), hirsutism (modified Ferriman-Gallwey 12), and acne. Polycystic ovarian syndrome was diagnosed 4 years ago by Rotterdam criteria. Her body mass index is 33 kg/m². Over the past 6 months she has lost 8% of her body weight with dietitian and exercise physiologist input and has had 2 spontaneous cycles in that time.

Her male partner has a normal semen analysis. Hysterosalpingogram demonstrates patent fallopian tubes bilaterally. Her AMH is 78 pmol/L (3-30) and antral follicle count is 35 (12-25). Day 21 progesterone in her last cycle was 5 nmol/L (>30 confirms ovulation). She has no diabetes; HbA1c 5.1%.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 78/min, BP 128/82 mmHg, RR 16/min, SpO2 99% room air, temperature 36.7 °C
data_table.Examination: BMI 33; modified Ferriman-Gallwey 12; mild facial acne; no acanthosis nigricans; pelvic examination unremarkable; transvaginal ultrasound bilateral polycystic ovary morphology
data_table.Investigations: TSH 1.8 mIU/L (0.4-4.0); prolactin 280 mIU/L (<500 non-pregnant); HbA1c 5.1%; AMH 78 pmol/L (3-30); 21-day progesterone 5 nmol/L (>30 ovulation confirmation)

lead_in: What is the most appropriate first-line ovulation induction agent?

options.text: Clomifene citrate 50 mg orally days 2-6 of cycle for up to six ovulatory cycles with cycle monitoring by transvaginal ultrasound and day 21 progesterone
options.rationale: Clomifene was previously first-line but PCOS Australia/RANZCOG and the 2023 International PCOS Guideline now recommend letrozole as superior first-line (higher live birth rate, lower twin rate). (Source: RANZCOG PCOS guidance)

options.text: Letrozole 2.5 mg orally on days 2-6 of cycle for up to six ovulatory cycles with cycle monitoring by transvaginal ultrasound and day 21 progesterone for ovulation confirmation
options.rationale: Letrozole is now first-line for PCOS ovulation induction per the 2023 International PCOS Guideline endorsed by RANZCOG; higher live birth rate vs clomifene (PPCOS II trial NEJM 2014), with lower multiple pregnancy rate. (Source: RANZCOG PCOS guidance)

options.text: Recombinant follicle stimulating hormone injection from day 2 of the cycle with cycle monitoring by transvaginal ultrasound and hCG trigger when lead follicle reaches 18 mm in diameter
options.rationale: Gonadotrophins are second-line after oral agents fail; significantly higher risk of multiple pregnancy and OHSS, requiring more intensive monitoring. (Source: RANZCOG PCOS guidance)

options.text: Combined oral contraceptive pill for three months to suppress and reset the hypothalamic-pituitary-ovarian axis, then a fourth cycle with hCG trigger after spontaneous follicle development
options.rationale: COCP suppresses ovulation rather than inducing it; this approach delays fertility treatment by 3 months without benefit. (Source: RANZCOG PCOS guidance)

options.text: Refer for in vitro fertilisation with gonadotrophin releasing hormone antagonist protocol and elective single embryo transfer before any first-line ovulation induction trial in this couple
options.rationale: IVF is reserved for failure of oral and gonadotrophin ovulation induction or for additional infertility factors; first-line is letrozole. (Source: RANZCOG PCOS guidance)

explanation.summary: The 2023 International Evidence-based Guideline for the Assessment and Management of Polycystic Ovary Syndrome (endorsed by RANZCOG and Monash University) now recommends letrozole as the first-line pharmacological agent for ovulation induction in anovulatory PCOS, based on PPCOS II (Legro et al, NEJM 2014) showing higher live birth rate (27.5% vs 19.1%) and lower multiple pregnancy rate compared with clomifene. Weight loss of 5-10% remains the first-line non-pharmacological intervention. Metformin can be added as adjunct, particularly in BMI >30. Gonadotrophins or IVF are reserved for failure of oral therapy.
key_points: Letrozole now first-line for PCOS ovulation induction (RANZCOG 2023).
Higher live birth rate and lower multiples vs clomifene (PPCOS II).
Letrozole 2.5 mg days 2-6, escalate to 5 mg then 7.5 mg if needed.
Weight loss of 5-10% improves spontaneous ovulation and treatment success.
Gonadotrophins and IVF reserved for oral therapy failure.
explanation.pearls: Letrozole 2.5 mg days 2-6 has displaced clomifene as first-line for PCOS ovulation induction in Australia - higher live birth, lower twin rate, and unbothered by clomifene's antiestrogenic endometrial effects.

subtopic_detail: Acute uterine inversion - immediate replacement with placenta in situ
stem:
A 28-year-old G1P1 has just had a normal vaginal birth of a 4.0 kg infant after a prolonged second stage. Active management of the third stage was performed with intramuscular oxytocin 10 IU. Controlled cord traction was applied while the registrar assessed uterine tone, which was felt to be soft. Within seconds of traction the patient develops sudden severe abdominopelvic pain and looks pale.

On rapid reassessment her pulse is 38 beats per minute and blood pressure 65/30 mmHg. She remains conscious but distressed. Inspection of the perineum reveals an inverted boggy mass protruding through the introitus with the placenta still attached and approximately 600 mL of blood loss already documented. The anaesthetist is in the room.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 38/min, BP 65/30 mmHg, RR 28/min, SpO2 96% room air, temperature 36.5 °C
data_table.Examination: Pale and distressed but conscious; abdominal palpation: uterine fundus not palpable; inverted boggy mass at introitus with attached placenta; estimated blood loss 600 mL ongoing
data_table.Investigations: FBC pre-delivery haemoglobin 122 g/L (115-165); group and save active; coagulation studies sent; no other investigations completed

lead_in: What is the most appropriate immediate next step?

options.text: Administer ergometrine 250 mcg intravenously immediately to contract the uterus before attempting replacement of the inverted fundus through the cervical ring during continuing resuscitation
options.rationale: Uterotonics BEFORE replacement worsen the cervical ring contracting around the inverted fundus, making replacement impossible; uterotonics are given only AFTER successful replacement. (Source: RANZCOG Major obstetric haemorrhage)

options.text: Remove the placenta first by manual separation before attempting to replace the inverted uterus through the cervical ring as ongoing resuscitation continues with IV access and fluids
options.rationale: Removing placenta from an inverted uterus dramatically worsens haemorrhage; leave placenta in situ during replacement and remove only after the uterus is replaced and contracted. (Source: RANZCOG Major obstetric haemorrhage)

options.text: Immediate manual replacement of the uterine fundus via the Johnson manoeuvre with the placenta still attached, while resuscitating with IV fluids and giving atropine 600 mcg IV for vagal bradycardia
options.rationale: Immediate replacement (Johnson manoeuvre) with placenta still attached is the AU first-line; atropine treats the parasympathetic-mediated bradycardia from cervical ring stretch; uterotonics follow once replaced. (Source: RANZCOG Major obstetric haemorrhage)

options.text: Urgent transfer to operating theatre for surgical replacement under general anaesthesia using the Huntington or Haultain procedure with no immediate attempt at manual replacement now
options.rationale: Surgery is reserved for failed manual replacement; the longer the delay, the more the cervical ring contracts and the harder replacement becomes. Manual attempt first. (Source: RANZCOG Major obstetric haemorrhage)

options.text: Bimanual uterine compression with intravenous tranexamic acid 1 g over 10 minutes and packing of the inverted segment without any attempt at replacement during ongoing fluid resuscitation today
options.rationale: Compression and packing does not address the inversion; only replacement restores anatomy and stops bleeding. TXA is appropriate adjunct AFTER replacement. (Source: RANZCOG Major obstetric haemorrhage)

explanation.summary: Acute uterine inversion is a rare obstetric emergency (1 in 2000-20000 births) characterised by sudden maternal collapse out of proportion to blood loss (vagal-mediated bradycardia and hypotension from cervical ring stretch) combined with PPH. Diagnosis is made on inspection (inverted fundus visible at introitus) or palpation (non-palpable fundus abdominally). Management: (1) immediate manual replacement (Johnson manoeuvre - upward pressure on inverted fundus with palm of hand) with placenta still attached, (2) resuscitation with IV fluids and atropine for vagal bradycardia, (3) uterotonics ONLY after replacement (oxytocin then ergometrine if no hypertension), (4) surgical replacement if manual fails (Huntington abdominal traction, Haultain posterior incision of cervical ring). Key teaching points: do NOT remove placenta before replacement, do NOT give uterotonics before replacement.
key_points: Sudden collapse + bradycardia + non-palpable fundus + inverted mass at introitus.
Johnson manoeuvre: immediate manual replacement with placenta still attached.
Atropine 600 mcg IV for vagal bradycardia.
Uterotonics ONLY after replacement (otherwise cervical ring traps fundus).
Surgical (Huntington or Haultain) if manual replacement fails.
explanation.pearls: In acute uterine inversion, leaving the placenta attached and skipping uterotonics until after Johnson manoeuvre replacement is the counter-intuitive sequence that saves the uterus and the patient.

stem:
A 38-year-old G4P3 at 40+2 weeks gestation had labour induced for postdates pregnancy. She has just had a normal vaginal birth of a 3.6 kg infant. Within 90 seconds of placental delivery she becomes acutely dyspnoeic, agitated and complains of an impending sense of doom, then rapidly loses consciousness. The midwife notes ongoing brisk vaginal bleeding that does not clot when applied to gauze.

The anaesthetist intubates the patient. Brief cardiac compressions are commenced before pulses return with low-dose adrenaline. ECG shows sinus tachycardia with a right heart strain pattern (S1Q3T3). Bedside echocardiogram performed by the intensivist shows a dilated right ventricle with septal flattening. There is no rash, no recent antibiotic exposure.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 140/min after adrenaline, BP 70/40 mmHg, RR ventilated, SpO2 88% on FiO2 1.0, temperature 36.4 °C
data_table.Examination: Intubated and ventilated; right heart strain on ECG and bedside echo with RV dilation and septal flattening; profuse non-clotting vaginal blood; estimated blood loss 1500 mL and rising
data_table.Investigations: Haemoglobin 88 g/L (115-165), platelets 70 x10⁹/L (150-400), INR 2.4 (0.9-1.2), fibrinogen 0.8 g/L (2.0-4.5); group O Rh positive; cross-match in progress; troponin pending

lead_in: What is the most appropriate blood-product strategy now?

options.text: Crystalloid resuscitation only with permissive hypotension targeting MAP 50 mmHg until cross matched packed red cells become available within the next 45 minutes from blood bank
options.rationale: Crystalloid alone in AFE-associated DIC worsens dilutional coagulopathy; immediate balanced blood product activation is required, not permissive hypotension in a pregnant collapsed patient. (Source: RANZCOG Major obstetric haemorrhage)

options.text: Packed red blood cells alone targeting haemoglobin above 70 g/L without immediate fresh frozen plasma or cryoprecipitate until further coagulation studies are available for review by haematology
options.rationale: Red cells alone in DIC dilutes already deficient coagulation factors and fibrinogen; balanced 1:1:1 MTP is the AU standard from the outset. (Source: NBA: Patient Blood Management - Obstetric)

options.text: Packed red cells with one early unit of cryoprecipitate but defer fresh frozen plasma transfusion until repeat fibrinogen returns from the laboratory in approximately 30 minutes
options.rationale: Delaying FFP and platelets in AFE-DIC worsens coagulopathy and PPH; AU MTP gives RBC, FFP, platelets and cryoprecipitate in balanced ratios immediately. (Source: NBA: Patient Blood Management - Obstetric)

options.text: Activate massive transfusion protocol with empirical 1:1:1 packed red cells, fresh frozen plasma and platelets, cryoprecipitate to keep fibrinogen above 2 g/L, plus tranexamic acid 1 g IV
options.rationale: AU MTP for obstetric haemorrhage gives balanced 1:1:1 ratio with cryoprecipitate (obstetric fibrinogen target >2 g/L, higher than non-obstetric); TXA <3 h from haemorrhage onset reduces mortality (WOMAN trial). (Source: NBA: Patient Blood Management - Obstetric)

options.text: Four-factor prothrombin complex concentrate 25 units per kilogram intravenously as the sole haemostatic resuscitation strategy without balanced blood products until further investigations available
options.rationale: PCC is not first-line in AFE-DIC; it lacks fibrinogen and platelets, both critical in this coagulopathy. Balanced MTP is the standard. (Source: NBA: Patient Blood Management - Obstetric)

explanation.summary: Amniotic fluid embolism is a rare (1 in 20,000-80,000 births) but devastating obstetric emergency presenting with sudden cardiovascular collapse, respiratory failure, and DIC during or shortly after labour and birth. Pathophysiology involves anaphylactoid response to fetal antigens entering maternal circulation, causing acute pulmonary vasoconstriction (RV failure) followed by left heart failure and consumptive coagulopathy. Diagnosis is clinical. Management is supportive: (1) high quality CPR if arrest, with left lateral tilt; (2) intubation and ventilation; (3) circulatory support with inotropes; (4) balanced massive transfusion targeting fibrinogen >2 g/L; (5) TXA 1 g IV within 3 hours; (6) perimortem caesarean within 4-5 minutes if arrest and undelivered. Maternal mortality remains 20-60%.
key_points: AFE: sudden collapse + respiratory failure + DIC in/after labour.
Pathophysiology: anaphylactoid response, RV failure, then coagulopathy.
Balanced 1:1:1 MTP from outset, target fibrinogen >2 g/L.
TXA 1 g IV within 3 hours of haemorrhage (WOMAN trial).
Perimortem caesarean within 4-5 min if arrest and undelivered fetus.
explanation.pearls: Obstetric fibrinogen target is over 2 g/L (higher than non-obstetric 1.5) because pregnancy doubles the normal range and DIC consumes it fast - cryoprecipitate goes in early during MTP for AFE.

stem:
A 31-year-old G2P1 woman has just delivered a 4.1 kg baby vaginally at term in a tertiary obstetric unit after spontaneous labour. The third stage was actively managed with intramuscular oxytocin 10 units at delivery of the anterior shoulder. Twenty minutes after delivery she has lost an estimated 900 mL of blood and continues to bleed.

The uterus feels soft on bimanual examination and rises above the umbilicus despite massage. The placenta delivered complete and the perineum has been inspected with no significant tear. An intravenous oxytocin infusion has just been started at 40 units in 1 L Hartmann's at 250 mL/hour. Tranexamic acid 1 g IV has been administered. The maternal team is preparing the next uterotonic at the bedside. Her booking blood pressure was 118/74 and her booking medical history is unremarkable.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 108/min, BP 124/82 mmHg, RR 20/min, SpO2 99% room air, temperature 37.0 °C
data_table.Examination: Boggy uterus above umbilicus, perineum intact, no retained products on examination; cannulae 2 x 16G antecubital fossa, blood group and antibody screen sent
data_table.Investigations: Haemoglobin (pre-delivery) 120 g/L, platelets 220 x10^9/L, INR 1.0, fibrinogen 3.8 g/L (2.5-5.0); urine output measured by indwelling catheter; cross-match 4 units

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next pharmacological uterotonic to give now?

options.text: Intravenous oxytocin 5 unit slow bolus repeated up to a total of 20 units in addition to the running oxytocin infusion already in progress at the bedside
options.rationale: An additional oxytocin bolus on top of an infusion does not add efficacy and may cause hypotension and arrhythmia; escalation is to a different-class uterotonic, not more oxytocin. (Source: RANZCOG Statement Management of Postpartum Haemorrhage)
source_refs: RANZCOG Statement Management of Postpartum Haemorrhage

options.text: Intramuscular carboprost 250 micrograms repeated every 15 minutes up to a maximum total dose of 2 mg before any other uterotonic is given to this patient
options.rationale: Carboprost is reserved for ergometrine failure or contraindication; jumping straight to carboprost skips a step in the RANZCOG escalation ladder and carries bronchospasm risk. (Source: RANZCOG Statement Management of Postpartum Haemorrhage)
source_refs: RANZCOG Statement Management of Postpartum Haemorrhage

options.text: Intramuscular ergometrine 250 micrograms repeated at 15 minute intervals up to a maximum of 1 mg in 24 hours alongside the oxytocin infusion
options.rationale: After oxytocin infusion and TXA, ergometrine 250 mcg IM is the next uterotonic step in PPH with uterine atony when there is no hypertensive or cardiac contraindication. (Source: RANZCOG Statement Management of Postpartum Haemorrhage; Therapeutic Guidelines: Obstetrics)
source_refs: RANZCOG Statement Management of Postpartum Haemorrhage

options.text: Rectal misoprostol 800 micrograms by single dose and reassess uterine tone and ongoing blood loss again within the next 15 minutes after administration
options.rationale: Misoprostol is a useful uterotonic where injectables are unavailable; in a tertiary unit with IV access and IM ergometrine available, ergometrine is preferred and has a faster onset. (Source: RANZCOG Statement Management of Postpartum Haemorrhage)
source_refs: RANZCOG Statement Management of Postpartum Haemorrhage

options.text: Intramyometrial carbetocin 100 micrograms single dose injected directly through the abdominal wall under ultrasound guidance by the obstetric registrar urgently
options.rationale: Carbetocin is a long-acting oxytocin analogue used as a single IM/IV dose at delivery for prophylaxis, not as escalation after a haemorrhage has already developed despite oxytocin infusion. (Source: RANZCOG Statement Management of Postpartum Haemorrhage)
source_refs: RANZCOG Statement Management of Postpartum Haemorrhage

explanation.summary: RANZCOG escalation for atonic PPH is sequential: bimanual compression and massage; oxytocin 10 units IM or 5 unit IV bolus then 40 unit infusion; TXA 1 g IV (within 3 hours of bleeding onset); ergometrine 250 mcg IM (contraindicated in hypertension, cardiac disease, severe pre-eclampsia); carboprost 250 mcg IM (contraindicated in asthma); misoprostol 800 mcg rectal as adjunct. Mechanical and surgical measures (intrauterine balloon tamponade, B-Lynch suture, uterine artery ligation, hysterectomy) follow if pharmacological steps fail.
key_points: Oxytocin first, then TXA, then ergometrine, then carboprost
Ergometrine contraindicated in hypertension, ischaemic heart disease, severe pre-eclampsia
Carboprost contraindicated in asthma due to bronchospasm risk
TXA effective when given within 3 hours of bleeding onset
Carbetocin is a prophylactic, not a rescue, uterotonic
explanation.pearls: Ergometrine 250 mcg IM is the standard second-line uterotonic after oxytocin failure; check BP and rule out severe pre-eclampsia before giving because hypertensive crisis is the main adverse effect.

sources.label: RANZCOG Statement Management of Postpartum Haemorrhage

stem:
A 28-year-old G1P0 woman at 27 weeks gestation attends a midwife-led shared-care clinic for a routine antenatal review. She has no significant past medical history and a BMI of 27 kg/m2. There is no family history of diabetes. The pregnancy has otherwise been uncomplicated and the dating ultrasound at 12 weeks was concordant with menstrual dates.

A 75 g oral glucose tolerance test was performed two days ago in the morning after an overnight fast. Fetal growth on most recent ultrasound is on the 50th centile, liquor volume normal, dopplers normal. Maternal blood pressure has been stable at booking values throughout. Symphysio-fundal height tracks with gestation. There is no proteinuria or glycosuria on dipstick today.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 78/min, BP 116/72 mmHg, RR 14/min, SpO2 99% room air, temperature 36.6 °C
data_table.Examination: Soft non-tender abdomen, gravid uterus consistent with dates, fetal heart rate 142/min by Doppler, no oedema, no proteinuria on dipstick
data_table.Investigations: 75 g OGTT (ADIPS): fasting 5.2 mmol/L (less than 5.1), 1 hour 9.8 mmol/L (less than 10.0), 2 hour 7.2 mmol/L (less than 8.5); HbA1c not performed; FBC and serum ferritin within normal limits

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step in management?

options.text: Repeat the 75 g oral glucose tolerance test in 4 weeks time to confirm a true diagnosis before any management changes are made to the pregnancy plan
options.rationale: Routine OGTT repeat is not required in pregnancy when a single ADIPS value is breached; the fasting value of 5.2 mmol/L exceeds the threshold and confirms GDM. (Source: ADIPS Consensus Guidelines for the Testing and Diagnosis of Hyperglycaemia in Pregnancy)

options.text: Send a confirmatory HbA1c level to differentiate undiagnosed pre-existing type 2 diabetes from new-onset gestational diabetes mellitus before any further intervention
options.rationale: HbA1c is recommended at booking to identify pre-existing diabetes, not as a confirmatory test after a 27 week OGTT; pre-existing diabetes is unlikely with these moderate values. (Source: ADIPS Consensus Guidelines)

options.text: Reassure the patient that the OGTT is normal because the 1 hour and 2 hour values are well below the upper limit of the gestational diabetes diagnostic ranges
options.rationale: ADIPS criteria require all three values to be below the cut-offs; a single breached value confirms GDM. The fasting of 5.2 mmol/L exceeds the 5.1 mmol/L threshold. (Source: ADIPS Consensus Guidelines)

options.text: Commence metformin 500 mg twice daily empirically as first-line pharmacotherapy without trial of diet and exercise modification first and arrange MDT follow up
options.rationale: Pharmacotherapy is escalated to only after a 1-2 week trial of dietary and lifestyle intervention with home blood glucose self-monitoring fails to meet targets; not empirical at diagnosis. (Source: ADIPS Consensus Guidelines)

options.text: Diagnose gestational diabetes and arrange referral to the multidisciplinary diabetes-in-pregnancy team for dietary education and blood glucose self-monitoring
options.rationale: ADIPS diagnoses GDM with ANY ONE value at or above fasting 5.1, 1 hour 10.0, or 2 hour 8.5 mmol/L; a fasting of 5.2 mmol/L is diagnostic and triggers MDT referral. (Source: ADIPS Consensus Guidelines for the Testing and Diagnosis of Hyperglycaemia in Pregnancy)

explanation.summary: ADIPS diagnoses gestational diabetes from a single 75 g OGTT at 24-28 weeks gestation with any one of: fasting plasma glucose 5.1 mmol/L or higher, 1 hour 10.0 mmol/L or higher, or 2 hour 8.5 mmol/L or higher. A single breached value is diagnostic. Management starts with diet and exercise modification with capillary glucose self-monitoring (targets: fasting under 5.1, 1 hour postprandial under 7.4, 2 hour postprandial under 6.7 mmol/L). Insulin or metformin is added if targets are missed despite lifestyle adherence over 1-2 weeks. Postnatal follow-up OGTT at 6-12 weeks reclassifies persistent dysglycaemia.
key_points: ADIPS thresholds: fasting 5.1, 1 hour 10.0, 2 hour 8.5 mmol/L
Any single breached value confirms GDM
First-line management is dietary and lifestyle modification with SMBG
Insulin or metformin added after 1-2 weeks of failed lifestyle targets
Postnatal OGTT at 6-12 weeks reclassifies persistent dysglycaemia
explanation.pearls: ADIPS GDM is diagnosed by ANY ONE of the three OGTT values being met; the fasting cut-off of 5.1 mmol/L is the most commonly breached and missed, particularly when the 1 and 2 hour values look reassuring.

sources.label: RANZCOG Diagnosis of Gestational Diabetes Mellitus

stem:
A 27-year-old G2P0 woman with blood group O Rhesus D negative presents to a metropolitan early pregnancy assessment clinic at 11 weeks gestation. She reports a single small painless bright red vaginal bleed yesterday with no associated pain. She had no previous antenatal anti-D administration in this pregnancy. Her first pregnancy ended in a 6 week miscarriage.

The abdomen is soft and non-tender on examination. A transvaginal ultrasound performed today shows a single live intrauterine pregnancy with a crown rump length consistent with 11 weeks and a 1 cm subchorionic haematoma. Fetal heart rate is 162 per minute. There is no cervical bleeding or open os on speculum examination. She has not started any anti-D yet in this pregnancy. Her antibody screen done at booking was negative.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 78/min, BP 110/68 mmHg, RR 14/min, SpO2 99% room air, temperature 36.6 °C
data_table.Examination: Soft non-tender abdomen, no cervical motion tenderness, closed os on speculum; small subchorionic haematoma seen on TVUS
data_table.Investigations: Blood group O Rhesus D negative, antibody screen negative; haemoglobin 122 g/L; transvaginal ultrasound 11 week live intrauterine pregnancy with 1 cm subchorionic haematoma; quantitative bhCG not required

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step regarding Rhesus D immunoprophylaxis?

options.text: Send fetal cell-free DNA Rhesus genotyping on a maternal sample and only administer anti-D once a Rhesus D positive fetus has been definitively confirmed
options.rationale: cffDNA RhD genotyping is available in some AU centres for routine 28 week prophylaxis but not for a sensitising event requiring action within 72 hours; treat empirically. (Source: NBA Anti-D Guidelines)

options.text: Administer anti-D immunoglobulin 625 IU intramuscularly within 72 hours of the bleed and document the dose on her antenatal record now
options.rationale: 625 IU is the dose for sensitising events at or beyond 12 weeks gestation (per NBA); at 11 weeks gestation the dose is 250 IU. (Source: NBA Anti-D Guidelines)

options.text: Hold anti-D immunoglobulin and reassess only at the next routine 28 week antenatal anti-D prophylaxis appointment if no further bleeding has occurred since today
options.rationale: A vaginal bleed at 11 weeks is a sensitising event regardless of subsequent bleeding; deferring anti-D risks alloimmunisation that cannot be reversed once antibodies are formed. (Source: NBA Anti-D Guidelines)

options.text: Send a maternal Kleihauer-Betke test to determine the size of any feto-maternal haemorrhage and dose the anti-D based on the calculated feto-maternal bleed
options.rationale: Kleihauer testing is required for sensitising events at or beyond 20 weeks to size larger feto-maternal haemorrhage; before 20 weeks the standard dose covers any plausible bleed. (Source: NBA Anti-D Guidelines)

options.text: Administer anti-D immunoglobulin 250 IU intramuscularly within 72 hours of the bleed and document the dose on her antenatal record now
options.rationale: Sensitising events before 12 weeks gestation (vaginal bleeding, ectopic, miscarriage) receive 250 IU anti-D IM within 72 hours; the Australian dose for first-trimester events is 250 IU. (Source: NBA Guidelines for the Prophylactic Use of Rh D Immunoglobulin (Anti-D) in Obstetrics)

explanation.summary: NBA Australia anti-D dosing depends on gestation: under 12 weeks 250 IU IM, 12 to under 20 weeks 250 IU IM, 20 weeks and beyond 625 IU IM plus Kleihauer-Betke quantification to detect bleeds greater than 6 mL fetal blood. Routine antenatal prophylaxis is 625 IU at 28 and 34 weeks (or single 1500 IU at 28-30 weeks per local policy). Post-delivery 625 IU within 72 hours if cord blood confirms RhD positive. Fetal RhD genotyping by cffDNA can avoid unnecessary routine prophylaxis but is not used for acute sensitising events.
key_points: Under 20 weeks sensitising event: 250 IU anti-D IM within 72 hours
20 weeks and over: 625 IU plus Kleihauer to size the bleed
Sensitising events include APH, abdominal trauma, ECV, amniocentesis, CVS, miscarriage, TOP, ectopic
Routine antenatal prophylaxis at 28 and 34 weeks (or 1500 IU at 28-30)
Fetal cffDNA RhD genotyping not used in acute sensitising events
explanation.pearls: Anti-D 250 IU IM is the dose for sensitising events under 20 weeks gestation in Australia, given within 72 hours; the dose steps up to 625 IU plus Kleihauer-Betke from 20 weeks onwards because feto-maternal haemorrhage volume can be larger.

sources.label: RANZCOG Statement Use of Rh D Immunoglobulin

stem:
A 33-year-old G3P1 woman at 33+2 weeks gestation is brought to a tertiary maternity unit by her partner with severe occipital headache and visual scotomas that started 2 hours ago. She has been managed in pregnancy on oral labetalol 200 mg three times daily for chronic hypertension. The booking BP was 138/88 mmHg. Her renal function and liver enzymes were normal at last review one week ago.

On arrival her BP is markedly elevated on two readings five minutes apart on the same arm. She has 3+ proteinuria. The fetus is in cephalic presentation with reassuring CTG. Magnesium sulfate loading has just been started for seizure prophylaxis. Her last labetalol dose was 6 hours ago. She has no known asthma but does have an autoimmune Raynaud phenomenon documented in her past medical history. The obstetric team has called for urgent intravenous antihypertensive therapy to be drawn up.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 96/min, BP 172/118 mmHg (repeated 168/116), RR 18/min, SpO2 99% room air, temperature 36.8 °C; fetal HR 140/min reassuring CTG
data_table.Examination: Brisk reflexes with 2 beats of clonus, no facial oedema, no right upper quadrant tenderness; visual fields intact to confrontation
data_table.Investigations: Urinalysis 3+ protein, urine protein:creatinine ratio 320 mg/mmol (less than 30); platelets 142 x10^9/L, ALT 28 U/L (<35), creatinine 72 micromol/L; uric acid 0.42 mmol/L

lead_in: What is the most appropriate single best intravenous antihypertensive choice now?

options.text: Intravenous glyceryl trinitrate infusion at 5 micrograms per minute titrated to a target maternal mean arterial pressure of 100 mmHg in the resuscitation bay
options.rationale: GTN is reserved for pre-eclampsia with concurrent pulmonary oedema or angina; standard severe hypertension management is hydralazine, labetalol, or nifedipine immediate-release. (Source: SOMANZ Hypertension in Pregnancy Guideline)

options.text: Intravenous labetalol 20 mg bolus repeated and doubled every 10 minutes up to a maximum of 220 mg titrated against the maternal blood pressure response
options.rationale: Beta-blockers including labetalol are best avoided in vasospastic disease such as Raynaud phenomenon because they can precipitate digital ischaemia; hydralazine is a safer first choice here. (Source: SOMANZ Hypertension in Pregnancy Guideline)

options.text: Sublingual nifedipine 10 mg immediate-release capsule and reassess the maternal blood pressure response after 30 minutes from administration in the resuscitation bay
options.rationale: Sublingual or immediate-release nifedipine is associated with abrupt and uncontrolled BP drop and is not recommended in severe pre-eclampsia; oral nifedipine immediate-release tablets are the alternative if available. (Source: SOMANZ Hypertension in Pregnancy Guideline)

options.text: Intravenous hydralazine 5 mg slow injection repeated every 20 minutes up to a maximum of 20 mg titrated against the maternal blood pressure response
