options.rationale: Hydralazine is the AU first-line IV agent when oral labetalol has failed and labetalol IV is relatively contraindicated (Raynaud phenomenon is a beta-blockade caution); hydralazine acts within 20 minutes. (Source: SOMANZ Hypertension in Pregnancy Guideline; RANZCOG)

options.text: Intravenous magnesium sulfate further 2 g bolus on top of the seizure prophylaxis loading dose targeted at lowering the maternal blood pressure to safe values
options.rationale: Magnesium is for seizure prophylaxis (eclampsia), not BP control; loading is 4 g over 20 min then 1 g/h infusion. It does not substantially lower BP and additional bolus risks toxicity. (Source: SOMANZ Hypertension in Pregnancy Guideline)

explanation.summary: SOMANZ defines severe hypertension in pregnancy as systolic 160 mmHg or above OR diastolic 110 mmHg or above on two readings; IV antihypertensives are required within 30 minutes. First-line options are IV labetalol, IV hydralazine, or oral nifedipine immediate release - choice is patient-tailored. Labetalol is avoided in vasospastic disease (Raynaud), asthma, and bradycardia. Hydralazine carries a small reflex tachycardia and maternal-fetal hypotension risk; pre-loading with 250 mL fluid before each bolus is suggested. Magnesium sulfate is given concurrently for seizure prophylaxis but does not control BP.
key_points: Severe hypertension threshold: 160/110 mmHg on 2 readings
First-line IV options: labetalol, hydralazine, or oral nifedipine IR
Labetalol avoided in Raynaud, asthma, bradycardia
Magnesium sulfate is seizure prophylaxis, NOT BP control
GTN reserved for concurrent pulmonary oedema or angina
explanation.pearls: Hydralazine 5 mg IV every 20 minutes up to 20 mg is the SOMANZ-recommended IV antihypertensive choice when labetalol is contraindicated or has failed; pre-load with 250 mL fluid to reduce reflex maternal hypotension.

stem:
A 34-year-old G3P2 woman has been pushing for 50 minutes at full dilation in a tertiary delivery suite. Her two previous deliveries were uncomplicated vaginal births of 3.6 kg and 3.8 kg infants. Antenatal estimated fetal weight by growth scan one week ago was 4.4 kg; her booking BMI was 32 kg/m2. She has a diet-controlled gestational diabetes diagnosis from this pregnancy.

The fetal head delivers with classical turtling against the perineum. With gentle downward axial traction by the registrar the anterior shoulder will not deliver. The emergency buzzer has been pressed and the obstetric consultant, anaesthetist, neonatal team, and senior midwife are arriving. The clock has just started. The mother is positioned semi-recumbent at the edge of the bed. She is haemodynamically stable. The midwife is asking what the first manoeuvre should be.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 102/min, BP 124/76 mmHg, RR 22/min, SpO2 99% room air, temperature 37.2 °C; fetal HR 138/min by Doppler immediately after head delivery
data_table.Examination: Fetal head delivered with turtling against perineum, no spontaneous restitution; anterior shoulder impacted behind maternal pubic symphysis on gentle axial traction
data_table.Investigations: Cardiotocograph was reassuring in second stage; no other investigations pending

lead_in: What is the most appropriate single best initial manoeuvre to attempt?

options.text: McRoberts manoeuvre with hyperflexion of the maternal hips against the abdomen by two assistants standing on either side of the delivery bed
options.rationale: McRoberts is the first-line manoeuvre in shoulder dystocia per HELPERR (Help, Evaluate for episiotomy, Legs in McRoberts, Pressure suprapubic, Enter rotational manoeuvres, Remove posterior arm, Roll); resolves over 40% of cases. (Source: RANZCOG Shoulder Dystocia; PROMPT Course)

options.text: Apply suprapubic pressure aimed in the downward and lateral direction to dislodge the impacted anterior shoulder from behind the maternal pubic symphysis
options.rationale: Suprapubic pressure is paired with McRoberts as the second step of HELPERR; the standard sequence runs McRoberts first, then add suprapubic pressure if McRoberts alone fails. (Source: RANZCOG Shoulder Dystocia; PROMPT Course)

options.text: Generous mediolateral episiotomy under local anaesthetic infiltration to enlarge the soft tissue space and allow direct access for the planned manoeuvres
options.rationale: Shoulder dystocia is a bony, not soft tissue, problem; episiotomy does not resolve the dystocia but may be performed selectively to enable internal manoeuvres later. (Source: RANZCOG Shoulder Dystocia)

options.text: Direct manual removal of the posterior arm of the fetus by sweeping it across the chest before any external manoeuvres have been attempted at this delivery
options.rationale: Posterior arm delivery is part of HELPERR but follows McRoberts and suprapubic pressure; it is a third-line internal manoeuvre, not a first-line approach. (Source: RANZCOG Shoulder Dystocia)

options.text: Apply firm downward fundal pressure by an assistant standing behind the maternal head to push the impacted anterior fetal shoulder downwards and forwards
options.rationale: Fundal pressure increases impaction and risks uterine rupture; it is contraindicated in shoulder dystocia. Suprapubic pressure (not fundal) is the correct external adjunct. (Source: RANZCOG Shoulder Dystocia)

explanation.summary: Shoulder dystocia is an unpredictable obstetric emergency requiring a sequenced response; the HELPERR mnemonic (Help, Evaluate for episiotomy, Legs in McRoberts, Pressure suprapubic, Enter rotational manoeuvres, Remove posterior arm, Roll the patient) provides a structured approach. McRoberts alone resolves over 40% of cases; combined McRoberts plus suprapubic pressure resolves over 80%. Internal manoeuvres (Rubin II, Woods screw, reverse Woods, posterior arm delivery) follow. Fundal pressure is absolutely contraindicated because it worsens impaction and risks uterine rupture and brachial plexus injury. Time-call documentation (head-to-body interval) and senior staff escalation begin immediately.
key_points: HELPERR is the standard structured sequence
McRoberts is always the first manoeuvre
Suprapubic pressure (NEVER fundal) is the next step
Internal manoeuvres only after external have failed
Time-call documentation begins from head delivery
explanation.pearls: McRoberts manoeuvre alone resolves over 40% of shoulder dystocia cases; pair with suprapubic pressure to lift resolution above 80% before progressing to internal manoeuvres.

subtopic_detail: Ovarian torsion diagnosis in normal Doppler
stem:
A 19-year-old nulliparous woman presents to a metropolitan emergency department with 8 hours of sudden onset severe right iliac fossa pain that began while she was at the gym doing burpees. She has vomited 4 times. The pain is constant with intermittent spikes. She is normally cycling, with her last menstrual period 12 days ago, and is sexually active using condoms.

On examination she is in significant pain at rest, lying still. The right iliac fossa is tender with voluntary guarding but no rebound. Her right adnexa is exquisitely tender on bimanual examination. Urine bhCG is negative. A transvaginal ultrasound reports a right ovary of 6.2 cm volume with a 3 cm haemorrhagic-appearing cyst, no free fluid in the pelvis, and preserved arterial and venous Doppler flow signals from the right ovarian vessels. The left ovary is normal at 4.1 cm volume. Pain control with oral oxycodone has not relieved her significantly.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 108/min, BP 122/74 mmHg, RR 22/min, SpO2 99% room air, temperature 37.4 °C
data_table.Examination: Right iliac fossa tenderness with voluntary guarding, exquisite right adnexal tenderness on bimanual; no peritonism, no cervical motion tenderness
data_table.Investigations: Urine bhCG negative; haemoglobin 130 g/L, WCC 12.4 x10^9/L, CRP 8 mg/L (<5); transvaginal ultrasound right ovary 6.2 cm volume with 3 cm haemorrhagic cyst, preserved arterial and venous Doppler signals; urine microscopy bland

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step in management?

options.text: Discharge home with oral analgesia and arrange outpatient gynaecology review in 1 week given that ultrasound Doppler signals from the right ovary are preserved
options.rationale: Doppler arterial and venous flow can be preserved in early or intermittent ovarian torsion (sensitivity around 50%); clinical findings of acute adnexal pain plus an enlarged ovary outweigh a reassuring Doppler. (Source: RANZCOG Position Statement: Ovarian Torsion; UpToDate)

options.text: Trial of intravenous opiate analgesia and antispasmodic medication and reassessment of clinical signs and pain scores after 2 hours of adequate analgesia first
options.rationale: Adequate analgesia is appropriate alongside surgical preparation but is not the definitive step; pain resolution may be misleading because the ovary can be necrosing while pain settles. (Source: RANZCOG Position Statement: Ovarian Torsion)

options.text: Repeat the transvaginal ultrasound with Doppler in 4 to 6 hours to look for any interval change in arterial or venous flow signals or any size increase
options.rationale: Watchful waiting for 4 to 6 hours risks irreversible ischaemia in a torsion; the diagnosis is surgical and must not be delayed by serial imaging. (Source: RANZCOG Position Statement: Ovarian Torsion)

options.text: Magnetic resonance imaging of the pelvis with contrast to clarify the ovarian appearances and viability before a final surgical decision is made by gynaecology
options.rationale: MRI is rarely indicated in acute torsion; it is time-consuming, often unavailable out of hours, and does not change the surgical pathway. (Source: RANZCOG Position Statement: Ovarian Torsion)

options.text: Urgent diagnostic laparoscopy by the gynaecology team aiming for ovarian detorsion and conservation regardless of macroscopic appearance at first inspection
options.rationale: Suspected ovarian torsion is a surgical diagnosis; preserved Doppler does not exclude it. Laparoscopy with detorsion and conservative management preserves fertility in most cases, even when the ovary looks ischaemic. (Source: RANZCOG Position Statement: Ovarian Torsion)

explanation.summary: Ovarian torsion is a clinical and surgical diagnosis; imaging is supportive but not exclusionary. Risk factors include ovarian enlargement above 5 cm volume, mass lesions (dermoid, functional cyst), pregnancy, ovulation induction, and sudden exertion. Doppler ultrasound has a sensitivity of only around 50% because the ovary has dual blood supply via ovarian and uterine arteries; preserved flow does NOT rule out torsion. The treatment of choice is urgent laparoscopic detorsion with conservation of the ovary regardless of macroscopic appearance at first inspection; up to 90% of black or purple ovaries recover after untwisting. Oophorectomy is reserved for clearly necrotic ovaries or post-menopausal patients.
key_points: Ovarian torsion is a clinical and surgical diagnosis
Doppler ultrasound sensitivity is only 50%
Conservative detorsion preserves the ovary in most cases
Black appearance at laparoscopy still warrants untwisting
Oophorectomy reserved for clear necrosis or post-menopausal patient
explanation.pearls: Preserved ovarian Doppler does NOT rule out torsion; the ovary has dual blood supply via ovarian and uterine arteries, and clinical suspicion plus an enlarged tender adnexa is enough to take a young woman to laparoscopy.

stem:
A 36-year-old G4P3 woman is reviewed in a tertiary maternal-fetal medicine clinic at 30 weeks gestation. She has had three previous caesarean sections without complication and is now booked for a fourth planned caesarean. The current pregnancy is uncomplicated. Fetal growth is on the 50th centile. Her booking BMI is 28 kg/m2 and she is otherwise well.

A detailed ultrasound at 28 weeks describes an anterior placenta covering the internal cervical os. The report flags loss of the retroplacental clear zone, two large placental lacunae with turbulent flow, and bridging vessels between the placenta and the bladder. A confirmatory MRI shows myometrial thinning to 1 mm between the placenta and the bladder, focal bulging of the placenta into the bladder serosa, but no clear breach of the bladder wall itself. She has been counselled that planned delivery will be early.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 80/min, BP 118/72 mmHg, RR 14/min, SpO2 99% room air, temperature 36.6 °C; fetal HR 142/min reassuring
data_table.Examination: Gravid uterus consistent with 30 weeks; no abdominal tenderness; symphysio-fundal height 30 cm; no vaginal bleeding
data_table.Investigations: Ultrasound and MRI consistent with placenta percreta involving bladder serosa; haemoglobin 118 g/L, ferritin 24 mcg/L (15-200), platelets 232 x10^9/L, group and antibody screen negative; cell saver and urology available at the tertiary unit

lead_in: What is the most appropriate planned mode and timing of delivery to recommend at the multidisciplinary planning meeting?

options.text: Spontaneous vaginal delivery at term with continuous CTG monitoring and active management of the third stage including immediate manual removal of placenta
options.rationale: Vaginal delivery is contraindicated in placenta percreta with placenta praevia; manual removal causes massive haemorrhage and bladder injury. (Source: RANZCOG Statement: Placenta Praevia and Accreta Spectrum; FIGO)
source_refs: RANZCOG Statement: Placenta Praevia and Accreta Spectrum
FIGO consensus guidelines on placenta accreta spectrum disorders

options.text: Planned caesarean hysterectomy at 34 to 36 weeks gestation at a tertiary centre with multidisciplinary team, cell saver, urology back-up, and antenatal corticosteroids
options.rationale: RANZCOG and FIGO recommend planned caesarean hysterectomy at 34-36+0 weeks for placenta accreta spectrum with MDT support; trying to remove the placenta or going to term is associated with catastrophic haemorrhage. (Source: RANZCOG Statement: Placenta Praevia and Accreta Spectrum; FIGO)
source_refs: RANZCOG Statement: Placenta Praevia and Accreta Spectrum
FIGO consensus guidelines on placenta accreta spectrum disorders

options.text: Planned caesarean section at 39 weeks gestation with attempted manual placental removal followed by uterotonics and balloon tamponade if heavy bleeding ensues
options.rationale: Term timing increases risk of unscheduled bleeding labour; attempted manual removal in placenta accreta spectrum is associated with massive haemorrhage and exsanguination. (Source: RANZCOG Statement: Placenta Praevia and Accreta Spectrum)
source_refs: RANZCOG Statement: Placenta Praevia and Accreta Spectrum

options.text: Planned caesarean section at 37 weeks gestation with placenta left in situ and outpatient methotrexate therapy aiming for delayed resorption over 6 months postpartum
options.rationale: Leaving the placenta in situ is an option in selected cases (fertility preserving) but is associated with sepsis, secondary haemorrhage, and DIC; not first-line in placenta percreta with bladder involvement. Methotrexate adds no proven benefit. (Source: RANZCOG Statement: Placenta Praevia and Accreta Spectrum)
source_refs: RANZCOG Statement: Placenta Praevia and Accreta Spectrum

options.text: Planned classical caesarean section at 32 weeks gestation followed by uterine artery embolisation in the angiography suite as planned definitive haemorrhage control
options.rationale: 32 weeks is too early without specific indication and exposes the neonate to avoidable prematurity morbidity; UAE is an adjunct, not a substitute for caesarean hysterectomy in placenta percreta with bladder involvement. (Source: RANZCOG Statement: Placenta Praevia and Accreta Spectrum)
source_refs: RANZCOG Statement: Placenta Praevia and Accreta Spectrum

explanation.summary: Placenta accreta spectrum (accreta, increta, percreta) is among the leading causes of maternal mortality due to massive haemorrhage. Major risk factors are prior caesarean section count (cumulative) plus placenta praevia. Antenatal ultrasound features include loss of the retroplacental clear zone, placental lacunae, abnormal vasculature, and bladder bulging; MRI defines bladder and parametrial involvement. Planned caesarean hysterectomy at 34-36+0 weeks gestation in a tertiary centre with cell saver, MDT, urology, interventional radiology, and ICU on standby is the standard of care; antenatal corticosteroids are given for fetal lung maturity. Conservative management (placenta left in situ) has a role in fertility preservation but is associated with significant late morbidity.
key_points: Planned delivery at 34-36+0 weeks at tertiary centre
Caesarean hysterectomy is standard of care for percreta with bladder involvement
MDT: obstetric, anaesthetic, urology, interventional radiology, blood bank, ICU
Antenatal corticosteroids before planned delivery for fetal lung maturity
Conservative management is fertility-preserving but with significant late morbidity
explanation.pearls: Placenta accreta spectrum delivery is planned at 34-36+0 weeks in a tertiary centre with cell saver and MDT support; never attempt manual placental removal because catastrophic haemorrhage is the rule.

sources.label: RANZCOG Statement: Placenta Praevia and Accreta Spectrum
FIGO consensus guidelines on placenta accreta spectrum disorders

subtopic_detail: VBAC counselling after one prior LSCS
stem:
A 32-year-old woman in her second pregnancy attends a 36-week midwife-led antenatal review. Her first child was delivered by emergency caesarean three years ago at 39 weeks gestation for a non-reassuring CTG in early labour. There were no complications during recovery, and she has had no other surgical procedures. This pregnancy has been uncomplicated.

She weighs 76 kg with a booking BMI of 26. The current pregnancy is singleton, cephalic, with an estimated fetal weight at the 50th centile. Placental position is fundal-posterior on the 32-week scan. Her midwife refers her to the obstetric clinic to discuss mode of birth. She tells you she is keen to attempt a vaginal birth this time but is worried about uterine rupture.

data_table.Vital signs: within normal limits
data_table.Examination: fundal height 36 cm, cephalic, longitudinal lie, fetal heart 140 bpm
data_table.Investigations: 32-week ultrasound: singleton cephalic, EFW at 50th centile, fundal-posterior placenta

lead_in: What is the most accurate counselling regarding planned vaginal birth after caesarean?

options.text: Vaginal birth success approximately 30 percent; uterine rupture risk approximately 5 percent
options.rationale: Both figures overstate risk and understate benefit by roughly an order of magnitude, which would unfairly bias the conversation against TOLAC. (Source: RANZCOG: Birth after previous caesarean)

options.text: Vaginal birth success approximately 60 percent; uterine rupture risk approximately 2 percent
options.rationale: The success rate is in the right region but the rupture rate is quadruple the cited RANZCOG figure for a single previous low transverse caesarean. (Source: RANZCOG: Birth after previous caesarean)

options.text: Vaginal birth success approximately 70 percent; uterine rupture risk approximately 0.5 percent
options.rationale: RANZCOG quotes 60 to 80 percent success for planned TOLAC after one prior low transverse caesarean, with uterine rupture in approximately 1 in 200. These are the figures to share in counselling. (Source: RANZCOG: Birth after previous caesarean)

options.text: Vaginal birth success approximately 90 percent; uterine rupture risk approximately 0.1 percent
options.rationale: This overstates the likelihood of vaginal delivery and understates rupture risk; quoting these figures would breach informed consent expectations. (Source: RANZCOG: Birth after previous caesarean)

options.text: Vaginal birth contraindicated; recommend elective repeat caesarean at 39 weeks gestation
options.rationale: A single previous low transverse caesarean is not a contraindication to TOLAC and RANZCOG explicitly recommends offering both options after balanced counselling. (Source: RANZCOG: Birth after previous caesarean)

explanation.summary: RANZCOG supports planned vaginal birth after one prior low transverse caesarean (TOLAC) provided there are no contraindications such as classical incision, two or more prior caesareans, placenta praevia, or prior uterine rupture. Counselling must quote a success rate of 60 to 80 percent (approximately 70 percent for single prior LSCS, no other risk factors) and uterine rupture risk of approximately 1 in 200 (0.5 percent). Continuous CTG monitoring is recommended in labour. Induction with prostaglandins increases rupture risk and is generally avoided.
key_points: TOLAC success rate after one LSCS: 60 to 80 percent (RANZCOG)
Uterine rupture risk approximately 1 in 200 (0.5 percent)
Continuous CTG monitoring in labour
Avoid prostaglandin induction; oxytocin augmentation with caution
explanation.pearls: After one prior low transverse caesarean, quote 70 percent success and 0.5 percent uterine rupture risk for planned TOLAC; rupture risk rises with prostaglandin induction.

sources.label: NSW Health: VBAC Clinical Practice Guideline

stem:
A 29-year-old woman in her first pregnancy attends for routine antenatal screening at 27 weeks gestation. She has no personal or family history of diabetes. Booking BMI was 24 and she has gained 9 kg in pregnancy so far. The pregnancy is otherwise uncomplicated, with normal morphology scan and a singleton cephalic fetus tracking the 55th centile for estimated weight.

She completes a 75 g oral glucose tolerance test as outpatient. Results: fasting venous plasma glucose 5.3 mmol/L, 1-hour 9.4 mmol/L, 2-hour 7.6 mmol/L. She is asymptomatic. Vital signs are within normal limits. Urine dipstick is negative for protein, glucose, and ketones.

data_table.Vital signs: within normal limits
data_table.Examination: uterus appropriate for dates, fetal heart 145 bpm, no peripheral oedema
data_table.Investigations: 75g OGTT: fasting 5.3 mmol/L, 1-h 9.4 mmol/L, 2-h 7.6 mmol/L; urinalysis negative

lead_in: What is the most appropriate interpretation of these results?

options.text: Normal pregnancy; repeat OGTT at 32 weeks if clinical concerns arise
options.rationale: The fasting value exceeds the ADIPS-IADPSG cut-off, which itself diagnoses GDM. Calling this normal would miss the diagnosis. (Source: ADIPS Consensus Guidelines for GDM)

options.text: Impaired glucose tolerance; arrange repeat 75 g OGTT in 6 weeks for confirmation
options.rationale: ADIPS in pregnancy does not use an intermediate IGT category; any single value above the threshold establishes GDM. Repeating the test delays nutritional and glycaemic management. (Source: ADIPS Consensus Guidelines for GDM)

options.text: Pre-existing type 2 diabetes; commence insulin and refer to endocrinology
options.rationale: Pre-existing diabetes is diagnosed by fasting at least 7.0 mmol/L, random at least 11.1 mmol/L, or HbA1c at least 6.5 percent, none of which apply. Labelling as type 2 would misdirect long-term follow-up. (Source: RACGP Diabetes Handbook)

options.text: Gestational diabetes; commence dietary advice, monitoring, and diabetes referral
options.rationale: ADIPS-IADPSG diagnostic thresholds on 75 g OGTT are fasting at least 5.1 mmol/L, 1-h at least 10.0, or 2-h at least 8.5; a single value above threshold qualifies. The fasting at 5.3 mmol/L establishes GDM. (Source: ADIPS Consensus Guidelines for GDM)

options.text: Borderline result; lifestyle advice only with no formal diabetes referral
options.rationale: ADIPS does not recognise a borderline category in pregnancy and labelling the diagnosis as borderline undertreats the fetal and maternal risk. (Source: ADIPS Consensus Guidelines for GDM)

explanation.summary: The ADIPS-IADPSG diagnostic criteria for GDM on the 75 g OGTT at 24 to 28 weeks gestation are: fasting at least 5.1 mmol/L, 1-h at least 10.0 mmol/L, or 2-h at least 8.5 mmol/L. A single value at or above any of these thresholds establishes GDM. Management begins with dietary modification (carbohydrate distribution, plate model) and home blood glucose monitoring (fasting and 2-h post-prandial), with pharmacotherapy (metformin or insulin) added if targets are not met within 1 to 2 weeks.
key_points: ADIPS-IADPSG GDM cut-offs: fasting >=5.1, 1-h >=10.0, 2-h >=8.5 mmol/L
Any single value at or above threshold diagnoses GDM
No intermediate IGT or borderline category in pregnancy
First-line management: diet + monitoring; pharmacotherapy if targets unmet
explanation.pearls: ADIPS-IADPSG 75 g OGTT at 24 to 28 weeks: fasting 5.1, 1-h 10.0, 2-h 8.5 mmol/L - a single value at threshold diagnoses GDM.

stem:
A 28-year-old woman, blood group O Rhesus-negative, presents to the early pregnancy assessment unit at 11+3 weeks gestation with one day of light per-vaginal bleeding and mild lower abdominal cramping. Her previous pregnancy was uncomplicated and resulted in a vaginal birth two years ago, after which she received post-natal anti-D 625 IU.

On examination she is haemodynamically stable. Speculum reveals a closed cervical os with a small amount of dark blood in the vault. Bimanual examination is unremarkable. Transvaginal ultrasound demonstrates a singleton intrauterine pregnancy with a fetal pole and cardiac activity at a gestational age of 11+4 weeks. Her partner is known to be Rhesus-positive. Indirect Coombs test confirms she has no detectable anti-D antibodies.

data_table.Vital signs: within normal limits
data_table.Examination: speculum closed os with small dark blood; bimanual unremarkable; abdomen non-tender
data_table.Investigations: TVS singleton IUP with cardiac activity at 11+4 wk; indirect Coombs negative; blood group O Rh-negative

lead_in: What is the most appropriate immunoglobulin management?

options.text: Anti-D immunoglobulin 625 IU intramuscularly within 72 hours of bleeding
options.rationale: The 625 IU dose is the standard antepartum and postpartum dose used at or beyond 20 weeks. Under 12 weeks the recommended dose is the lower 250 IU per NBA guidance. (Source: NBA: Guidelines on the use of Rh(D) Immunoglobulin)
source_refs: NBA: Guidelines on the use of Rh(D) Immunoglobulin

options.text: Anti-D immunoglobulin 1500 IU intramuscularly within 72 hours of bleeding
options.rationale: 1500 IU is reserved for large feto-maternal haemorrhage (over 6 mL fetal blood) such as that detected by Kleihauer-Betke testing after major events, not first-trimester threatened miscarriage. (Source: NBA: Guidelines on the use of Rh(D) Immunoglobulin)
source_refs: NBA: Guidelines on the use of Rh(D) Immunoglobulin

options.text: No anti-D required for threatened miscarriage with closed os under 12 weeks
options.rationale: NBA Australia does recommend anti-D 250 IU for any sensitising event in a Rhesus-negative woman under 12 weeks, including threatened miscarriage with bleeding, regardless of cervical os status. (Source: NBA: Guidelines on the use of Rh(D) Immunoglobulin)
source_refs: NBA: Guidelines on the use of Rh(D) Immunoglobulin

options.text: Defer anti-D and arrange Kleihauer-Betke test to quantify feto-maternal haemorrhage
options.rationale: Kleihauer-Betke testing is unreliable and not recommended before 20 weeks because fetal red cell volume is too small to quantify. Anti-D is given empirically by gestational-age band. (Source: NBA: Guidelines on the use of Rh(D) Immunoglobulin)
source_refs: NBA: Guidelines on the use of Rh(D) Immunoglobulin

options.text: Anti-D immunoglobulin 250 IU intramuscularly within 72 hours of bleeding
options.rationale: NBA recommends anti-D 250 IU for sensitising events under 12 weeks gestation in a Rhesus-negative woman, including threatened miscarriage with bleeding. Timing within 72 hours is critical to prevent sensitisation. (Source: NBA: Guidelines on the use of Rh(D) Immunoglobulin)
source_refs: NBA: Guidelines on the use of Rh(D) Immunoglobulin

explanation.summary: NBA anti-D dosing in Australia is banded by gestational age. Under 12 weeks the dose for any sensitising event (including bleeding in threatened, complete, or incomplete miscarriage) is 250 IU within 72 hours. From 12 weeks onwards the dose is 625 IU. Routine antenatal prophylaxis is given at 28 and 34 weeks (625 IU each). Postpartum dose is 625 IU plus dose adjustment by Kleihauer if FMH exceeds 6 mL fetal blood. Kleihauer testing is not used before 20 weeks because of poor reliability.
key_points: Anti-D under 12 weeks: 250 IU within 72 hours of sensitising event
Anti-D 12 weeks and over: 625 IU within 72 hours
Routine antenatal prophylaxis at 28 and 34 weeks
Kleihauer testing not used before 20 weeks
explanation.pearls: In a Rhesus-negative woman with bleeding under 12 weeks, give anti-D 250 IU IM within 72 hours; the dose doubles to 625 IU from 12 weeks onward.

sources.label: NBA: Guidelines on the use of Rh(D) Immunoglobulin

subtopic_detail: Mode of delivery for DCDA twins at 37 weeks
stem:
A 31-year-old primigravida with a spontaneous dichorionic diamniotic twin pregnancy attends a 36-week obstetric review. Both fetuses are alive and growing concordantly, with estimated fetal weights at the 50th and 55th centiles and an inter-twin discordance of 6 percent. She has no medical co-morbidities and the pregnancy has been uncomplicated.

On examination her symphysis-fundal height is 42 cm. Twin 1 is cephalic with engaged presenting part; twin 2 is transverse with the fetal back inferior. Cervical examination reveals a closed, posterior cervix. Both placentas are fundal-anterior on the most recent ultrasound, with normal umbilical artery Doppler. She is keen to plan a vaginal birth at 37+5 weeks gestation, the unit's standard timing for DCDA twins.

data_table.Vital signs: within normal limits
data_table.Examination: SFH 42 cm; twin 1 cephalic engaged; twin 2 transverse; cervix closed posterior
data_table.Investigations: 36-wk ultrasound: DCDA twins, EFW 50th and 55th centile (6% discordance), fundal-anterior placentas, normal umbilical Doppler

lead_in: What is the most appropriate counselling regarding mode of birth?

options.text: Recommend elective caesarean at 37+5 weeks because twin 2 is non-cephalic
options.rationale: RANZCOG and the AAOM joint statement permit planned vaginal birth for DCDA twins only if twin 1 is cephalic AND twin 2 is cephalic or amenable to internal podalic version after delivery of twin 1. A transverse second twin is generally an indication for caesarean unless an experienced obstetrician is available for breech extraction or external version. (Source: RANZCOG: Management of twin pregnancy)

options.text: Plan vaginal birth at 37+5 weeks with internal podalic version of twin 2 in labour
options.rationale: Internal podalic version is acceptable only when performed by an obstetrician experienced in the manoeuvre. Listing it without confirmed clinician competency exposes mother and twin 2 to avoidable risk. (Source: RANZCOG: Management of twin pregnancy)

options.text: Plan vaginal birth at 38+5 weeks regardless of twin 2 presentation in labour
options.rationale: Continuing the DCDA pregnancy beyond 37+6 increases the risk of stillbirth, and the proposed plan ignores the non-cephalic second twin entirely. (Source: RANZCOG: Management of twin pregnancy)

options.text: Defer delivery decision until spontaneous labour and manage twin 2 in labour
options.rationale: RANZCOG advises elective birth of DCDA twins by 37+6 weeks. Waiting for spontaneous labour delays a planned decision and leaves the unit reacting to a transverse second twin at presentation. (Source: RANZCOG: Management of twin pregnancy)

options.text: Recommend elective caesarean at 36+0 weeks due to twin pregnancy risk profile
options.rationale: DCDA twins are delivered at 37+0 to 37+6 weeks unless complications dictate earlier. Bringing the delivery forward to 36+0 without indication adds avoidable neonatal respiratory morbidity. (Source: RANZCOG: Management of twin pregnancy)

explanation.summary: RANZCOG and AAOM recommend planned birth of uncomplicated DCDA twins at 37+0 to 37+6 weeks. Mode of birth depends on the presentation of twin 1 and the unit's expertise. Planned vaginal birth is appropriate when twin 1 is cephalic AND twin 2 is cephalic, breech in a unit experienced in vaginal breech, or transverse with a clinician confident in internal podalic version. A transverse second twin without that expertise is an indication for elective caesarean. MCMA twins always deliver by caesarean at 32 to 34 weeks; MCDA at 36 to 37 weeks.
key_points: DCDA twins delivered electively at 37+0 to 37+6 weeks
Planned vaginal birth requires cephalic twin 1; twin 2 presentation determines further pathway
Transverse twin 2 without experienced clinician for podalic version: caesarean
MCMA twins by caesarean at 32 to 34 weeks; MCDA at 36 to 37
explanation.pearls: DCDA twins with non-cephalic twin 2 and no clinician confident in internal podalic version: elective caesarean at 37+5 weeks, not vaginal.

subtopic_detail: Timing of caesarean for asymptomatic placenta praevia
stem:
A 35-year-old multigravida (G3 P2) attends antenatal clinic at 34+5 weeks gestation. A transabdominal scan at 32 weeks identified placenta praevia with the placental edge covering the internal cervical os by 18 mm. A repeat transvaginal scan at 34 weeks confirmed a major praevia with the lower edge 12 mm across the os. She has had no per-vaginal bleeding throughout the pregnancy.

On examination she is well, vital signs within normal limits, with a soft non-tender abdomen. The fetus is in transverse lie with an estimated fetal weight at the 50th centile. Her previous two deliveries were uncomplicated vaginal births. The pregnancy is otherwise low-risk and she has had antenatal corticosteroids in a prior preterm threatened labour at 31 weeks (fetus born at term).

data_table.Vital signs: within normal limits
data_table.Examination: soft non-tender abdomen, fetus transverse, no per-vaginal bleeding
data_table.Investigations: TVS at 34 weeks: placenta covering internal os by 12 mm (major praevia), EFW 50th centile, normal umbilical Doppler

lead_in: What is the most appropriate elective delivery plan?

options.text: Schedule elective lower-segment caesarean at 36+0 to 37+0 weeks gestation
options.rationale: RANZCOG recommends elective caesarean for uncomplicated major placenta praevia at 36+0 to 37+0 weeks to balance neonatal respiratory morbidity against the rising risk of unplanned bleeding at term. (Source: RANZCOG: Placenta praevia and placenta accreta)
source_refs: RANZCOG: Placenta praevia and placenta accreta

options.text: Schedule elective lower-segment caesarean at 39+0 weeks gestation
options.rationale: Waiting until 39 weeks for major praevia accepts a meaningful interval risk of unscheduled antepartum haemorrhage requiring emergent surgery. RANZCOG specifically pulls the planned date earlier. (Source: RANZCOG: Placenta praevia and placenta accreta)
source_refs: RANZCOG: Placenta praevia and placenta accreta

options.text: Schedule elective lower-segment caesarean at 34+0 weeks gestation
options.rationale: 34 weeks delivery for uncomplicated major praevia is too early and incurs avoidable neonatal respiratory morbidity. Earlier delivery is justified only if symptomatic with bleeding. (Source: RANZCOG: Placenta praevia and placenta accreta)
source_refs: RANZCOG: Placenta praevia and placenta accreta

options.text: Plan trial of labour with continuous CTG and an experienced obstetrician on standby
options.rationale: Major praevia is an absolute contraindication to vaginal birth. Any cervical change risks catastrophic haemorrhage as the placenta separates from the lower segment. (Source: RANZCOG: Placenta praevia and placenta accreta)
source_refs: RANZCOG: Placenta praevia and placenta accreta

options.text: Repeat ultrasound at 37 weeks before deciding on delivery timing
options.rationale: Repeat scanning will not move a placenta covering the os by 12 mm; the decision to schedule caesarean before 37 weeks is already established. Further imaging adds delay without changing the plan. (Source: RANZCOG: Placenta praevia and placenta accreta)
source_refs: RANZCOG: Placenta praevia and placenta accreta

explanation.summary: For uncomplicated major placenta praevia (placental edge covering the internal os by more than 20 mm, or persistent praevia after 32 weeks), RANZCOG recommends elective lower-segment caesarean at 36+0 to 37+0 weeks. Earlier delivery is indicated if there has been antepartum haemorrhage. The lower segment caesarean must be performed by an experienced obstetrician with consultant anaesthesia, cross-matched blood available, and consideration of placenta accreta spectrum imaging if there are risk factors (prior caesarean, IVF). Major praevia is an absolute contraindication to vaginal birth.
key_points: Uncomplicated major praevia: elective LSCS 36+0 to 37+0 weeks (RANZCOG)
Symptomatic praevia (bleeding): earlier delivery individualised by gestation and bleeding
Major praevia absolutely contraindicates vaginal birth
Screen for accreta spectrum if prior caesarean or IVF
explanation.pearls: Asymptomatic major placenta praevia: elective LSCS at 36 to 37 weeks, with cross-matched blood and consultant cover; earlier delivery only for bleeding.

sources.label: RANZCOG: Placenta praevia and placenta accreta

subtopic_detail: Management of PPROM at 34 to 36 weeks (RANZCOG)
stem:
A 27-year-old primigravida at 34+5 weeks gestation presents with a 4-hour history of clear fluid loss per vaginam. She felt a small gush followed by ongoing dampness. There is no abdominal pain, no per-vaginal bleeding, and the fetus is moving normally.

On examination she is afebrile with pulse 78, blood pressure 118 by 72 mmHg, respiratory rate 16, SpO2 99 percent on room air, temperature 36.8 degrees Celsius. Speculum reveals a pool of clear fluid in the posterior fornix that ferns on slide testing. The cervix is closed. CTG shows a baseline of 140 with normal variability and accelerations. White cell count 9.2 x10^9/L (4-11) and CRP 4 mg/L (<5). Group B streptococcus screen at 28 weeks was negative.

data_table.Vital signs: HR 78, BP 118/72, RR 16, SpO2 99% room air, temperature 36.8 degrees Celsius
data_table.Examination: speculum: clear fluid pool, ferning positive, cervix closed; abdomen soft non-tender
data_table.Investigations: WCC 9.2 x10^9/L (4-11), CRP 4 mg/L (<5), GBS negative at 28 wk, CTG baseline 140 normal variability with accelerations

lead_in: What is the most appropriate immediate management plan?

options.text: Admit, commence IV benzylpenicillin and erythromycin and induce labour with oxytocin now
options.rationale: Active induction at 34+5 weeks is not the default RANZCOG position because the PPROMT trial showed worse neonatal outcomes with immediate delivery between 34+0 and 36+6 compared with expectant management in well-monitored women. (Source: RANZCOG: PPROM; PPROMT Trial 2016)
source_refs: RANZCOG: Preterm prelabour rupture of membranes

options.text: Admit, latency erythromycin and expectant management with daily CTG and inflammatory markers
options.rationale: RANZCOG recommends expectant management for PPROM between 34+0 and 36+6 weeks in the absence of chorioamnionitis, fetal compromise, or placental abruption, following PPROMT trial evidence of reduced neonatal respiratory distress with expectant care. Latency antibiotics reduce ascending infection. (Source: RANZCOG: PPROM)
source_refs: RANZCOG: Preterm prelabour rupture of membranes

options.text: Discharge home on oral amoxicillin with daily clinic review and self-temperature monitoring
options.rationale: PPROM management requires inpatient surveillance with CTG and inflammatory markers; discharge home cannot reliably detect early chorioamnionitis. (Source: RANZCOG: PPROM)
source_refs: RANZCOG: Preterm prelabour rupture of membranes

options.text: Administer betamethasone 11.4 mg IM and proceed to elective caesarean at 35+0 weeks
options.rationale: Beyond 34+0 weeks the benefit of antenatal corticosteroids is uncertain and routine use is not recommended in PPROM at this gestation. Proceeding to caesarean adds surgical morbidity without clear benefit. (Source: RANZCOG: Antenatal corticosteroids)

options.text: Administer tocolysis with nifedipine and continue surveillance until 37 weeks gestation
options.rationale: Tocolysis is not indicated in PPROM because membranes are already ruptured and prolonging gestation in the presence of broken membranes risks ascending infection without clear benefit. (Source: RANZCOG: PPROM)
source_refs: RANZCOG: Preterm prelabour rupture of membranes

explanation.summary: RANZCOG management of PPROM is gestation-banded. Under 34+0 weeks, expectant care with antenatal corticosteroids, magnesium sulfate (under 30 weeks), and erythromycin latency antibiotics is standard. Between 34+0 and 36+6 weeks, the PPROMT trial demonstrated lower neonatal respiratory morbidity with expectant management compared with immediate delivery; expectant care with daily monitoring is preferred unless there is chorioamnionitis, fetal compromise, abruption, or active labour. From 37+0 weeks, induction is reasonable.
key_points: PPROM 34+0 to 36+6 weeks: expectant management is RANZCOG default (post-PPROMT)
Latency antibiotics (erythromycin) given until labour or delivery
Daily CTG and inflammatory markers to detect chorioamnionitis early
Triggers for immediate delivery: chorioamnionitis, abruption, fetal compromise, labour
explanation.pearls: PPROM between 34+0 and 36+6 weeks without chorioamnionitis or fetal compromise: expectant management with latency erythromycin (PPROMT trial 2016).

sources.label: RANZCOG: Preterm prelabour rupture of membranes

subtopic_detail: Ectopic in only remaining tube after prior contralateral salpingectomy
stem:
A 33-year-old woman G2 P0 presents to the early pregnancy assessment service with three days of right iliac fossa pain and a positive home pregnancy test. Her last menstrual period was 7 weeks ago. Three years ago she had an emergency laparoscopic left salpingectomy for a ruptured ectopic pregnancy; she has no other gynaecological surgery and no children. She would like to preserve every reasonable chance of future spontaneous conception.

On examination she is haemodynamically stable. Abdomen is soft with mild right iliac fossa tenderness without peritonism. Transvaginal ultrasound shows an empty uterus with a 3 cm right adnexal mass containing a yolk sac but no fetal cardiac activity, with a small amount of free fluid in the pouch of Douglas. Serum bhCG is 2400 IU/L. FBC, group and hold, and electrolytes are within normal limits. The left ovary is structurally normal and the left tube is absent on imaging.

data_table.Vital signs: within normal limits
data_table.Examination: abdomen soft with mild RIF tenderness, no peritonism, no cervical excitation
data_table.Investigations: TVS: empty uterus, 3 cm right adnexal mass with yolk sac, no cardiac activity, small free fluid in pouch of Douglas; bhCG 2400 IU/L; left tube absent (prior salpingectomy)

lead_in: What is the most appropriate surgical procedure if she opts for operative management?

options.text: Laparoscopic right salpingostomy with conservative tube preservation
options.rationale: Salpingostomy preserves the affected tube but carries a 4 to 15 percent risk of persistent trophoblast requiring further treatment, plus higher risk of recurrent ipsilateral ectopic. In a single-tube setting where future ectopic in the same tube would be catastrophic, salpingectomy gives better long-term outcomes. (Source: RANZCOG GPS: Tubal ectopic pregnancy)

options.text: Methotrexate 50 mg/m2 IM single-dose protocol with weekly bhCG follow-up
options.rationale: Methotrexate is medical not surgical management, and the question asks about the surgical procedure. Methotrexate is also a legitimate alternative here given bhCG below 5000 and stable haemodynamics, but is outside the lead-in. (Source: RANZCOG GPS: Tubal ectopic pregnancy)

options.text: Laparoscopic ipsilateral oophorectomy with tubal preservation
options.rationale: The ovary is not implicated in tubal ectopic pregnancy; removing it would compromise fertility (through reduced ovarian reserve and contralateral compensation issues) without addressing the ectopic. (Source: RANZCOG GPS: Tubal ectopic pregnancy)

options.text: Laparoscopic right salpingectomy with histopathology of the resected tube
options.rationale: Despite this being her remaining tube, the historical-bilaterality flip applies: with no contralateral tube, recurrent ipsilateral ectopic risk dominates fertility planning, and salpingectomy with subsequent IVF gives better cumulative live-birth outcomes than salpingostomy with the risks of persistent trophoblast and recurrence. RANZCOG endorses salpingectomy in this scenario. (Source: RANZCOG GPS: Tubal ectopic pregnancy)

options.text: Laparotomy with right salpingectomy and contralateral tube preservation review
options.rationale: Laparotomy is reserved for haemodynamic instability or limited laparoscopic access. The patient is stable and laparoscopy is preferred, with shorter recovery and equivalent outcomes. (Source: RANZCOG GPS: Tubal ectopic pregnancy)

explanation.summary: Contrary to the intuitive 'preserve the only remaining tube' approach, RANZCOG and the recent meta-analytic evidence favour laparoscopic salpingectomy over salpingostomy when an ectopic occurs in the sole remaining tube after prior contralateral salpingectomy. Salpingostomy carries 4 to 15 percent persistent trophoblast risk and substantially higher recurrent ipsilateral ectopic risk; subsequent ectopic in that single tube would necessitate emergency salpingectomy under worse conditions. Cumulative live-birth rates via salpingectomy plus planned IVF exceed those of salpingostomy attempting natural conception. Medical management with methotrexate is an acceptable alternative given bhCG below 5000 and stable haemodynamics, but if operative is chosen, salpingectomy is preferred.
key_points: Historical-bilaterality flip: prior contralateral salpingectomy changes the calculus
Salpingostomy in sole remaining tube: high persistent trophoblast and recurrence risk
Salpingectomy + planned IVF gives better cumulative live-birth than salpingostomy
Methotrexate (medical) is a legitimate alternative under RANZCOG criteria (bhCG <5000, no cardiac activity, no rupture)
explanation.pearls: Ectopic in the only remaining tube after prior contralateral salpingectomy: prefer salpingectomy plus planned IVF over salpingostomy because the recurrence and persistent trophoblast risks dominate.

sources.label: Cochrane: Interventions for tubal ectopic pregnancy

stem:
A 36-year-old woman attends your general practice for a routine cervical screening test. She has had previous normal screening tests at age 30 and 25; she has no symptoms of abnormal bleeding and is not pregnant. She is up to date with HPV vaccination from school years. She has been with the same partner for 8 years.

The self-collected vaginal swab returns oncogenic HPV (non 16, non 18) positive. A reflex liquid-based cytology from the same sample reports low-grade squamous intraepithelial lesion (LSIL).

data_table.Vital signs: within normal limits
data_table.Examination: asymptomatic; speculum examination not performed for self-collected screen
data_table.Investigations: HPV PCR: oncogenic non 16/18 detected; reflex LBC: LSIL

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step in screening management?

options.text: Refer urgently for colposcopy and directed biopsy within 8 weeks
options.rationale: Direct colposcopy is reserved for oncogenic HPV 16 or 18, for any HPV positive with HSIL on cytology, or persistent intermediate risk on the 12-month repeat. LSIL with non 16/18 HPV does not meet the immediate referral threshold. (Source: National Cervical Screening Program Clinical Guidelines)
source_refs: National Cervical Screening Program Clinical Guidelines

options.text: Repeat the cervical screening test in 12 months as intermediate risk
options.rationale: Under the NCSP, oncogenic HPV (not 16/18) with reflex LBC of LSIL is intermediate risk. Management is a repeat HPV test in 12 months. Most clear within that interval and avoid unnecessary colposcopy. (Source: National Cervical Screening Program Clinical Guidelines)
source_refs: National Cervical Screening Program Clinical Guidelines

options.text: Repeat cervical screening test in 5 years as standard low-risk recall
options.rationale: Routine 5-yearly recall applies only to HPV-negative results. Any positive HPV pulls the woman onto either the intermediate risk (12 month repeat) or higher risk (colposcopy) pathway. (Source: National Cervical Screening Program Clinical Guidelines)
source_refs: National Cervical Screening Program Clinical Guidelines

options.text: Refer for endometrial sampling and a pelvic ultrasound at this visit
options.rationale: Endometrial assessment is indicated for abnormal uterine bleeding or postmenopausal bleeding, not for cervical screening abnormalities. (Source: National Cervical Screening Program Clinical Guidelines)
source_refs: National Cervical Screening Program Clinical Guidelines

options.text: Prescribe topical imiquimod and recheck cytology in 6 months from now
options.rationale: Imiquimod is for external genital warts, not for cervical screening management. No topical or destructive therapy is indicated for LSIL detected on screening; it is followed by surveillance. (Source: National Cervical Screening Program Clinical Guidelines)
source_refs: National Cervical Screening Program Clinical Guidelines

explanation.summary: The Australian NCSP stratifies cervical screening results by HPV status: HPV negative returns to 5-year recall; oncogenic 16/18 goes directly to colposcopy; oncogenic non 16/18 with negative or LSIL cytology becomes intermediate risk and repeats HPV at 12 months; oncogenic non 16/18 with HSIL+ goes to colposcopy. Self-collected vaginal swabs are now accepted as primary screening for HPV detection across the eligible age range. Persistent HPV at the 12-month repeat or any HSIL upgrades to colposcopy.
key_points: Non 16/18 oncogenic HPV with LSIL is intermediate risk: repeat in 12 months
16/18 oncogenic HPV or HSIL on cytology: colposcopy regardless of subtype
HPV negative: return to 5-year recall
Self-collected vaginal swabs are accepted for primary HPV screening across the eligible age range
explanation.pearls: NCSP: 16/18 oncogenic HPV or HSIL cytology to colposcopy; non 16/18 oncogenic HPV with negative or LSIL cytology to repeat HPV at 12 months; HPV negative back to 5-year recall.

sources.label: National Cervical Screening Program Clinical Guidelines

stem:
A 24-year-old woman attends your general practice for advice about irregular periods and growing dark hair on her chin and lower abdomen over the past two years. Her periods come every 50 to 70 days. Her BMI is 28. She is not on contraception and is currently sexually active with a male partner.

Clinical examination confirms terminal hair on the chin, around the umbilicus, and on the lower back. There is no acanthosis nigricans. Pelvic ultrasound was performed last week; the report describes both ovaries containing more than 20 antral follicles 2 to 9 mm in diameter, with normal stromal volume.

data_table.Vital signs: within normal limits
data_table.Examination: modified Ferriman-Gallwey score 10, BMI 28 kg/m^2, no virilising features such as clitoromegaly or deepened voice
data_table.Investigations: fasting glucose 5.2 mmol/L (3.9 to 5.4); total testosterone 2.6 nmol/L (less than 2.0); SHBG 28 nmol/L; prolactin 280 mIU/L (less than 500); TSH 1.8 mIU/L; 17-hydroxyprogesterone within normal limits

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step in confirming the diagnosis?

options.text: Order serum DHEAS, androstenedione, and a 1 mg dexamethasone suppression test
options.rationale: Further androgen workup is reserved for severe or rapidly progressive hyperandrogenism, virilisation, or testosterone well above the female reference. Her testosterone is only mildly raised and CAH is already excluded. (Source: 2023 International Evidence Based Guideline for PCOS)
source_refs: 2023 International Evidence Based Guideline for PCOS

options.text: Repeat pelvic ultrasound in 3 months to confirm ovarian morphology
options.rationale: A single representative ultrasound consistent with PCOS morphology suffices. The threshold under the 2023 update is over 20 follicles per ovary on high-frequency transvaginal scanning. (Source: 2023 International Evidence Based Guideline for PCOS)
source_refs: 2023 International Evidence Based Guideline for PCOS

options.text: Diagnose PCOS and counsel on lifestyle plus long-term metabolic risk
options.rationale: She meets the Rotterdam criteria (2018 International PCOS Guideline endorsed by the NHMRC and Monash Centre for Health Research): two of three of oligo/anovulation, clinical or biochemical hyperandrogenism, and polycystic ovarian morphology. All three are present, and thyroid, prolactin, and CAH have been excluded. (Source: 2023 International Evidence Based Guideline for PCOS)
source_refs: 2023 International Evidence Based Guideline for PCOS

options.text: Request an MRI of the adrenals and ovaries to exclude an androgen-secreting tumour
options.rationale: Imaging for androgen-secreting tumours is indicated when testosterone is grossly elevated or virilisation is present. Neither applies here. (Source: 2023 International Evidence Based Guideline for PCOS)
source_refs: 2023 International Evidence Based Guideline for PCOS

options.text: Defer the diagnosis pending a 2-hour 75 g oral glucose tolerance test
options.rationale: OGTT is recommended after the diagnosis to screen for impaired glucose tolerance and type 2 diabetes, especially with raised BMI. It is part of follow-up workup, not a diagnostic criterion. (Source: 2023 International Evidence Based Guideline for PCOS)
source_refs: 2023 International Evidence Based Guideline for PCOS

explanation.summary: PCOS is diagnosed by the Rotterdam criteria: two of three of oligo/anovulation, clinical or biochemical hyperandrogenism, and polycystic ovarian morphology on ultrasound. The 2023 Australian-led International Evidence Based Guideline raised the follicle count threshold to over 20 per ovary on high-frequency transvaginal scans, reflecting modern imaging. Thyroid disease, hyperprolactinaemia, and non-classical congenital adrenal hyperplasia must be excluded first. After diagnosis, screen for impaired glucose tolerance with a 75 g OGTT and assess cardiovascular and endometrial risk.
key_points: Rotterdam: two of three of oligo/anovulation, hyperandrogenism, polycystic morphology
2023 morphology threshold: over 20 follicles per ovary on high-frequency transvaginal scan
Exclude thyroid disease, hyperprolactinaemia, and non-classical CAH before diagnosis
After diagnosis: OGTT for IGT/T2DM and endometrial risk assessment
explanation.pearls: PCOS by Rotterdam: two of three of oligo/anovulation, hyperandrogenism, polycystic morphology (over 20 follicles per ovary on high-frequency transvaginal scan). Exclude thyroid, prolactin, and CAH first; then OGTT for metabolic screening.

sources.label: 2023 International Evidence Based Guideline for PCOS

stem:
A 23-year-old woman attends with painful periods that have worsened over the past two years. The pain starts the day before her period, peaks on day 2, and stops her attending university for 1 to 2 days each cycle. She also has deep pain during intercourse. She has never been pregnant and is not currently planning pregnancy; she uses condoms for contraception.

General and pelvic examination are unremarkable. There is no adnexal tenderness on bimanual examination and no nodularity is felt on rectovaginal palpation. She has tried ibuprofen with limited effect. She has no contraindications to combined hormonal contraception (no smoking history, no migraine with aura, no thrombotic risk factors, normal blood pressure).

data_table.Vital signs: within normal limits
data_table.Examination: normal vulva and vagina, soft non-tender cervix, no adnexal mass, no rectovaginal nodularity
data_table.Investigations: transvaginal ultrasound: normal-sized anteverted uterus, no endometrioma, ovaries normal volume, no deep infiltrating lesions identified

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step?

options.text: Refer for diagnostic laparoscopy as the first management step
options.rationale: Laparoscopy is no longer required to label endometriosis-related pain. Empirical medical therapy is recommended first under RANZCOG and ESHRE; laparoscopy is reserved for treatment failure or suspected deep infiltrating disease. (Source: RANZCOG Endometriosis Guideline)

options.text: Trial a continuous combined oral contraceptive pill plus regular ibuprofen
options.rationale: RANZCOG and the European Society of Human Reproduction and Embryology endorse empirical medical therapy for suspected endometriosis-related pain when imaging is normal, particularly in younger women not seeking pregnancy. Continuous (skipping the placebo week) combined hormonal contraception is first-line. Diagnostic laparoscopy is reserved for failure of empirical treatment or features suggestive of deep disease. (Source: RANZCOG Endometriosis Guideline)

options.text: Commence a 3-month course of GnRH agonist with hormonal add-back therapy
options.rationale: GnRH agonists are second or third line after failure of combined hormonal contraception and progestogens. They have bone-density and menopausal-symptom trade-offs and need add-back therapy. (Source: RANZCOG Endometriosis Guideline)

options.text: Reassure her that primary dysmenorrhoea is benign and review in 12 months
options.rationale: Pain that stops her attending university and is associated with deep dyspareunia is not consistent with simple primary dysmenorrhoea. RANZCOG recommends active treatment. (Source: RANZCOG Endometriosis Guideline)

options.text: Order serum CA-125 to confirm or exclude an endometriosis diagnosis
options.rationale: CA-125 is non-specific and not used for diagnosis or exclusion. It may be elevated in endometriosis but also in many other conditions and is not part of the RANZCOG diagnostic pathway. (Source: RANZCOG Endometriosis Guideline)

explanation.summary: RANZCOG and ESHRE allow empirical medical management of suspected endometriosis without surgical confirmation, particularly for younger women not currently seeking pregnancy. Continuous combined hormonal contraception is the recommended first-line, with progestogen-only options (oral, depot, or LNG-IUS) as alternatives if combined contraception is contraindicated. NSAIDs are adjunctive. Laparoscopy is reserved for failure of medical therapy, features of deep infiltrating disease, or fertility-driven assessment. CA-125 is not part of the diagnostic pathway.
key_points: Empirical continuous combined hormonal contraception is first-line
Progestogen-only options if combined contraception is contraindicated
Laparoscopy for failure of medical therapy or suspected deep infiltrating disease
CA-125 is non-diagnostic; transvaginal ultrasound for endometriomas and DIE only
explanation.pearls: Suspected endometriosis-related pain in a young non-pregnancy-seeking woman: empirical continuous combined hormonal contraception plus NSAIDs first-line. Laparoscopy only after failed medical therapy or features of deep infiltrating disease.

stem:
A 62-year-old woman attends your practice with a single episode of light vaginal bleeding three days ago, the first since her menopause at age 53. She is otherwise well, takes no medication, has never used hormone replacement therapy, and is not on tamoxifen. Her BMI is 34 and she has type 2 diabetes managed with metformin.

On examination there is no obvious vulval or vaginal lesion, the cervix appears healthy, and bimanual examination is unremarkable. There is no active bleeding at the time of review. Cervical screening is up to date and negative.

data_table.Vital signs: within normal limits
data_table.Examination: atrophic vulva and vagina, healthy cervix, no adnexal mass, no rectovaginal nodularity
data_table.Investigations: transvaginal ultrasound: endometrial thickness 7 mm with irregular endomyometrial junction

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step?

options.text: Repeat the transvaginal ultrasound in 3 months for surveillance
options.rationale: Once the threshold is exceeded, the next step is tissue sampling, not surveillance imaging. Delay risks progression of an underlying neoplasm. (Source: RANZCOG Investigation of Postmenopausal Bleeding)

options.text: Reassure that one episode of bleeding does not require investigation
options.rationale: Any episode of postmenopausal bleeding warrants investigation under RANZCOG, regardless of volume or whether it recurs. Endometrial cancer can present with a single bleed. (Source: RANZCOG Investigation of Postmenopausal Bleeding)

options.text: Commence vaginal oestrogen for atrophy and review in 6 months
options.rationale: Vaginal oestrogen treats atrophic vaginitis but does not address the suspicious endometrial finding. Empirical treatment without sampling risks missing endometrial hyperplasia or carcinoma. (Source: RANZCOG Investigation of Postmenopausal Bleeding)

options.text: Refer for outpatient hysteroscopy with directed endometrial biopsy
options.rationale: Postmenopausal bleeding with endometrial thickness over 4 mm on transvaginal ultrasound exceeds the RANZCOG threshold to proceed to endometrial sampling. The combination of obesity, type 2 diabetes, and unopposed oestrogen exposure further raises endometrial cancer risk. Hysteroscopy with directed biopsy is the diagnostic standard. (Source: RANZCOG Investigation of Postmenopausal Bleeding)

options.text: Order an MRI pelvis to characterise the endometrium before any sampling
options.rationale: MRI is used to stage known endometrial cancer or assess myometrial invasion, not as a primary diagnostic test. Tissue sampling comes first. (Source: RANZCOG Investigation of Postmenopausal Bleeding)

explanation.summary: Any postmenopausal bleeding warrants investigation. Transvaginal ultrasound is the first-line test, with an endometrial thickness over 4 mm prompting endometrial sampling. Obesity, diabetes, polycystic ovary syndrome, tamoxifen use, unopposed oestrogen, and Lynch syndrome are major risk factors that lower the threshold for early biopsy. Hysteroscopy with directed biopsy is preferred over blind pipelle when focal lesions or polyps are suspected.
key_points: Any episode of postmenopausal bleeding needs investigation
TVUS endometrial thickness over 4 mm: proceed to endometrial sampling
Hysteroscopy with directed biopsy is preferred when focal pathology is suspected
Obesity, T2DM, unopposed oestrogen, and tamoxifen are major risk factors
explanation.pearls: Postmenopausal bleeding: TVUS first; endometrial thickness over 4 mm prompts hysteroscopy and biopsy. Obesity, T2DM, unopposed oestrogen, and tamoxifen lower the threshold.

sources.label: Cancer Council Australia Endometrial Cancer Statement

stem:
A 28-year-old G1P0 woman at 34+2 weeks is referred from her shared-care GP to the birthing unit with a 24-hour history of headache and visual flashing lights. Her booking blood pressure was 110/70 mmHg. On arrival now her readings are repeatedly elevated and she has hyperreflexia with three beats of ankle clonus.

Fetal CTG shows a normal baseline with reassuring variability and accelerations. Her urine dipstick is 3+ for protein and the spot urine protein-creatinine ratio is 84 mg/mmol (less than 30). She is for admission with senior obstetric and anaesthetic input. She has had no seizures and is GCS 15. The midwife asks what to commence first.

data_table.Vital signs: pulse 92 /min, blood pressure 168/112 mmHg, respiratory rate 18 /min, SpO2 98% on room air, temperature 36.8 degrees Celsius
data_table.Examination: hyperreflexia, three beats of clonus, headache with visual sparkles, no focal deficit
data_table.Investigations: platelets 142 x10^9/L (150 to 400); ALT 78 U/L (5 to 35); creatinine 88 micromol/L (45 to 90); urate 0.42 mmol/L; spot UPCR 84 mg/mmol; CTG reassuring

lead_in: What is the single best initial intervention?

options.text: Withhold magnesium given the borderline creatinine and observe closely
options.rationale: Renal impairment is not a contraindication to magnesium; it is a reason to adjust the maintenance infusion and monitor magnesium levels and reflexes more closely. Withholding seizure prophylaxis in this setting is not safe. (Source: SOMANZ Hypertension in Pregnancy Guidelines)

options.text: IV labetalol 20 mg bolus and proceed to delivery within 30 minutes
options.rationale: BP control with labetalol or hydralazine is essential but is concurrent with magnesium, and immediate delivery is not always required at 34+2 weeks with reassuring CTG. Steroid cover for fetal lung maturity and stabilisation precede delivery in this window. (Source: SOMANZ Hypertension in Pregnancy Guidelines)

options.text: IV phenytoin 15 mg/kg loading dose over 30 minutes for seizure prophylaxis
options.rationale: The Magpie trial established magnesium as superior to phenytoin and diazepam for eclampsia prevention. Phenytoin is no longer recommended for this indication. (Source: SOMANZ Hypertension in Pregnancy Guidelines)

options.text: Oral nifedipine 20 mg immediate release stat and review in one hour
options.rationale: Nifedipine is a valid BP-lowering option but does not prevent seizures and is not the single best initial intervention with this constellation of cerebral irritation features. (Source: SOMANZ Hypertension in Pregnancy Guidelines)

options.text: IV magnesium sulfate 4 g loading dose over 20 minutes, then 1 g per hour infusion
options.rationale: Severe pre-eclampsia with cerebral features (headache, visual disturbance, hyperreflexia, clonus) carries imminent eclampsia risk. The RANZCOG and SOMANZ standard is magnesium sulfate IV 4 g over 20 minutes then 1 g per hour for 24 hours, with reflex and respiratory rate monitoring. BP control with labetalol or hydralazine follows but seizure prophylaxis is the immediate priority. (Source: SOMANZ Hypertension in Pregnancy Guidelines)

explanation.summary: Severe pre-eclampsia is defined by SOMANZ as systolic BP at least 160 mmHg or diastolic at least 110 mmHg, or BP elevation plus end-organ involvement (cerebral features, pulmonary oedema, oliguria, raised transaminases, thrombocytopenia, raised creatinine, fetal compromise). Magnesium sulfate IV is the standard seizure prophylaxis (Magpie trial) and is given as a loading dose of 4 g over 20 minutes followed by 1 g per hour for at least 24 hours, with reflex, respiratory rate, and urine output monitoring. Antihypertensive therapy (IV labetalol or hydralazine, or oral immediate-release nifedipine) is concurrent. Delivery is the definitive treatment but stabilisation, magnesium, and antenatal corticosteroid cover (if under 35 weeks) precede it where possible.
key_points: Magnesium IV 4 g over 20 min then 1 g per hour for 24 hours is seizure prophylaxis
Magpie trial: magnesium is superior to phenytoin and diazepam for eclampsia prevention
Renal impairment requires dose adjustment and closer monitoring, not omission
BP control and delivery planning are concurrent priorities, not substitutes for magnesium
explanation.pearls: Severe pre-eclampsia with cerebral features: IV magnesium sulfate 4 g over 20 minutes then 1 g per hour for 24 hours. Concurrent BP control with labetalol or hydralazine; antenatal corticosteroids if under 35 weeks.

stem:
A 31-year-old G2P1 woman at 36+5 weeks attends antenatal clinic having been told at her routine appointment last week that the baby was breech. The previous delivery was an uncomplicated vaginal birth of a cephalic baby at 39 weeks. She has no significant past medical history and the current pregnancy has been uncomplicated.

Today's ultrasound confirms frank breech presentation with an estimated fetal weight on the 60th centile, normal liquor volume (deepest vertical pocket 5 cm), anterior placenta not low lying, and reassuring umbilical artery Doppler. The CTG performed on arrival is reassuring. There is no history of antepartum haemorrhage, no uterine scar, and she has not yet decided on her birth plan.

data_table.Vital signs: maternal vital signs within normal limits; fetal heart rate baseline 138 /min, reactive CTG
data_table.Examination: soft non-tender abdomen, fundal height 36 cm, breech palpable in the pelvis, fetal heart auscultated in upper quadrant
data_table.Investigations: ultrasound: frank breech, EFW 60th centile, DVP 5 cm, anterior placenta not low lying, UA Doppler normal

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step?

options.text: Refer for moxibustion at acupuncture points BL67 as the first intervention
options.rationale: Moxibustion has weak and inconsistent evidence; it is an adjunct rather than a first-line intervention under RANZCOG. ECV is the recommended primary offer. (Source: RANZCOG Management of Breech Presentation)

options.text: Book elective caesarean section at 39 weeks without offering ECV
options.rationale: Defaulting to caesarean section without offering ECV does not meet RANZCOG standards. ECV should be discussed as it can convert to cephalic presentation, allowing vaginal birth in many cases. (Source: RANZCOG Management of Breech Presentation)

options.text: Recommend immediate vaginal breech delivery planning given multiparity
options.rationale: Planned vaginal breech birth has higher perinatal morbidity than planned caesarean (Term Breech Trial); it is an option only after detailed risk counselling and in select cases with experienced operators. It is not the default in a multiparous woman without an attempt at ECV. (Source: RANZCOG Management of Breech Presentation)

options.text: Trial a knee-to-chest position three times daily and review in 2 weeks
options.rationale: Postural manoeuvres have not been shown to convert breech presentation in meta-analyses. They delay ECV during the optimal window. (Source: RANZCOG Management of Breech Presentation)

options.text: Offer external cephalic version at 37 weeks with tocolysis after counselling
options.rationale: RANZCOG recommends offering ECV from 36 weeks for nulliparous women and 37 weeks for multiparous women with breech presentation, reassuring fetal welfare, no contraindications, and normal liquor. Success rates are around 50% (higher in multiparous women with adequate liquor) and serious complications such as placental abruption are rare. Tocolysis with subcutaneous terbutaline improves success. (Source: RANZCOG Management of Breech Presentation)

explanation.summary: RANZCOG recommends offering external cephalic version from 36 weeks (nulliparous) or 37 weeks (multiparous) to women with breech presentation at term, with reassuring fetal status and no contraindications (significant antepartum haemorrhage, scarred uterus, oligohydramnios, abnormal CTG, multiple pregnancy after first twin). Tocolysis with subcutaneous terbutaline 250 micrograms improves success. Counselling covers success rates (around 50%, higher in multiparous women), the small risk of emergency caesarean for non-reassuring CTG or abruption, and the alternatives of planned vaginal breech or planned caesarean. Anti-D is given to RhD-negative women.
key_points: Offer ECV from 36 weeks (nulliparous) or 37 weeks (multiparous)
Success around 50%, higher in multiparous women with adequate liquor
Tocolysis with subcutaneous terbutaline 250 micrograms improves success
Give anti-D 625 IU to RhD-negative women after ECV
explanation.pearls: Term breech RANZCOG: offer ECV from 36 weeks (nulliparous) or 37 weeks (multiparous) with tocolysis (subcut terbutaline 250 micrograms). Success around 50%; anti-D 625 IU if RhD-negative.

stem:
A 27-year-old G2P1 woman at 28+4 weeks presents to the birthing unit with a sudden gush of clear fluid one hour ago, followed by ongoing leaking. There are no contractions, no per vaginal bleeding, and fetal movements are normal. Her previous pregnancy ended in spontaneous vaginal delivery at term.

Sterile speculum confirms pooling of clear fluid in the posterior fornix. Cervix appears closed; no digital examination is performed. Maternal observations and CTG are reassuring. Ultrasound shows oligohydramnios with a deepest vertical pocket of 1.8 cm; estimated fetal weight is on the 45th centile; the fetus is cephalic. There are no clinical features of chorioamnionitis (no fever, uterine tenderness, or offensive discharge).

data_table.Vital signs: pulse 88 /min, blood pressure 118/72 mmHg, respiratory rate 16 /min, SpO2 99% on room air, temperature 36.7 degrees Celsius
data_table.Examination: no contractions, soft non-tender uterus, sterile speculum shows pooling of clear amniotic fluid
data_table.Investigations: FBC WCC 9.8 x10^9/L (4 to 11); CRP 6 mg/L; high vaginal swab and urine culture sent; CTG reassuring; group B streptococcus status unknown

lead_in: What is the most appropriate initial management bundle?

options.text: Induce labour immediately with oxytocin to minimise infection risk
options.rationale: Active induction before 34 weeks in the absence of chorioamnionitis, fetal compromise, or other indication for delivery harms neonatal outcomes through prematurity. Expectant management with prophylactic antibiotics is the standard. (Source: RANZCOG PPROM Guideline)
source_refs: RANZCOG Preterm Prelabour Rupture of Membranes Guideline

options.text: Admit for IM betamethasone, oral erythromycin, and IV magnesium for neuroprotection
options.rationale: PPROM under 34 weeks without chorioamnionitis is managed expectantly with antenatal corticosteroids (IM betamethasone 11.4 mg, two doses 24 hours apart), prophylactic erythromycin for 10 days (or until delivery) to prolong latency, and magnesium sulfate for neuroprotection when delivery within 24 hours is anticipated or below 30 weeks. The ORACLE trial supports erythromycin over amoxicillin with clavulanic acid, which increased neonatal necrotising enterocolitis. (Source: RANZCOG Preterm Prelabour Rupture of Membranes Guideline)
source_refs: RANZCOG Preterm Prelabour Rupture of Membranes Guideline

options.text: Admit, give a single dose of dexamethasone, and start IV amoxicillin with clavulanic acid for 10 days
options.rationale: Amoxicillin with clavulanic acid is contraindicated for prophylaxis in PPROM by ORACLE because of increased neonatal necrotising enterocolitis. Two doses of corticosteroid are required, not one, to achieve the surfactant effect. (Source: RANZCOG PPROM Guideline)
source_refs: RANZCOG Preterm Prelabour Rupture of Membranes Guideline

options.text: Discharge home on oral metronidazole with daily fetal movement counting
options.rationale: PPROM warrants inpatient observation for chorioamnionitis, fetal welfare, and cord prolapse risk. Metronidazole is not the prophylactic agent of choice and outpatient management is not first-line under RANZCOG. (Source: RANZCOG PPROM Guideline)
source_refs: RANZCOG Preterm Prelabour Rupture of Membranes Guideline

options.text: Perform a digital cervical examination to plan timing of induction
options.rationale: Digital examination in PPROM increases infection risk and is avoided unless labour is established or imminent. Sterile speculum is sufficient for assessment. (Source: RANZCOG PPROM Guideline)
source_refs: RANZCOG Preterm Prelabour Rupture of Membranes Guideline

explanation.summary: Preterm prelabour rupture of membranes under 34 weeks without chorioamnionitis is managed expectantly. Admission allows monitoring for infection, abruption, and fetal compromise. Antenatal corticosteroids (IM betamethasone 11.4 mg, two doses 24 hours apart) accelerate fetal lung maturity. Prophylactic erythromycin 250 mg four times daily for 10 days (or until delivery) prolongs latency. Magnesium sulfate is given for neuroprotection if delivery is anticipated within 24 hours or below 30 weeks. Digital cervical examination is avoided to reduce infection risk.
key_points: Antenatal corticosteroids: two doses of IM betamethasone 11.4 mg 24 hours apart
Prophylactic erythromycin 250 mg four times daily for 10 days (ORACLE); amoxicillin with clavulanic acid contraindicated
Magnesium for neuroprotection if delivery anticipated within 24 hours or below 30 weeks
Avoid digital cervical examination; use sterile speculum
explanation.pearls: PPROM under 34 weeks without chorioamnionitis: betamethasone 11.4 mg x 2 doses 24 hours apart, erythromycin 250 mg qid for 10 days (NOT amoxicillin with clavulanic acid per ORACLE), magnesium for neuroprotection if delivery imminent or under 30 weeks. Avoid digital exam.

sources.label: RANZCOG Preterm Prelabour Rupture of Membranes Guideline

stem:
A 32-year-old primigravida is admitted to the birth suite at 34 plus 2 weeks gestation with a 24 hour history of a frontal headache and 'spots' in her vision. She has been monitored as an outpatient for proteinuria (1+) since 30 weeks. Her partner says she was confused for a few minutes at home but recovered before they arrived.

On examination she is alert and oriented now. Knee jerks are 3+ and symmetrical. The uterus is non-tender, the cervix is closed on speculum, and the cardiotocograph baseline is 140 with two accelerations and no decelerations over a 30 minute trace. Her partner reports she had a single self-limiting tonic-clonic seizure on the corridor as they walked into the assessment area, lasting 90 seconds. Maternal vital signs and bloods are below.

data_table.Vital signs: pulse rate 102, blood pressure 172/112, respiratory rate 18, SpO2 98 percent on room air, temperature 36.7 degrees, fetal heart rate 140
data_table.Investigations: platelets 88 x10^9/L (150-400), ALT 142 U/L (<40), creatinine 96 micromol/L (45-90), urine protein:creatinine 320 mg/mmol (<30), lactate dehydrogenase 612 U/L, haptoglobin within normal limits, urate 0.42 mmol/L

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step?

options.text: Immediate caesarean section without antiseizure prophylaxis on the basis that delivery is the definitive cure for eclampsia
options.rationale: Delivery is definitive but maternal stabilisation with MgSO4 and antihypertensive control precedes operative birth to reduce maternal stroke and recurrent seizure risk. Operating on an unstable patient increases morbidity. (Source: SOMANZ Hypertension in Pregnancy)

options.text: Intravenous diazepam 10 mg bolus and intravenous phenytoin loading at 18 mg/kg, with antihypertensive therapy afterward
options.rationale: Diazepam and phenytoin are inferior to MgSO4 in eclampsia (Collaborative Eclampsia Trial showed 50 percent fewer recurrent seizures with MgSO4 than phenytoin and 67 percent fewer than diazepam). Australian guidelines specify MgSO4 first line. (Source: SOMANZ Hypertension in Pregnancy)

options.text: Magnesium sulfate 4 g intravenously over 20 minutes then 1 g/hour, with labetalol to target blood pressure under 160/110
options.rationale: After an eclamptic seizure (single tonic-clonic seizure with documented severe pre-eclampsia), MgSO4 4 g IV over 20 minutes then 1 g/hour for 24 hours is the Australian standard alongside antihypertensive control targeting under 160/110 (labetalol 20 to 40 mg IV bolus, repeatable). MgSO4 reduces recurrent eclampsia by 50 percent versus placebo. (Source: SOMANZ Hypertension in Pregnancy)
