options.text: Intravenous hydralazine 5 mg bolus every 20 minutes targeting blood pressure under 130/80 without antiseizure prophylaxis
options.rationale: Target blood pressure in severe pre-eclampsia is under 160/110 (not under 130/80), and antiseizure prophylaxis with MgSO4 is mandatory after an eclamptic seizure. Over-rapid blood pressure lowering risks placental hypoperfusion. (Source: SOMANZ Hypertension in Pregnancy)

options.text: Commence intramuscular betamethasone 11.4 mg and admit for outpatient blood pressure and proteinuria surveillance
options.rationale: Although antenatal corticosteroids are given at 34+2 if delivery is anticipated within seven days, they do not address the immediate need for MgSO4, blood pressure control, and planning for delivery. Outpatient surveillance is unsafe after an eclamptic seizure. (Source: SOMANZ Hypertension in Pregnancy)

explanation.summary: Eclampsia is defined as a generalised seizure on a background of pre-eclampsia. Immediate priorities are maternal airway and stabilisation, MgSO4 loading 4 g IV over 20 minutes then 1 g/hour for 24 hours, blood pressure control to less than 160/110 with labetalol or hydralazine, and planning urgent delivery once stable. MgSO4 also reduces severe maternal morbidity (placental abruption, ICU admission) by around 25 percent in severe pre-eclampsia without seizures.
key_points: MgSO4 first line for eclampsia (loading 4 g IV over 20 min, then 1 g/hour for 24 hours)
Target BP < 160/110 with labetalol 20 to 40 mg IV bolus repeatable, or hydralazine 5 mg IV bolus
Monitor Mg toxicity: respiratory rate, deep tendon reflexes, urine output - reverse with calcium gluconate 1 g IV
MgSO4 also indicated in severe pre-eclampsia without seizure to prevent eclampsia
Delivery is definitive but maternal stabilisation precedes operative birth
explanation.pearls: MgSO4 toxicity manifests at serum magnesium 3.5 mmol/L (loss of patellar reflex), 5 mmol/L (respiratory depression), and 6 mmol/L (cardiac arrest) - reverse with 10 mL of 10 percent calcium gluconate IV over 10 minutes.

stem:
A 33-year-old G3P2 woman has just delivered a 3.9 kg baby by spontaneous vaginal birth at 40 plus 3 weeks after a four hour active second stage. She received active third stage management with 10 units intramuscular oxytocin. The placenta delivered complete at 12 minutes. Twenty minutes after delivery she has soaked through two large pads with fresh red blood and a third is in progress. The midwife has called for help and started bimanual uterine massage.

On examination the uterus is large and soft despite massage. There is no perineal or vaginal wall tear on inspection, the cervix appears intact, and the placenta is confirmed complete. Two 16 gauge cannulas are in. Her booking blood pressure was 132/86 and antenatal blood pressure has remained around 135/85 throughout pregnancy. She has no asthma. Vital signs are below.

data_table.Vital signs: pulse rate 116, blood pressure 102/64, respiratory rate 20, SpO2 99 percent on room air, temperature 36.6 degrees
data_table.Investigations: estimated blood loss 1100 mL and ongoing, haemoglobin pre-delivery 124 g/L, group and screen on file, fibrinogen pending

lead_in: After ongoing uterine massage and an infusion of oxytocin 40 units in 1 L normal saline, which is the most appropriate next pharmacological step?

options.text: Intramuscular carboprost (15-methyl PGF2 alpha) 250 micrograms with intravenous tranexamic acid 1 g over 10 minutes
options.rationale: Carboprost is the third line uterotonic after oxytocin and ergometrine. Skipping ergometrine misses a safe, cheap, first-after-oxytocin step in a woman with no contraindication to ergot agents. (Source: RANZCOG Postpartum Haemorrhage)

options.text: Intramuscular ergometrine 250 micrograms with concurrent intravenous tranexamic acid 1 g over 10 minutes
options.rationale: After oxytocin infusion, the next uterotonic in the Australian PPH algorithm is ergometrine 250 micrograms IM or 250 micrograms slow IV (avoid in hypertension, severe cardiac disease, or pre-eclampsia). Tranexamic acid 1 g IV within three hours of birth (WOMAN trial) reduces death from bleeding by around one third and is given concurrently. (Source: RANZCOG Postpartum Haemorrhage)

options.text: Sublingual misoprostol 800 micrograms with intravenous calcium gluconate 1 g over 10 minutes for tone augmentation
options.rationale: Misoprostol is reserved for settings without injectable uterotonics or as adjunct after first and second line agents have failed. Calcium gluconate is not a uterotonic. (Source: RANZCOG Postpartum Haemorrhage)

options.text: Intravenous oxytocin further bolus of 10 units repeated every five minutes until uterine tone is restored
options.rationale: Bolus oxytocin in this dose can cause hypotension and is not the recommended escalation; the algorithm moves to ergometrine after the oxytocin infusion is established. (Source: RANZCOG Postpartum Haemorrhage)

options.text: Intramuscular carboprost 250 micrograms with concurrent insertion of an intrauterine Bakri balloon for tamponade
options.rationale: Balloon tamponade is an option after pharmacological measures fail, not before ergometrine has been trialled. Carboprost is similarly third line. (Source: RANZCOG Postpartum Haemorrhage)

explanation.summary: Primary postpartum haemorrhage (PPH) is blood loss of 500 mL or more in the first 24 hours after birth, or any blood loss causing haemodynamic compromise. The 'four Ts' (tone, trauma, tissue, thrombin) frame the workup. The Australian uterotonic ladder is oxytocin infusion, then ergometrine 250 micrograms IM (or carbetocin 100 micrograms IV in caesarean), then carboprost 250 micrograms IM up to eight doses, then misoprostol 800 micrograms PR or SL. Tranexamic acid 1 g IV is given concurrently if within three hours of birth. Mechanical (bimanual compression, balloon tamponade) and surgical (B-Lynch, uterine artery ligation, hysterectomy) measures follow.
key_points: Oxytocin infusion 40 units in 1 L over 4 hours after the initial 10 units IM
Ergometrine 250 micrograms IM (contraindicated in hypertension, pre-eclampsia)
Carboprost 250 micrograms IM, repeat up to 8 doses (contraindicated in asthma)
Tranexamic acid 1 g IV within 3 hours of birth (WOMAN trial)
Mechanical: bimanual compression, intrauterine balloon tamponade; surgical: B-Lynch, internal iliac ligation, hysterectomy
explanation.pearls: WOMAN trial: tranexamic acid 1 g IV within 3 hours of birth reduces death due to bleeding by 31 percent (number needed to treat about 250); after 3 hours there is no mortality benefit and possible harm from clot stabilisation.

stem:
A 36-year-old G2P1 woman of South Asian background is reviewed at the joint obstetric-endocrine clinic at 30 weeks gestation. She was diagnosed with gestational diabetes at 26 weeks on a positive 75 g OGTT. She has completed two weeks of structured dietitian-led carbohydrate counselling and 30 minutes of post-meal walking. She is monitoring fasting and one hour post-meal capillary blood glucose four times per day.

Her body mass index pre-pregnancy was 27.6 kg/m^2. Fetal growth ultrasound at 28 weeks showed abdominal circumference on the 78th centile and estimated fetal weight on the 72nd centile. There has been no maternal hypoglycaemia. She has no proteinuria, normal blood pressure, and no obstetric or medical contraindications to oral therapy or insulin. The seven-day capillary record is summarised below.

data_table.Investigations: fasting glucose 24 of 28 readings above 5.0 mmol/L (range 4.9 to 6.4), one hour post-meal glucose 18 of 63 readings above 7.4 mmol/L (range 5.6 to 8.8), HbA1c at diagnosis 5.4 percent, no ketonuria, urine albumin:creatinine ratio normal

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step?

options.text: Continue lifestyle and dietary measures alone with reassessment of capillary blood glucose readings in two weeks
options.rationale: ADIPS thresholds are exceeded persistently (fasting target less than 5.0, one hour post-meal less than 7.4); ongoing reliance on diet and exercise risks fetal macrosomia, polyhydramnios, and neonatal hypoglycaemia. (Source: ADIPS GDM Guidelines)

options.text: Commence rapid acting insulin aspart 4 units subcutaneously before each main meal only without basal coverage
options.rationale: Prandial insulin alone targets post-meal glucose; here the dominant abnormality is fasting hyperglycaemia, which needs basal insulin. Prandial may be added later if post-meal targets are not met. (Source: ADIPS GDM Guidelines)

options.text: Commence metformin 500 mg twice daily with a stop date if fetal growth accelerates beyond the 95th centile on scan
options.rationale: Metformin is acceptable second line or where insulin is declined; ADIPS and RANZCOG prefer insulin because of better fasting glycaemic control and the long term neonatal safety data. Metformin crosses the placenta and ongoing offspring data are accumulating. (Source: ADIPS GDM Guidelines)

options.text: Commence basal insulin (isophane or detemir) 0.1 to 0.2 units/kg subcutaneously at bedtime and titrate to fasting target
options.rationale: Fasting hyperglycaemia (most readings above 5.0 over two weeks of lifestyle optimisation) is best treated with basal insulin starting at 0.1 to 0.2 units/kg at bedtime and titrating to a fasting target of less than 5.0 mmol/L. ADIPS supports insulin as first line pharmacotherapy in GDM. (Source: ADIPS GDM Guidelines)

options.text: Commence glibenclamide 2.5 mg orally daily and continue dietetic review monthly for the remainder of pregnancy
options.rationale: Sulfonylureas are not Australian first line for GDM; glibenclamide crosses the placenta and increases neonatal hypoglycaemia compared with insulin. (Source: ADIPS GDM Guidelines)

explanation.summary: Australian Diabetes in Pregnancy Society (ADIPS) thresholds for self-monitoring are fasting less than 5.0 mmol/L and one or two hour post-meal less than 7.4 or 6.7 mmol/L respectively. After two weeks of dietary and exercise optimisation, persistent above-target readings warrant pharmacotherapy. Insulin remains first line: basal (NPH or detemir) at bedtime for fasting hyperglycaemia, rapid acting (aspart) pre-meal for post-meal hyperglycaemia, doses titrated every three days. Metformin is acceptable second line. Targets reduce macrosomia, polyhydramnios, neonatal hypoglycaemia, and shoulder dystocia.
key_points: ADIPS targets: fasting < 5.0; 1 hour post-meal < 7.4; 2 hour post-meal < 6.7 mmol/L
Insulin is first line; basal for fasting hyperglycaemia, prandial for post-meal
Starting dose basal insulin 0.1 to 0.2 units/kg at bedtime
Metformin acceptable second line if insulin declined
All GDM women should have 75 g OGTT 6 to 12 weeks postpartum
explanation.pearls: Pre-pregnancy BMI above 35 plus persistent fasting glucose above 5.0 on diet doubles the chance of needing insulin during pregnancy; start basal insulin without waiting for the four-week food diary trial.

stem:
A 34-year-old woman attends general practice asking to restart the combined oral contraceptive pill after a four year gap. She is otherwise well, a non-smoker, with a body mass index of 24.6 kg/m^2 and no personal history of venous thromboembolism. Her mother had a deep vein thrombosis at age 58 following an orthopaedic operation but no younger relatives are affected.

She has migraine with aura twice a year (visual scintillations followed by unilateral throbbing headache) which respond to oral sumatriptan. Her last episode was six weeks ago. Blood pressure is 122/78. She has had three normal cervical screening test results and no abnormal bleeding. She does not want a long-acting reversible contraceptive method and has not had children.

data_table.Investigations: haemoglobin 134 g/L, thyroid function within normal limits, urine pregnancy test negative, blood pressure repeated 122/78

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step?

options.text: Commence a 30 microgram levonorgestrel combined oral contraceptive pill from day one of her next menstrual period
options.rationale: Migraine with aura at any age is a UKMEC and WHO MEC category 4 (unacceptable risk) for combined hormonal contraception because of the doubled ischaemic stroke risk; absolute risk is small but synergistic with oestrogen. (Source: Family Planning Australia: Contraception)

options.text: Refer for full thrombophilia screening before deciding on a combined hormonal method or a progestogen-only method
options.rationale: Routine thrombophilia screening is not recommended before contraceptive prescribing because of low yield and management does not change in the absence of a personal VTE history. Migraine with aura already excludes the combined pill. (Source: Family Planning Australia: Contraception)

options.text: Commence the combined vaginal ring on the basis that lower systemic oestrogen exposure is safe in migraine with aura
options.rationale: All combined hormonal contraceptives (pill, patch, ring) share the migraine-with-aura contraindication regardless of the route, because systemic oestrogen exposure is the relevant exposure. (Source: Family Planning Australia: Contraception)

options.text: Continue with a combined oral contraceptive but advise her to stop immediately if she has another migraine with aura
options.rationale: Migraine with aura is a baseline contraindication to combined hormonal contraception; she should not be commenced on it with a conditional plan to stop. The risk is established before any further events. (Source: Family Planning Australia: Contraception)

options.text: Commence the progestogen-only desogestrel pill 75 micrograms daily or recommend depot medroxyprogesterone instead
options.rationale: Progestogen-only methods (desogestrel pill, depot medroxyprogesterone) and intrauterine devices (copper or levonorgestrel) are UKMEC category 1 or 2 in migraine with aura. The progestogen-only pill is a reasonable starting point given her preference against LARC. (Source: Family Planning Australia: Contraception)

explanation.summary: The UK Medical Eligibility Criteria (UKMEC, used in Australia by Family Planning) classify contraceptive options against medical conditions on a 1 (no restriction) to 4 (unacceptable risk) scale. Migraine with aura is category 4 for combined hormonal contraception (any route) at any age due to roughly doubled ischaemic stroke risk. Progestogen-only methods, copper IUD, and levonorgestrel IUD are category 1 or 2. Hypertension above 140/90 controlled, BMI 30 to 34, and age 35 or older with light smoking are commonly missed UKMEC restrictions.
key_points: Migraine with aura: UKMEC 4 for any combined hormonal contraception
Migraine without aura: UKMEC 2 for initiation, UKMEC 3 for continuation
BP 140 to 159/90 to 99: UKMEC 3 for CHC; BP > 160/100: UKMEC 4
Smoking > 15 per day plus age 35 or older: UKMEC 4 for CHC
All progestogen-only methods, copper IUD, and LNG-IUD are UKMEC 1 or 2 in migraine with aura
explanation.pearls: After 6 weeks postpartum a woman who has never had migraine with aura before pregnancy who develops aura on the combined pill should switch to a progestogen-only or non-hormonal method - the new aura raises ischaemic stroke risk to UKMEC 4 level.

sources.label: UK Medical Eligibility Criteria for Contraceptive Use

stem:
A 28-year-old G3P2 woman presents to the maternity assessment unit at 32 weeks gestation with a sudden 200 mL fresh bright red vaginal bleed at home that has now slowed. She is not in pain. Her two previous births were both caesareans for breech and arrest. She has had no abdominal trauma. Her partner reports that she was hanging washing when the bleed started.

On examination she is alert and pink. The uterus is soft and non-tender to palpation. She has not had a speculum examination in this unit yet. The mid-trimester morphology scan (booking the dates the booking ultrasound recorded at 20 weeks) reported a low-lying anterior placenta with a placental edge covering the internal os; a follow-up scan has not yet been performed. Vital signs are below.

data_table.Vital signs: pulse rate 96, blood pressure 118/72, respiratory rate 16, SpO2 99 percent on room air, temperature 36.7 degrees, fetal heart rate 142 on intermittent Doppler
data_table.Investigations: haemoglobin 112 g/L, group and antibody screen on file (group O Rh negative, antibody negative), repeat group and screen and crossmatch 4 units sent

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step?

options.text: Arrange urgent transvaginal ultrasound to localise the placenta, admit, give betamethasone 11.4 mg, and give anti-D 625 IU
options.rationale: Transvaginal ultrasound is the gold standard for placental localisation and is safer than digital examination in praevia. Admission, antenatal corticosteroids at 32 weeks (and again as part of a planned LSCS by 36 to 37 weeks), and anti-D prophylaxis in this Rh negative woman complete the package. (Source: RANZCOG Placenta Praevia and Placenta Accreta)
source_refs: RANZCOG Placenta Praevia and Placenta Accreta

options.text: Digital cervical examination in the assessment room to determine cervical dilatation and station before any imaging
options.rationale: Digital cervical examination is contraindicated in suspected placenta praevia because of the risk of catastrophic haemorrhage. Imaging precedes examination. (Source: RANZCOG Placenta Praevia and Placenta Accreta)
source_refs: RANZCOG Placenta Praevia and Placenta Accreta

options.text: Discharge home with weekly outpatient cardiotocography after the bleeding settles and plan vaginal birth at full term
options.rationale: A sentinel bleed in suspected placenta praevia requires inpatient admission. Vaginal birth is contraindicated when the placenta covers the internal os and elective caesarean is planned 36+0 to 37+0 weeks. (Source: RANZCOG Placenta Praevia and Placenta Accreta)
source_refs: RANZCOG Placenta Praevia and Placenta Accreta

options.text: Proceed directly to category 1 caesarean section without imaging because of the painless fresh red vaginal bleeding
options.rationale: Maternal haemodynamic stability and a reassuring fetal heart trace allow time for imaging and corticosteroids. Category 1 caesarean is reserved for unstable mother or non-reassuring fetal status. (Source: RANZCOG Placenta Praevia and Placenta Accreta)
source_refs: RANZCOG Placenta Praevia and Placenta Accreta

options.text: Insert a cervical tamponade balloon to reduce ongoing bleeding before further imaging or specialist obstetric review
options.rationale: Cervical balloon tamponade has no antepartum role in praevia; it is reserved for postpartum haemorrhage. Antepartum management is imaging, admission, steroids, anti-D, and planned LSCS. (Source: RANZCOG Placenta Praevia and Placenta Accreta)
source_refs: RANZCOG Placenta Praevia and Placenta Accreta

explanation.summary: Painless fresh bright red bleeding with a soft non-tender uterus suggests placenta praevia, whereas constant pain, a hard tender uterus, and concealed bleeding suggest placental abruption. The two often coexist after vaginal manipulation, so digital examination is contraindicated until ultrasound has excluded praevia. Management of sentinel bleeds in known or suspected praevia involves admission, antenatal corticosteroids if before 34+6 weeks (and consideration of magnesium sulfate for neuroprotection under 30 weeks), and anti-D in Rh negative women. Elective caesarean is planned at 36+0 to 37+0 weeks unless bleeding forces earlier delivery.
key_points: Painless bright red bleeding plus soft uterus suggests praevia; painful tender uterus suggests abruption
Digital cervical examination is contraindicated until praevia excluded
Transvaginal ultrasound is safer and more accurate than transabdominal for placental localisation
Antenatal corticosteroids 24+0 to 34+6 weeks if delivery within 7 days is anticipated
Anti-D 625 IU IM in Rh negative women after any antepartum bleed (and any indicated post-event)
explanation.pearls: Two or more previous caesarean sections plus an anterior praevia raises placenta accreta spectrum risk above 40 percent - request MRI of the lower segment and plan delivery in a centre with interventional radiology and massive transfusion support.

sources.label: RANZCOG Placenta Praevia and Placenta Accreta

stem:
A 30-year-old G3P0+2 woman attends a high risk antenatal clinic at 18 weeks gestation. Her two previous pregnancies ended at 21 and 23 weeks with painless cervical dilatation and bulging membranes followed by spontaneous preterm birth and neonatal death. There is no history of cervical surgery or LLETZ. The current dating ultrasound was concordant with menstrual dates.

On examination the abdomen is soft and there is no contraction. A transvaginal ultrasound today shows a singleton with normal anatomy and a cervical length of 18 mm with funnelling at the internal os. There are no signs of intra-amniotic infection: she is afebrile, the maternal CRP is 4 mg/L, white cells 9.2 x10^9/L, and there is no discharge. The vaginal swab and urine culture are negative.

data_table.Investigations: cervical length 18 mm, funnelling at internal os, fetus appropriate for dates with normal anatomy, no membrane prolapse, CRP 4 mg/L (<5), white cells 9.2 x10^9/L

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step?

options.text: Perform an emergency rescue cervical cerclage today even though the membranes are not prolapsed and cervix is closed
options.rationale: Rescue cerclage is reserved for dilated cervix with prolapsing membranes (physical examination indicated). With closed cervix and short ultrasound length, ultrasound-indicated (not rescue) cerclage is appropriate. (Source: RANZCOG Cervical Insufficiency)

options.text: Insert an Arabin cervical pessary and avoid surgical cerclage to minimise procedural and anaesthetic risk for her
options.rationale: Arabin pessary trials (PECEP, ProTWIN) have not consistently reduced preterm birth and Australian practice favours cerclage with this history. Pessary is a second line option when cerclage is contraindicated or declined. (Source: RANZCOG Cervical Insufficiency)

options.text: Commence weekly intramuscular 17 hydroxyprogesterone caproate as monotherapy in the second and third trimester
options.rationale: Subsequent trials (PROLONG) failed to replicate the benefit of weekly intramuscular 17 OH-progesterone, and Australian guidance now prefers vaginal progesterone for short cervix. (Source: RANZCOG Cervical Insufficiency)

options.text: Recommend strict bed rest in hospital until 34 weeks gestation without procedural intervention or progesterone
options.rationale: Bed rest does not reduce preterm birth and increases venous thromboembolism and deconditioning risk. It is not standard care for cervical insufficiency. (Source: RANZCOG Cervical Insufficiency)

options.text: Schedule an ultrasound indicated transvaginal cervical cerclage and continue vaginal progesterone 200 mg nightly
options.rationale: Two or more prior second trimester losses with painless cervical dilatation, current short cervix under 25 mm before 24 weeks, and no infection signs is a textbook indication for ultrasound-indicated cervical cerclage. Vaginal progesterone is added because the cervix is shorter than 25 mm. (Source: RANZCOG Cervical Insufficiency)

explanation.summary: Cervical insufficiency presents as painless cervical dilatation and second trimester loss. Three cerclage indications exist: history-indicated (three or more prior second trimester losses, place at 12 to 14 weeks), ultrasound-indicated (one or more prior preterm birth plus cervical length under 25 mm before 24 weeks), and physical examination-indicated (rescue) when membranes prolapse. Vaginal progesterone reduces preterm birth in women with cervical length under 25 mm regardless of history. Active intra-amniotic infection, vaginal bleeding, ruptured membranes, and active labour contraindicate cerclage.
key_points: History-indicated cerclage at 12 to 14 weeks for 3 or more prior second trimester losses
Ultrasound-indicated cerclage for prior preterm birth plus cervical length < 25 mm before 24 weeks
Rescue cerclage for dilated cervix with prolapsing membranes
Vaginal progesterone 200 mg nightly for short cervix (< 25 mm)
Remove cerclage at 36 to 37 weeks or earlier if labour, rupture of membranes, or chorioamnionitis
explanation.pearls: Ultrasound-indicated cerclage halves the preterm birth rate (number needed to treat about 8) in singleton pregnancies with prior preterm birth and cervical length under 25 mm - the benefit is lost in twin pregnancies.

stem:
A 31-year-old G2P1 woman with an in-vitro fertilisation singleton pregnancy reaches 35 plus 4 weeks gestation. Her morphology scan reported a velamentous cord insertion with a bilobed placenta, and a third trimester scan at 32 weeks confirmed a vessel running across the internal cervical os without supporting placental tissue. She has been admitted at 34 weeks for surveillance and completed a course of antenatal corticosteroids.

This afternoon she has a brisk fresh red vaginal bleed of about 100 mL after her membranes ruptured spontaneously. The midwife describes the liquor as port-wine coloured. She has no abdominal pain and the uterus is soft. Cardiotocography shows a baseline of 110 falling to 90 with a sinusoidal pattern over the past four minutes. Her vital signs are stable.

data_table.Vital signs: pulse rate 92, blood pressure 122/76, respiratory rate 18, SpO2 99 percent on room air, temperature 36.8 degrees, fetal heart rate 110 with sinusoidal pattern
data_table.Investigations: maternal full blood count and coagulation within normal limits, group and screen on file, Apt test of vaginal blood positive for fetal haemoglobin

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step?

options.text: Augment labour with intravenous oxytocin aiming for vaginal birth given the gestation of 35 plus 4 weeks today
options.rationale: Augmentation accelerates fetal blood loss through the torn vasa praevia and is contraindicated. Vasa praevia is an absolute indication for caesarean. (Source: RANZCOG Antepartum Haemorrhage)

options.text: Immediate category 1 caesarean section with the neonatal resuscitation team and uncrossmatched O negative blood ready
options.rationale: Confirmed vasa praevia with rupture of membranes producing port-wine vaginal blood, a positive Apt test (fetal haemoglobin), and a sinusoidal CTG indicates fetal exsanguination from a torn velamentous vessel. Category 1 caesarean is the only intervention that prevents fetal death; antenatal diagnosis converts mortality from 60 percent to under 5 percent. (Source: RANZCOG Antepartum Haemorrhage)

options.text: Insert an intrauterine pressure catheter and observe with continuous cardiotocography over the next sixty minutes
options.rationale: Sinusoidal cardiotocography indicates established fetal anaemia and ongoing observation risks fetal death. Definitive delivery is the only treatment. (Source: RANZCOG Antepartum Haemorrhage)

options.text: Administer maternal intravenous tranexamic acid 1 g and reassess the fetal heart trace in fifteen minutes' time
options.rationale: Tranexamic acid does not address fetal vessel rupture and delays definitive delivery. The bleeding is fetal in origin, not maternal. (Source: RANZCOG Antepartum Haemorrhage)

options.text: Repeat the Apt test on vaginal blood in 15 minutes and proceed to caesarean only if it is positive a second time
options.rationale: The Apt test is already positive and the CTG is sinusoidal; further confirmation wastes time when fetal exsanguination is occurring. Caesarean must proceed immediately. (Source: RANZCOG Antepartum Haemorrhage)

explanation.summary: Vasa praevia is the presence of fetal vessels within the membranes overlying the internal os, usually from velamentous cord insertion or accessory placental lobes. Antenatal diagnosis (by colour Doppler transvaginal ultrasound) allows planned caesarean at 34 to 36 weeks and converts mortality from 60 to 90 percent (undiagnosed, rupture of membranes setting) to under 5 percent. Risk factors include IVF pregnancies, low-lying or bilobed placentas, velamentous insertion, and multiple pregnancy. The Apt test distinguishes fetal from maternal blood at the bedside (fetal haemoglobin is alkali-resistant).
key_points: Antenatal diagnosis converts mortality from > 60 percent to under 5 percent
Risk factors: IVF, low-lying placenta, velamentous cord, bilobed/succenturiate placenta
Plan elective LSCS at 34 to 36 weeks after antenatal corticosteroids
Sinusoidal CTG plus port-wine vaginal blood after rupture of membranes is fetal exsanguination
Apt test (alkali denaturation) at the bedside distinguishes fetal from maternal blood
explanation.pearls: Vasa praevia type 1 follows velamentous cord insertion within the lower segment; type 2 connects two placental lobes; both warrant planned 34 to 36 week LSCS after corticosteroids.

subtopic_detail: Selective fetal growth restriction in MCDA twins
stem:
A 27-year-old G2P1 woman with a monochorionic diamniotic (MCDA) twin pregnancy is reviewed at the maternal fetal medicine clinic at 26 plus 5 weeks. Both twins were grown concordantly at the 18 week scan. The 24 week scan showed an estimated fetal weight discordance of 22 percent. Today's scan shows further discordance.

Twin A is appropriately grown on the 35th centile with normal umbilical artery Doppler. Twin B is on the 4th centile with an intermittent absent end-diastolic flow pattern in the umbilical artery that cycles between forward, absent, and reversed (positive then negative then positive) every several minutes when watched for 15 minutes. The middle cerebral artery peak systolic velocity is within normal limits in both twins. Amniotic fluid volumes are normal in both sacs. Maternal blood pressure is normal and there is no proteinuria.

data_table.Investigations: twin A estimated fetal weight 35th centile, umbilical artery PI within normal limits; twin B estimated fetal weight 4th centile, intermittent absent and reversed end-diastolic flow (Gratacos type III); middle cerebral artery peak systolic velocities within normal limits in both; amniotic fluid normal in both sacs; no anatomical anomalies

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step?

options.text: Plan elective caesarean section at 36 weeks after antenatal corticosteroids and weekly outpatient surveillance
options.rationale: Gratacos type III selective IUGR carries an unpredictable risk of sudden fetal death of twin B (around 15 percent) and 20 percent neurological injury in twin A from acute fetofetal transfusion at the moment of death. Awaiting 36 weeks is unsafe. (Source: ISUOG Multiple Pregnancy)

options.text: Refer to a tertiary maternal fetal medicine unit for fetoscopic laser ablation or selective bipolar cord occlusion
options.rationale: Gratacos type III selective IUGR (intermittent absent/reversed end-diastolic flow) reflects a single large arterio-arterial anastomosis; spontaneous demise of twin B carries around 20 percent risk of neurological injury to twin A from acute hypotension across the anastomosis. Tertiary fetoscopic dichorionisation by laser ablation or selective reduction by bipolar cord occlusion are the recognised options. (Source: ISUOG Multiple Pregnancy)

options.text: Administer maternal oral sildenafil to augment placental perfusion in the growth restricted twin from this week
options.rationale: The STRIDER trial of maternal sildenafil for severe early onset IUGR was halted because of neonatal pulmonary hypertension and excess deaths. Sildenafil is not recommended. (Source: ISUOG Multiple Pregnancy)

options.text: Commence weekly outpatient cardiotocography and repeat umbilical artery Doppler assessment again in two weeks
options.rationale: Weekly intermittent surveillance is inadequate for the unpredictable cycling Doppler pattern of Gratacos type III, which can precede acute demise within days. Inpatient or tertiary referral is needed. (Source: ISUOG Multiple Pregnancy)

options.text: Deliver both twins by emergency caesarean section today at 26 plus 5 weeks regardless of viability considerations
options.rationale: Pre-viable iatrogenic preterm delivery to rescue twin B sacrifices both twins to extreme prematurity (around 35 percent mortality at 26 weeks and high major morbidity). Tertiary intervention to dichorionise the placentae is preferred. (Source: ISUOG Multiple Pregnancy)

explanation.summary: Selective fetal growth restriction (sFGR) in MCDA twins is classified by umbilical artery Doppler in the growth restricted twin: type I (positive end-diastolic flow), type II (persistent absent or reversed end-diastolic flow), and type III (intermittent absent or reversed end-diastolic flow). Type III is the highest risk because of unpredictable sudden death of twin B and around 20 percent risk of neurological injury to the larger co-twin from acute exsanguination across a single large arterio-arterial anastomosis. Tertiary management options include fetoscopic laser dichorionisation or selective bipolar cord occlusion; both convert MCDA to a functional dichorionic pregnancy at the placental level.
key_points: Gratacos classification of sFGR in MCDA twins (type I, II, III)
Type III intermittent absent/reversed UA EDF: 15 percent demise risk, 20 percent neuro injury risk in co-twin
Tertiary options: fetoscopic laser ablation, selective bipolar cord occlusion
Maternal sildenafil contraindicated (STRIDER trial harm signal)
Pre-viable iatrogenic delivery causes worse outcomes than expectant management at tertiary centre
explanation.pearls: In Gratacos type III selective FGR a single large arterio-arterial anastomosis carries the cycling Doppler pattern; fetoscopic laser ablation converts the placenta functionally to dichorionic and removes the catastrophic 20 percent neurological injury risk to the larger twin if its co-twin dies.

stem:
A 32-year-old G3P3 has just had a spontaneous vaginal delivery at 39+5 weeks of a 4.1 kg baby with rapid third stage. Her booking pregnancy was complicated by pregnancy-induced hypertension and she has been on oral labetalol 200 mg three times daily since 32 weeks with home blood pressures around 138/86. Her placenta delivered apparently intact ten minutes ago.

On assessment now her uterus is boggy at the umbilicus despite fundal massage and she has had 800 mL of fresh red blood loss into the drape in the last 15 minutes. The midwife has called for senior review and a second wide-bore intravenous line is being placed. She is alert but pale and clammy. The placenta has been re-examined and looks complete with intact cotyledons and membranes. There is no vaginal or perineal laceration on inspection.

data_table.Vital signs: pulse rate 110, blood pressure 95/60, respiratory rate 22, SpO2 98 percent on room air, temperature 36.8 degrees

lead_in: Which uterotonic regimen is most appropriate?

options.text: Ergometrine 250 micrograms intramuscular as first line and a 40 unit oxytocin infusion in 1000 mL Hartmann's over four hours
options.rationale: Ergometrine is contraindicated in pregnancy-induced hypertension because of severe rebound vasoconstriction and stroke risk; an alternative uterotonic must be used here. (Source: RANZCOG: Postpartum Haemorrhage)

options.text: Sublingual misoprostol 800 micrograms with intrauterine vaginal packing in the delivery room while awaiting senior review
options.rationale: Misoprostol is a second-line uterotonic when oxytocin fails. Intrauterine packing is not recommended ahead of oxytocin escalation and a Bakri balloon. (Source: RANZCOG: Postpartum Haemorrhage)

options.text: Carboprost 250 micrograms intramuscular every fifteen minutes for up to eight doses as primary uterotonic for atony
options.rationale: Carboprost is reserved for refractory uterine atony and is contraindicated in asthma. It is not the first uterotonic to escalate to when oxytocin has not yet been used at therapeutic doses. (Source: RANZCOG: Postpartum Haemorrhage)

options.text: Oxytocin 10 units intramuscular plus a 40 unit oxytocin infusion in 1000 mL Hartmann's over four hours, and intravenous tranexamic acid 1 g
options.rationale: Oxytocin is first line for postpartum haemorrhage and is safe in pregnancy-induced hypertension. Tranexamic acid 1 g within three hours of onset reduces mortality per the WOMAN trial and is endorsed by RANZCOG. (Source: RANZCOG: Postpartum Haemorrhage)

options.text: Bakri balloon insertion at the bedside and immediate transfer to the operating theatre for examination under anaesthesia
options.rationale: Mechanical tamponade and theatre are reserved for failed medical management with ongoing haemorrhage. Stepwise escalation begins with oxytocin and tranexamic acid. (Source: RANZCOG: Postpartum Haemorrhage)

explanation.summary: First-line medical management of atonic postpartum haemorrhage in Australia is oxytocin (10 units intramuscular plus 40 unit infusion in 1000 mL crystalloid over four hours) plus 1 g intravenous tranexamic acid within three hours of onset. Ergometrine is a useful second-line agent but is contraindicated in pregnancy-induced hypertension. Misoprostol, carboprost (avoid in asthma), mechanical tamponade, and surgical escalation follow if haemorrhage continues despite oxytocin.
key_points: Oxytocin is first line for atonic postpartum haemorrhage
Tranexamic acid 1 g intravenous within 3 hours reduces mortality (WOMAN trial)
Ergometrine is contraindicated in hypertension and pre-eclampsia
Carboprost is contraindicated in asthma
Misoprostol, Bakri balloon, and laparotomy escalate sequentially if oxytocin fails
explanation.pearls: In a woman with pregnancy-induced hypertension or pre-eclampsia the second-line uterotonic switches from ergometrine (contraindicated) to carboprost (still contraindicated in asthma) and then misoprostol, before mechanical and surgical escalation.

subtopic_detail: Intrapartum GBS prophylaxis with penicillin allergy
stem:
A 28-year-old G2P1 at 38+0 weeks presents to delivery suite in early labour. Her vaginal-rectal screening swab at 36 weeks grew group B streptococcus. She has a previous vaginal delivery at 39 weeks without complications. Her first child had no neonatal sepsis. She is otherwise well.

She tells you she developed a generalised pruritic rash and lip swelling when prescribed amoxicillin two years ago for tonsillitis and was told to avoid penicillins by the emergency department doctor at the time. She has not had any antibiotic since then. She is currently 4 cm dilated with regular contractions and ruptured membranes one hour ago at home. The midwife has commenced intravenous access and a syntocinon augmentation has not yet been started.

data_table.Vital signs: pulse rate 92, blood pressure 118/76, respiratory rate 18, SpO2 99 percent on room air, temperature 36.9 degrees, fetal heart rate 142 with normal variability

lead_in: Which intrapartum antibiotic regimen is most appropriate?

options.text: Intravenous clindamycin 600 mg every eight hours from now until delivery, confirming GBS susceptibility on the laboratory antibiogram
options.rationale: Severe penicillin allergy (anaphylaxis or angioedema) precludes both penicillin and cefazolin. Clindamycin is recommended if the GBS isolate is documented as clindamycin susceptible; otherwise vancomycin is used. (Source: RANZCOG: Maternal Group B Streptococcus)

options.text: Intravenous cefazolin 2 g loading dose then 1 g every eight hours until delivery, after a graded penicillin challenge in labour
options.rationale: Cefazolin is acceptable for mild non-anaphylactic penicillin allergy but is contraindicated when the index reaction is severe (angioedema or anaphylaxis). Graded challenge is not appropriate in active labour. (Source: RANZCOG: Maternal Group B Streptococcus)

options.text: Intravenous benzylpenicillin 3 g loading dose then 1.8 g every four hours until delivery, with adrenaline drawn up at the bedside
options.rationale: Benzylpenicillin is contraindicated in confirmed severe penicillin allergy regardless of pre-drawn adrenaline. (Source: RANZCOG: Maternal Group B Streptococcus)

options.text: Oral cefalexin 500 mg every six hours until delivery and a single intravenous dose at the time of delivery to cover the neonate
options.rationale: Oral antibiotics do not achieve adequate amniotic fluid levels in time for intrapartum GBS prophylaxis. Intravenous administration is required. (Source: RANZCOG: Maternal Group B Streptococcus)

options.text: No antibiotics required because she had a previous uncomplicated vaginal delivery and the colony count is unknown
options.rationale: A positive screening swab at 35 to 37 weeks is itself an indication for intrapartum prophylaxis regardless of previous delivery course or colony count. (Source: RANZCOG: Maternal Group B Streptococcus)

explanation.summary: RANZCOG recommends intrapartum GBS prophylaxis with intravenous benzylpenicillin (or ampicillin) for women with a positive 35 to 37 week vaginal-rectal swab, previous GBS infant, GBS bacteriuria during pregnancy, intrapartum fever, or membranes ruptured 18 hours or more. For severe penicillin allergy, clindamycin is used if the isolate is susceptible; otherwise vancomycin. Cefazolin is used only for mild penicillin allergy.
key_points: Indications: positive 35-37 week swab, GBS bacteriuria, previous GBS infant, fever, ROM >= 18 h
First line: intravenous benzylpenicillin 3 g load then 1.8 g every 4 hours
Mild penicillin allergy: intravenous cefazolin
Severe penicillin allergy with clindamycin-susceptible isolate: intravenous clindamycin
Severe penicillin allergy with resistant or unknown isolate: intravenous vancomycin
explanation.pearls: Severe penicillin allergy and a clindamycin-susceptible GBS isolate get intravenous clindamycin 600 mg every eight hours; if the isolate is resistant or unknown, default to intravenous vancomycin rather than cefazolin.

subtopic_detail: Pregnancy of uncertain viability and Anti-D
stem:
A 25-year-old G1P0 at 7+2 weeks by last menstrual period presents to early pregnancy unit with 24 hours of light vaginal bleeding and mild lower abdominal cramps. She has had no syncopal episodes and no shoulder tip pain. Her blood group on a booking blood test today is documented as RhD negative.

On examination her observations are normal. Speculum reveals a closed cervical os with a small amount of dark blood pooling in the posterior fornix. Bimanual examination shows a soft anteverted uterus, no cervical motion tenderness, and no adnexal mass or tenderness. There has been no previous miscarriage and she conceived spontaneously. There is no significant past gynaecological history and she takes no medications.

data_table.Vital signs: pulse rate 84, blood pressure 116/72, respiratory rate 16, SpO2 99 percent on room air, temperature 36.7 degrees
data_table.Investigations: serum beta-hCG 14000 IU/L, transvaginal ultrasound: single intrauterine gestational sac with yolk sac and embryo with crown-rump length 3.5 mm, no fetal cardiac activity demonstrated, no adnexal mass, no free fluid

lead_in: What is the most appropriate management?

options.text: Admit for intravenous antibiotics and uterine evacuation in theatre for a presumed septic incomplete miscarriage with retained products
options.rationale: There is no fever, no offensive discharge, and no inflammatory markers raised. Septic management is not indicated and would be invasive on an indeterminate scan. (Source: RANZCOG: Miscarriage)

options.text: Administer intramuscular methotrexate 50 mg/m squared and arrange serial beta-hCG measurements every 48 hours for one week
options.rationale: Methotrexate is used for tubal ectopic pregnancy meeting RANZCOG medical management criteria. An intrauterine sac is visible on ultrasound, making ectopic unlikely and methotrexate contraindicated. (Source: RANZCOG: Miscarriage)

options.text: Discharge home with repeat transvaginal ultrasound and beta-hCG in 7 to 10 days, give Anti-D 250 IU intramuscular, and provide written safety netting advice
options.rationale: An embryo with crown-rump length less than 7 mm without cardiac activity is indeterminate, not miscarriage; repeat scan in 7 to 10 days is required. RANZCOG recommends 250 IU Anti-D for any RhD-negative woman with first-trimester bleeding. (Source: RANZCOG: Miscarriage)

options.text: Commence vaginal misoprostol 800 micrograms now and a second dose at 24 hours for medical management of a missed miscarriage
options.rationale: Medical evacuation requires the diagnostic threshold for miscarriage to be met (crown-rump length 7 mm or more without cardiac activity, or mean sac diameter 25 mm or more empty). The current scan is indeterminate. (Source: RANZCOG: Miscarriage)

options.text: Admit for 48 hour observation and offer dilatation and curettage if vaginal bleeding has not stopped by review the following morning
options.rationale: Inpatient observation is not standard for haemodynamically stable threatened miscarriage. Surgical evacuation is offered only once miscarriage is confirmed and after patient counselling. (Source: RANZCOG: Miscarriage)

explanation.summary: RANZCOG diagnostic criteria for first-trimester miscarriage on transvaginal ultrasound require either a crown-rump length of 7 mm or more without cardiac activity, or a mean gestational sac diameter of 25 mm or more without a visible embryo. Below these cut-offs the scan is indeterminate and warrants a repeat in 7 to 10 days. Any RhD-negative woman with first-trimester bleeding receives 250 IU Anti-D within 72 hours.
key_points: CRL >= 7 mm without cardiac activity = miscarriage diagnostic
Mean sac diameter >= 25 mm without embryo = miscarriage diagnostic
Below thresholds: repeat ultrasound in 7-10 days
Anti-D 250 IU intramuscular for RhD-negative first trimester bleeding
Beta-hCG should approximately double every 48 hours in viable intrauterine pregnancy
explanation.pearls: The diagnostic cut-off for miscarriage on transvaginal ultrasound is a crown-rump length of 7 mm without cardiac activity; anything smaller is an indeterminate scan and the rest plan is repeat ultrasound in 7 to 10 days.

stem:
A 32-year-old G2P1 at 35+2 weeks self-presents to triage with two hours of frontal headache, blurry vision with scotomata, and epigastric pain. Her booking blood pressure was 118/74 and her antenatal record shows no prior hypertension. Fetal movements have been normal today.

On examination she is alert and orientated. There is mild hyperreflexia at the knees without clonus. There is no peripheral oedema and no rash. Urine dipstick is 3+ protein. Cardiotocograph shows a baseline of 140 with normal variability and no decelerations. Speculum is not yet performed. Her observation chart is shown below. There is no abdominal tenderness on uterine palpation between contractions and no PV bleeding.

data_table.Vital signs: pulse rate 102, blood pressure 168/112, respiratory rate 20, SpO2 99 percent on room air, temperature 36.8 degrees
data_table.Investigations: haemoglobin 124 g/L (115-145), platelets 142 x10^9/L (150-400), ALT 80 U/L (<35), urate 0.42 mmol/L (<0.36), creatinine 78 micromol/L (45-90), urine protein:creatinine ratio 220 mg/mmol

lead_in: What is the most appropriate immediate management?

options.text: Oral nifedipine 20 mg now, repeat in thirty minutes if blood pressure is not below 150/100, and arrange emergency caesarean section under general anaesthesia
options.rationale: Oral nifedipine is acceptable for acute blood pressure control but emergency caesarean under general anaesthesia is not the next step before seizure prophylaxis is commenced and the patient is stabilised. (Source: SOMANZ Hypertension in Pregnancy)

options.text: Intravenous labetalol infusion alone and tocolysis with nifedipine to prolong gestation by 48 hours for corticosteroid completion
options.rationale: Tocolysis is not used in severe pre-eclampsia; the focus is maternal seizure prophylaxis and stabilisation prior to controlled delivery. (Source: SOMANZ Hypertension in Pregnancy)

options.text: Oral methyldopa 250 mg three times daily and outpatient antenatal day-assessment unit review in twenty four hours for blood pressure trend
options.rationale: Methyldopa is too slow in onset for severe pre-eclampsia and outpatient review is unsafe with blood pressure 168/112 and neurological symptoms. (Source: SOMANZ Hypertension in Pregnancy)

options.text: Intravenous diazepam 10 mg slow bolus for seizure prophylaxis and intravenous hydralazine 5 mg boluses every twenty minutes
options.rationale: Diazepam is not the recommended seizure prophylaxis or treatment in pre-eclampsia; magnesium sulfate is superior in both prevention and treatment of eclamptic seizures per the MAGPIE trial. (Source: SOMANZ Hypertension in Pregnancy)

options.text: Intravenous magnesium sulfate 4 g loading over 20 minutes then 1 g/hour infusion plus intravenous labetalol for blood pressure control, and admit
options.rationale: Severe pre-eclampsia (blood pressure 160/110 or more plus neurological or epigastric symptoms or end-organ involvement) is the SOMANZ threshold for magnesium sulfate seizure prophylaxis at 4 g load then 1 g/hour, with concurrent antihypertensive treatment. (Source: SOMANZ Hypertension in Pregnancy)

explanation.summary: Severe pre-eclampsia is defined by SOMANZ as blood pressure 160/110 or more, end-organ dysfunction (hepatic, renal, neurological, haematological, placental, or pulmonary oedema), or persistent severe symptoms. Magnesium sulfate seizure prophylaxis (4 g intravenous load over 20 minutes then 1 g/hour for 24 hours) is indicated. Antihypertensive treatment runs in parallel (labetalol, nifedipine, or hydralazine). Delivery is the definitive treatment after maternal stabilisation.
key_points: SOMANZ severe pre-eclampsia: BP 160/110+ or end-organ damage or severe symptoms
Magnesium sulfate 4 g load over 20 min then 1 g/hour for 24 hours
Target BP under 160/110 acutely with labetalol, nifedipine, or hydralazine
Watch for magnesium toxicity: reflex loss, respiratory depression, oliguria
Delivery is the definitive treatment after stabilisation
explanation.pearls: The SOMANZ trigger for intravenous magnesium sulfate seizure prophylaxis is severe pre-eclampsia (BP 160/110 plus headache, visual symptoms, epigastric pain, or end-organ derangement), not eclampsia itself.

subtopic_detail: Preterm prelabour rupture of membranes at 32 weeks
stem:
A 28-year-old G1P0 at 32+1 weeks presents to delivery suite four hours after a sudden gush of clear fluid at home. She has no contractions. Her pregnancy has been low risk and she is fully vaccinated including booster pertussis. Her 35-week vaginal-rectal swab is not yet due. Booking blood group is A positive.

On examination she is well and afebrile. Speculum demonstrates clear amniotic pooling in the posterior fornix with a closed cervix. There is no offensive odour and the umbilical cord is not visible. Fetal cardiotocograph shows baseline 138 with normal variability, no contractions, and no decelerations. Ultrasound estimates the fetus is in a cephalic presentation with normal liquor outside the membrane defect, and weight on the 60th centile. She has no allergy.

data_table.Vital signs: pulse rate 86, blood pressure 112/70, respiratory rate 16, SpO2 99 percent on room air, temperature 36.8 degrees
data_table.Investigations: white cells 11.0 x10^9/L (4-11), CRP 8 mg/L (<5), high vaginal swab pending, urinalysis nil active

lead_in: What is the most appropriate management plan?

options.text: Induction of labour with vaginal misoprostol now and intravenous benzylpenicillin given the unknown group B streptococcus status
options.rationale: Routine immediate induction at 32 weeks in well preterm prelabour rupture of membranes increases neonatal morbidity from prematurity. Expectant management to 34 weeks is preferred in stable women. (Source: RANZCOG: Term Prelabour Rupture of Membranes and PPROM)
source_refs: RANZCOG: Term Prelabour Rupture of Membranes and PPROM

options.text: Admit and give oral erythromycin 250 mg six hourly for ten days with antenatal betamethasone twice and expectant management to thirty four weeks
options.rationale: RANZCOG recommends admission, antenatal corticosteroids (betamethasone 11.4 mg intramuscular two doses 24 hours apart) before 34 weeks, prophylactic antibiotics (10 days oral erythromycin) to prolong latency and reduce neonatal sepsis (ORACLE I), and expectant management to 34 weeks if no contraindication. (Source: RANZCOG: Term Prelabour Rupture of Membranes and PPROM)
source_refs: RANZCOG: Term Prelabour Rupture of Membranes and PPROM

options.text: Outpatient management with twice weekly cardiotocograph reviews and serial inflammatory marker checks until thirty six weeks gestation
options.rationale: Preterm prelabour rupture of membranes requires inpatient observation for chorioamnionitis, abruption, and cord prolapse. Outpatient management is not standard in Australia. (Source: RANZCOG: Term Prelabour Rupture of Membranes and PPROM)
source_refs: RANZCOG: Term Prelabour Rupture of Membranes and PPROM

options.text: Tocolysis with nifedipine for 48 hours plus betamethasone, then discharge home for outpatient maternal-fetal medicine review
options.rationale: Tocolysis is not recommended in preterm prelabour rupture of membranes because it does not improve outcomes and risks masking infection; the patient also requires inpatient surveillance. (Source: RANZCOG: Term Prelabour Rupture of Membranes and PPROM)
source_refs: RANZCOG: Term Prelabour Rupture of Membranes and PPROM

options.text: Emergency caesarean section now for imminent cord prolapse risk with immediate neonatal intensive care unit admission planning
options.rationale: The cord is not visible and the fetus is cephalic with a normal cardiotocograph. Emergency caesarean is not indicated. (Source: RANZCOG: Term Prelabour Rupture of Membranes and PPROM)
source_refs: RANZCOG: Term Prelabour Rupture of Membranes and PPROM

explanation.summary: Preterm prelabour rupture of membranes between 24 and 34 weeks is managed inpatient with antenatal corticosteroids (betamethasone 11.4 mg intramuscular at 24 hour intervals for two doses), prophylactic erythromycin 250 mg orally six hourly for 10 days to prolong latency and reduce neonatal sepsis (ORACLE I), and expectant management to 34 weeks unless chorioamnionitis, abruption, or non-reassuring fetal status develops. Magnesium sulfate for neuroprotection is given if delivery becomes imminent before 30 weeks.
key_points: Admit for inpatient surveillance, twice daily observations and CTG
Antenatal betamethasone 11.4 mg intramuscular two doses 24 hours apart before 34 weeks
Oral erythromycin 250 mg six hourly for 10 days (ORACLE I)
Expectant management to 34 weeks unless chorioamnionitis or non-reassuring CTG
Magnesium sulfate neuroprotection if delivery imminent before 30 weeks
explanation.pearls: ORACLE I demonstrated that 10 days of oral erythromycin in preterm prelabour rupture of membranes prolongs latency and reduces neonatal sepsis, while amoxicillin with clavulanic acid increases necrotising enterocolitis risk and is avoided.

sources.label: RANZCOG: Term Prelabour Rupture of Membranes and PPROM

stem:
A 30-year-old G2P1 attends antenatal clinic at 28+0 weeks for review of her routine gestational diabetes screening. She had a previous baby weighing 4.3 kg born at 40+1 weeks. Her booking BMI was 31 kg per square metre. She has no family history of type 2 diabetes and her first pregnancy did not require diabetes screening because of a different antenatal provider.

She completed a 75 g two-hour oral glucose tolerance test yesterday after an overnight fast. She is asymptomatic and her fetus is active. There is no glycosuria on urine dipstick today and her blood pressure is normal. She has no symptoms of polyuria or polydipsia. Her medications are routine pregnancy multivitamin only and she does not smoke. Her booking HbA1c was 5.4 percent.

data_table.Vital signs: pulse rate 78, blood pressure 122/76, respiratory rate 16, SpO2 99 percent on room air, temperature 36.7 degrees
data_table.Investigations: OGTT fasting plasma glucose 5.4 mmol/L (target < 5.1), one hour 10.8 mmol/L (target < 10.0), two hour 8.6 mmol/L (target < 8.5)

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step?

options.text: Reassure her that the oral glucose tolerance test is within normal range and review her at the routine 36 week appointment with no further action
options.rationale: All three OGTT timepoints exceed ADIPS thresholds. The diagnosis of gestational diabetes is made when any one of fasting >= 5.1, one hour >= 10.0, or two hour >= 8.5 mmol/L is met. (Source: ADIPS Consensus Guidelines for GDM)

options.text: Repeat the oral glucose tolerance test in four weeks because results are only marginally elevated and might normalise spontaneously
options.rationale: Repeat testing is not part of the ADIPS pathway when threshold criteria are met. The diagnosis is made on a single abnormal value. (Source: ADIPS Consensus Guidelines for GDM)

options.text: Commence insulin glargine 10 units at night and review with diabetes educator and dietitian once weekly until delivery and the postnatal review
options.rationale: First-line therapy for gestational diabetes is lifestyle intervention and home blood glucose monitoring. Insulin is added only when glycaemic targets are not met after 1 to 2 weeks of diet and exercise. (Source: ADIPS Consensus Guidelines for GDM)

options.text: Diagnose GDM, refer to diabetes educator and dietitian, start home blood glucose monitoring with fasting target under 5.1 and two hour postprandial under 6.7 mmol/L
options.rationale: All three OGTT values exceed ADIPS criteria, confirming GDM. First-line management is education, dietary modification, exercise, and home glucose monitoring with fasting target less than 5.1 and two-hour postprandial less than 6.7 mmol/L; pharmacotherapy is added if targets not met. (Source: ADIPS Consensus Guidelines for GDM)

options.text: Diagnose GDM and commence oral metformin 500 mg twice daily as first-line pharmacotherapy with dietitian review at the next clinic visit
options.rationale: Pharmacotherapy is escalated only when lifestyle measures fail to achieve targets over 1 to 2 weeks. Metformin remains a second-line option after insulin in Australian practice. (Source: ADIPS Consensus Guidelines for GDM)

explanation.summary: ADIPS diagnostic criteria for GDM on the 75 g 2-hour OGTT are fasting plasma glucose 5.1 or more, one hour 10.0 or more, or two hour 8.5 or more mmol/L. Any one value confirms the diagnosis. First-line management is dietary advice, exercise, and home blood glucose monitoring with targets fasting under 5.1 and two-hour postprandial under 6.7 mmol/L. Insulin is the preferred first-line pharmacotherapy when targets are not met; metformin is second line in Australian practice.
key_points: ADIPS thresholds (any one): fasting >= 5.1, 1-hour >= 10.0, 2-hour >= 8.5 mmol/L
First-line: lifestyle, dietitian, home blood glucose monitoring
Targets: fasting < 5.1, two hour postprandial < 6.7 mmol/L
Pharmacotherapy if targets not met after 1-2 weeks lifestyle
Postpartum OGTT at 6-12 weeks to detect persistent dysglycaemia
explanation.pearls: ADIPS uses fasting cut-off 5.1 mmol/L (lower than non-pregnant 6.1) reflecting the heightened risk of large-for-gestational-age and neonatal hypoglycaemia even at modest fasting elevations.

stem:
A 24-year-old G1P0 at 38+2 weeks is in established labour in the delivery suite. The registrar performs an artificial rupture of membranes for slow progress. Cervix is 6 cm dilated, head is high at station minus one, contractions are three in ten and strong. Immediately after the artificial rupture of membranes the midwife observes a 6 cm length of umbilical cord prolapsing through the cervix into the vagina.

Fetal cardiotocograph immediately falls from a baseline of 140 to 80 with a flat trace. The mother is positioned supine on the bed. The emergency caesarean section is called overhead and the obstetric registrar arrives at the bedside within one minute. The anaesthetic team is paged and a theatre is being prepared on the floor below. The mother is calm but anxious and has had no opioid analgesia in the last six hours.

data_table.Vital signs: maternal pulse rate 96, blood pressure 118/72, respiratory rate 20, SpO2 99 percent on room air, temperature 36.8 degrees, fetal heart rate 80

lead_in: What is the most appropriate immediate action?

options.text: Replace the cord into the vagina manually with continuous fetal monitoring and proceed to ventouse-assisted vaginal delivery in the delivery suite
options.rationale: Manual cord replacement is not recommended because it does not reliably restore fetal circulation and ventouse is not feasible at 6 cm dilation. The head is also too high for instrumental delivery. (Source: RANZCOG: Cord Prolapse)

options.text: Position the mother left lateral, administer terbutaline 250 micrograms subcutaneously for tocolysis, and observe over five minutes
options.rationale: Tocolysis may be considered as an adjunct to relieve contractions while preparing for caesarean, but it is not sufficient definitive management when the cord is prolapsed and fetal bradycardia is present. (Source: RANZCOG: Cord Prolapse)

options.text: Elevate the presenting part with the examining hand, adopt knee-chest or steep Trendelenburg position, and transfer immediately to theatre for emergency caesarean section
options.rationale: Manual elevation of the presenting part to relieve cord compression plus a knee-chest or steep Trendelenburg position and immediate transfer to theatre for category-one caesarean section is the recommended management. Decision-to-delivery interval target is under 30 minutes. (Source: RANZCOG: Cord Prolapse)

options.text: Apply suprapubic pressure with simultaneous fundal pressure and instruct the mother to push with each contraction for rapid vaginal delivery
options.rationale: Pushing increases cord compression and worsens fetal asphyxia. Vaginal delivery is not appropriate at 6 cm dilation with a high head. (Source: RANZCOG: Cord Prolapse)

options.text: Insert urinary catheter and instill 500 mL of saline to elevate the presenting part, then proceed to instrumental delivery in delivery suite
options.rationale: Bladder filling can be used as a bridging measure when caesarean delivery is delayed (for example in transit), but it does not replace manual elevation and immediate theatre transfer. (Source: RANZCOG: Cord Prolapse)

explanation.summary: Cord prolapse is a category-one obstetric emergency. Immediate management is manual elevation of the presenting part to relieve cord compression, knee-chest or steep Trendelenburg position, and transfer to theatre for emergency caesarean section under general anaesthesia, targeting a decision-to-delivery interval under 30 minutes. Tocolysis (terbutaline 250 micrograms subcutaneous) and bladder filling are bridging adjuncts when transfer is delayed. The cord should be kept warm and moist and not handled excessively.
key_points: Immediate manual elevation of the presenting part
Knee-chest or steep Trendelenburg position
Category-one caesarean: decision-to-delivery under 30 minutes
Tocolysis with terbutaline and bladder filling are bridging adjuncts
Keep cord warm and moist, avoid excessive handling
explanation.pearls: Bladder filling with 500 mL of saline through a urinary catheter is a bridging manoeuvre for cord prolapse during transfer (e.g. retrieval to a tertiary centre) and does not replace continued manual elevation.

subtopic_detail: Severe HELLP delivery timing with steroid uncertainty
stem:
A 29-year-old G1P0 at 33+0 weeks is transferred to your tertiary delivery suite from a regional hospital with severe pre-eclampsia. She has had epigastric pain and nausea for 12 hours and her blood pressure has risen to 175/115 despite oral labetalol 200 mg three times daily. She has had no seizures. Fetal movements remain normal.

On examination she has right upper quadrant tenderness without peritonism and is alert (GCS 15) with hyperreflexia. Cardiotocograph is reactive, baseline 140, normal variability, no decelerations. Fetal estimated weight on ultrasound today is 1900 g (50th centile). Cervix is unfavourable on examination (Bishop score 2). Tertiary neonatal intensive care is available. Magnesium sulfate has been loaded and a labetalol infusion is running. No corticosteroid has yet been administered.

data_table.Vital signs: pulse rate 108, blood pressure 168/108 on labetalol infusion, respiratory rate 22, SpO2 99 percent on room air, temperature 36.8 degrees, fetal heart rate 144 reactive
data_table.Investigations: haemoglobin 96 g/L (115-145, was 122 yesterday), platelets 78 x10^9/L (150-400, was 140 yesterday), ALT 312 U/L (was 80 yesterday), LDH 580 U/L (110-230), haptoglobin 0.1 g/L (0.3-2.0), peripheral blood film schistocytes present, urine protein:creatinine ratio 380 mg/mmol, creatinine 92 micromol/L

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step?

options.text: Continue magnesium sulfate and labetalol infusion and proceed to induction of labour with prostaglandin pessary targeting vaginal delivery within 24 hours
options.rationale: Induction with an unfavourable cervix (Bishop 2) and severe progressive HELLP is unsafe; the time required for induction is incompatible with the rate of maternal decline. (Source: SOMANZ Hypertension in Pregnancy)

options.text: Continue magnesium sulfate and labetalol infusion plus give antenatal betamethasone and expectant management for 48 hours to complete the steroid course
options.rationale: Expectant management for the full 48 hour steroid window is contraindicated when HELLP is progressing rapidly (platelets falling 140 to 78, ALT rising 80 to 312 within 24 hours). Maternal compromise outweighs the benefit of a second betamethasone dose. (Source: SOMANZ Hypertension in Pregnancy)

options.text: Continue magnesium and labetalol infusion plus give antenatal betamethasone and intravenous dexamethasone 10 mg twice daily as treatment for HELLP itself
options.rationale: High-dose dexamethasone does not improve maternal or perinatal outcomes in HELLP (Cochrane 2010) and is not a substitute for delivery. (Source: SOMANZ Hypertension in Pregnancy)

options.text: Continue magnesium and labetalol infusion, transfuse platelets to greater than 100, and book elective caesarean section in twelve hours after platelet recovery
options.rationale: Routine prophylactic platelet transfusion in HELLP is not indicated unless platelets are below 20 or there is bleeding or planned regional anaesthesia at very low counts. Delaying delivery for twelve hours allows further deterioration. (Source: SOMANZ Hypertension in Pregnancy)

options.text: Continue magnesium and labetalol infusion, give a first dose of antenatal betamethasone, and expedite caesarean section the same day without waiting for the second steroid dose
options.rationale: Progressive severe HELLP with rapidly falling platelets and rising transaminases mandates expedited delivery without completing the 48 hour steroid window. A single betamethasone dose still provides partial benefit. Caesarean is preferred over induction with unfavourable cervix. (Source: SOMANZ Hypertension in Pregnancy)

explanation.summary: Delivery timing in severe pre-eclampsia and HELLP under 34 weeks balances neonatal benefits of antenatal corticosteroids against rapid maternal deterioration. Stable disease can be temporised for 48 hours to complete betamethasone, but progressive HELLP (falling platelets, rising transaminases, neurological symptoms, oliguria, abruption, eclampsia, or non-reassuring fetal status) mandates expedited delivery the same day regardless of steroid status. Caesarean is preferred when the cervix is unfavourable.
key_points: Severe HELLP under 34 weeks: try to give betamethasone but do not delay delivery if progressive
Indications for immediate delivery: uncontrolled BP, eclampsia, abruption, falling platelets, rising ALT/LDH, non-reassuring CTG
Single dose of betamethasone provides partial neonatal benefit
Routine platelet transfusion only if < 20 or bleeding
Caesarean preferred when cervix unfavourable
explanation.pearls: Progressive HELLP with platelets falling more than 50 percent in 24 hours mandates same-day delivery: the maternal mortality curve outpaces the steroid window benefit, and a single betamethasone dose still reduces neonatal respiratory distress syndrome.

subtopic_detail: Ectopic with prior contralateral salpingectomy - historical-bilaterality flip
stem:
A 33-year-old G3P1 woman presents to the early pregnancy assessment unit with a positive urine pregnancy test, 6 weeks of amenorrhoea, right iliac fossa pain rated 5 out of 10, and minimal vaginal spotting. She is haemodynamically stable.

Her obstetric history includes a left tubal ectopic pregnancy three years ago managed by laparoscopic left salpingectomy, and a normal vaginal birth two years ago. She and her partner have been trying to conceive for 5 months and she very much hopes to have at least one more child.

Transvaginal ultrasound shows an empty uterus, a 28 mm right adnexal mass with a yolk sac and no fetal cardiac activity, and a small amount of free fluid in the pouch of Douglas. Beta-hCG today is 4800 IU/L. The right fallopian tube on prior imaging and intra-operative records from her left salpingectomy is structurally normal. There is no other contralateral pelvic pathology.

The gynaecology team is choosing between methotrexate medical management, laparoscopic right salpingostomy with tube preservation, and laparoscopic right salpingectomy.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 84 bpm, BP 118/72 mmHg, RR 16, SpO2 99% on room air, temperature 36.8 degrees C
data_table.Examination: Right iliac fossa tenderness, no peritonism, no cervical motion tenderness
data_table.Investigations: TVUS as described; Hb 122 g/L (115-160); blood group A Rh positive; LFTs and renal function within normal limits
data_table.Past surgical history: Laparoscopic left salpingectomy three years ago; structurally normal right tube on prior records

lead_in: What would you first recommend as her definitive management?

options.text: Single-dose methotrexate 50 mg/m^2 intramuscularly with serial beta-hCG day 1, day 4, and day 7; expect more than 15 per cent fall in beta-hCG between day 4 and day 7
options.rationale: Methotrexate medical management is appropriate when beta-hCG is below 5000 IU/L, the mass is less than 3.5 cm, there is no fetal cardiac activity, the patient is haemodynamically stable, and she can attend reliable follow-up. This patient is at the upper end (beta-hCG 4800, mass 28 mm); a yolk sac alone (without fetal cardiac activity) does not exclude medical management. However the dominant clinical concern here is the prior contralateral salpingectomy: the right tube is now her only remaining tube and the risk of a recurrent ectopic in the SAME tube after persistence following methotrexate (or after salpingostomy) is substantial. The Royal Australian and New Zealand College of Obstetricians and Gynaecologists notes recurrent ipsilateral ectopic risk around 15 per cent after salpingostomy; persistence risk after methotrexate adds further complexity. Would be the appropriate first recommendation if the contralateral tube were intact. (Source: RANZCOG: Ectopic Pregnancy)

options.text: Laparoscopic right salpingostomy with linear incision over the antimesenteric border, evacuation of the ectopic, and haemostasis without tube removal, with serial beta-hCG follow-up
options.rationale: Salpingostomy is the standard first-line surgical option when the contralateral tube is intact and the woman wishes to preserve fertility; it leaves the affected tube in situ for future natural conception. This patient has NO contralateral tube (prior left salpingectomy). Preserving the affected right tube exposes her to a recurrent ipsilateral ectopic in her ONLY remaining tube (approximately 15 per cent risk per RANZCOG) and to persistent trophoblast requiring methotrexate. With a structurally normal right tube confirmed pre-operatively, definitive salpingectomy is the preferred management given the historical-bilaterality consideration. Would be the appropriate first surgical choice if the left tube were intact. (Source: RANZCOG: Ectopic Pregnancy)

options.text: Laparoscopic right salpingectomy with removal of the affected tube, with counselling that future conception will require in vitro fertilisation (IVF) given the prior contralateral salpingectomy
options.rationale: This is the appropriate first recommendation. With a prior contralateral salpingectomy, the affected right tube is the patient's only remaining tube. Recurrent ipsilateral ectopic risk after salpingostomy or methotrexate is approximately 15 per cent per RANZCOG; persistent trophoblast after methotrexate or salpingostomy can require repeat intervention. Definitive salpingectomy removes this risk at the cost of natural conception, with IVF as the path to future pregnancy. Counselling on fertility implications and shared decision-making are required, and the rationale acknowledges that the patient hopes for another child. RANZCOG recommends salpingectomy when the contralateral tube has previously been removed, even where standard criteria would favour tube preservation. (Source: RANZCOG: Ectopic Pregnancy)

options.text: Two-dose methotrexate protocol with methotrexate 50 mg/m^2 IM on day 0 and day 4, with serial beta-hCG day 1, day 4, day 7, and weekly until negative
options.rationale: The two-dose protocol is an option for ectopics with beta-hCG between 3000 and 5000 IU/L or with a larger mass than the single-dose pathway accommodates; it can be appropriate where single-dose methotrexate is borderline. The dominant issue here remains the prior contralateral salpingectomy and the persistence risk to her only remaining tube. Would be a defensible non-surgical option only if she declined salpingectomy after counselling. (Source: RANZCOG: Ectopic Pregnancy)

options.text: Expectant management with weekly outpatient beta-hCG and TVUS, intervention reserved for failure to fall by more than 50 per cent at one week or for clinical deterioration
options.rationale: Expectant management is reserved for very early ectopics with beta-hCG below 1000 to 1500 IU/L, falling levels, and absent or minimal symptoms. This patient has beta-hCG of 4800 IU/L, a defined adnexal mass with a yolk sac, and active symptoms; expectant management is not appropriate and risks tubal rupture in her only remaining tube. (Source: RANZCOG: Ectopic Pregnancy)

explanation.summary: This question tests the historical-bilaterality flip in ectopic pregnancy management. The textbook hierarchy preserves the affected tube where the contralateral tube is intact; salpingostomy and methotrexate both have salvage rates around 70 to 85 per cent. The flip occurs when the patient has already had a contralateral salpingectomy: the affected tube is the only remaining tube and the recurrent ipsilateral ectopic risk plus persistence risk make definitive salpingectomy preferred, with IVF as the path to future conception. The Royal Australian and New Zealand College of Obstetricians and Gynaecologists explicitly addresses this scenario in its Ectopic Pregnancy guideline. In context, prior contralateral surgical history of any reproductive structure (mastectomy, nephrectomy, orchidectomy, salpingectomy) can invert the standard fertility-preserving or organ-preserving answer.
key_points: Standard ectopic management favours tube preservation (salpingostomy or methotrexate) when the contralateral tube is intact.
Prior contralateral salpingectomy inverts this: definitive ipsilateral salpingectomy is preferred over preservation, with IVF as the future-conception path.
RANZCOG recurrent ipsilateral ectopic risk after salpingostomy is approximately 15 per cent.
Counselling on fertility implications and shared decision-making is required - the rationale acknowledges shared decision-making but the question asks the first recommendation.
explanation.pearls: Prior contralateral surgical history flips fertility-preserving answers across many domains: ectopic, breast cancer, renal mass, testicular mass. Always check what the patient still has.
